topic: AA Amyloidosis secondary to chronic arthritis

page.mentor_intro: AA amyloidosis is a complication of sustained inflammation, so control of the underlying disease is the treatment. Autoinflammatory syndromes (FMF, CAPS, TRAPS), uncontrolled adult-onset Still's disease and injecting-related soft-tissue infection are recognised causes.

teaching_points.claim: In familial Mediterranean fever, IL-1 inhibitors are effective and relatively safe for colchicine non-responders, and tocilizumab might be of interest in selected patients with established AA amyloidosis resistant to colchicine and IL-1 inhibitors.

A systematic review of causes listed 48 disease associations as strong, 19 weak, 23 unclear and 60 unlikely, and proposed a pragmatic diagnostic approach for AA amyloidosis without an obvious underlying disease.

In cryopyrin-associated periodic syndrome, AA amyloidosis occurred in nearly all subtypes; deaths were in patients who never received IL-1 inhibitors, and 89% of those treated had a greater than 50% fall in proteinuria.
TRAPS is revealed by AA amyloidosis in most cases, so clinical features of TRAPS should be screened for in AA patients, and IL-1 antagonists can preserve renal function.

AA amyloidosis is a rare, severe complication of uncontrolled active adult-onset Still's disease that could be prevented by early diagnosis and better disease control, including more frequent use of biologic therapy.
There is strong evidence linking skin and soft-tissue infections to AA amyloidosis among people who inject drugs.

uncertainties: Optimal treatment of AA amyloidosis secondary to chronic arthritis is not covered by the retrieved excerpts.
case_hooks: Long-standing inflammatory arthritis with new nephrotic-range proteinuria.

standard_knowledge.claim: AA amyloidosis is driven by chronic elevation of acute-phase reactant serum amyloid A (SAA); sustained suppression of SAA to < 10 mg/L halts renal progression and improves survival.
Renal involvement is the primary clinical manifestation (> 90% of cases), presenting initially as asymptomatic albuminuria progressing to nephrotic syndrome and end-stage kidney disease.
Biopsy confirmation using Congo red stain demonstrates characteristic apple-green birefringence under cross-polarized light, with immunohistochemistry differentiating AA from AL and ATTR amyloidosis.

Targeted biologic therapies suppressing chronic inflammation (IL-6 receptor antagonist tocilizumab or TNF inhibitors in inflammatory arthritis) produce dramatic biochemical and renal remissions in AA amyloidosis.

page.standard_overview: AA (secondary/reactive) amyloidosis results from sustained overproduction of serum amyloid A (SAA) protein by hepatocytes during chronic systemic inflammation (rheumatoid arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, adult-onset Still's disease, or chronic infection). Insoluble amyloid fibrils deposit in tissues, predominantly causing nephrotic-range proteinuria, progressive renal failure, and hepatosplenomegaly, while cardiac involvement is rare compared to AL or ATTR amyloidosis. Diagnosis requires Congo red staining of tissue biopsies (abdominal fat pad, rectum, or kidney) showing apple-green birefringence under polarized light and positive anti-SAA immunohistochemistry. Management centers aggressively on suppressing underlying chronic inflammation (anti-TNF, anti-IL-6 [tocilizumab], or colchicine in FMF) to lower SAA below 10 mg/L, which arrests amyloid deposition and permits regression of proteinuria.

topic: Abatacept in RA: T-cell co-stimulation blockade, seropositive advantage, safety profile

page.mentor_intro: Abatacept (T-cell co-stimulation blockade) is one of several biologic options in RA. Evidence suggests it is a plausible choice in RA-associated interstitial lung disease, and weight or BMI may influence response to some biologics.

teaching_points.claim: The EULAR 2022 and 2025 systematic reviews of DMARD efficacy informed the update of the RA management recommendations, and strategic and head-to-head studies helped refine the established treatment algorithm.

Current evidence suggests abatacept may be a plausible alternative for RA patients with interstitial lung disease, with a lower relative risk of ILD deterioration at 24 months than TNF inhibitors and csDMARDs and no unexpected adverse events.
Janus kinase inhibitors in RA-ILD were well tolerated and might offer comparable safety and efficacy to abatacept and rituximab.
Weight and BMI should be considered when planning treatment, with the effect more pronounced for TNF inhibitors than for other biologics; similar evidence exists for tocilizumab and abatacept.
A meta-analysis found no difference in cardiovascular outcomes between abatacept and TNF inhibitors (OR 1.08), while tocilizumab may be associated with a lower MACE risk than TNF inhibitors.
Early treatment of at-risk individuals may delay RA onset, though whether it prevents RA remains undetermined.

The head-to-head AMPLE trial found subcutaneous abatacept non-inferior to adalimumab (both with methotrexate) for ACR20 response at 1 year (64.8% vs 63.4%), with similar inhibition of radiographic progression at 2 years.

page.standard_overview: Abatacept is a soluble recombinant fusion protein consisting of the extracellular domain of human CTLA-4 linked to the modified Fc portion of human IgG1 (CTLA-4-Ig). It selectively modulates T-cell co-stimulation by binding to CD80 and CD86 on antigen-presenting cells, thereby blocking CD28 interaction on T cells and inhibiting T-cell activation. In the landmark AMPLE trial (first head-to-head biologic comparison in RA), subcutaneous abatacept demonstrated non-inferior clinical efficacy to adalimumab with comparable radiographic inhibition, but with fewer injection-site reactions and fewer serious infections. Abatacept exhibits superior clinical responsiveness in seropositive (anti-CCP and RF positive) patients and appears to carry a lower risk of tuberculosis reactivation than TNF inhibitors, although tuberculosis screening is still required.

topic: Abdominal aortic aneurysm: surveillance thresholds, EVAR vs open repair

page.mentor_intro: Retrieved AAA evidence covers detection and risk rather than the surveillance-threshold question: point-of-care ultrasound is highly accurate, smoking carries twice the relative risk in women, and advanced EVAR has better short-term but not better long-term outcomes than open repair.

teaching_points.claim: SVS 2018 AAA: Level of recommendation 2 (Weak) Quality of evidence B (Moderate) We suggest deferring open aneurysm repair for at least 6 months after drug-eluting coronary stent placement or, alternatively, performing EVAR with continuation of dual antiplatelet therapy.
European Society for Vascular Surgery 2019: Morphology of small abdominal aortic aneurysms should be considered before continued ultrasound surveillance.
ACR Appropriateness Criteria address screening for abdominal aortic aneurysm.
Point-of-care ultrasound by emergency physicians is highly accurate for AAA (pooled sensitivity 98.33%, specificity 99.84%), even with limited training.
The relative risk of AAA among current smokers is almost twice as high in women as in men, with no strong association with inflammatory markers.
Obesity is positively but nonlinearly correlated with AAA presence, and BMI relates to postoperative mortality in a U-shaped curve.
Metformin use hints at a potential role in limiting annual AAA growth, events and risk.
Women undergoing EVAR experience higher perioperative morbidity and less favourable long-term outcomes than men, including after rupture (8-year survival 36.7% versus 49.5%).
Advanced (fenestrated) EVAR had better short-term outcomes than open surgery for complex AAA but higher long-term mortality (RR 1.46).
The SVS and ESVS guidelines support considering elective repair of an abdominal aortic aneurysm at a diameter of 5.5 cm or more in men and 5.0 cm or more in women.
In the UK EVAR trial 1, 30-day operative mortality was 1.7% with endovascular repair versus 4.7% with open repair.

At up to 15 years of follow-up in UK EVAR trial 1, all-cause mortality was similar after endovascular and open repair (adjusted hazard ratio 1.11, 95% CI 0.97 to 1.27), although the early survival benefit of EVAR was lost and aneurysm-related mortality was higher in the EVAR group after about 8 years.

standard_knowledge.claim: Classification of endoleaks: Type I (attachment cuff leak; requires urgent repair), Type II (collateral lumbar/IMA back-bleeding; observe unless sac expands), Type III (graft fabric/modular disconnection; requires urgent repair).

page.standard_overview: Abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA) is defined as an infrarenal aortic diameter >= 3.0 cm (or > 50% increase over normal). Rupture carries > 80% overall mortality. Ultrasound surveillance intervals depend on diameter and guideline: SVS recommends approximately every 3 years for 3.0-3.9 cm, annually for 4.0-4.9 cm, and every 6-12 months for 5.0-5.4 cm; ESVS intervals differ and should be checked for the applicable version. Elective repair is indicated at diameter >= 5.5 cm in men, >= 5.0 cm in women, or with rapid expansion (> 1.0 cm/year or > 0.5 cm in 6 months), or symptomatic aneurysms. Landmark trials (EVAR-1, DREAM, OVER) proved that Endovascular Aneurysm Repair (EVAR) significantly reduces 30-day perioperative mortality compared to open surgical repair (1.2-1.7% vs 4.7-5.0%), but this early survival benefit converges by 2-3 years, with EVAR carrying higher lifetime re-intervention rates for endoleaks (especially Type I and III) requiring lifelong CT/ultrasound surveillance.

page.mentor_intro: Intra-abdominal hypertension is common in critical illness, raises acute kidney injury risk and predicts mortality, including in severe pancreatitis. standard_knowledge.claim: Transvesical bladder pressure measurement at end-expiration instilling 20-25 mL sterile saline with transducer zeroed at mid-axillary line is the clinical gold standard.

ACS pathophysiology produces a triad of cardiovascular collapse (decreased preload, elevated SVR), respiratory compromise (high peak airway pressures), and oliguric renal failure resistant to fluid challenges.

page.standard_overview: Abdominal compartment syndrome (ACS) is defined by the WSACS consensus as a sustained intra-abdominal pressure (IAP) > 20 mmHg (with or without an abdominal perfusion pressure [APP = MAP - IAP] < 60 mmHg) associated with new or worsening single- or multiple-organ dysfunction. Intra-abdominal hypertension (IAH) is defined as sustained IAP >= 12 mmHg. Measurement of bladder pressure via an indwelling Foley catheter at end-expiration in the supine position is the gold standard diagnostic method. High IAP compresses the IVC (lowering venous return and cardiac output), impedes renal vein and parenchymal perfusion (oliguria and acute tubular necrosis), and elevates hemidiaphragms (peak airway pressures rise, producing hypercapnia and hypoxemia). Medical therapy encompasses nasogastric/colonic decompression, paracentesis of ascites, neuromuscular blockade, and judicious fluid management; refractory ACS is a surgical emergency mandating decompressive laparotomy with temporary open abdominal closure.

page.standard_overview: Abnormal uterine bleeding (AUB) in non-pregnant reproductive-age women is classified according to the FIGO PALM-COEIN system into structural causes (Polyp, Adenomyosis, Leiomyoma, Malignancy/hyperplasia) and non-structural causes (Coagulopathy, Ovulatory dysfunction, Endometrial, Iatrogenic, Not otherwise classified). Initial AUB evaluation includes pregnancy testing and CBC, with transvaginal ultrasound when structural disease is suspected; endometrial biopsy is indicated at age >=45 years and at younger ages with risk factors such as chronic anovulation, obesity, tamoxifen exposure, or Lynch syndrome. First-line medical therapy for ovulatory or non-structural AUB is the 52 mg levonorgestrel intrauterine system (LNG-IUS; Mirena), which reduces menstrual blood loss by > 70-90%, followed by oral tranexamic acid, combined oral contraceptives, or cyclical oral progestins. When medical treatment fails or is unsuitable, procedural options are selected by the cause and reproductive goals: endometrial ablation for appropriate nonstructural bleeding, UAE particularly for fibroid-related bleeding, and hysterectomy as definitive treatment.

page.standard_overview: Childhood Absence Epilepsy (CAE) and Juvenile Myoclonic Epilepsy (JME) are idiopathic generalized epilepsies (IGEs) characterized by bilateral, synchronous 3-Hz spike-and-wave discharges on EEG (CAE) or rapid 4-6 Hz polyspike-and-wave discharges (JME). Ethosuximide is the drug of first choice for pure absence seizures: the landmark NIH randomized controlled trial proved ethosuximide and valproic acid have superior seizure freedom rates (~53-58%) compared to lamotrigine (29%), with ethosuximide causing significantly fewer attentional/cognitive side effects. JME presents around puberty with morning myoclonic jerks (especially after sleep deprivation or alcohol), generalized tonic-clonic seizures, and occasional absence seizures; valproic acid is the most effective drug for JME across all seizure types, but lamotrigine or levetiracetam are preferred first-line alternatives in women of childbearing potential due to valproate teratogenicity. Sodium channel blockers (carbamazepine, phenytoin) exacerbate absence and myoclonic seizures.

standard_knowledge.claim: AAC occurs in critically ill, burned, trauma, or post-cardiac surgery patients through a combination of bile stasis (TPN, fasting) and microvascular ischemia.

Antibiotic therapy must cover enteric Gram-negative bacilli, Enterococcus, and anaerobes (e.g. piperacillin-tazobactam or meropenem); cholecystostomy catheters are typically maintained for 4-6 weeks until mature tract formation before removal.

page.standard_overview: Acute acalculous cholecystitis (AAC) is an acute necroinflammatory gallbladder disease occurring without cholelithiasis, accounting for ~5-10% of acute cholecystitis cases but carrying 30-50% mortality. It typically arises in critically ill ICU patients, severe trauma, extensive burns, sepsis, major surgery, or prolonged total parenteral nutrition (TPN). The cause of acute acalculous cholecystitis is multifactorial and likely results from bile stasis or ischaemia, or both; bile stasis follows fasting, obstruction, or postsurgical ileus and parenteral nutrition. Ultrasound and CT criteria include gallbladder wall thickening (> 3 mm), pericholecystic fluid, intramural gas, and subserosal halo sign without gallstones. Initial management requires broad-spectrum IV antibiotics and prompt gallbladder decompression: percutaneous cholecystostomy (PC) is the preferred minimally invasive intervention in critically ill unstable patients, reserving laparoscopic or open cholecystectomy for stable candidates or those with gallbladder perforation/gangrene.

overview_support.note: CGH 2010 Pathophysiology: "The etiology of AAC is multifactorial and likely results from bile stasis or ischemia (or both). Bile stasis can be caused by fasting, obstruction, postsurgical/procedural irritation or ileus (TPN)". The endotoxin-mediated mucosal necrosis wording is not stated.

standard_knowledge.claim: Chronic systemic inflammation drives endothelial injury, increases circulating adhesion molecules (ICAM-1, VCAM-1), promotes dense necrotic core lipid plaques, and doubles premature myocardial infarction rates.
Aggressive disease suppression with methotrexate and biologic DMARDs (anti-TNF, anti-IL-6) reduces vascular inflammation and decreases incident cardiovascular events by 20-30%.

page.standard_overview: Systemic autoimmune and chronic inflammatory diseases increase premature ASCVD risk through disease activity and traditional factors; the magnitude varies by disease and population rather than uniformly being 2-3-fold or equivalent to diabetes. Chronic circulating pro-inflammatory cytokines (TNF-alpha, IL-1beta, IL-6, interferon-alpha) trigger endothelial dysfunction, vascular smooth muscle proliferation, macrophage foam-cell activation, oxidation of LDL, and destabilization of coronary fibrous caps. EULAR recommends a 1.5 multiplication factor for conventional cardiovascular risk estimates in eligible patients with rheumatoid arthritis; under the 2015 rule this applied when at least two of disease duration >=10 years, RF or anti-CCP positivity, and severe extra-articular manifestations were present, while current guidance should be applied by version and disease activity. Controlling inflammatory disease activity with appropriate DMARDs may reduce vascular risk and should be combined with conventional prevention, including statins when indicated, blood-pressure control, and smoking cessation.

page.standard_overview: ACE inhibitors (or ARNI), beta-blockers and MRAs are foundational therapy for heart failure with reduced ejection fraction. Use in hypertension, post-myocardial infarction and proteinuric CKD rests on other guidelines. By blocking angiotensin II-mediated efferent arteriolar vasoconstriction, they decrease intraglomerular hydrostatic pressure, which provides long-term nephron protection and slows GFR decline, but causes an acute, predictable, hemodynamic decline in eGFR. A serum-creatinine rise of up to 30% after starting an ACE inhibitor or ARB can be hemodynamic and does not automatically require discontinuation if it stabilizes; reassess volume status, potassium, interacting drugs, and progressive kidney dysfunction. Routine monitoring of serum creatinine and potassium is required 1-2 weeks post-initiation. Hyperkalemia, commonly defined as potassium >5.0 mmol/L, is managed according to severity by reviewing diet and potassium-retaining drugs, using diuretics when appropriate, and considering patiromer or sodium zirconium cyclosilicate to enable continued RAAS inhibition.

overview_support.note: ESC 2021: "The triad of an ACE-I/ARNI, a beta-blocker, and an MRA is recommended as cornerstone" for HFrEF. Hypertension, post-MI and CKD indications are not in this source.

page.mentor_intro: Achalasia treatment options are pneumatic dilation, Heller myotomy and POEM. POEM has durable efficacy (87% long-term) with stable post-procedure reflux, and subtype 3 favours POEM; guidelines from ASGE, UEG/ESNM and SAGES cover choice and follow-up.

teaching_points.claim: The 2024 SAGES update gives a conditional recommendation for either POEM or Heller with fundoplication in subtypes 1 and 2, and prefers POEM for subtype 3; POEM should be used with appropriate PPI use.

European UEG/ESNM guidelines cover diagnosis, medical, endoscopic and surgical therapy, treatment failure, follow-up and oesophageal cancer risk in adult achalasia.
ESGE advises G-POEM in carefully selected patients in expert centres only, preferably within clinical trials, because data are limited.
A POEM centre should maintain a prospective registry of procedures, techniques and adverse events.
A meta-analysis found long-term clinical efficacy of POEM persisted in 87% of patients, with a pooled severe adverse event rate of 1.5% and minimal risk of Barrett's oesophagus and peptic strictures.
The global incidence and prevalence of achalasia have increased notably, with large worldwide variation.

standard_knowledge.claim: High-Resolution Manometry (Chicago Classification) is the gold standard diagnostic tool, classifying achalasia into Type I (classic), Type II (panesophageal pressurization), and Type III (spastic).
POEM achieves excellent dysphagia relief (> 90%) across all subtypes and is the treatment of choice for Type III (spastic) achalasia due to the ability to perform a long proximal esophageal myotomy.
Laparoscopic Heller Myotomy combined with partial fundoplication (Dor or Toupet) provides durable 5-10 year clinical success with lower rates of post-procedure reflux compared to POEM.

Pneumatic dilation with graded balloon sizes (30, 35, 40 mm) achieves success comparable to myotomy in older adults with Type II achalasia, but carries a 1-3% perforation risk requiring emergency surgical backup.

page.standard_overview: Achalasia is a primary esophageal motility disorder characterized by incomplete lower esophageal sphincter (LES) relaxation and absent esophageal peristalsis due to autoimmune loss of inhibitory nitric oxide/VIP-producing ganglion cells in the myenteric (Auerbach) plexus. Diagnosis is confirmed by High-Resolution Manometry (HRM) according to the Chicago Classification v4.0, defining three subtypes based on panesophageal pressurization: Type I (classic, no pressurization), Type II (panesophageal pressurization; highest therapeutic success > 90%), and Type III (spastic, premature contractions). Definitive treatment aims to mechanically disrupt the LES and encompasses Per-Oral Endoscopic Myotomy (POEM), Laparoscopic Heller Myotomy with partial fundoplication (LHM), and Graded Pneumatic Dilation (PD; serial 30, 35, 40 mm balloons). POEM is especially useful for type III achalasia and has comparable dysphagia efficacy to Heller myotomy for types I and II, but post-POEM reflux is common and may require testing, surveillance, or proton-pump-inhibitor treatment rather than universal daily PPI therapy.

standard_knowledge.claim: In ALPS, neither amiodarone nor lidocaine improved survival to discharge or good neurological outcome compared with placebo in out-of-hospital arrest with shock-refractory VF or pulseless VT; both remain options (amiodarone 300 mg then 150 mg; lidocaine 1 to 1.5 mg/kg).
Giving epinephrine 1 mg as early as possible in non-shockable rhythms increases return of spontaneous circulation and survival, with little effect on good neurological outcome (PARAMEDIC2).
In comatose survivors of cardiac arrest, TTM2 found that targeted hypothermia at 33 C did not improve survival compared with normothermia with early treatment of fever; fever should be prevented.

page.standard_overview: Advanced Cardiovascular Life Support (ACLS) guidelines from the AHA and ERC structure adult cardiac arrest resuscitation around rapid rhythm identification, high-quality cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR), and prompt defibrillation for shockable rhythms. VF and pulseless VT require unsynchronized biphasic defibrillation followed by 2 minutes of CPR; AHA gives epinephrine 1 mg after the second shock, whereas ERC gives it after the third, and amiodarone or lidocaine is considered after the third shock, with ALPS showing no significant overall survival-to-discharge advantage over placebo. Non-shockable rhythms (Asystole and Pulseless Electrical Activity [PEA]) require immediate epinephrine 1 mg as early as possible and urgent investigation of reversible etiologies using the 'H's and T's' framework (Hypovolemia, Hypoxia, Hydrogen ion acidosis, Hypo/hyperkalemia, Hypothermia, Tension pneumothorax, Tamponade, Toxins, Thrombosis PE/coronary).

page.standard_overview: Acromegaly is a chronic systemic endocrine disease caused by excessive growth hormone (GH) secretion, in > 98% from a benign pituitary somatotroph adenoma. Elevated serum Insulin-like Growth Factor 1 (IGF-1) is the screening test of choice. Confirmation requires an Oral Glucose Tolerance Test (OGTT; 75 g oral glucose), where failure to suppress nadir GH < 1.0 ug/L (or < 0.4 ug/L with ultrasensitive assays) confirms autonomous GH hypersecretion. Transsphenoidal pituitary adenomectomy is the first-line definitive therapy, achieving biochemical cure in > 70-85% of microadenomas and 40-50% of macroadenomas. For persistent or recurrent disease, first-line medical therapy is first-generation long-acting Somatostatin Receptor Ligands (SRLs: octreotide LAR, lanreotide autogel; targeting SSTR2). Second-line therapies for SRL-resistant disease include the growth hormone receptor antagonist pegvisomant (normalizes IGF-1 in most patients (roughly 60 to 90%) without lowering GH), pasireotide LAR (multi-receptor SRL targeting SSTR5; carries high hyperglycemia risk), or cabergoline (dopamine agonist for modest IGF-1 elevation).

standard_knowledge.claim: STEMI mandates emergency primary PCI with target door-to-balloon time < 90 minutes, or fibrinolytic therapy within 10 minutes of ECG if primary PCI transfer time exceeds 120 minutes.

page.standard_overview: Acute Coronary Syndrome (ACS) encompasses ST-Elevation Myocardial Infarction (STEMI), Non-ST-Elevation Myocardial Infarction (NSTEMI), and Unstable Angina (UA), defined by myocardial ischemia with or without high-sensitivity cardiac troponin (hs-cTn) elevation. ESC 2017: fibrinolysis is recommended if primary PCI cannot be performed within 120 minutes of STEMI diagnosis; the fibrinolytic bolus should be given within 10 minutes of diagnosis. NSTEMI requires validated risk stratification (GRACE score > 140) to direct early invasive coronary angiography (< 24 hours). ACS management usually combines aspirin with a P2Y12 inhibitor, preferably ticagrelor or prasugrel when suitable, plus anticoagulation and high-intensity statin therapy; clopidogrel is an alternative for bleeding, access, or contraindication issues, prasugrel is used in PCI and avoided after stroke/TIA, and beta-blockers and ACE inhibitors are added for appropriate cardiac indications.

page.standard_overview: Active pulmonary tuberculosis (TB) is caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis, presenting with chronic cough, hemoptysis, fevers, drenching night sweats, weight loss, and upper lobe cavitary or nodular infiltrates on chest radiography. Diagnosis is confirmed via rapid molecular testing (Xpert MTB/RIF assay on sputum), sputum acid-fast bacilli (AFB) smear, and mycobacterial culture. Standard first-line therapy for drug-susceptible TB consists of a 6-month regimen: a 2-month intensive phase with 4 drugs (Rifampin [RIF], Isoniazid [INH], Pyrazinamide [PZA], and Ethambutol [EMB] - 'RIPE'), followed by a 4-month continuation phase with Rifampin and Isoniazid (2RH). Pyridoxine 25-50 mg daily is given with isoniazid to patients at increased risk of peripheral neuropathy, including malnutrition, diabetes, HIV infection, renal failure, alcohol misuse, pregnancy, or breastfeeding; it is not universally mandatory for every patient. Baseline visual acuity and red-green color discrimination must be verified before starting ethambutol to detect optic neuritis; baseline and serial hepatic transaminases must be monitored for drug-induced liver injury (PZA > INH > RIF).

page.standard_overview: The acute abdomen encompasses rapid-onset, severe abdominal pain reflecting life-threatening surgical emergencies (perforated viscus, acute peritonitis, bowel obstruction, acute mesenteric ischemia, ruptured ectopic pregnancy, or ruptured AAA). Diagnostic evaluation prioritizes hemodynamic stability, early resuscitation, and structured clinical evaluation: localized peritoneal signs (involuntary guarding, percussion tenderness, rebound) mandate emergent surgical consultation. Contrast-enhanced CT is often the first-line definitive test for adults with severe or undifferentiated acute abdominal pain, but diagnostic accuracy and the optimal modality depend on the suspected condition; ultrasound, MRI, endoscopy, or immediate surgery may be more appropriate in selected cases. POCUS can rapidly identify hemoperitoneum, an abdominal aortic aneurysm, and features of acute cholecystitis, helping prioritize urgent treatment, although it does not by itself reliably prove aneurysm rupture. Analgesia with IV opioids should NOT be withheld as it facilitates physical examination without masking surgical pathology.

standard_knowledge.claim: Concurrent prescription of opioids and benzodiazepines quadruples the risk of fatal respiratory depression and is strongly discouraged unless strictly clinically necessary.

Naloxone should be offered to patients on opioids with overdose risk factors, including doses of 50 MME/day or more, concurrent benzodiazepines, sleep apnoea, renal or hepatic impairment, or substance use history.

page.standard_overview: Pain assessment requires validated multidimensional scales and careful clinical differentiation between nociceptive, neuropathic, and nociplastic mechanisms. In acute pain, multimodal analgesia combining acetaminophen, NSAIDs (unless contraindicated by CKD, peptic ulcer, or cardiovascular disease), regional/neuraxial anesthesia, and non-pharmacologic interventions maximizes pain control while minimizing opioid requirements ('opioid-sparing strategy'). For chronic non-cancer pain, CDC guidelines emphasize non-opioid pharmacotherapies (gabapentinoids, SNRIs, tricyclics, topical agents) and non-pharmacologic modalities (CBT, physical therapy). When opioids are necessary, use immediate-release formulations at the lowest effective dose, usually only a few days for acute pain; for longer-term prescribing, assess misuse risk, review the PDMP, avoid benzodiazepine combinations where possible, and offer naloxone at >=50 MME/day or with other overdose-risk factors.

standard_knowledge.claim: Weight-adjusted colchicine dosing (0.5 mg daily if < 70 kg, or 0.5 mg BID if >= 70 kg) is maintained for 3 months for first-episode acute pericarditis and 6 months for recurrences.

page.standard_overview: Acute pericarditis is diagnosed clinically by the presence of at least 2 of 4 cardinal ESC criteria: 1) sharp, pleuritic chest pain improved by sitting upright and leaning forward, 2) pericardial friction rub on auscultation, 3) widespread concave-upward ST-segment elevation with PR depression on ECG, and 4) new or worsening pericardial effusion. Viral infections are among the most common causes of pericardial inflammation in developed countries. ESC guidelines mandate combination therapy with high-dose NSAIDs (e.g. ibuprofen 600-800 mg TID or aspirin 750-1000 mg TID) PLUS weight-adjusted oral colchicine (0.5 mg daily if < 70 kg, 0.5 mg BID if >= 70 kg) for 3 months in acute pericarditis (ICAP trial) and 6 months in recurrent pericarditis (CORP trials). Colchicine inhibits tubulin polymerization and leukocyte chemotaxis, halving recurrence rates from 37% to 16%. Systemic corticosteroids are second-line agents strictly reserved for NSAID contraindications, autoimmune etiologies, or pregnancy, as early corticosteroid use independently increases the risk of chronic recurrence.

topic: Acute aortic dissection diagnosis and management

page.mentor_intro: Retrieved evidence centres on outcomes rather than the diagnostic pathway: type A dissection carries organ-specific malperfusion risk that predicts in-hospital death, and for type B the question is whether and when to add TEVAR to medical therapy. Guideline-level recommendations were not in the retrieved set.

teaching_points.claim: In acute type A aortic dissection, in-hospital survival varies with the type of malperfusion; mesenteric, coronary and cerebral malperfusion carried the highest in-hospital mortality, so organ-specific malperfusion should inform perioperative risk and surgical planning.
Women with type A dissection more often had pericardial effusion or tamponade, while in-hospital surgical mortality did not differ by sex (RR 1.02), suggesting a personalised approach.

A meta-analysis found TEVAR was associated with lower mortality than best medical therapy in type B dissection, especially in patients aged 65 or older, at the cost of longer hospital and ICU stays, with randomised trials still needed.

For uncomplicated type B dissection, the role of TEVAR remains debated: it improves aortic remodelling but there is no definitive survival evidence, and trials and guidelines that include high-risk features are needed.
Meta-analyses of TEVAR timing found the subacute phase (14-90 days from onset) associated with better long-term outcomes, including lower aortic-related death and reintervention.
Retrograde type A dissection after TEVAR is rare but carries high mortality (about 42%), especially in the first month and with proximal bare-stent grafts.
The GERAADA score showed better calibration than EuroSCORE II for 30-day mortality after surgery for acute type A dissection, though discrimination of both was moderate.
AI tools can feasibly detect aortic dissection on CT but do not yet demonstrate clinical applicability, and most studies were low quality.

uncertainties: Whether pre-emptive TEVAR improves survival in uncomplicated type B dissection.

page.standard_overview: Acute aortic syndromes include dissection, intramural hematoma, and penetrating atherosclerotic ulcer, typically presenting with sudden severe chest or back pain; hypertension is common, but hypotension or shock can occur with complications. Stanford classification determines emergency management: Type A involves the ascending aorta (surgical emergency requiring immediate open surgical graft replacement to prevent pericardial tamponade, aortic rupture, or coronary malperfusion); Type B involves the descending aorta distal to the left subclavian artery (managed with medical anti-impulse therapy, reserving Thoracic Endovascular Aortic Repair [TEVAR] for complicated dissection: malperfusion, refractory pain, rapid expansion, or rupture). In aortic dissection, intravenous beta-blockers are started to reduce heart rate and lower systolic blood pressure to 100-120 mmHg, after excluding aortic regurgitation; other agents may be added to reach the target. Giving vasodilators before beta-blockers precipitates reflex tachycardia and accelerates dissection tear propagation.

page.mentor_intro: Retrieved evidence centres on outcomes rather than the diagnostic pathway: type A dissection carries organ-specific malperfusion risk that predicts in-hospital death, and for type B the question is whether and when to add TEVAR to medical therapy. Guideline-level recommendations were not in the retrieved set.

teaching_points.claim: In acute type A aortic dissection, in-hospital survival varies with the type of malperfusion; mesenteric, coronary and cerebral malperfusion carried the highest in-hospital mortality, so organ-specific malperfusion should inform perioperative risk and surgical planning.
Women with type A dissection more often had pericardial effusion or tamponade, while in-hospital surgical mortality did not differ by sex (RR 1.02), suggesting a personalised approach.

A meta-analysis found TEVAR was associated with lower mortality than best medical therapy in type B dissection, especially in patients aged 65 or older, at the cost of longer hospital and ICU stays, with randomised trials still needed.

For uncomplicated type B dissection, the role of TEVAR remains debated: it improves aortic remodelling but there is no definitive survival evidence, and trials and guidelines that include high-risk features are needed.
Meta-analyses of TEVAR timing found the subacute phase (14-90 days from onset) associated with better long-term outcomes, including lower aortic-related death and reintervention.
Retrograde type A dissection after TEVAR is rare but carries high mortality (about 42%), especially in the first month and with proximal bare-stent grafts.
The GERAADA score showed better calibration than EuroSCORE II for 30-day mortality after surgery for acute type A dissection, though discrimination of both was moderate.
AI tools can feasibly detect aortic dissection on CT but do not yet demonstrate clinical applicability, and most studies were low quality.

uncertainties: Whether pre-emptive TEVAR improves survival in uncomplicated type B dissection.

teaching_points.claim: The Italian paediatric acute-asthma guideline advises against epinephrine, allows IV magnesium sulfate in severe attacks or FEV1 below 60% unresponsive to inhaled therapy, allows heliox in life-threatening attacks, and does not recommend leukotriene receptor antagonists.

Adherence of 80% or more lowered the odds of severe exacerbation (OR 0.53), and discontinuing therapy raised it.

standard_knowledge.claim: Systemic corticosteroids administered within 1 hour of emergency department presentation accelerate airflow recovery, prevent relapses, and reduce hospitalization rates.
Intravenous magnesium sulfate (2 g IV over 20 minutes) is indicated in acute severe asthma with PEF < 50% failing initial bronchodilators, significantly improving FEV1 and reducing admission.

A 'normal' or elevated PaCO2 (> 40-45 mmHg) in a tachypneic asthmatic is an ominous sign of respiratory muscle exhaustion, signaling impending arrest requiring ICU monitoring and preparation for intubation.

page.standard_overview: Acute severe asthma exacerbation is characterized by progressive dyspnea, wheezing, chest tightness, and airflow obstruction, quantified by Peak Expiratory Flow (PEF) < 50% predicted or personal best. Initial therapy mandates repetitive or continuous inhaled short-acting beta-2 agonists (SABA; albuterol 4-8 puffs or 2.5-5 mg nebulized) combined with inhaled ipratropium bromide (500 ug nebulized q20min x 3 doses), which reduces hospital admissions by roughly a quarter. Systemic corticosteroids (oral prednisone 40-50 mg daily for 5-7 days, or IV methylprednisolone 60-80 mg in severe cases) must be administered early within 1 hour of presentation to accelerate resolution of airway inflammation. In severe exacerbations unresponsive to initial nebulization, single-dose intravenous magnesium sulfate (2 g IV over 20 min) provides safe, potent bronchodilation and reduces hospitalizations. Controlled oxygen therapy should target SpO2 93-95% (avoiding hyperoxia, which worsens V/Q mismatch and hypercapnia). A 'normal' or rising PaCO2 (> 40 mmHg) or silent chest signals respiratory muscle fatigue and impending fatal respiratory arrest.

page.mentor_intro: Bacterial meningitis is time-critical: antibiotics later than two hours after presentation roughly double mortality. Case fatality has fallen over eighty years but remains high; molecular and host-marker tests may help when cultures are negative.

teaching_points.claim: NICE 2002: Therefore, we recommend dexamethasone treatment for all patients with acute bacterial meningitis.

In community-acquired bacterial meningitis, odds of mortality increase markedly when antibiotics are given later than two hours after presentation, and delay raised the odds of neurological impairment (aOR 1.79).
Case fatality of community-acquired bacterial meningitis has declined over the last century but a high burden remains.
Aetiology of bacterial meningitis differs by age group and region.
Metagenomic next-generation sequencing has moderate diagnostic accuracy for bacterial meningitis/encephalitis and may help when standard diagnosis fails.
16S/18S rRNA gene PCR with Sanger sequencing can diagnose non-growing pathogens and may change antibiotic treatment when cultures stay negative.
Heparin-binding protein has high diagnostic accuracy for bacterial infections including meningitis (sensitivity and specificity 87% at a cut-off of 32.868 ng/ml).
Febrile neonates have about twice the rate of bacteraemia and meningitis as febrile infants in the second month of life.

In a European randomised trial in adults with bacterial meningitis, dexamethasone 10 mg every 6 hours for 4 days, started before or with the first antibiotic dose, reduced unfavourable outcome and mortality, with the greatest benefit in pneumococcal meningitis.

uncertainties: Role of adjunctive dexamethasone is not covered by the retrieved excerpts.

CT of the head prior to lumbar puncture is indicated ONLY if specific high-risk features exist: immunocompromised state, history of CNS disease, new-onset seizures, papilledema, abnormal consciousness, or focal neurologic deficit.
If CT head is required before LP, blood cultures must be drawn immediately and empiric antibiotics plus dexamethasone administered WITHOUT waiting for CT completion.

page.standard_overview: The classic triad of fever, neck stiffness and altered mental status is described in adult acute bacterial meningitis, but its sensitivity is limited. Most common community pathogens in adults are Streptococcus pneumoniae and Neisseria meningitidis; Listeria monocytogenes must be covered in adults >= 50 years, alcoholics, or immunocompromised individuals. Empiric therapy in adults < 50 is IV ceftriaxone (2 g q12h) plus vancomycin (15-20 mg/kg q8-12h); adults >= 50 require the addition of IV ampicillin (2 g q4h) to cover Listeria. Adjuvant dexamethasone (10 mg IV) must be given BEFORE or WITH the first antibiotic dose: the landmark European randomized trial showed dexamethasone reduced unfavourable outcome and mortality, with a clear benefit in pneumococcal meningitis. ESCMID 2016: blood cultures are strongly recommended before the first dose of antibiotics. If cranial CT delays lumbar puncture, empiric treatment must start immediately on suspicion. Dexamethasone is advised with the first dose of antibiotics.

overview_support.note: EFNS 2008: refers to "the sensitivity of the classic triad of fever, neck stiffness and [altered mental status]" in a Dutch adult cohort. The Kernig/Brudzinski signs are not mentioned in the matched text.

ESCMID 2016: ceftriaxone 2 g q12h plus vancomycin; "Age >50 years, or Age >18 and <50 years plus risk factors for Listeria monocytogenes": add amoxicillin/ampicillin. The age threshold is >50, not >=50.

ESCMID 2016: "empiric treatment must be started immediately upon clinical suspicion even if the diagnosis has not been established... blood cultures must be drawn before initiating antibiotics"; "it is advised to start dexamethasone with the first dose of antibiotics".

standard_knowledge.claim: Empiric antimicrobial regimen: ceftriaxone 2 g q12h plus vancomycin for all adults; add ampicillin 2 g q4h in adults >= 50 years or immunocompromised hosts to cover Listeria monocytogenes.

CT of the head prior to lumbar puncture is indicated ONLY if specific high-risk features exist: immunocompromised state, history of CNS disease, new-onset seizures, papilledema, abnormal consciousness, or focal neurologic deficit.
If CT head is required before LP, blood cultures must be drawn immediately and empiric antibiotics plus dexamethasone administered WITHOUT waiting for CT completion.

page.standard_overview: The classic triad of fever, neck stiffness and altered mental status is described in adult acute bacterial meningitis, but its sensitivity is limited. Most common community pathogens in adults are Streptococcus pneumoniae and Neisseria meningitidis; Listeria monocytogenes must be covered in adults >= 50 years, alcoholics, or immunocompromised individuals. Empiric therapy in adults < 50 is IV ceftriaxone (2 g q12h) plus vancomycin (15-20 mg/kg q8-12h); adults >= 50 require the addition of IV ampicillin (2 g q4h) to cover Listeria. Adjuvant dexamethasone (10 mg IV) must be given BEFORE or WITH the first antibiotic dose: the landmark European randomized trial showed dexamethasone reduced unfavourable outcome and mortality, with a clear benefit in pneumococcal meningitis. ESCMID 2016: blood cultures are strongly recommended before the first dose of antibiotics. If cranial CT delays lumbar puncture, empiric treatment must start immediately on suspicion. Dexamethasone is advised with the first dose of antibiotics.

overview_support.note: EFNS 2008: refers to "the sensitivity of the classic triad of fever, neck stiffness and [altered mental status]" in a Dutch adult cohort. The Kernig/Brudzinski signs are not mentioned in the matched text.

ESCMID 2016: ceftriaxone 2 g q12h plus vancomycin; "Age >50 years, or Age >18 and <50 years plus risk factors for Listeria monocytogenes": add amoxicillin/ampicillin. The age threshold is >50, not >=50.

ESCMID 2016: "empiric treatment must be started immediately upon clinical suspicion even if the diagnosis has not been established... blood cultures must be drawn before initiating antibiotics"; "it is advised to start dexamethasone with the first dose of antibiotics".

standard_knowledge.claim: A structured stepwise approach begins with non-pharmacologic de-escalation, reserving chemical sedation for patients presenting immediate physical danger to themselves or staff.
Benzodiazepines (lorazepam, midazolam) are the first-line sedatives for agitation driven by sympathomimetic intoxication (cocaine, methamphetamines) or alcohol withdrawal.
Antipsychotics (haloperidol, olanzapine, droperidol) provide effective sedation for psychotic agitation and delirium, but require ECG monitoring for QTc prolongation.
Intramuscular ketamine (3-4 mg/kg IM) produces rapid, reliable dissociation within 3-5 minutes in extreme, life-threatening violent agitation failing other agents, under dedicated airway monitoring.

page.standard_overview: Acute behavioural disturbance (ABD) and severe agitation in the emergency and acute inpatient setting represent medical emergencies that threaten patient and staff safety. Most common causes include acute delirium, intoxication (sympathomimetics, alcohol, synthetic cannabinoids), sedative withdrawal, severe psychiatric psychosis, metabolic derangements, and traumatic brain injury. Clinical management follows a staged de-escalation hierarchy: environmental adaptation and verbal de-escalation are attempted first. When de-escalation fails and there is immediate danger, medication is selected by cause and contraindications; haloperidol, a typical antipsychotic, or olanzapine may be options for severe undifferentiated agitation, but neither is universally first-line for delirium. For stimulant toxicity or alcohol withdrawal, intravenous or intramuscular benzodiazepines (lorazepam 1-2 mg or midazolam 2.5-5 mg) are the treatments of choice. For life-threatening agitation refractory to other measures, intramuscular ketamine may produce rapid sedation when used by experienced clinicians with immediate airway, ventilation, and cardiovascular monitoring; evidence and protocols vary, and excited delirium is not a uniformly defined diagnosis.

page.standard_overview: Acute cholecystitis and acute cholangitis represent common biliary infections governed by the international Tokyo Guidelines (TG18). Acute cholecystitis is defined by local inflammation (Murphy's sign, RUQ tenderness), systemic inflammation (fever, elevated CRP/WBC), and confirmatory imaging (ultrasound showing gallbladder wall thickening >= 4 mm, pericholecystic fluid, sonographic Murphy's sign). Laparoscopic cholecystectomy performed early within 72 hours of symptom onset (or during index admission) is the gold standard, achieving shorter hospital stays and fewer complications than delayed surgery. Acute cholangitis is a medical emergency caused by biliary tract obstruction (primarily choledocholithiasis) with bacterial superinfection, presenting with Charcot's triad (fever, jaundice, RUQ pain) or Reynolds' pentad (adding hypotension and altered mental status in septic shock). TG18 management includes resuscitation and empiric antibiotics, with biliary drainage timing based on severity: urgent drainage after stabilization for severe grade III disease, early drainage for moderate grade II disease, and drainage for mild disease that does not respond to initial treatment.

Delirium is common in critically ill patients with AKI and is associated with worse outcomes and longer hospital stay (WMD 4.78 days).

page.standard_overview: Acute confusion (delirium) is an acute, fluctuating neurocognitive disturbance characterized by inattention, altered level of consciousness, and disorganized thinking, triggered by underlying acute medical illness, surgery, or toxidrome. CAM and 4AT are validated tools that support delirium screening and recognition, while diagnostic confirmation remains a clinical assessment of acute fluctuating inattention and associated cognitive or consciousness changes. The Hospital Elder Life Program-style intervention uses standardised protocols for orientation, sleep enhancement, early mobilisation, vision and hearing, and minimising sedative drugs. Routine antipsychotic treatment has not been shown to shorten delirium or reduce mortality; haloperidol, a typical antipsychotic, and selected atypical agents should generally be reserved for short-term control of dangerous agitation after correcting causes and implementing nonpharmacologic care. Formal mental capacity assessment must be decision-specific and time-specific, assessing the ability to understand, retain, weigh information, and communicate a choice.

overview_support.note: Lancet 2014: "Key diagnostic features include an acute onset and fluctuating course of symptoms, inattention, impaired level of consciousness, and disturbance of cognition". "Disorganised thinking" is not the wording used.

NEJM 1999 Table 1: orientation, nonpharmacologic sleep protocol, sleep enhancement, and "change in rate of use of sedative drugs". Anticholinergic avoidance and "evidence-based first-line cornerstone" are not stated.

page.mentor_intro: The 2025 ACC/AHA ACS guideline and the Australian guideline set current care; P2Y12 monotherapy may prove better than aspirin for long-term prevention and CYP2C19 genotyping may guide P2Y12 choice. Secondary prevention uses stricter LDL targets and PCSK9 inhibitors.

teaching_points.claim: The Australian ACS guideline supports selective intravascular imaging in NSTEACS, updated P2Y12 timing, stricter LDL-C targets and PCSK9 inhibitor use in secondary prevention.
Commentary on the 2025 ACS guideline urges that CYP2C19-guided P2Y12 inhibitor selection be incorporated, especially for patients at high bleeding risk.
New data from HOST-EXAM and SMART CHOICE 3 suggest P2Y12 monotherapy may be better than aspirin for long-term prevention of major adverse cardiovascular events.
A UK guideline addresses CYP2C19 genotype testing for clopidogrel.
Where HIT patients need cardiac surgery with negative functional assays, limited intraoperative heparin re-exposure carries a low risk of HIT recurrence with postoperative monitoring.
Mental disorders, particularly PTSD and sleep disorders, are significant risk factors for ACS.
Prasugrel and ticagrelor are significantly superior to clopidogrel in ACS, reducing ischemic death and stent thrombosis (TRITON-TIMI 38 and PLATO trials).
The head-to-head ISAR-REACT 5 trial demonstrated that a prasugrel-based strategy significantly reduced ischemic events compared to ticagrelor without increasing major bleeding in ACS.

uncertainties: Optimal long-term antiplatelet monotherapy.

page.standard_overview: Acute Coronary Syndrome (ACS) management centers on rapid risk stratification, coronary revascularization, and potent antithrombotic therapy. After ACS PCI, aspirin plus a P2Y12 inhibitor is the default antiplatelet strategy, commonly for 12 months when bleeding risk is acceptable; ticagrelor or prasugrel is preferred when suitable, while clopidogrel and shorter regimens are used for contraindications or high bleeding risk. In the randomized head-to-head ISAR-REACT 5 trial, prasugrel was superior to ticagrelor in reducing composite death, MI, or stroke (6.9% vs 9.3%) without increasing major bleeding. High-bleeding-risk (HBR) patients can safely undergo abbreviated DAPT (1-3 months) followed by P2Y12 inhibitor monotherapy (ticagrelor or clopidogrel; TWILIGHT and STOPDAPT-2 trials), which substantially reduces bleeding without increasing ischemic events. Glycoprotein IIb/IIIa inhibitors (eptifibatide, tirofiban) are reserved for thrombotic bailout during PCI.

overview_support.note: ESC 2023 ACS: "There is no strong evidence for any additional benefit with the routine use of GP IIb/IIIa inhibitors... their use should be considered for bailout if there is evidence of no-reflow or a thrombotic complication during PCI."

page.mentor_intro: Diuretic response in acute heart failure can be guided by urinary sodium, and acetazolamide is an effective add-on increasing decongestion without mortality change. Lung ultrasound aids diagnosis, and deprescribing diuretics is feasible in selected patients.

teaching_points.claim: Urinary sodium analysis may allow fast titration of diuretics in acute decompensated heart failure, with a point-of-care sensor enabling immediate readings.
Diuretic discontinuation could be safe and feasible in carefully selected patients, though high-quality evidence is lacking.
A systematic review of guidelines on diuretic appropriateness found few offered actionable deprescribing support, calling for implementation-ready guidance.
A European consensus provides a framework for guideline-directed therapy in patients with heart failure and obesity.
Acetazolamide as add-on therapy increased diuresis, natriuresis and clinical decongestion (RR 1.35) but was not associated with mortality differences.
Prehospital lung ultrasound has similar diagnostic characteristics for ADHF as in the ED, and a positive scan may justify early treatment.

In the DOSE trial in acute decompensated heart failure, high-dose intravenous furosemide (2.5 times the oral dose) showed a nonsignificant trend toward greater symptom improvement (P=0.06) than low-dose, with no significant difference in change in creatinine.

In the ADVOR trial, adding intravenous acetazolamide (500 mg daily) to loop diuretics increased the likelihood of successful decongestion (risk ratio 1.46) in acute decompensated heart failure with volume overload.
Adding a thiazide diuretic (CLOROTIC trial: oral hydrochlorothiazide added to IV furosemide) significantly enhances weight loss and diuresis in patients with loop diuretic resistance.

uncertainties: Optimal diuretic strategy beyond urinary sodium guidance.

page.standard_overview: In acute heart failure the objectives of treatment are identification of precipitants and decongestion; adequate decongestion is needed before discharge, as persistent congestion predicts death and rehospitalisation. Intravenous loop diuretics (furosemide, bumetanide) are the foundation of therapy: the DOSE trial found that high-dose IV loop diuretic therapy (2.5x oral home dose) gave greater fluid loss and a nonsignificant trend toward better symptom relief, with no significant difference in renal function compared with low-dose therapy, with continuous infusion offering no superiority over bolus dosing. Sequential nephron blockade can overcome diuretic resistance: intravenous acetazolamide 500 mg daily improved successful decongestion in ADVOR, and thiazide-like agents such as oral metolazone or intravenous chlorothiazide increase natriuresis in CLOROTIC and related practice. SGLT2 inhibitors (dapagliflozin, empagliflozin) initiated early during index hospitalization improve decongestion and overall clinical benefit (EMPULSE trial), without a clear difference in mortality alone.

overview_support.note: ESC 2021 section 11.2: "The objectives of treatment are identification of precipitants, decongestion, and in rare instances, correction of hypoperfusion." "Aggressive, early" is not stated.

page.mentor_intro: ADEM in adults has worse outcomes than in children, with residual deficits in about half of cases. COVID-19-associated ADEM resembles classic ADEM; MOGAD is a related antibody-mediated disease with its own French and European guidance.

French guidelines for MOG antibody-associated disease stress multidisciplinary management.
Neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder consensus recommendations cover diagnosis, treatment, paediatric patients and pregnancy.
Adults with ADEM had worse outcomes than children, with a mortality rate of 7.8% and a 47.5% risk of residual deficits.
SARS-CoV-2-associated ADEM, though rare, shares most features of classic ADEM, and ADEM and acute haemorrhagic leukoencephalitis after COVID-19 had high haemorrhage rates and poor outcomes.
Brain MRI in neurologically symptomatic COVID-19 patients commonly showed infarction, olfactory bulb abnormalities, white matter abnormalities and microbleeds.

page.standard_overview: Acute Disseminated Encephalomyelitis (ADEM) is an acute, immune-mediated, monophasic inflammatory demyelinating disease of the central nervous system, predominantly affecting children and young adults typically 1-3 weeks following a viral illness or vaccination. Clinical presentation combines encephalopathy (altered behavior, lethargy, or coma - a mandatory diagnostic feature in pediatric consensus criteria) with multifocal neurologic deficits (ataxia, cranial nerve palsies, hemiparesis, optic neuritis). Brain and spine MRI with gadolinium is the imaging modality of choice, demonstrating large, bilateral, asymmetric, poorly marginated, fluffy hyperintensities on T2/FLAIR predominantly involving cerebral white matter, deep gray nuclei (thalami, basal ganglia), and spinal cord, with punctate or open-ring enhancement. Serum myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein (MOG) antibodies are positive in roughly a third to a half of children with ADEM. First-line therapy is high-dose intravenous methylprednisolone (30 mg/kg/day, up to 1 g daily for 3-5 days) followed by an oral prednisone taper; intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG 2 g/kg over 2-5 days) or plasma exchange (PLEX) are second-line rescue therapies.

page.standard_overview: Acute gouty arthritis is an intensely painful inflammatory arthritis driven by the deposition of monosodium urate (MSU) crystals in synovial fluid and periarticular tissues, triggering the NLRP3 inflammasome and interleukin-1beta (IL-1beta) release. Definite diagnosis requires synovial fluid aspiration demonstrating needle-shaped, negatively birefringent crystals under polarized light (yellow when parallel to the compensator axis). First-line therapies for acute flares are low-dose oral colchicine (1.2 mg initial loading dose, followed by 0.6 mg 1 hour later, then 0.6 mg once or twice daily; AGREE trial), oral NSAIDs (e.g. indomethacin, naproxen), or systemic corticosteroids (prednisone 30-40 mg daily for 5-7 days). In hospitalized patients, oral colchicine and NSAIDs are frequently contraindicated by acute kidney injury, chronic kidney disease (eGFR < 30 mL/min), or anticoagulant therapy; in this setting, systemic corticosteroids (oral, IV, or intra-articular) are the first-line therapy of choice. Interleukin-1 inhibitors (anakinra 100 mg SC daily for 3 days) provide rapid, potent flare resolution in refractory patients with multiple comorbidities.

page.standard_overview: Acute gouty arthritis is an intensely painful inflammatory arthritis driven by the deposition of monosodium urate (MSU) crystals in synovial fluid and periarticular tissues, triggering the NLRP3 inflammasome and interleukin-1beta (IL-1beta) release. Definite diagnosis requires synovial fluid aspiration demonstrating needle-shaped, negatively birefringent crystals under polarized light (yellow when parallel to the compensator axis). First-line therapies for acute flares are low-dose oral colchicine (1.2 mg initial loading dose, followed by 0.6 mg 1 hour later, then 0.6 mg once or twice daily; AGREE trial), oral NSAIDs (e.g. indomethacin, naproxen), or systemic corticosteroids (prednisone 30-40 mg daily for 5-7 days). In hospitalized patients, oral colchicine and NSAIDs are frequently contraindicated by acute kidney injury, chronic kidney disease (eGFR < 30 mL/min), or anticoagulant therapy; in this setting, systemic corticosteroids (oral, IV, or intra-articular) are the first-line therapy of choice. Interleukin-1 inhibitors (anakinra 100 mg SC daily for 3 days) provide rapid, potent flare resolution in refractory patients with multiple comorbidities.

page.standard_overview: In acute heart failure the objectives of treatment are identification of precipitants and decongestion; adequate decongestion is needed before discharge, as persistent congestion predicts death and rehospitalisation. Intravenous loop diuretics (furosemide, bumetanide) are the foundation of therapy: the DOSE trial found that high-dose IV loop diuretic therapy (2.5x oral home dose) gave greater fluid loss and a nonsignificant trend toward better symptom relief, with no significant difference in renal function compared with low-dose therapy, with continuous infusion offering no superiority over bolus dosing. Sequential nephron blockade can overcome diuretic resistance: intravenous acetazolamide 500 mg daily improved successful decongestion in ADVOR, and thiazide-like agents such as oral metolazone or intravenous chlorothiazide increase natriuresis in CLOROTIC and related practice. SGLT2 inhibitors (dapagliflozin, empagliflozin) initiated early during index hospitalization improve decongestion and overall clinical benefit (EMPULSE trial), without a clear difference in mortality alone.

page.mentor_intro: The 2026 AHA/ASA acute stroke guideline updates reperfusion care. Tenecteplase 0.25 mg/kg is an effective alternative to alteplase, intra-arterial thrombolysis after successful thrombectomy may help selected patients, and early DOAC initiation after stroke with AF appears safe.

teaching_points.claim: The 2026 AHA/ASA guideline modifies the approach to thrombolysis contraindications and highlights remaining knowledge gaps.
Early DOAC initiation after acute ischaemic stroke with non-valvular AF appears safe and potentially more effective than delayed treatment.
Tenecteplase was superior for excellent functional outcomes and not inferior for major neurological improvement or death versus alteplase, with 0.25 mg/kg the optimal dose.
Tenecteplase 0.25 mg/kg gives better efficacy, while alteplase remains safer for symptomatic intracranial haemorrhage, so thrombolytic selection should be individualised.
A network meta-analysis found alteplase 0.6 mg/kg safer, and tenecteplase 0.25 mg/kg and alteplase 0.6 mg/kg preferable beyond 4.5 hours with tissue window assessment.
Adjunctive intra-arterial thrombolysis after successful thrombectomy appears to benefit selected patients, such as those with higher NIHSS or cardioembolic aetiology.
Fibrinogen depletion was seen only after alteplase and tended to accompany more major haemorrhagic complications.
Intravenous alteplase 0.9 mg/kg given within 3 hours (NINDS) and up to 4.5 hours (ECASS III) after stroke onset improves functional outcome at 3 months.

The DAWN trial showed that thrombectomy 6 to 24 hours after onset, selected by a mismatch between clinical deficit and infarct volume, improved 90-day outcomes, with functional independence in 49% versus 13% of controls.

page.standard_overview: Acute ischemic stroke management is defined by rapid reperfusion to salvage the ischemic penumbra. Intravenous thrombolysis with alteplase (0.9 mg/kg, max 90 mg; NINDS trial) or tenecteplase (0.25 mg/kg, max 25 mg; EXTEND-IA TNK trial) is indicated within 4.5 hours of symptom onset in eligible patients after intracranial hemorrhage is excluded on non-contrast CT head. For anterior-circulation large-vessel occlusion, thrombectomy is standard within 6 hours for eligible internal carotid or proximal M1 occlusions; selected M2 occlusions may also benefit depending on anatomy, deficit, and accessible thrombus. Furthermore, landmark trials revolutionized late-window therapy: the DAWN trial (6 to 24 hours using clinical-core mismatch on diffusion MRI or CT perfusion) and DEFUSE-3 trial (6 to 16 hours using perfusion-core mismatch: ischemic core < 70 mL, mismatch ratio >= 1.8) proved that EVT dramatically improves functional independence (mRS 0-2: 45-49% vs 13-17%; NNT ~2-3) in selected patients with salvageable penumbral tissue out to 24 hours.

standard_knowledge.claim: Muddy brown granular casts are characteristic of acute tubular necrosis, whereas red cell casts indicate glomerulonephritis.

Urgent indications for renal replacement therapy follow the 'AEIOU' mnemonic: refractory Acidemia (pH < 7.15), refractory Hyperkalemia (K+ > 6.5 mmol/L), Intoxications, volume Overload, and Uremic pericarditis/encephalopathy.

page.standard_overview: Acute Kidney Injury (AKI) is an abrupt decline in glomerular filtration rate defined by KDIGO consensus as an increase in serum creatinine by >= 0.3 mg/dL within 48 hours, a >= 1.5-fold increase over baseline within 7 days, or urine output < 0.5 mL/kg/h for >= 6 hours. Clinical evaluation categorizes etiology into prerenal (volume depletion, renal hypoperfusion), intrinsic renal (acute tubular necrosis [ATN], acute interstitial nephritis [AIN], glomerulonephritis), and postrenal (urinary tract obstruction). Urinalysis with microscopic sediment examination is essential: muddy brown granular casts indicate ATN, white cell casts/eosinophils suggest AIN, dysmorphic red cells and RBC casts signal glomerulonephritis, and bland sediment points to prerenal azotemia. Renal ultrasound is indicated in unexplained AKI when urinary obstruction cannot be excluded clinically, and urgently when anuria, renal colic, bladder dysfunction, or other obstructive features are present. Management prioritizes restoring euvolemia with balanced crystalloids, discontinuing nephrotoxins (NSAIDs, aminoglycosides, contrast), and initiating renal replacement therapy for urgent refractory complications (AEIOU: Acidosis pH < 7.15, Electrolytes K+ > 6.5, Ingestion toxins, Overload pulmonary edema, Uremia encephalopathy/pericarditis).

KDIGO 2012 describes prerenal azotemia, intrinsic causes (ATN, glomerulonephritis, interstitial nephritis, vasculitis) and acute postrenal obstructive nephropathy (Table 5 lists causes of AKI).

page.mentor_intro: Contrast-associated AKI risk is raised by hypertension, and the potential need for dialysis should be explained, especially after intra-arterial contrast. Biomarkers such as NGAL, cystatin-C and KIM-1 may predict it; RenalGuard-guided hydration may be safer than conventional hydration.

teaching_points.claim: The risk of dialysis should be communicated to patients undergoing procedures requiring contrast, especially intra-arterial exposure.
Hypertension is an independent risk factor for contrast-associated AKI and can be used for risk stratification.
RenalGuard is more secure than conventional hydration for preventing contrast-associated AKI, though its role in TAVR is questionable.
NGAL had the highest diagnostic performance for contrast-induced nephropathy, followed by cystatin-C and urinary KIM-1.
Pre-angiography CRP and some haematological indices are associated with contrast-induced nephropathy, and NLR shows potential as a cost-effective predictor.

In the landmark PRESERVE trial of 5,177 patients undergoing angiography, neither intravenous sodium bicarbonate nor oral N-acetylcysteine reduced the 90-day risk of death, need for dialysis, or persistent decline in kidney function compared with intravenous isotonic saline.

The AMACING randomized trial established non-inferiority of withholding prophylactic intravenous hydration compared with standard hydration in elective contrast procedures for patients with eGFR 30-59 mL/min/1.73m2, showing no increase in contrast-induced nephropathy.

page.standard_overview: Contrast-associated acute kidney injury (CA-AKI) represents a frequent inpatient consult where historic dogma often drives unnecessary prophylactic interventions. PRESERVE found no benefit of sodium bicarbonate over saline or acetylcysteine over placebo; AMACING found that prophylactic hydration could be withheld in the studied stable elective outpatients with eGFR 30-59 mL/min/1.73m2, excluding higher-risk groups. Preventive care focuses on minimizing contrast dose, avoiding unnecessary repeat exposures, addressing hemodynamic risk, and stopping nonessential nephrotoxins where feasible; contrast-volume/eGFR ratios are risk guides rather than a universally validated <3.0 rule.

page.standard_overview: Acute Leukemia of Ambiguous Lineage (ALAL) comprises rare, biologically aggressive leukemias that cannot be classified as purely myeloid or lymphoid. Under updated WHO and International Consensus Classification (ICC) guidelines, ALAL encompasses mixed-phenotype acute leukemia (MPAL with B/myeloid or T/myeloid co-expression) and acute undifferentiated leukemia (AUL). Multiparameter flow cytometry plus cytogenetic and molecular profiling, including BCR::ABL1 and KMT2A assessment, is essential; ALL-like or lineage-directed induction is generally favored, and allogeneic transplantation in CR1 is considered according to response, genetics, and patient factors rather than assumed superior for everyone.

standard_knowledge.claim: Rutherford classification defines clinical urgency: Stage I is viable without sensory/motor loss; Stage IIa is marginally threatened with minimal sensory loss and audible arterial Doppler; Stage IIb is immediately threatened with motor weakness and inaudible arterial Doppler; Stage III is irreversible with profound anesthesia and paralysis.

Immediate intravenous unfractionated heparin bolus and infusion prevents microvascular thrombosis propagation and reduces amputation risk, and should be administered immediately upon clinical suspicion before diagnostic imaging.

TOPAS found catheter-directed thrombolysis gave amputation-free survival similar to surgery with less operative morbidity in acute limb ischaemia of under 14 days, while STILE favoured surgery in longer-standing ischaemia.

For immediately threatened limbs (Rutherford IIb), emergent open surgical revascularization (balloon catheter embolectomy, endarterectomy, or bypass) is required to restore perfusion within 6 hours to prevent permanent neuromuscular necrosis; prophylactic four-compartment fasciotomy is indicated if ischemia duration exceeds 4-6 hours.

page.standard_overview: Acute limb ischemia is a time-critical vascular emergency in which sudden hypoperfusion can threaten limb viability; severely threatened limbs often require revascularization within hours, but no universal 4-6-hour safe window applies to every presentation. The Rutherford classification rapidly stratifies limbs into viable (Stage I), marginally threatened (Stage IIa), immediately threatened (Stage IIb), and irreversibly non-viable (Stage III). Unless contraindicated, immediate unfractionated heparin should be given to limit thrombus propagation; immediately threatened IIb limbs need urgent revascularization, while selected IIa limbs may undergo catheter-directed thrombolysis or endovascular treatment.

page.standard_overview: Acute liver failure (ALF) is a rapid-onset syndrome characterized by severe hepatocyte death, international normalized ratio (INR) >= 1.5, and hepatic encephalopathy in a patient without pre-existing cirrhosis, evolving within 26 weeks. Early administration of intravenous N-acetylcysteine improves transplant-free survival even in non-acetaminophen ALF with early-grade encephalopathy, and aggressive supportive ICU care targeting cerebral edema and multi-organ failure serves as a bridge to spontaneous recovery or emergency liver transplantation.

page.standard_overview: The combination of the selective oral BCL-2 inhibitor venetoclax with a hypomethylating agent (azacitidine or decitabine) has transformed the therapeutic landscape for older adults (>= 75 years) or younger patients unfit for intensive chemotherapy. In the landmark VIALE-A trial, venetoclax plus azacitidine demonstrated marked improvements in complete remission rates and overall survival over azacitidine monotherapy. Patients on azacitidine-venetoclax were hospitalised for tumour lysis syndrome prophylaxis and monitoring around the first venetoclax dose.

overview_support.note: NEJM 2020: patients ineligible for intensive chemotherapy because of coexisting conditions or age 75 or older received azacitidine plus venetoclax; azacitidine/decitabine are the usual hypomethylating agents; survival and remission were higher than with azacitidine alone.

NEJM 2020: "All the patients were hospitalized on or before day 1 of cycle 1 and for at least 24 hours after... to receive prophylaxis against the tumor lysis syndrome". Day-28 marrow reassessment and growth-factor support are not stated.

topic: Acute myocarditis: Dallas criteria, cardiac MRI, immunosuppression indications

page.mentor_intro: Cardiac magnetic resonance is the key non-invasive test for acute myocarditis: mapping techniques match or exceed the Lake Louise criteria, and late gadolinium enhancement is an independent prognostic marker. Genetic variants are common, and steroid use in COVID-19 myocarditis is individualised.

teaching_points.claim: ESC 2013 myocarditis: Immunosuppression should be started only after ruling out active infection on EMB by PCR.
A European and US expert consensus describes the role of histology in defining myocarditis subtypes with prognostic and therapeutic implications.
Novel CMR mapping techniques provide high diagnostic accuracy in acute myocarditis and are promising successors of classic Lake Louise elements, with only T1 mapping surpassing them.
Extracellular volume and native T1 and T2 mapping give diagnostic performance comparable to Lake Louise criteria, and native T1 had significantly better sensitivity.
Late gadolinium enhancement on baseline CMR is an independent prognostic marker of adverse cardiac outcomes in acute myocarditis.

Pathogenic variants in cardiomyopathy genes were found in a large proportion of acute myocarditis patients (58% of adults and 71% of children in the cited analysis), varying with age and presentation.
In COVID-19 myocarditis outcomes with steroid therapy appeared favourable, but treatment should be individualised until larger studies exist.
Temporary mechanical circulatory support can bridge myocarditis patients in cardiogenic shock to durable LVAD.

Under the 2018 Updated Lake Louise Criteria, CMR diagnosis of acute myocarditis requires at least one T2-based criterion (myocardial edema on T2-weighted imaging or elevated myocardial T2 relaxation time) and at least one T1-based criterion (late gadolinium enhancement, increased myocardial T1 relaxation time, or extracellular volume fraction).

AHA/ACC/ESC guidelines reserve endomyocardial biopsy for specific clinical scenarios: new-onset heart failure of < 2 weeks' duration associated with hemodynamic compromise, or heart failure of 2 weeks to 3 months with ventricular arrhythmias, conduction block, or failure to respond to standard therapy within 1-2 weeks.

Routine immunosuppression is not recommended for mild lymphocytic myocarditis with preserved ejection fraction; management consists of standard guideline-directed medical therapy for heart failure, arrhythmia surveillance, and strict avoidance of competitive exercise for 3 to 6 months.

Giant cell myocarditis carries a median survival of < 6 months without transplantation; Cooper et al. demonstrated that combined aggressive immunosuppression (cyclosporine, corticosteroids, and azathioprine or anti-thymocyte globulin) prolonged transplant-free survival to 12.3 months.

uncertainties: Immunosuppression indications beyond biopsy-proven subtypes.

page.standard_overview: Myocarditis is myocardial inflammation due to viral infection and autoimmune reactions. Initial evaluation requires high-sensitivity cardiac troponin, 12-lead ECG, echocardiography, and multiparametric cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR; updated Lake Louise Criteria). Haemodynamically stable heart failure from myocarditis is treated with diuretics, ACE inhibitor or ARB and beta-blockade. Physical activity should be restricted during the acute phase; athletes are reassessed before resuming sport, and similar advice is reasonable for non-athletes. In fulminant myocarditis manifesting as cardiogenic shock, life-threatening ventricular arrhythmias, or advanced heart block, emergency mechanical circulatory support (ECMO, Impella) and endomyocardial biopsy (EMB) to detect giant cell or eosinophilic myocarditis for targeted immunosuppression are life-saving.

overview_support.note: ESC 2013 describes viral and autoimmune myocarditis. Immune checkpoint inhibitors are not mentioned in this 2013 document.

topic: Acute necrotising pancreatitis and step-up management approach

page.mentor_intro: Lactated Ringer's solution may reduce progression to moderate-to-severe acute pancreatitis compared with saline. CRP is a useful severity marker, early nutrition is recommended when oral intake is insufficient, and hypertriglyceridaemia-induced pancreatitis has a poorer prognosis.

teaching_points.claim: Pol Arch Intern Med 2025: If oral nutrition becomes insufficient, we recommend enteral nutrition as the next step in patients with a functional gastrointestinal tract (quality of evidence: moderate; strength of recommendation: strong).

IAP/APA 2013: Percutaneous catheter or endoscopic transmural drainage should be the first step in the treatment of patients with suspected or confirmed (walled-off) infected necrotizing pancreatitis. (GRADE 1A, strong agreement)
A clinical nutrition guideline recommends nutrition within 72 hours of admission in all patients in whom oral intake does not cover 60% of protein-calorie requirements.
The Ibero-Latin American guideline (iLATAM-AP) covers medical, endoscopic and surgical approaches to acute pancreatitis.
Lactated Ringer's solution versus saline resuscitation reduced progression to moderate-to-severe acute pancreatitis, with no notable differences in other complications.
CRP has significant value as a biomarker for acute pancreatitis severity, but history, signs and imaging should also be considered.
Hypertriglyceridaemia-induced acute pancreatitis is more frequent in Eastern countries, has poorer prognosis than other causes and may warrant aggressive management.
Ulinastatin, alone or combined, was associated with improved outcomes and reduced mortality in severe acute pancreatitis.
Postoperative hyperamylasaemia and post-pancreatectomy acute pancreatitis definitions stratify risk of complications.

International Association of Pancreatology / American Pancreatic Association (IAP/APA) guidelines recommend delaying invasive drainage or debridement until walled-off necrosis (WON) has matured, typically at least 4 weeks after symptom onset, unless rapid clinical collapse dictates emergency drainage.

In the landmark Dutch PANTER randomized trial (88 patients), the minimally invasive step-up approach reduced the composite endpoint of major complications or death by 43% compared with primary open necrosectomy, driven by lower rates of new-onset multi-organ failure (12% vs 40%).
Over one-third of patients (35%) treated in the step-up arm of the PANTER trial were successfully cured by percutaneous catheter drainage alone, avoiding surgical necrosectomy entirely.

The randomized TENSION trial demonstrated that an endoscopic step-up approach (transluminal endoscopic drainage followed by endoscopic necrosectomy) was comparable to the surgical step-up approach in mortality and major morbidity, with fewer pancreaticocutaneous fistulae and shorter hospital stays.
