page.standard_overview: Acute necrotising pancreatitis is a distinct type of acute pancreatitis; secondary infection of pancreatic necrosis is associated with increased morbidity and mortality. In infected necrotizing pancreatitis, PANTER established a step-up approach beginning with percutaneous catheter drainage and reserving minimally invasive retroperitoneal necrosectomy for patients who do not improve. PANTER found less new-onset multiple-organ failure with the step-up approach than open necrosectomy, 12% versus 40%, and fewer incisional hernias, without demonstrating lower mortality.

overview_support.note: Atlanta 2012: "The development of secondary infection in pancreatic necrosis is associated with increased morbidity and mortality". The 20% incidence is not stated.

guideline_recommendations.source: IAP/APA evidence-based guidelines for the management of acute pancreatitis (2013)

items.text: Intravenous antibiotic prophylaxis is not recommended for the prevention of infectious complications in acute pancreatitis.

Routine percutaneous fine needle aspiration of peripancreatic collections to detect bacteria is not indicated, because clinical signs (i.e. persistent fever, increasing inflammatory markers) and imaging signs (i.e. gas in peripancreatic collections) are accurate predictors of infected necrosis in the majority of patien ts. Although the diagnosis of infection can be confirmed by fine needle aspiration (FNA), there is a risk of false-negative results.

Indications for intervention (either radiological, endoscopical or surgical) in sterile necrotizing pancreatitis are: 1) Ongoing gastric out let, intestinal, or biliary obstruction due to mass effect of walled-off necrosis (i.e. arbitrarily >4-8 weeks after onset of acute pancreatitis), 2) Persistent symptoms (e.g. pain, ‘persistent unwellness') in patients with walled-off necrosis without signs of infection (i.e. arbitrarily >8 weeks after onset of acute pancreatitis), 3) Disconnected duct syndrome (i.e. full transection of the pancreatic duct in the presence of pancreatic necrosis) with persisting symptomatic (e.g. pain, obstruction) collect ion(s) with necrosis without signs of infections (i.e. arbitrarily >8 weeks after onset of acute pancreatitis).

For patients with proven or suspected infected necrotizing pancreatitis, invasive intervention (i.e. percutaneous catheter drainage, endosc opic transluminal drainage/ necrosectomy, minimally invasive or open necrosectomy) should be delayed where possible until at least 4 weeks after initial presentation to allow t he collection to become ‘walled-off'.

The best available evidence suggests that surgical necrosectomy should ideally be delayed until collections have become walled-off, typically 4 weeks after the onset of pancreatitis, in all patients with complications of necrosis. No subgroups have been identified that might benefit from earlier or delayed intervention.

The optimal interventional strategy for patients with suspected or confirmed infected necrotizing pancreatitis is initial image-guided percutaneous (retroperitoneal) catheter drainage or endoscopic transluminal drainage, followed, if necessary, by endoscopic or surgical necrosectomy.(GRADE 1A, strong agreeme nt).
Percutaneous catheter or endoscopic transmural drainage should be the first step in the treatment of patients with suspected or confirmed (walled-off) infected necrotizing pancreatitis.
There are insufficient data to define subgroups of patients with suspected or confirmed infected necrotizing pancreatitis who would benefit from a different treatment strategy.

page.standard_overview: Acute otitis media (AOM) is a rapid-onset middle ear infection characterized by erythema, purulent middle ear effusion, and distinct bulging of the tympanic membrane. Observation with analgesia and reliable follow-up for 48-72 hours is an option for selected children >=2 years with nonsevere AOM and for some 6-23-month-olds with nonsevere unilateral disease; immediate high-dose amoxicillin is used for severe illness, otorrhea, bilateral AOM in children <2 years, or age <6 months.

standard_knowledge.claim: Diagnosis under the Revised Atlanta Classification requires at least 2 of 3 features: (1) characteristic epigastric pain radiating to the back; (2) serum lipase or amylase > 3x upper limit of normal; (3) contrast CT, MRI, or transabdominal ultrasound demonstrating pancreatitis.

Persistent organ failure (> 48 hours)—defined using the modified Marshall scoring system for cardiovascular (hypotension), renal (elevated creatinine), or respiratory (decreased PaO2/FiO2) systems—is the primary determinant of mortality in severe acute pancreatitis.

page.standard_overview: Acute pancreatitis is an acute inflammatory process of the pancreas diagnosed by fulfilling at least two of three criteria: characteristic epigastric abdominal pain radiating to the back, serum lipase or amylase elevated >= 3 times the upper limit of normal, and characteristic cross-sectional abdominal imaging findings. Under the Revised Atlanta Classification, pancreatitis is stratified into mild (no organ failure or local complications), moderately severe (transient organ failure < 48 hours or local complications), and severe (persistent organ failure > 48 hours). Management focuses on etiology identification, goal-directed moderate fluid resuscitation, and early enteral nutrition.

overview_support.note: IAP/APA 2013: "The definition of acute pancreatitis is based on the fulfillment of 2 out of 3 of the following criteria: clinical (upper abdominal pain), laboratory (serum amylase or lipase >3x upper limit of normal) and/or imaging". Radiation to the back is not stated.

guideline_recommendations.source: IAP/APA evidence-based guidelines for the management of acute pancreatitis (2013)

items.text: The definition of acute pancreatitis is based on the ful fillment of ‘2 out of 3' of the following criteria: clinical (upper abdominal pain), laboratory (serum amylase or lipase >3x upper limit of normal) and/or imaging (CT, MRI, ultrasonography) criteria.

On admission, the etiology of acute pancreatitis should be determined using detailed personal (i.e. previous acute pancreatitis, known gallstone disease, alcohol intake, medication and drug intake, known hyperlipidemia, trauma, recent invasive procedures such as ERCP) and family history of pancreatic disease, physical examination, laboratory serum tests (i.e. liver enzymes, calcium, triglycerides), and imaging (i.e. right upper quadrant ultrasonography).(GRADE 1B, strong a greement).

In patients considered to have idiopathic acute pancreatitis, after negative routine work-up for biliary etiology, endoscopic ultrasonography (EUS) is recommended as the first step to assess for occult microlithiasis, neoplasms and chronic pancreatitis. If EUS is negative, (secretin-stimulated) MRCP is advised as a second step to identify rare morphologic abnormalities. CT of the abdomen should be performed. If etiology remains unidentified, especially after a second attack of idiopathic pancreatitis, genetic counseling (not necessarily genetic testing) should be considered.
Systemic inflammatory response syndrome (SIRS) is advised to predict severe acute pancreatitis at admission and persistent SIRS at 48 hours.

During admission, a 3-dimension approach is advised to predict outcome of acute pancreatitis combining host risk factors (e.g. age, co-morbidity , body mass index), clinical risk strati fication (e.g. persistent SIRS) and monitoring response to initial therapy (e.g. persistent SIRS, blood urea nitrogen, creatinine).

The indication for initial CT assessment in acute pancreatitis can be: 1) diagnostic uncertainty, 2) confirmation of severity based on clinical predictors of severe acute pancreatitis, or 3) failure to respond to conservative treatment or in the setting of clinical deterioration. Optimal timing for initial CT assessment is at least 72 e96 hours after onset of symptoms.
Follow up CT or MR in acute pancreatitis is indicated when there is a lack of clinical improvement, clinical deterioration, or especially when invasive intervention is considered.

It is recommended to perform multidetector CT with thin collimation and slice thickness (i.e. 5mm or less), 100 e150 ml of non-ionic intra-venous contrast material at a rate of 3mL/s, during the pancreatic and/or portal venous phase (i.e. 50 e70 seconds delay). During follow up only a portal venous phase (monophasic) is generally sufficient. For MR, the recommendation is to perform axial FS-T2 and FS-T1 scanning before and after intravenous gadolinium contrast administration.
Ringer 's lactate is recommended for initial fluid resuscitation in acute pancreatitis.

The preferred approach to assessing the response to fluid resuscitation should be based on one or more of the following: 1) non-invasive clinical targets of heart rate < 120/min, mean arterial pressure between 65-85 mmHg (8.7 e11.3 kPa), and urinary output > 0.5e1ml/kg/h, 2) invasive clinical targets of stroke volume variation, and intrathoracic blood volume determination, and 3) biochemical targets of hematocrit 35-44%.

Patients diagnosed with acute pancreatitis and one or more of the parameters identified at admission as defined by the guidelines of the Society of Critical Care Medicine (SCCM). Furthermore, patients with severe acute pancreatitis as defined by the revised Atlanta Classi fication (i.e. persistent organ failure) should be treated in an intensive care setting.

Management in, or referral to, a specialist center is necessary for patients with severe acute pancreatitis and for those who may need interventio nal radiologic, endoscopic, or surgical intervention.

A specialist center in the management of acute pancreatitis is defined as a high volume center with up-to-date intensive care facilities including options for organ replacement therapy, and with daily (i.e. 7 days per week) access to interventional radiology, interventional endoscopy with EUS and ERCP assistanc e as well as surgical expertise in managing necrotizing pancreatitis. Patients should be enrolled in prospective audits for quality control issues and into clinical tri als whenever possible.
Early fluid resuscitation within the first 24 hours of admission for acute pancreatitis is associated with decreased rates of persistent SIRS and organ failure.
Abdominal compartment syndrome (ACS) is defined as a sustained intra-abdominal pressure > 20 mmHg that is associated with new onset organ failure.

Medical treatment of ACS should target 1) hollow-viscera volume, 2) intra/extra vascular fluid and 3) abdominal wall expansion. Invasive treatment should only be used after multidisciplinary discussion in patients with a sustained intra-abdominal pressure >25mmHg with new onset organ failure refractory to medical therapy and nasogastric/ rectal decompression. Invasive treatment options include percutaneous catheter drainage of ascites, midline laparostomy, bilater al subcostal laparostomy, or subcutaneous linea alba fasciotomy. In case of surgical decompression, the retroperitoneal cavity and the omental bursa should be left intact to r educe the risk of infecting peripancreatic and pancreatic necrosis.
Intravenous antibiotic prophylaxis is not recommended for the prevention of infectious complications in acute pancreatitis.
Selective gut decontamination has shown some benefits in preventing infectious complications in acute pancreatitis, but further studies are needed.
Probiotic prophylaxis is not recommended for the prevention of infectious complications in acute pancreatitis.
Oral feeding in predicted mild pancreatitis can be restarted once abdominal pain is decreasing and inflammatory markers are improving.
Enteral tube feeding should be the primary therapy in patients with predicted severe acute pancreatitis who require nutritional support.
Either elemental or polymeric enteral nutrition formulations can be used in acute pancreatitis.
Enteral nutrition in acute pancreatitis can be administered via either the nasojejunal or nasogastric route.
Parenteral nutrition can be administered in acute pancreatitis as second-line therapy if nasojejunal tube feeding is not tolerated and nutritio nal support is required.
ERCP is not indicated in predicted mild biliary pancreatitis without cholangitis.
Urgent ERCP ( <24 hrs) is required in patients with acute cholangitis. Currently, there is no evidence regarding the optimal timing of ERCP in patients with biliary pancreatitis without cholangitis.

MRCP and EUS may prevent a proportion of ERCPs that would otherwise be performed for suspected common bile duct stones in patients with biliary panc reatitis who do not have cholangitis, without in fluencing the clinical course. EUS is superior to MRCP in excluding the presence of small ( <5mm) gallstones. MRCP is less invasive, less operator-dependent and probably more widely available than EUS. Therefore, in clinical practice there is no clear superiority for either MRCP o r EUS.

Common indications for intervention (either radiological, endoscopical or surgical) in necrotizing pancreatitis are: 1) Clinical suspicion o f, or documented infected necrotizing pancreatitis with clinical deterioration, preferably when the necrosis has become walled-off, 2) In the absence of documented infecte d necrotizing pancreatitis, ongoing organ failure for several weeks after the onset of acute pancreatitis, preferably when the necrosis has become walled-off.(G RADE 1C, strong agreement).

Routine percutaneous fine needle aspiration of peripancreatic collections to detect bacteria is not indicated, because clinical signs (i.e. persistent fever, increasing inflammatory markers) and imaging signs (i.e. gas in peripancreatic collections) are accurate predictors of infected necrosis in the majority of patien ts. Although the diagnosis of infection can be confirmed by fine needle aspiration (FNA), there is a risk of false-negative results.

Indications for intervention (either radiological, endoscopical or surgical) in sterile necrotizing pancreatitis are: 1) Ongoing gastric out let, intestinal, or biliary obstruction due to mass effect of walled-off necrosis (i.e. arbitrarily >4-8 weeks after onset of acute pancreatitis), 2) Persistent symptoms (e.g. pain, ‘persistent unwellness') in patients with walled-off necrosis without signs of infection (i.e. arbitrarily >8 weeks after onset of acute pancreatitis), 3) Disconnected duct syndrome (i.e. full transection of the pancreatic duct in the presence of pancreatic necrosis) with persisting symptomatic (e.g. pain, obstruction) collect ion(s) with necrosis without signs of infections (i.e. arbitrarily >8 weeks after onset of acute pancreatitis).

For patients with proven or suspected infected necrotizing pancreatitis, invasive intervention (i.e. percutaneous catheter drainage, endosc opic transluminal drainage/ necrosectomy, minimally invasive or open necrosectomy) should be delayed where possible until at least 4 weeks after initial presentation to allow t he collection to become ‘walled-off'.

The best available evidence suggests that surgical necrosectomy should ideally be delayed until collections have become walled-off, typically 4 weeks after the onset of pancreatitis, in all patients with complications of necrosis. No subgroups have been identified that might benefit from earlier or delayed intervention.

The optimal interventional strategy for patients with suspected or confirmed infected necrotizing pancreatitis is initial image-guided percutaneous (retroperitoneal) catheter drainage or endoscopic transluminal drainage, followed, if necessary, by endoscopic or surgical necrosectomy.(GRADE 1A, strong agreeme nt).
Percutaneous catheter or endoscopic transmural drainage should be the first step in the treatment of patients with suspected or confirmed (walled-off) infected necrotizing pancreatitis.
There are insufficient data to define subgroups of patients with suspected or confirmed infected necrotizing pancreatitis who would benefit from a different treatment strategy.

Cholecystectomy during index admission for mild biliary pancreatitis appears safe and is recommended. Interval cholecystectomy after mild bil iary pancreatitis is associated with a substantial risk of readmission for recurrent biliary events, especially recurrent biliary pancreatitis.

Cholecystectomy should be delayed in patients with peripancreatic collections until the collections either resolve or if they persist beyond 6 w eeks, at which time cholecystectomy can be performed safely.

In patients with biliary pancreatitis who have undergone sphincterotomy and are fit for surgery, cholecystectomy is advised, because ERCP and sphincterotomy prevent recurrence of biliary pancreatitis but not gallstone related gallbladder disease, i.e. biliary colic and cholecystitis.

topic: Acute pancreatitis fluid and nutrition strategy

page.mentor_intro: Lactated Ringer's solution may reduce progression to moderate-to-severe acute pancreatitis compared with saline. CRP is a useful severity marker, early nutrition is recommended when oral intake is insufficient, and hypertriglyceridaemia-induced pancreatitis has a poorer prognosis.

teaching_points.claim: Pol Arch Intern Med 2025: We recommend early initiation of oral nutrition in patients with predicted mild acute pancreatitis after resolution of complaints, regardless of lipase activity.
A clinical nutrition guideline recommends nutrition within 72 hours of admission in all patients in whom oral intake does not cover 60% of protein-calorie requirements.
The Ibero-Latin American guideline (iLATAM-AP) covers medical, endoscopic and surgical approaches to acute pancreatitis.
Lactated Ringer's solution versus saline resuscitation reduced progression to moderate-to-severe acute pancreatitis, with no notable differences in other complications.
CRP has significant value as a biomarker for acute pancreatitis severity, but history, signs and imaging should also be considered.
Hypertriglyceridaemia-induced acute pancreatitis is more frequent in Eastern countries, has poorer prognosis than other causes and may warrant aggressive management.
Ulinastatin, alone or combined, was associated with improved outcomes and reduced mortality in severe acute pancreatitis.
Postoperative hyperamylasaemia and post-pancreatectomy acute pancreatitis definitions stratify risk of complications.

The WATERFALL randomized trial showed that aggressive hydration roughly tripled the incidence of fluid overload (20.5% vs 6.3%) without improving clinical outcomes; guidelines now favour moderate hydration with Ringer's lactate (10 mL/kg bolus only if hypovolaemic, then 1.5 mL/kg/h).

The multicenter Dutch PYTHON randomized trial demonstrated that very early nasoenteric tube feeding (within 24 hours) did not reduce infected necrosis or death compared to an on-demand strategy allowing oral diet at 72 hours in predicted severe pancreatitis, with 69% of patients tolerating oral food without needing a feeding tube.

uncertainties: Role of ulinastatin outside trials.

Enteral nutrition is vastly superior to total parenteral nutrition (TPN), significantly reducing infectious complications, systemic inflammatory response syndrome (SIRS), multi-organ failure, and overall mortality by preserving intestinal barrier function.

page.standard_overview: Fluid stewardship and nutritional support have undergone a paradigm shift in acute pancreatitis management. The historic practice of aggressive volume resuscitation ('forced hydration') was conclusively refuted by the landmark WATERFALL trial, establishing goal-directed moderate fluid resuscitation with balanced crystalloids (Ringer's lactate) as the modern standard. Early enteral nutrition replaces prolonged fasting: oral feeding is restarted as tolerated in mild pancreatitis, and enteral tube feeding is used in severe disease when oral intake is inadequate, generally within about 72 hours, to support gut-barrier function.

page.standard_overview: Critically ill patients with severe acute pancreatitis in the ICU suffer high mortality (20-30%) driven by a biphasic clinical trajectory: early multi-organ failure from massive systemic inflammatory response syndrome (SIRS), followed by late sepsis from infected pancreatic necrosis. Early bedside risk stratification utilizing the Bedside Index for Severity in Acute Pancreatitis (BISAP) or APACHE-II score identifies patients at risk of rapid deterioration. Management centers on lung-protective ventilation, restrictive fluid therapy after initial stabilization, avoiding prophylactic antibiotics or routine probiotics (disproven in PROPATRIA), and multidisciplinary coordination.

items.text: Systemic inflammatory response syndrome (SIRS) is advised to predict severe acute pancreatitis at admission and persistent SIRS at 48 hours.

During admission, a 3-dimension approach is advised to predict outcome of acute pancreatitis combining host risk factors (e.g. age, co-morbidity , body mass index), clinical risk strati fication (e.g. persistent SIRS) and monitoring response to initial therapy (e.g. persistent SIRS, blood urea nitrogen, creatinine).
Ringer 's lactate is recommended for initial fluid resuscitation in acute pancreatitis.

The preferred approach to assessing the response to fluid resuscitation should be based on one or more of the following: 1) non-invasive clinical targets of heart rate < 120/min, mean arterial pressure between 65-85 mmHg (8.7 e11.3 kPa), and urinary output > 0.5e1ml/kg/h, 2) invasive clinical targets of stroke volume variation, and intrathoracic blood volume determination, and 3) biochemical targets of hematocrit 35-44%.

Patients diagnosed with acute pancreatitis and one or more of the parameters identified at admission as defined by the guidelines of the Society of Critical Care Medicine (SCCM). Furthermore, patients with severe acute pancreatitis as defined by the revised Atlanta Classi fication (i.e. persistent organ failure) should be treated in an intensive care setting.

Management in, or referral to, a specialist center is necessary for patients with severe acute pancreatitis and for those who may need interventio nal radiologic, endoscopic, or surgical intervention.

A specialist center in the management of acute pancreatitis is defined as a high volume center with up-to-date intensive care facilities including options for organ replacement therapy, and with daily (i.e. 7 days per week) access to interventional radiology, interventional endoscopy with EUS and ERCP assistanc e as well as surgical expertise in managing necrotizing pancreatitis. Patients should be enrolled in prospective audits for quality control issues and into clinical tri als whenever possible.
Early fluid resuscitation within the first 24 hours of admission for acute pancreatitis is associated with decreased rates of persistent SIRS and organ failure.
Abdominal compartment syndrome (ACS) is defined as a sustained intra-abdominal pressure > 20 mmHg that is associated with new onset organ failure.

Medical treatment of ACS should target 1) hollow-viscera volume, 2) intra/extra vascular fluid and 3) abdominal wall expansion. Invasive treatment should only be used after multidisciplinary discussion in patients with a sustained intra-abdominal pressure >25mmHg with new onset organ failure refractory to medical therapy and nasogastric/ rectal decompression. Invasive treatment options include percutaneous catheter drainage of ascites, midline laparostomy, bilater al subcostal laparostomy, or subcutaneous linea alba fasciotomy. In case of surgical decompression, the retroperitoneal cavity and the omental bursa should be left intact to r educe the risk of infecting peripancreatic and pancreatic necrosis.
Intravenous antibiotic prophylaxis is not recommended for the prevention of infectious complications in acute pancreatitis.

topic: Acute pericarditis: colchicine, NSAIDs, recurrence prevention

page.mentor_intro: The first combined ESC guidelines on myocarditis and pericarditis highlight interleukin-1 antagonists for recurrent pericarditis. A network meta-analysis found colchicine and anti-IL-1 agents both reduce recurrence, with anti-IL-1 agents causing more non-serious adverse events.

teaching_points.claim: ESC 2015 pericardial diseases: Aspirin or NSAIDs are recommended as first-line therapy for acute pericarditis with gastroprotection (Class I, level A)
ESC 2015 pericardial diseases: Colchicine is recommended as first-line therapy for acute pericarditis as an adjunct to aspirin/NSAID therapy (Class I, level A)
ESC 2015 pericardial diseases: Colchicine is recommended at low, weight-adjusted doses to improve the response to medical therapy and prevent recurrences.
The first combined European guidelines on myocarditis and pericarditis bring interleukin-1 antagonists to the fore for pericarditis and consider genetic factors in recurrent forms.
An international position statement on pericardial diseases emphasises multimodality cardiac imaging and new therapeutics.
Canadian imaging referral guidelines cover pericardial syndromes among cardiovascular indications.
In frail older patients, optimal pleuro-myopericarditis treatment may differ from guideline-based strategies when patient-specific risks outweigh benefits.

Colchicine and anti-interleukin-1 agents are both effective in reducing the risk of recurrent pericarditis; anti-IL-1 agents cause more frequent non-serious adverse events, with serious adverse event evidence inconclusive.
For pericardial complications after open heart surgery, evidence for some preventive and treatment interventions is relatively weak and large trials are needed.

The 2015 ESC Pericardial Diseases Guidelines recommend high-dose NSAIDs (ibuprofen 600-800 mg TID or aspirin 750-1000 mg TID) with gastroprotection plus colchicine for 3 months as first-line therapy, with tapering guided by symptom resolution and C-reactive protein (CRP) normalization.

In the ICAP randomized trial (240 patients), adding colchicine (0.5 mg once or twice daily for 3 months) to standard anti-inflammatory therapy reduced recurrent or persistent pericarditis from 37.5% to 16.7% (relative risk reduction 0.56).
The COPE trial found that adding colchicine to aspirin in a first episode of acute pericarditis reduced 18-month recurrence (10.7% vs 32.3%) and symptom persistence at 72 hours.

uncertainties: Evidence in frail older patients.

page.standard_overview: Acute pericarditis is diagnosed by fulfilling at least two of four cardinal criteria: pleuritic chest pain, pericardial friction rub, new widespread PR-segment depression or ST-segment elevation, and new or worsening pericardial effusion. High-dose NSAIDs (e.g., ibuprofen 600-800 mg TID or indomethacin 50 mg TID) combined with weight-adjusted colchicine (0.5 mg BID, or 0.5 mg daily if weight < 70 kg) for 3 months represent the first-line evidence-based regimen. The landmark ICAP and COPE trials proved that adding colchicine halves recurrence rates and accelerates symptom remission, whereas systemic corticosteroids should be avoided as first-line therapy due to increased recurrence risk.

sources.title: Acute phosphate nephropathy following oral sodium phosphate bowel purgative: an underrecognized cause of chronic renal failure.

standard_knowledge.claim: The course is often biphasic: an early asymptomatic rise in creatinine followed by progressive loss of renal function, and full recovery to baseline is uncommon.

Major clinical risk factors include baseline CKD (eGFR < 60 mL/min/1.73m2), volume contraction, hypertension, advanced age (> 65 years), and concurrent medications that compromise renal hemodynamics: ACE inhibitors, ARBs, diuretics, and NSAIDs.

Oral sodium phosphate bowel preparations carry an FDA boxed warning; they should be avoided in CKD, heart failure, cirrhosis and electrolyte disturbance, and polyethylene glycol preparations are used instead.

page.standard_overview: Acute phosphate nephropathy is a form of kidney injury caused by the deposition of calcium phosphate crystals within the renal tubules and interstitium, typically following the ingestion of oral sodium phosphate (OSP) bowel purgatives for colonoscopy. Patients present with either acute kidney injury shortly after exposure or insidious, irreversible chronic kidney disease diagnosed weeks to months later. Advanced age, pre-existing chronic kidney disease (CKD), volume depletion, and concurrent therapy with renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS) inhibitors, NSAIDs, or diuretics are major risk factors; PEG-based bowel preparations are the safer standard of care.

page.mentor_intro: APL is a highly curable but urgent leukaemia: prompt recognition avoids early death. ATRA plus arsenic trioxide may be preferred to ATRA plus chemotherapy, particularly in low-to-intermediate risk disease, and FLT3 mutations and obesity predict worse outcomes.

teaching_points.claim: Brazilian consensus guidelines describe APL as highly curable through differentiation therapy, yet a serious and urgent condition needing prompt recognition and management to avoid early mortality.
International recommendations address treatment of APL in older patients, highlighting consensus, gaps and research opportunities.
Japanese DIC guidelines address anticoagulants in DIC, weakly recommending against heparin and serine protease inhibitors beyond selected options.
A meta-analysis indicated ATRA plus arsenic trioxide may be preferred to ATRA plus chemotherapy, especially in low-to-intermediate risk APL, with larger trials needed in high-risk disease.
FLT3-ITD and FLT3-D835 mutations are associated with higher presenting white cell count and poorer prognosis in APL.
High BMI predicts adverse outcomes in APL, with a higher risk of differentiation syndrome (HR 1.53).

European LeukemiaNet (ELN) guidelines emphasize that ATRA must be started immediately at the earliest clinical suspicion of APL without waiting for molecular confirmation, alongside aggressive platelet and cryoprecipitate transfusions to maintain fibrinogen > 150 mg/dL and platelets > 50,000/uL.

In the APL0406 trial (Lo-Coco), ATRA plus arsenic trioxide was non-inferior and then superior to ATRA plus idarubicin in low-to-intermediate risk APL, with 2-year event-free survival of about 97% versus 86%.

In the UK NCRI AML17 randomized trial, ATRA plus arsenic trioxide was feasible in low-risk and high-risk acute promyelocytic leukaemia, with a high cure rate and less relapse than ATRA plus idarubicin; survival did not differ and quality of life was not improved.

uncertainties: Optimal therapy in high-risk APL.

page.standard_overview: Acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL) is a medical emergency driven by the t(15;17)(q24.1;q21.2) chromosomal translocation encoding the PML::RARA fusion oncoprotein, leading to severe consumptive coagulopathy (disseminated intravascular coagulation and hyperfibrinolysis) and catastrophic hemorrhage. Immediate initiation of all-trans retinoic acid (ATRA) upon morphological suspicion—before cytogenetic confirmation—is mandatory. In standard- and intermediate-risk APL (WBC <= 10,000/uL), chemotherapy-free dual differentiation therapy with ATRA and arsenic trioxide (ATO) is the curative standard of care, achieving 95-98% complete remission and event-free survival rates superior to chemotherapy.

topic: Acute psychosis: assessment, management and antipsychotic therapy

page.mentor_intro: After two antipsychotics fail, a trial of clozapine is supported. Metformin can prevent antipsychotic-induced weight gain, shorter duration of untreated psychosis relates to outcomes, and sex-sensitive prescribing guidance exists for females.

teaching_points.claim: Findings support a trial of clozapine after two other antipsychotics prove ineffective.
A consensus-validated guideline recommends metformin for preventing antipsychotic-induced weight gain, including co-commencement.
A guideline on the first antipsychotic for females in first-episode psychosis supports safer, sex-sensitive prescribing.
The US VA/DoD guideline synopsis gives pharmacological and somatic treatment recommendations for first-episode psychosis and schizophrenia, with many decision points lacking data.
An appraisal of early intervention in psychosis guidelines found a need for more methodologically robust and implementation-oriented guidance.
Longer duration of untreated psychosis correlates with poorer outcomes, though whether it causes them needs study and a consensus definition of long DUP is needed.
Treatment strategies for antipsychotic-induced akathisia rest on low to very low confidence evidence.

NICE clinical guideline CG178 recommends oral second-generation antipsychotics as first-line therapy for acute psychosis, advising individualized choice based on side-effect profiles (metabolic vs extrapyramidal vs hyperprolactinemia) in collaborative discussion with the patient.

A network meta-analysis of 402 randomised trials (Huhn, Lancet 2019) found that all antipsychotics reduce psychotic symptoms more than placebo, with small efficacy differences (clozapine, amisulpride and olanzapine ranking highest) but marked differences in weight gain, sedation and extrapyramidal effects.

In the TREC-India randomized trial, intramuscular olanzapine and haloperidol plus promethazine tranquillised similar proportions of agitated patients at 15 minutes (87% vs 91%), but more patients given olanzapine needed additional drugs over four hours (43% vs 21%).

uncertainties: Evidence for add-on agents against akathisia is weak.

standard_knowledge.claim: Physical restraints should be an absolute intervention of last resort, with continuous 1-to-1 nursing observation and regular vital sign/airway monitoring every 15 minutes to prevent restraint-related asphyxia and positional death.

page.standard_overview: Acute psychosis is characterized by hallucinations, delusions, thought disorganization, and loss of reality testing, precipitated by primary psychiatric disorders (schizophrenia, bipolar mania), substance intoxication/withdrawal, or underlying medical illness (encephalitis, endocrine disorders, systemic lupus). Initial management prioritizes safety, medical clearance, and calm, structured non-coercive verbal de-escalation. For a primary psychotic disorder, an oral second-generation antipsychotic selected by efficacy, adverse effects, and patient preference is standard first-line pharmacotherapy; secondary psychosis requires treatment of the cause, and rapid tranquilization is reserved for dangerous agitation.

topic: Acute pulmonary oedema: NIV, morphine controversy, nitrates, ultrafiltration

page.mentor_intro: Retrieved evidence concerns respiratory support in acute hypoxaemic failure rather than cardiogenic pulmonary oedema specifically: high-flow nasal oxygen probably reduces intubation versus standard oxygen, helmet NIV may reduce intubation, and HFNC may be inferior to NIV in hypercapnic COPD exacerbations.

teaching_points.claim: European Society of Cardiology 2021: Short-acting nitrates should be used with caution in patients with HF as they cause hypotension.

ESC 2021 heart failure: routine use of opiates in AHF is not recommended although they may be considered in selected patients, particularly in case of severe/intractable pain or anxiety or in the setting of palliation.
The ACP suggests high-flow nasal oxygen rather than conventional oxygen for hospitalised adults with postextubation hypoxaemic respiratory failure (conditional recommendation, low certainty).
The AARC guideline suggests considering high-flow oxygen immediately after extubation to avoid reintubation and humidification for flows above 4 L/min.
In acute hypoxaemic respiratory failure, high-flow nasal cannula probably reduces the risk of invasive mechanical ventilation and may be as comfortable as standard oxygen.
Compared with facemask NIV, helmet NIV may reduce mortality and intubation, while its effect versus high-flow nasal cannula remains uncertain.
In AECOPD with hypercapnic failure, HFNC was associated with more treatment failure and switch to NIV, which may mask HFNC inferiority.
Sugammadex reversal was associated with fewer postoperative pulmonary complications than neostigmine.
The 2021 ESC heart failure guideline supports intravenous nitrates in acute pulmonary oedema with systolic pressure above 110 mmHg, and opioids are not used routinely.

The 3CPO trial (1,069 patients) found that non-invasive ventilation (CPAP or bilevel) produced faster improvement in dyspnoea, acidosis and hypercapnia than standard oxygen therapy, without a difference in 7-day mortality.

The UNLOAD trial showed that early venous ultrafiltration in hypervolemic heart failure produced greater weight loss and fluid removal with significantly lower 90-day heart failure rehospitalizations compared to continuous intravenous diuretics.

uncertainties: Direct trials in acute cardiogenic pulmonary oedema are not covered by the retrieved excerpts.

page.standard_overview: Acute pulmonary edema secondary to decompensated heart failure represents an extreme emergency characterized by alveolar flooding, severe dyspnea, tachypnea, hypoxemia, and diaphoresis. Initial management includes upright positioning and oxygen as needed, NIV for significant respiratory distress without contraindication, and intravenous nitrates for hypertensive pulmonary edema when blood pressure permits. Historic routine administration of intravenous morphine is no longer recommended routinely because observational data link it with more intubation, ICU admission and mortality. Intravenous loop diuretics should be dosed dynamically, with ultrafiltration reserved for refractory diuretic resistance.

standard_knowledge.claim: American Academy of Ophthalmology (AAO) Preferred Practice Patterns emphasize identifying red flags: deep boring pain, photophobia, reduced visual acuity, ciliary flush, and corneal abnormalities, which rule out benign conjunctivitis and require immediate specialist care.

Acute angle-closure glaucoma presents with severe unilateral ocular pain, headache, nausea, steamy/hazy cornea, and a fixed mid-dilated pupil, requiring emergency medical lowering of intraocular pressure (timolol, apraclonidine, IV acetazolamide, and topical pilocarpine) followed by bilateral laser peripheral iridotomy.

Corneal fluorescein staining under cobalt blue light is essential in contact lens wearers presenting with acute red eye to detect Pseudomonas or Acanthamoeba keratitis; topical corticosteroids must never be prescribed empirically without slit-lamp examination due to catastrophic corneal melting or herpes simplex worsening.

Viral conjunctivitis (adenovirus) is characterized by watery discharge, preauricular lymphadenopathy, and follicular conjunctival response; it is self-limiting and requires strict hand hygiene rather than topical antibiotic therapy.

page.standard_overview: Acute red eye is one of the most frequent ophthalmic presentations in primary care and emergency departments. Accurate differential diagnosis hinges on distinguishing benign, self-limiting superficial conditions (viral/bacterial conjunctivitis, episcleritis, subconjunctival hemorrhage) from sight-threatening emergencies requiring immediate ophthalmologic consultation: acute angle-closure glaucoma, acute anterior uveitis, bacterial/fungal keratitis, and endophthalmitis. The presence of 'red flag' symptoms—severe ocular pain, decreased visual acuity, photophobia, ciliary flush (perilimbal injection), corneal opacity, or a fixed mid-dilated pupil—mandates urgent specialist evaluation.

page.mentor_intro: Non-invasive support is central in acute respiratory failure: NIV works especially in hypercapnic failure and cardiogenic pulmonary oedema, high-flow nasal oxygen suits hypoxaemic and post-extubation failure, and awake proning helps in COVID-19. Preoxygenation technique prolongs safe apnoea time.

teaching_points.claim: Guidelines on non-invasive mechanical ventilation in acute respiratory failure support its use in hypercapnic respiratory failure and pulmonary oedema, including in the prehospital setting, and in paediatric ICU patients with monitoring.
The ACP suggests high-flow nasal oxygen rather than conventional oxygen for hospitalised adults with postextubation acute hypoxaemic respiratory failure (conditional recommendation, low certainty).
A rapid practice guideline recommends a trial of awake prone positioning in COVID-19 acute hypoxaemic respiratory failure, with monitoring by staff experienced in recognising deterioration.
A 2026 guideline covers acute respiratory insufficiency treated with invasive ventilation and extracorporeal support, conveying where certainty of evidence is limited.
The AARC patient-ventilator assessment guideline gives a strong, high-certainty recommendation on measures to decrease ventilator-associated pneumonia risk.
The ESICM guideline on fluid therapy in critically ill adults gives eleven recommendations on resuscitation fluid choice.
A network meta-analysis found head-up position likely the most effective technique to prolong safe apnoea time during preoxygenation.

British Thoracic Society (BTS) emergency oxygen guidelines recommend target SpO2 ranges of 94-98% for most acutely ill patients, but a restricted target of 88-92% for patients at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure (COPD, neuromuscular disease, morbid obesity hypoventilation).

In the FLORALI trial of non-hypercapnic acute hypoxemic respiratory failure, the intubation rate (primary outcome) did not differ significantly between high-flow oxygen (38%), standard oxygen (47%) and non-invasive ventilation (50%), but high-flow oxygen gave more ventilator-free days at day 28 (24 vs 22 vs 19) and a lower 90-day mortality (hazard ratio for death 2.01 with standard oxygen and 2.50 with non-invasive ventilation, versus high-flow oxygen).

For acute hypercapnic respiratory failure in COPD (pH below 7.35 and PaCO2 above 6 kPa), non-invasive ventilation reduces intubation and roughly halves hospital mortality.

page.standard_overview: Acute respiratory failure is categorized into Type 1 (hypoxemic: PaO2 < 60 mmHg [8 kPa] with normal or low PaCO2) and Type 2 (hypercapnic: PaCO2 > 45-50 mmHg [6-6.5 kPa] with respiratory acidemia). Type 1 failure results from ventilation-perfusion mismatch, intrapulmonary shunt, or diffusion impairment (e.g., ARDS, pneumonia, pulmonary edema), while Type 2 failure reflects ventilatory pump failure, central hypoventilation, or neuromuscular weakness (e.g., severe COPD, myasthenia gravis, drug overdose). Oxygen is usually targeted to SpO2 92%-96%, or 88%-92% when hypercapnic respiratory failure is a risk; HFNC is preferred for many hypoxemic patients, while NIV is first-line for selected hypercapnic COPD or cardiogenic pulmonary-edema presentations.

page.mentor_intro: Acute asthma care centres on bronchodilators and systemic corticosteroids; high-dose inhaled corticosteroids may add benefit, and IV magnesium helps children. Prevention depends on adherence, eosinophilic phenotype and inhaler technique.

teaching_points.claim: The Italian paediatric acute-asthma guideline advises against epinephrine, allows IV magnesium sulfate in severe attacks or FEV1 below 60% unresponsive to inhaled therapy, allows heliox in life-threatening attacks, and does not recommend leukotriene receptor antagonists.

A meta-analysis found moderate evidence that high-dose inhaled corticosteroids added to systemic corticosteroids reduce hospital admission (OR 0.73) in ED treatment of moderate-to-severe exacerbations.
In children, intravenous magnesium sulfate improved pulmonary function and reduced hospitalisation and further treatment, whereas nebulised magnesium had no significant effect.
Adherence of 80% or more lowered the odds of severe exacerbation (OR 0.53), and discontinuing therapy raised it.
Blood eosinophils of 200 cells/microlitre or more are associated with exacerbation (a modifiable factor in asthma management).
Inhaler technique education reduced exacerbation rates in older adults with asthma or COPD (pooled risk ratio 0.71).
Oral timolol and infusion propranolol were associated with higher asthma attack risk and should be avoided in patients at risk of asthma.
GORD and asthma exacerbation are only weakly associated.

British Thoracic Society (BTS/SIGN) and GINA guidelines classify asthma exacerbations into Moderate, Severe (PEF 33-50%, RR >= 25, HR >= 110, unable to complete sentences), and Life-threatening (PEF < 33%, SpO2 < 92%, silent chest, cyanosis, exhaustion, confusion, or normal/elevated PaCO2).

Intravenous magnesium sulfate (1.2 to 2 g over 20 minutes) is added for severe asthma not responding to initial bronchodilators; Cochrane data show fewer admissions in adults, whereas nebulised magnesium did not help in the 3Mg trial.

uncertainties: Optimal role of inhaled steroids in the emergency department.

page.standard_overview: Acute severe asthma is a life-threatening exacerbation defined clinically by peak expiratory flow (PEF) 33-50% of predicted/best, inability to complete sentences in one breath, respiratory rate >= 25 bpm, or heart rate >= 110 bpm. Initial treatment uses repeated high-dose inhaled salbutamol with ipratropium and early systemic corticosteroids; a single intravenous magnesium-sulfate infusion is an adjunct for severe exacerbations that do not respond to initial inhaled therapy.

page.mentor_intro: The 2026 AHA/ASA acute stroke guideline updates reperfusion care. Tenecteplase 0.25 mg/kg is an effective alternative to alteplase, intra-arterial thrombolysis after successful thrombectomy may help selected patients, and early DOAC initiation after stroke with AF appears safe.

teaching_points.claim: The 2026 AHA/ASA guideline modifies the approach to thrombolysis contraindications and highlights remaining knowledge gaps.
Early DOAC initiation after acute ischaemic stroke with non-valvular AF appears safe and potentially more effective than delayed treatment.
Tenecteplase was superior for excellent functional outcomes and not inferior for major neurological improvement or death versus alteplase, with 0.25 mg/kg the optimal dose.
Tenecteplase 0.25 mg/kg gives better efficacy, while alteplase remains safer for symptomatic intracranial haemorrhage, so thrombolytic selection should be individualised.
A network meta-analysis found alteplase 0.6 mg/kg safer, and tenecteplase 0.25 mg/kg and alteplase 0.6 mg/kg preferable beyond 4.5 hours with tissue window assessment.
Adjunctive intra-arterial thrombolysis after successful thrombectomy appears to benefit selected patients, such as those with higher NIHSS or cardioembolic aetiology.
Fibrinogen depletion was seen only after alteplase and tended to accompany more major haemorrhagic complications.

The NINDS rt-PA trial showed that alteplase within 3 hours of ischaemic stroke increased the chance of minimal or no disability at 3 months by at least 30% (OR about 1.7), with a symptomatic intracranial haemorrhage rate of 6.4%.

uncertainties: Optimal selection for adjunctive intra-arterial thrombolysis.

STREAM showed that pre-hospital fibrinolysis (half-dose tenecteplase in those aged 75 or over) followed by timely angiography was an effective alternative to primary PCI when PCI could not be delivered within about 60 to 90 minutes.

Absolute contraindications to systemic thrombolysis include prior intracranial hemorrhage, known structural cerebral vascular lesion or neoplasm, ischemic stroke within 3 months, active internal bleeding, and recent severe head/facial trauma within 3 months.

page.standard_overview: Acute thrombolytic therapy with recombinant tissue plasminogen activators (alteplase, tenecteplase) offers rapid reperfusion in life-threatening thrombotic emergencies, but carries catastrophic intracranial hemorrhage risks requiring strict patient selection. Eligible acute ischemic-stroke patients benefit from intravenous thrombolysis within 4.5 hours: NINDS and ECASS-3 established alteplase across the early and 3-4.5-hour windows, while separate randomized evidence supports tenecteplase 0.25 mg/kg within 4.5 hours. Systemic thrombolysis is recommended for high-risk PE with shock or persistent hypotension; in intermediate-high-risk PE, PEITHO found no overall mortality advantage to routine upfront tenecteplase and supports rescue thrombolysis if hemodynamic decompensation occurs. In STEMI, thrombolysis is indicated within 12 hours when primary PCI cannot be achieved within 120 minutes (STREAM trial).

An ISHLT consensus conference on emerging antibody and AMR science lays a platform for future studies.

standard_knowledge.claim: First-line therapy for acute TCMR consists of intravenous methylprednisolone (500-1000 mg/day for 3 days), which reverses > 80% of Grade IA/IB rejection episodes; steroid-resistant TCMR or vascular rejection (Banff II/III) warrants rabbit anti-thymocyte globulin (rATG).

Acute ABMR is diagnosed by the triad of graft dysfunction, histological microvascular inflammation (peritubular capillaritis/glomerulitis or C4d deposition), and circulating donor-specific anti-HLA antibodies (DSA).

Management of acute active ABMR centers on rapid removal and neutralization of donor-specific antibodies using therapeutic plasma exchange (PLEX) coupled with high-dose intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG 1-2 g/kg).

page.standard_overview: Acute allograft rejection presents as acute graft dysfunction categorized histologically under the international Banff classification into T cell-mediated rejection (TCMR) and antibody-mediated rejection (ABMR). Indication allograft biopsy is the definitive gold standard to differentiate rejection from calcineurin inhibitor nephrotoxicity, BK polyomavirus nephropathy, or acute tubular necrosis. Acute cellular rejection is treated with intravenous methylprednisolone, commonly 250-500 mg daily for 3 days. Treatment with an anti-T-cell antibody (ATG) is more effective than corticosteroids in restoring kidney function and preventing graft loss. Conversely, ABMR—driven by donor-specific anti-HLA antibodies (DSA) and microvascular inflammation—requires multimodal desensitization combining therapeutic plasma exchange, intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG), and optimization of baseline immunosuppression.

page.mentor_intro: EAES/SAGES and WSES guidelines guide acute diverticulitis management; colorectal cancer prevalence is 1.9% after acute diverticulitis and higher after complicated disease. Abscesses are treated non-operatively first, with surgery reserved for failure.

page.standard_overview: Uncomplicated diverticulitis is localised diverticular inflammation without abscess or perforation; the modified Hinchey classification names it stage 0 (mild clinical diverticulitis) and stage Ia (confined pericolic inflammation). Landmark randomized clinical trials (AVOD and DIABOLO) demonstrated that observational management without antibiotics yields equivalent healing, symptom resolution, complication rates, and recurrence compared to routine antibiotic therapy in immunocompetent patients. Antibiotics can be used selectively rather than routinely in immunocompetent patients with mild uncomplicated diverticulitis, and are strongly advised in immunocompromised patients.

page.standard_overview: Adrenal crisis is an acute life-threatening manifestation of severe absolute or relative glucocorticoid deficiency characterized by profound hypotension refractory to fluid resuscitation and vasopressors, hypovolemic shock, fever, hypoglycemia, and electrolyte derangements (hyponatremia, hyperkalemia). standard_knowledge.claim: The standard 250 ug cosyntropin (short Synacthen) stimulation test is the diagnostic reference standard: peak serum cortisol < 500 nmol/L (18 ug/dL) at 30 or 60 minutes confirms adrenal insufficiency.

Plasma ACTH measured concurrently with morning cortisol differentiates primary (markedly elevated ACTH, usually > 2x upper limit of normal) from secondary/tertiary adrenal insufficiency (low or inappropriately normal ACTH).

In primary adrenal insufficiency, 21-hydroxylase autoantibodies confirm autoimmune adrenalitis (> 80-90% of cases in developed nations); adrenal CT is indicated if autoantibodies are negative to evaluate tuberculosis, hemorrhage, or infiltration.

Physiological glucocorticoid replacement consists of hydrocortisone 15-25 mg daily divided into 2-3 doses (highest dose upon waking) or oral cortisone acetate; primary disease additionally requires fludrocortisone (0.05-0.2 mg daily) titrated to seated/standing blood pressure and plasma renin activity.

page.standard_overview: Adrenal insufficiency encompasses primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison disease: adrenal cortex destruction, loss of both glucocorticoids and mineralocorticoids, elevated ACTH) and secondary/tertiary adrenal insufficiency (hypothalamic-pituitary failure or exogenous steroid suppression, deficient ACTH, preserved mineralocorticoid secretion). Patients present insidiously with fatigue, weight loss, orthostatic hypotension, nausea, and in primary disease, cutaneous hyperpigmentation from pro-opiomelanocortin (POMC) cleavage. Evaluation uses morning cortisol and ACTH followed when needed by a 250-microgram cosyntropin test; a peak cortisol below the assay-specific threshold, commonly around 500 nmol/L, supports adrenal insufficiency, but early secondary disease can produce a falsely normal response.

page.standard_overview: Adrenocortical carcinoma (ACC) is a rare, aggressive malignancy carrying a 5-year survival of < 40-50%. Clinical presentation comprises symptoms of hormone excess (Cushing syndrome, virilization, feminization) in 60% of cases, abdominal pain/mass effect in 30%, or an incidental discovery. Staging utilizes the European Network for the Study of Adrenal Tumors (ENSAT) system (Stages I-IV). Complete surgical resection with negative margins (R0 en bloc adrenalectomy with lymphadenectomy) performed by high-volume endocrine surgeons is the sole curative modality. Adjuvant mitotane is considered for patients at high risk of recurrence; for advanced or metastatic ACC, EDP plus mitotane is a commonly used first-line regimen, with alternatives and sequencing individualized to fitness and disease.

Secondary erythrocytosis in cyanotic ACHD is an adaptive physiological response to chronic tissue hypoxemia; routine prophylactic phlebotomy is contraindicated and induces severe iron-deficient microcytosis and hyperviscosity-related stroke.

page.standard_overview: Eisenmenger syndrome represents the most extreme manifestation of pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) associated with adult congenital heart disease (ACHD), developing from a large uncorrected congenital systemic-to-pulmonary shunt (VSD, ASD, PDA). Chronic cyanosis causes secondary erythrocytosis as an adaptive response to hypoxaemia. Closure of an atrial septal defect is not recommended in Eisenmenger physiology. Management relies on pulmonary vasodilators (endothelin receptor antagonists, PDE-5 inhibitors), avoidance of dehydration or pregnancy, and restrictive phlebotomy indications.

page.standard_overview: Adult-Onset Still's Disease (AOSD) is a rare systemic autoinflammatory disorder driven by dysregulated innate immunity, hyperactivation of the NLRP3 inflammasome, and massive overproduction of pro-inflammatory cytokines, specifically interleukin-1 (IL-1beta, IL-18) and interleukin-6 (IL-6). For severe or glucocorticoid-refractory/dependent AOSD, anakinra, an IL-1 receptor antagonist, canakinumab, an anti-IL-1-beta antibody, or the IL-6 receptor antagonist tocilizumab can produce rapid disease control and improve ferritin; prevention of MAS is not established for every patient.

Under the validated Yamaguchi criteria, diagnosis requires >= 5 criteria (with at least 2 major criteria): Major criteria include fever >= 39°C lasting >= 1 week, arthralgia/arthritis >= 2 weeks, typical salmon-pink maculopapular rash, and leukocytosis >= 10,000/uL (>= 80% neutrophils).
Minor Yamaguchi criteria include sore throat, lymphadenopathy and/or splenomegaly, abnormal liver enzymes (transaminitis), and negative antinuclear antibody (ANA) and rheumatoid factor (RF).

The Fautrel criteria introduced biological markers into diagnostic classification, incorporating extreme hyperferritinemia and glycosylated ferritin <= 20%, which provides high diagnostic specificity (98.5%) for AOSD.

page.standard_overview: Adult-Onset Still's Disease (AOSD) is a diagnosis of exclusion requiring rigorous elimination of occult infections, hematologic malignancies (especially lymphoma), and other systemic autoimmune diseases. The Yamaguchi criteria represent the most widely validated and sensitive (sensitivity above 90%) diagnostic framework, requiring at least five criteria with at least two major criteria: high quotidian fever (>= 39°C for >= 1 week), arthralgias/arthritis (>= 2 weeks), typical evanescent non-pruritic salmon-pink maculopapular rash, and leukocytosis (>= 10,000/uL with >= 80% granulocytes). Ferritin above five times the upper limit of normal and glycosylated ferritin below 20% can support an AOSD diagnosis in the appropriate clinical setting, but neither is specific or independently diagnostic and glycosylated ferritin is not universally available.

standard_knowledge.claim: The rash of AOSD is characteristically an evanescent, non-pruritic or mildly pruritic salmon-pink macular or maculopapular eruption, predominantly appearing on the trunk and proximal extremities during high evening fever spikes and disappearing as temperature normalizes.

Extreme hyperferritinemia (> 5-to-10-fold upper limit of normal, often exceeding 10,000 ug/L) reflects massive reticuloendothelial histiocyte activation and directly correlates with disease activity and response to treatment.

Macrophage Activation Syndrome (MAS/sHLH) develops in 10-15% of AOSD patients; laboratory clues include acute fall in erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) with rising CRP, sudden bicytopenia/pancytopenia, hypofibrinogenemia, elevated triglycerides, and hyperferritinemia > 10,000 ug/L.

Emergency management of AOSD-associated MAS mandates high-dose intravenous pulse methylprednisolone (1 g/day for 3 days) combined with high-dose intravenous or subcutaneous anakinra (100-200 mg every 6-8 hours) to arrest the fatal cytokine cascade.

page.standard_overview: The classic clinical triad of adult-onset Still disease (AOSD) is high spiking quotidian fever, an evanescent salmon-pink maculopapular rash that often accompanies fever, and arthralgia or arthritis; marked hyperferritinemia is a supportive laboratory feature rather than part of the classic triad. Macrophage activation syndrome (MAS), a form of secondary hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis, is a life-threatening AOSD complication marked by cytokine storm, cytopenias, transaminitis, coagulopathy, and sometimes a paradoxically falling ESR from hypofibrinogenemia; emergency management commonly uses high-dose glucocorticoids with an IL-1 inhibitor such as anakinra, with additional immunosuppression individualized to severity and response.

page.mentor_intro: Retrieved evidence centres on vasopressors rather than steroids: vasopressin or analogues added to catecholamines are suggested in distributive shock, and a network meta-analysis found norepinephrine, terlipressin and vasopressin associated with lower 28-day mortality than dopamine. Corticosteroid trial data were not retrieved.

teaching_points.claim: The Canadian Critical Care Society guideline suggests using vasopressin or analogues in addition to catecholamines rather than catecholamines alone in distributive shock (conditional recommendation, low certainty).
Global expert consensus statements address management of adult sepsis in resource-limited settings.
A consensus blood transcriptomic framework aligns sepsis subgroupings to assist precision medicine and trial design.
A network meta-analysis found dopamine associated with higher 28-day mortality in septic shock than norepinephrine, terlipressin and vasopressin.
Vasopressin and glucocorticoids improved return of spontaneous circulation compared with placebo in in-hospital cardiac arrest, with larger trials needed for longer-term outcomes.

The 2021 Surviving Sepsis Campaign guidelines issue a weak recommendation for low-dose corticosteroid therapy (IV hydrocortisone 200 mg/day) in adult septic shock patients who have an ongoing requirement for vasopressor therapy (norepinephrine or epinephrine >= 0.25 ug/kg/min) for at least 4 hours.

The landmark ADRENAL trial (3,800 patients, Venkatesh et al., NEJM) showed that continuous hydrocortisone (200 mg/day for 7 days) significantly accelerated shock resolution (median 3 vs 4 days), shortened time to ICU discharge, and reduced blood transfusion requirements, though 90-day mortality was not significantly different (27.9% vs 28.8%).

The French APROCCHSS trial (1,241 patients with severe septic shock, Annane et al., NEJM) demonstrated that combined hydrocortisone (50 mg IV q6h) plus oral fludrocortisone (50 ug daily) significantly reduced 90-day all-cause mortality from 49.1% to 43.0% (hazard ratio 0.88, p=0.03).

Neither trial reported an increase in secondary hospital-acquired infections or gastrointestinal bleeding with low-dose corticosteroids, although hydrocortisone was associated with higher rates of manageable hyperglycemia.

page.standard_overview: The ADRENAL trial randomised 3800 patients (primary outcome known for 3658) to hydrocortisone or placebo in septic shock; APROCCHSS tested hydrocortisone plus fludrocortisone. While ADRENAL evaluated continuous intravenous hydrocortisone (200 mg/day) monotherapy and demonstrated faster shock resolution and shorter mechanical ventilation without 90-day mortality benefit, APROCCHSS evaluated hydrocortisone (50 mg IV q6h) plus oral fludrocortisone (50 ug daily) in severe shock and demonstrated a statistically significant 90-day all-cause mortality reduction (43.0% vs 49.1%). Immune-related adverse events (colitis, hepatitis, hypophysitis, pneumonitis, myocarditis) require protocolized grading and prompt high-dose systemic corticosteroids (prednisone 1-2 mg/kg/day or IV methylprednisolone); refractory colitis responds rapidly to infliximab or vedolizumab.

page.standard_overview: The therapeutic paradigm for advanced/metastatic melanoma has been revolutionized by immune checkpoint blockade targeting PD-1 and CTLA-4. In the benchmark CheckMate 067 trial, dual checkpoint inhibition with nivolumab plus ipilimumab achieved unprecedented durable 6.5-year overall survival (49% vs 42% for nivolumab alone and 23% for ipilimumab alone), with median overall survival reaching 72.1 months. While dual therapy yields the highest response rates (58%) and intracranial control, it induces severe Grade 3/4 immune-related adverse events (irAEs) in 59% of patients, necessitating proactive monitoring, prompt high-dose corticosteroid intervention, and careful risk-benefit stratification against anti-PD-1 monotherapy.

page.standard_overview: The treatment landscape of locally advanced or metastatic urothelial carcinoma has been fundamentally transformed by the antibody-drug conjugate (ADC) enfortumab vedotin paired with the anti-PD-1 inhibitor pembrolizumab. In the practice-changing EV-302 phase 3 trial, enfortumab vedotin plus pembrolizumab nearly doubled median overall survival compared to traditional platinum-based chemotherapy (gemcitabine plus cisplatin or carboplatin), establishing a new frontline standard of care regardless of cisplatin eligibility. In patients receiving initial platinum chemotherapy, the JAVELIN Bladder 100 trial proved that switch maintenance avelumab significantly extends survival in those without disease progression.

page.standard_overview: Agitation in hospitalized adult medical and surgical patients represents a clinical emergency reflecting underlying delirium, substance intoxication or withdrawal, toxic-metabolic encephalopathy, or acute exacerbation of psychiatric illness. standard_knowledge.claim: Venous air embolism entering the right ventricle creates a mechanical 'air lock' obstructing the pulmonary artery, producing acute pulmonary hypertension, acute cor pulmonale, profound hypotension, and sudden drop in end-tidal CO2 (EtCO2).

Immediate bedside rescue positioning for suspected venous air embolism is the Durant maneuver: placing the patient in the left lateral decubitus and Trendelenburg position, which traps the air bubble at the apex of the right ventricle away from the pulmonary outflow tract.

Administration of 100% inspired oxygen accelerates bubble reabsorption by washing out systemic nitrogen, creating a steep nitrogen concentration gradient from the bubble into blood and reducing bubble volume.

Hyperbaric oxygen therapy (HBOT at 2.8 to 3.0 atmospheres absolute) is the definitive treatment of choice for arterial gas embolism and severe venous embolism with neurological or hemodynamic impairment, rapidly compressing bubble diameter (Boyle's law) and restoring microvascular tissue perfusion.

page.standard_overview: Gas in the arterial system can occlude cerebral arteries and cause ischaemic stroke; venous gas embolism can follow iatrogenic procedures. Venous air or gas embolism can occur during central venous catheter insertion or removal, sitting-position neurosurgery, or laparoscopic insufflation (usually carbon dioxide rather than air), potentially causing right ventricular outflow obstruction and cardiovascular collapse. Immediately stop further gas entry and administer 100% oxygen; positioning such as the Durant maneuver may be considered for venous air embolism but has limited evidence, while urgent hyperbaric oxygen is especially important for cerebral or other arterial gas embolism rather than mandatory for every venous event.

overview_support.note: AHA 2025 Part 10: "Gas in the arterial system rises to the least dependent vascular bed. Cerebral arterial gas embolism can occlude arteries, causing ischemic stroke." The venous/arterial classification wording is not stated.

page.standard_overview: Endotracheal intubation in the intensive care unit is a high-risk procedure carrying a much higher incidence of life-threatening complications (severe hypoxemia, cardiovascular collapse, cardiac arrest) compared to elective operating room intubations. page.standard_overview: Malignant central airway obstruction (CAO) is a life-threatening complication occurring in up to 20-30% of advanced lung cancers and metastatic malignancies (esophagus, thyroid, melanoma, breast). Malignant central airway obstruction causes dyspnoea (from exertion to rest), cough, haemoptysis, difficulty clearing secretions, and post-obstructive or recurrent infections. Emergency management requires prompt oxygenation and multidisciplinary airway or interventional-pulmonology assessment; heliox can transiently reduce resistance where flow is turbulent, and corticosteroids are used selectively when airway edema or a steroid-responsive tumor contribution is suspected rather than universally. Rigid bronchoscopy is the optimal platform to secure the airway, de-bulk endobronchial tumor via ablative modalities (electrocautery, APC, cryotherapy), and deploy self-expanding metallic or silicone tracheobronchial stents.

page.standard_overview: Acute kidney injury (AKI) diagnosis and management focuses on early detection, etiology identification, avoidance of compounding toxicities, and fluid stewardship. KDIGO recommends serial serum creatinine and urine-output assessment for AKI detection and staging, with hourly urine-output monitoring when clinically appropriate in high-risk or critically ill patients, followed by stage-based supportive care. In resuscitating patients at risk of or suffering from AKI, the landmark SMART and SALT-ED randomized trials demonstrated that balanced crystalloids (Plasma-Lyte or Lactated Ringer's) significantly reduce Major Adverse Kidney Events at 30 days (MAKE30) compared to 0.9% normal saline, avoiding hyperchloremia-induced renal arteriolar vasoconstriction.

The cause of AKI should be determined whenever possible.
W e recommend that patients be stratified for risk of AKI according to their susceptibilities and exposures.

Manage patients with AKI according to the stage (see Figure 4) and cause.

In the absence of hemorrhagic shock, we suggest using isotonic crystalloids rather than colloids (albumin or starches) as initial management for expansion of intravascular volume in patients at risk for AKI or with AKI.

In critically ill patients, we suggest insulin therapy targeting plasma glucose 110- 149 mg/dl (6.1- 8.3 mmol/l).
W e suggest achieving a total energy intake of 20- 30 kcal/kg/d in patients with any stage of AKI.
W e suggest to avoid restriction of protein intake with the aim of preventing or delaying initiation of RRT.
W e suggest administering 0.8- 1.0 g/kg/d of protein in noncatabolic AKI patients without need for dialysis.
W e suggest providing nutrition preferentially via the enteral route in patients with AKI.
W e recommend not using diuretics to prevent AKI.

page.standard_overview: KDIGO diagnosis and staging use changes in serum creatinine and urine output; serial creatinine and appropriately frequent urine-output monitoring are required, with hourly urine-output measurement particularly useful in high-risk or critically ill monitored patients rather than mandatory in every setting. Urine-output criteria can detect AKI earlier than serum creatinine because creatinine is a delayed, indirect marker of changing kidney function; the delay varies with the severity of injury, baseline creatinine, fluid balance, and kinetics rather than always requiring 24 to 48 hours. The Acute Disease Quality Initiative (ADQI) consensus emphasizes that combining functional staging (creatinine and urine output) with structural injury biomarkers (TIMP-2, IGFBP7, NGAL) defines subclinical AKI, guiding risk-adapted monitoring and preventing secondary iatrogenic insult.

page.standard_overview: Acamprosate and naltrexone are the medications recommended for moderate to severe alcohol use disorder; the benefit is small but outweighs harms when non-pharmacological approaches have not worked. Acamprosate is renally cleared, so first-line use is avoided in mild to moderate renal impairment; naltrexone is an alternative. Naltrexone is an opioid receptor antagonist; labelling warns against use in acute hepatitis or liver failure, and it reduces the effectiveness of opioid analgesia.

Alcohol-related cirrhosis requires systematic hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) screening with ultrasound +/- AFP every 6 months and endoscopic variceal screening.
Sustained alcohol abstinence is the single most powerful determinant of survival and portal pressure reduction across all stages of alcohol-related liver disease.

page.standard_overview: Chronic heavy alcohol use can cause hepatic steatosis, fibrosis, and cirrhosis and can contribute to nutritional and metabolic brain injury, although these complications do not develop in every person with alcohol use disorder. Wernicke encephalopathy is a medical emergency caused by thiamine (vitamin B1) deficiency, classic triad of confusion, ataxia, and ophthalmoplegia (nystagmus/lateral rectus palsy) occurring in only one-third of cases. Prompt parenteral thiamine is urgent treatment for suspected Wernicke encephalopathy and can prevent progression and reduce the risk of persistent Korsakoff syndrome, but established memory impairment is not always reversible.

Diazepam and chlordiazepoxide provide smoother withdrawal control due to long-acting active metabolites (desmethyldiazepam), reducing withdrawal seizure frequency.

Alcohol withdrawal seizures typically occur 6 to 48 hours after the last drink, are generalised tonic-clonic, and are treated with benzodiazepines rather than phenytoin.

page.standard_overview: Alcohol withdrawal syndrome (AWS) ranges from mild tremulousness to life-threatening delirium tremens and withdrawal seizures. Benzodiazepines are the mainstay of alcohol-withdrawal treatment; symptom-triggered CIWA-Ar protocols are preferred for appropriate mild-to-moderate cases with reliable assessment, while severe withdrawal, delirium, seizures, or unreliable symptom scoring may require fixed-schedule or loading-dose regimens and close monitoring. In hepatic cirrhosis, short-acting agents without active metabolites (lorazepam, oxazepam) avoid drug accumulation.

standard_knowledge.claim: Delirium tremens carries up to 5-15% mortality without intensive care; mortality is driven by hyperthermia, cardiac arrhythmias, and aspiration pneumonia.
Phenobarbital monotherapy or protocolized combination with benzodiazepines achieves faster symptom control, lower intubation rates, and decreased ICU length of stay in severe refractory withdrawal.
Dexmedetomidine reduces sympathetic overdrive and tachycardia as an adjunctive sedative, but does not prevent seizures or delirium and cannot substitute for GABAergic agents.
Severe hypomagnesemia and hypophosphatemia are common in severe withdrawal and must be corrected aggressively to prevent refractory seizures and refractory hypokalemia.

page.standard_overview: Delirium tremens (DT) is a severe medical emergency characterized by profound delirium, hallucinations, agitation, fever, and severe autonomic instability, typically developing 48-96 hours after alcohol cessation. Severe delirium tremens requires a closely monitored setting, often an ICU, escalating benzodiazepine therapy with phenobarbital as an adjunct or alternative in selected protocols, careful airway and respiratory assessment, thiamine, fluids as indicated, and correction of electrolytes such as magnesium and potassium.

Omalizumab reduced exacerbations and oral corticosteroid use and improved lung function and asthma control in ABPA, and was well tolerated.
Omalizumab, dupilumab and mepolizumab showed clinical benefit in ABPA, with larger randomised trials needed.

page.standard_overview: Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (ABPA) is a hypersensitivity response to Aspergillus fumigatus colonization in patients with asthma or cystic fibrosis. Current ABPA criteria require a predisposing condition or compatible presentation, demonstrated fungal sensitization and total serum IgE at least 500 IU/mL, plus two of Aspergillus-specific IgG, peripheral eosinophilia, or suggestive imaging; central bronchiectasis and IgE above 1,000 IU/mL are no longer mandatory in every case. ABPA treatment is individualized: oral corticosteroids or oral itraconazole are first-line options for acute exacerbation, combination therapy may be used for recurrent or difficult disease, and selected patients may benefit from a type-2 biologic.

Moderate-to-severe symptoms are managed first-line with intranasal corticosteroids (INCS) or combination INCS and intranasal antihistamines (e.g. fluticasone/azelastine). Allergen immunotherapy (SLIT or SCIT) is the only disease-modifying intervention for IgE-confirmed refractory disease.

Abnormal liver chemistries imply hepatocellular disease or biliary obstruction, and liver biopsy may be considered when other tests fail to establish a diagnosis.

page.standard_overview: Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency (AATD) is an autosomal codominant genetic disorder characterized by low circulating levels of AAT (a serine protease inhibitor protecting lung elastin). Homozygosity for the Z allele (Pi*ZZ) predisposes to early-onset panacinar emphysema (predominating in lower lung zones) and liver cirrhosis from misfolded polymer accumulation in hepatocytes.

overview_support.note: ATS/ERS 2003: PI*ZZ gives low serum AAT; "Pulmonary emphysema of the panacinar type is the most prevalent clinical correlate"; liver disease is second; PAS-D-positive inclusions of polymerised Z AAT in hepatocytes. Lower-zone predominance not located.

page.mentor_intro: Alport syndrome is managed with genetic diagnosis and RAAS blockade started early to delay kidney failure. The ERKNet/ERA/ESPN 2024 guideline covers diagnosis and management of COL4A3/4/5 variant carriers, including donor assessment.

teaching_points.claim: Alport genetic diagnosis consensus 2019: All three COL4A5, COL4A3 and COL4A4 genes should be examined in individuals undergoing genetic testing for Alport syndrome.

The 2024 ERKNet/ERA/ESPN guideline covers diagnosis and management of individuals with pathogenic COL4A3/4/5 variants, and heterozygous carriers should be considered for living kidney donation only as a last resort.
A molecular diagnostics consensus notes heterozygous COL4A3 and COL4A4 variants are common incidental findings, and interpreting hypomorphic variants remains challenging.
Expert consensus guidelines on genetic diagnosis note genetic and non-genetic factors contribute to phenotypic variability.
A Chinese expert consensus updated in 2023 covers genetic testing, variant interpretation and treatment follow-up.
RAAS blockers delay end-stage kidney disease in Alport syndrome of any genetic type, especially early in disease, with more effective therapies to be added on top of this standard of care.
Ocular manifestations of Alport syndrome mean ophthalmologists can aid diagnosis, and early diagnosis lessens blindness and retinal detachment risk.
A review of potential renal damage biomarkers in Alport syndrome highlights markers of kidney disease progression risk.

International consensus guidelines recommend early initiation of ACE inhibitors at the onset of persistent microalbuminuria (or at diagnosis in males with X-linked Alport syndrome) to delay end-stage kidney disease by decades.
