page.standard_overview: Alport syndrome is an inherited progressive type IV collagen nephropathy caused by pathogenic variants in COL4A3, COL4A4, or COL4A5 genes. It presents with persistent microscopic hematuria in childhood, progressive proteinuria, hypertension, progressive renal failure, high-frequency sensorineural hearing loss, and anterior lenticonus. Early ACE inhibitor therapy significantly delays progression to end-stage kidney disease.

overview_support.note: JASN 2013: "Alport syndrome is characterised by hematuria, progressive renal failure, hearing loss, lenticonus, and retinal flecks". Proteinuria and hypertension are not in that sentence.

topic: Alport syndrome and inherited collagen nephropathies

page.mentor_intro: Alport syndrome is managed with genetic diagnosis and RAAS blockade started early to delay kidney failure. The ERKNet/ERA/ESPN 2024 guideline covers diagnosis and management of COL4A3/4/5 variant carriers, including donor assessment.

teaching_points.claim: Alport genetic diagnosis consensus 2019: All three COL4A5, COL4A3 and COL4A4 genes should be examined in individuals undergoing genetic testing for Alport syndrome.

The 2024 ERKNet/ERA/ESPN guideline covers diagnosis and management of individuals with pathogenic COL4A3/4/5 variants, and heterozygous carriers should be considered for living kidney donation only as a last resort.
A molecular diagnostics consensus notes heterozygous COL4A3 and COL4A4 variants are common incidental findings, and interpreting hypomorphic variants remains challenging.
Expert consensus guidelines on genetic diagnosis note genetic and non-genetic factors contribute to phenotypic variability.
A Chinese expert consensus updated in 2023 covers genetic testing, variant interpretation and treatment follow-up.
RAAS blockers delay end-stage kidney disease in Alport syndrome of any genetic type, especially early in disease, with more effective therapies to be added on top of this standard of care.
Ocular manifestations of Alport syndrome mean ophthalmologists can aid diagnosis, and early diagnosis lessens blindness and retinal detachment risk.

Next-generation sequencing multigene panels have replaced routine renal biopsy as the preferred first-line diagnostic investigation for suspected inherited collagen IV disorders.
Heterozygous females with X-linked Alport syndrome (COL4A5) have a lifelong risk of developing proteinuria (up to 75%) and ESRD (up to 15-30% by age 60), requiring lifelong annual monitoring.

page.standard_overview: Alport syndrome and thin basement membrane nephropathy are related COL4A3/COL4A4/COL4A5 disorders; the 2013 expert guidelines continue to use the term thin basement membrane nephropathy. COL4A3, COL4A4, and COL4A5 testing helps establish the diagnosis, inheritance pattern, and progression risk, but heterozygous COL4A3 or COL4A4 variants are not uniformly benign; some individuals develop proteinuria, focal segmental glomerulosclerosis, or chronic kidney disease and require long-term surveillance.

overview_support.note: Alport genetic diagnosis consensus 2019: COL4A3/4/5 variants cause these conditions; the guideline notes the term "Thin basement membrane nephropathy" is "widely understood". A benign-to-severe continuum is not stated.

topic: alteplase acute ischemic stroke NINDS trial

page.mentor_intro: The 2026 AHA/ASA acute stroke guideline updates reperfusion care. Tenecteplase 0.25 mg/kg is an effective alternative to alteplase, intra-arterial thrombolysis after successful thrombectomy may help selected patients, and early DOAC initiation after stroke with AF appears safe.

teaching_points.claim: The 2026 AHA/ASA guideline modifies the approach to thrombolysis contraindications and highlights remaining knowledge gaps.
Early DOAC initiation after acute ischaemic stroke with non-valvular AF appears safe and potentially more effective than delayed treatment.
Tenecteplase was superior for excellent functional outcomes and not inferior for major neurological improvement or death versus alteplase, with 0.25 mg/kg the optimal dose.
Tenecteplase 0.25 mg/kg gives better efficacy, while alteplase remains safer for symptomatic intracranial haemorrhage, so thrombolytic selection should be individualised.
A network meta-analysis found alteplase 0.6 mg/kg safer, and tenecteplase 0.25 mg/kg and alteplase 0.6 mg/kg preferable beyond 4.5 hours with tissue window assessment.
Adjunctive intra-arterial thrombolysis after successful thrombectomy appears to benefit selected patients, such as those with higher NIHSS or cardioembolic aetiology.
Fibrinogen depletion was seen only after alteplase and tended to accompany more major haemorrhagic complications.

Mechanical thrombectomy for acute large vessel occlusion (internal carotid or M1 middle cerebral artery) is standard within 6 hours of onset (HERMES meta-analysis) and benefits selected patients up to 24 hours (DAWN, DEFUSE 3).

The landmark NINDS rt-PA Stroke Study demonstrated that patients treated with intravenous alteplase within 3 hours had a 30% higher likelihood of minimal or no disability at 3 months (mRS 0-1) despite a 6.4% symptomatic intracerebral hemorrhage rate.
The ECASS III trial showed that alteplase given 3 to 4.5 hours after symptom onset increased the likelihood of a favourable outcome at 90 days in eligible patients.

uncertainties: Optimal selection for adjunctive intra-arterial thrombolysis.

topic: alzheimer s disease anti amyloid immunotherapy

page.mentor_intro: Anti-amyloid antibodies slow decline in early Alzheimer disease but their effects are small, below the minimal clinically important difference in one analysis, and they carry meaningful harms including ARIA. MRI protocols to detect ARIA are recommended.

teaching_points.claim: Imaging recommendations for anti-amyloid therapies include implementing MRI protocols to detect ARIA in diverse practice settings.
FDA-approved anti-amyloid monoclonal antibodies slow disease progression on CDR-SB and other scales, at the cost of increased side effects.
Monoclonal antibodies targeting amyloid give small benefits on cognitive and functional scales that are far below the minimal clinically important difference, with clinically meaningful harms.
Aducanumab, lecanemab and donanemab do not appear to differ in effect on cognitive function, and low-dose lithium may be safer.
A critical assessment suggests benefits of the newest antibodies could be cumulative over time, leading to larger clinical effects in subsequent years.
A meta-analysis of phase III trials found anti-amyloid antibodies associated with improved ADAS-Cog and CDR-SB.
Appropriate Use Criteria mandate pre-treatment confirmation of amyloid pathology via CSF biomarkers or amyloid PET imaging.
Lecanemab slowed 18-month cognitive and functional decline (CDR-SB) by 27% compared to placebo in the CLARITY AD trial.

uncertainties: Long-term clinical benefit and cost-effectiveness.
case_hooks: Early Alzheimer's disease with amyloid-positive PET considering lecanemab.

Reviews summarise the diagnostic features and clinical implications of inherited bone marrow failure syndromes including congenital amegakaryocytic thrombocytopenia.
Radioulnar synostosis with amegakaryocytic thrombocytopenia type 2 is reviewed with management considerations including transplantation.
Thrombopoietin-receptor agonists are used selectively in rare inherited thrombocytopenias.
Anti-thymocyte globulin-based treatment is used for acquired bone marrow failure in adults.
Amegakaryocytic thrombocytopenia with later aplastic anaemia has been associated with Epstein-Barr virus infection, and recovery may reflect natural history.
CRISPR/Cas9 gene editing is a promising strategy in haematological disorders, with delivery into stem cells a bottleneck.

page.standard_overview: Congenital amegakaryocytic thrombocytopenia (CAMT) is a severe marrow failure disorder characterized by isolated severe thrombocytopenia and absent megakaryocytes on bone marrow biopsy. CAMT is caused by biallelic loss-of-function MPL mutations (TPO receptor), typically progressing to aplastic anemia or leukemia; allogeneic hematopoietic cell transplantation is the definitive curative treatment.

page.mentor_intro: AML evolving from MPN has a poor outlook. Combination of hypomethylating agents with venetoclax or ruxolitinib improved outcomes over HMA alone in accelerated or blast phase, and allogeneic transplant is a potential option for selected therapy-related myeloid neoplasms.

teaching_points.claim: Combination therapy with hypomethylating agents plus venetoclax or ruxolitinib was associated with improved outcomes over HMAs alone in MPN accelerated or blast phase, with randomised trials needed.
Allogeneic transplant remains a potential treatment for carefully selected patients with therapy-related myeloid neoplasms, with relapse the commonest cause of death.
TP53 mutations strongly predict poorer survival in adult AML.
CPX-351 showed superior efficacy and comparable safety to standard chemotherapy across diverse AML populations in a systematic review.
Post-chemotherapy G-CSF may increase relapse risk in paediatric and secondary AML (RR 1.26 and 1.12 in subgroups).
Cutaneous involvement in Ph-negative MPN has prognostic relevance and histological heterogeneity.

page.standard_overview: Acute myeloid leukemia transformed from myeloproliferative neoplasms (MPN-blast phase / secondary AML) carries an aggressive clinical course and dismal prognosis. Management typically uses hypomethylating agents plus venetoclax or intensive chemotherapy in fit patients, with allogeneic stem cell transplantation the only potentially curative option.

topic: Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS): El Escorial criteria, riluzole, non-invasive ventilation

page.mentor_intro: ALS care is multidisciplinary, including respiratory support and nutrition. Tofersen slows progression and lowers NfL in SOD1-ALS; respiratory muscle training may help function, and biomarker diagnosis alone risks misclassification.

teaching_points.claim: The Japanese ALS guideline covers respiration, rehabilitation, nutrition, metabolism and care support.
A US expert consensus sets a standard for ALS home health and durable medical equipment.
Tofersen reduces SOD1 and NfL levels and slows disease progression in SOD1 ALS.
Respiratory muscle training may improve pulmonary function, particularly respiratory muscle strength, in people with ALS, with limited evidence of benefit on quality of life and survival.
Blood and CSF biomarkers used alone for ALS diagnosis carry a considerable risk of misclassification and should be integrated into multimodal frameworks.
No association was found between viral infections and ALS risk, unlike Alzheimer's and Parkinson's disease.
Genetic mutations in ALS and FTD genes have distinct effects on behavioural and cognitive change, suggesting tailored care.
Revised El Escorial and Gold Coast criteria establish diagnosis based on upper and lower motor neuron signs across progressive body regions.
Riluzole (50 mg orally twice daily) extends median survival by 2 to 3 months and reduces tracheostomy risk (Cochrane review).

uncertainties: Evidence for respiratory muscle training is limited.

page.standard_overview: Anaemia of chronic disease (ACD / anaemia of inflammation) is a cytokine-driven normocytic or mildly microcytic anaemia. Interleukin-6 induces hepatic hepcidin synthesis, which mediates the hypoferraemia of inflammation. Typical findings in anemia of inflammation are low serum iron, low or normal transferrin/TIBC, and normal or elevated ferritin as an acute-phase reactant; ferritin need not exceed 100 ng/mL, and hepcidin elevation explains the mechanism but is not a routine diagnostic laboratory requirement.

page.standard_overview: Anaphylaxis is an acute, life-threatening systemic hypersensitivity reaction with rapid onset involving airway, breathing, circulation, or skin/mucosa. Intramuscular epinephrine (adrenaline) 1 mg/mL (1:1,000), 0.01 mg/kg up to a usual adult maximum of 0.5 mg, injected into the mid-anterolateral thigh is the immediate first-line treatment; auto-injector strength should be appropriate to body weight. Antihistamines and corticosteroids are adjuncts only and must not delay or replace intramuscular epinephrine.

page.standard_overview: ANCA-associated vasculitis (AAV) encompasses Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis (GPA; PR3-ANCA), Microscopic Polyangiitis (MPA; MPO-ANCA), and Eosinophilic Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis (EGPA). Remission induction for organ- or life-threatening disease combines high-dose glucocorticoids with rituximab or cyclophosphamide. Avacopan (C5a receptor antagonist) enables significant glucocorticoid-sparing induction.

page.mentor_intro: Recent guidance (ACR/VF 2021, EULAR 2022, KDIGO 2024, BSR 2025) favours reduced-dose glucocorticoid induction; reduced-dose regimens probably reduce serious infections without increasing ESKD. Rituximab maintenance lowers relapse risk compared with azathioprine in Japanese review evidence.

teaching_points.claim: Reduced-dose glucocorticoid regimens probably reduce serious infections by about 5.9% to 12.8% and probably do not increase ESKD, according to a practice guideline on plasma exchange and glucocorticoid dosing.
The KDIGO 2024 executive summary notes the case for lower-dose glucocorticoid induction or complete replacement has strengthened.
The 2021 ACR/Vasculitis Foundation guideline provides the first endorsed recommendations for ANCA-associated vasculitis management.
The 2025 BSR recommendations include research and audit recommendations to support equitable access.
A systematic review for the 2023 Japanese guidelines compared rituximab and azathioprine maintenance for relapse risk.
A review summarises recent guidelines including KDIGO glomerular diseases and EULAR 2022 for AAV management.
An evidence-based guideline addresses diagnosis and management of eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis.
EULAR 2022 recommendations establish rituximab (375 mg/m2 weekly x 4 or 1000 mg x 2) as equivalent to cyclophosphamide for induction and superior for relapsing disease.
Avacopan (30 mg twice daily), an oral complement C5a receptor antagonist, produces sustained remission at 52 weeks while significantly reducing glucocorticoid-related toxicity (ADVOCATE trial).

PEXIVAS trial demonstrated that routine plasma exchange does not reduce end-stage kidney disease or all-cause mortality, and a reduced-dose glucocorticoid regimen is non-inferior with fewer severe infections.
In the MAINRITSAN trial, maintenance rituximab 500 mg every 6 months for 18 months was superior to azathioprine for preventing relapse in ANCA-associated vasculitis.

uncertainties: Optimal role of plasma exchange.
case_hooks: Patient with haemoptysis, glomerulonephritis and positive PR3-ANCA.

page.mentor_intro: The 2023 AHA/ASA guideline updates aneurysmal SAH care. Lumbar drainage was associated with less vasospasm, infarction and mortality in meta-analysis, and risk factors for delayed cerebral ischaemia help target ICU monitoring.

teaching_points.claim: The 2023 AHA/ASA guideline updates many earlier aneurysmal SAH recommendations and adds new ones, including patient and family priorities.
Multimodality neuromonitoring practice standards were developed by Delphi consensus, covering technologies, implementation and training.
A multidisciplinary practical consensus statement offers a protocol for acute care of aneurysmal SAH, not evidence-based guidelines.
A Chinese guideline covers evaluation, treatment selection, anaesthesia and perioperative care of ruptured intracranial aneurysms.
Lumbar CSF drainage in aneurysmal SAH was associated with benefits in vasospasm, secondary cerebral infarction and mortality (RR 0.75 for poor outcome at 6 months) without more adverse events.

Risk factors for delayed cerebral ischaemia include pre-existing hypertension, vasospasm, high admission white cell count, intracranial infection and female sex, so such patients need careful ICU monitoring.
Machine learning shows potential to forecast delayed cerebral ischaemia and poor outcomes but methodology needs standardising.

In the ISAT trial, endovascular coiling of ruptured aneurysms suitable for either treatment gave better 1-year outcomes than neurosurgical clipping, and the AHA/ASA guideline favours coiling when an aneurysm is amenable to both.

uncertainties: Standardised prediction tools.
case_hooks: Thunderclap headache with SAH on CT.

Blood pressure should be controlled with titratable IV infusions (labetalol, nicardipine) targeting SBP < 140-160 mmHg prior to aneurysm securing.
Maintenance of euvolemia is recommended; hypervolemic 'triple-H' therapy is no longer recommended due to cardiopulmonary complications.

page.standard_overview: Aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage (aSAH) is an acute neurosurgical emergency presenting with sudden thunderclap headache. Emergent non-contrast head CT is the first-line investigation; a high-quality CT performed within 6 hours can be highly sensitive in appropriate patients, but lumbar puncture is reserved for cases where CT is negative or nondiagnostic and clinical suspicion remains. Management prioritizes early aneurysm securing by endovascular coiling or surgical clipping as anatomically and clinically appropriate, oral nimodipine for 21 days, and maintenance of euvolemia to reduce delayed cerebral ischemia.

page.mentor_intro: The WAO/EAACI guideline sets global standards for hereditary angioedema, with separate paediatric, normal-C1-inhibitor and resource-limited guidance. Urticaria-associated angioedema is covered by the international urticaria guideline.

teaching_points.claim: The international WAO/EAACI hereditary angioedema guideline (2021 revision and update) aims to establish global standards, including disease activity, impact and control.
A 2026 international guideline addresses diagnosis and management of paediatric hereditary angioedema and promotes HAE centres and registries.
Hereditary angioedema with normal C1 inhibitor recommendations are all based on expert opinion.
The International/Canadian HAE guideline targets all specialists who may encounter patients with HAE.
Indian consensus recognises that resource-constrained settings often cannot follow international evaluation algorithms or access recommended therapy.
The 2026 international urticaria guideline covers definition, classification, diagnosis and treatment of urticaria subtypes.
On-demand HAE treatment guidelines evolved with trial and real-world data, changing trial designs.
WAO/EAACI guidelines recommend icatibant (bradykinin B2 receptor antagonist) or plasma-derived C1-inhibitor concentrate for acute attacks of hereditary angioedema.

standard_knowledge.claim: ACE inhibitor-induced angioedema is caused by impaired bradykinin degradation; ACE inhibitors must be permanently discontinued, and ARBs should be avoided in acute severe airway presentation.
Hereditary angioedema (HAE) Type 1 (85%) has low C4 and low antigenic/functional C1-INH; Type 2 (15%) has low C4, normal antigenic but low functional C1-INH.
Emergent airway protection (fiberoptic intubation or cricothyroidotomy) takes precedence over pharmacotherapy in progressive laryngeal edema.

page.standard_overview: Angioedema is asymmetric swelling of the deep dermis and subcutaneous or submucosal tissues. It is critical to differentiate histamine-mediated angioedema (associated with urticaria/pruritus, responds to epinephrine, antihistamines, and steroids) from bradykinin-mediated angioedema (ACE-inhibitor induced or hereditary angioedema [HAE]). Bradykinin-mediated angioedema lacks urticaria and does NOT respond to antihistamines or steroids.

topic: angiotensin ii for catecholamine refractory vasodilatory shock

page.mentor_intro: Angiotensin II raises blood pressure and spares catecholamines in vasodilatory shock without clearly lowering mortality. It is a rescue (third-line) vasopressor, and patients with high renin may respond best.

teaching_points.claim: Expert consensus recognises angiotensin II as useful to reduce catecholamine requirements in vasopressor-resistant septic shock, while stressing the need for more trials.
A meta-analysis of distributive shock found angiotensin II did not reduce mortality but allowed significant adjunctive vasopressor reduction at 3 hours without more reported adverse events.
In vasoplegic shock, angiotensin II showed comparable in-hospital mortality to standard therapy but produced a significant mean arterial pressure rise.
A systematic review suggests angiotensin II may be a third-line vasopressor if the target MAP is not reached after noradrenaline above 200 ng/kg/min for more than 6 hours.
An exploratory analysis found a greater response in patients with elevated baseline plasma renin and a reduction in renal replacement therapy initiation.
Safety concerns include thromboembolism with angiotensin II, and in cardiogenic shock reported adverse events included hepatic injury, digital ischaemia and thrombotic events.

An overview of reviews found angiotensin II consistently improved MAP by more than 10 mmHg, with gaps in the definition of catecholamine-resistant shock, initiation thresholds and biomarker-guided treatment.
Surviving Sepsis Campaign guidelines recommend adding vasopressin (0.03 U/min) rather than escalating norepinephrine to high levels (> 0.25 mcg/kg/min).
ATHOS-3 randomized trial demonstrated that synthetic human angiotensin II significantly increased mean arterial pressure and reduced background catecholamine requirements in vasodilatory shock.

uncertainties: Optimal initiation threshold and renin-guided selection.
Effect on hard outcomes beyond MAP and catecholamine sparing.
mcq_angles: Thromboembolic risk as a key adverse effect.
case_hooks: Septic shock on noradrenaline 0.5 microgram/kg/min with MAP still 55.

page.standard_overview: Catecholamine-refractory vasodilatory shock is characterized by persistent severe hypotension and inadequate organ perfusion despite high-dose catecholamine vasopressors; vasopressin may already have been added but is not required for the definition. Synthetic human angiotensin II acts through the AT1 receptor, providing a non-adrenergic vasoconstrictor mechanism. Management may include vasopressin, commonly at 0.03 units/min, hydrocortisone for selected patients with refractory septic shock, and angiotensin II as an adjunct for catecholamine-refractory vasodilatory shock.

page.mentor_intro: Axial spondyloarthritis is increasingly treated as a single entity across radiographic and non-radiographic disease. Upadacitinib improves disease activity and function, and tapering (not withdrawing) biologics preserves remission in more patients.

teaching_points.claim: SPARTAN members strongly support treating axSpA as a single entity in the update of the ACR/SAA/SPARTAN guideline.
Tapering biologic DMARDs does not significantly compromise remission or low disease activity, whereas complete withdrawal reduces the likelihood of maintaining inactive or low disease activity.
A guideline on biomarkers in axSpA addresses their clinical significance and composes a clinical toolkit for healthcare professionals.
A Chinese 2024 guideline covers diagnosis and treatment of non-radiographic axSpA with 37 clinical questions including drug tapering.
The ESPOGUIA guideline aims to reduce unjustified variability in managing axial spondyloarthritis and psoriatic arthritis.
A meta-analysis supports upadacitinib as a new treatment for axSpA, improving disease activity, physical function and wellbeing.
A meta-analysis found gut microbiota dysbiosis in ankylosing spondylitis, suggesting a possible therapeutic target.
ASAS/EULAR 2022 recommendations recommend continuous NSAIDs at maximum tolerated doses as first-line medical therapy for active axial spondyloarthritis.

uncertainties: Optimal tapering strategy.
case_hooks: Young man with inflammatory back pain and sacroiliitis on MRI.

page.standard_overview: Ankylosing spondylitis (radiographic axial spondyloarthritis) is a chronic inflammatory arthritis predominantly affecting the axial skeleton and sacroiliac joints. Ankylosing spondylitis typically begins before age 45 with inflammatory back pain, including prolonged morning stiffness, improvement with exercise and night pain, although later onset and atypical presentations occur. NSAIDs are first-choice pharmacological therapy, with dose and continuous versus on-demand use individualized; persistently active disease despite NSAIDs may require a TNF inhibitor, IL-17 inhibitor or an appropriate JAK inhibitor.

Functional defecation disorders are common in European children.

page.standard_overview: Common benign anorectal disorders include hemorrhoidal disease, anal fissures, anorectal abscesses, and fistula-in-ano. Thrombosed external hemorrhoids present with acute severe perianal pain and a tender bluish lump; excision can be considered for severe symptoms presenting within about 72 hours, while conservative treatment is appropriate in many cases. Acute anal fissures cause tearing pain during defecation and bright-red bleeding; initial management includes stool softening, fiber and sitz baths, with topical diltiazem or nitroglycerin commonly used when symptoms persist. Anorectal abscesses require prompt incision and drainage.

page.mentor_intro: Anterior mediastinal masses are mostly thymic epithelial tumours, managed by surgery with video-assisted or robotic approaches for suitable cases. Anaesthesia needs care because of airway and vascular compression risk.

teaching_points.claim: A China Anti-Cancer Association guideline provides integrative management for thymic epithelial tumours including systemic therapy for advanced disease and follow-up after resection.
Anaesthetic management of patients with an anterior mediastinal mass has evolved, with new approaches for safe induction and maintenance of general anaesthesia.
Robotic-assisted, video-assisted and open thymectomy for thymoma were compared, with robotic use constrained by cost, surgeon training and a lack of high-quality prospective data.
Thoracoscopic and robotic mediastinal tumour resection show insignificant differences in tumour size and operation time, with robotic surgery increasing hospitalisation costs.
In children, video-assisted resection of mediastinal tumours can be safe with low length of stay, while more complex tumours still need open surgery.
AI models for diagnosis and prognosis of thymic epithelial tumours are not yet ready for clinical implementation.

uncertainties: Long-term oncologic adequacy of robotic resection in children.
mcq_angles: Thymoma is the commonest anterior mass.
case_hooks: Patient with myasthenia gravis and an anterior mediastinal mass.

Complete surgical resection (thymectomy) is the mainstay of treatment for non-invasive and locally advanced resectable thymomas (Masaoka-Koga stage I-II).

page.standard_overview: Anterior mediastinal masses encompass the classic '4 Ts': Thymoma/thymic carcinoma, Teratoma (germ cell tumors), Thyroid (substernal goiter), and Terrible lymphoma. Evaluation usually includes contrast-enhanced chest CT; AFP, beta-hCG and LDH are obtained when a germ-cell tumor is suspected, myasthenia gravis testing is guided by the clinical context, and biopsy and treatment are planned multidisciplinary rather than biopsying every lesion automatically.

page.mentor_intro: Cancer therapy-related cardiac dysfunction is addressed through baseline risk assessment, imaging (including cardiac CT), prevention strategies and quality indicators. Paediatric oncology patients have a tailored approach to screening and follow-up.

teaching_points.claim: Prevention of cancer therapy-related cardiac dysfunction and heart failure combines lifestyle modification and pharmacological interventions within a holistic cardio-oncology management approach.
ESC quality indicators quantify adherence to guideline-recommended practice for prevention and management of cancer therapy-related cardiovascular toxicity.
A Delphi consensus gives paediatric oncology patients an approach to risk and baseline assessment, screening and follow-up specific to the cancer therapeutic.
An expert consensus summarises evidence for cardiac CT applications in cardio-oncology with practice recommendations.
A multidisciplinary consensus statement addresses cardiovascular manifestations from therapeutic radiation.
Expert panel discussion highlights gaps in evidence and drug-drug interactions in cardio-oncology.
A position paper addresses interventional cardiology in cancer patients.

ESC 2022 cardio-oncology guidance defines cancer therapy-related cardiac dysfunction by LVEF and strain: a fall in LVEF of 10 points or more to below 50%, or a relative fall in global longitudinal strain of over 15%, indicates dysfunction.

uncertainties: Optimal cardioprotective drug strategy.
case_hooks: Breast cancer patient on doxorubicin with falling LVEF.

standard_knowledge.claim: Cumulative lifetime doxorubicin dose is the strongest risk factor: heart failure incidence rises sharply above 400-500 mg/m2.
Dexrazoxane (iron-chelating topoisomerase II-beta inhibitor) significantly reduces anthracycline-induced cardiotoxicity without compromising oncological efficacy in high-risk patients.
Guideline-directed neurohormonal blockade (carvedilol, enalapril) initiated for early subclinical strain deterioration or asymptomatic LVEF drop prevents progression to clinical heart failure.

page.standard_overview: Anthracyclines such as doxorubicin and epirubicin can cause cumulative dose-related myocardial injury through topoisomerase II-beta-mediated effects, oxidative stress and cardiomyocyte death, with some injury becoming irreversible. Surveillance relies on baseline and serial echocardiography with global longitudinal strain (GLS). Dexrazoxane may be used for cardioprotection in selected high-risk patients receiving anthracyclines, and ACE inhibitors or beta-blockers may be considered according to cardiovascular risk and clinical findings.

topic: Antibiotic prophylaxis for infective endocarditis: high-risk procedures and patients

page.mentor_intro: Antibiotic prophylaxis before invasive dental procedures lowers infective endocarditis incidence in high-risk individuals, supporting AHA and ESC recommendations, with no proven association in low or unknown risk groups. S. aureus is now the most common causative organism.

teaching_points.claim: The 2023 ESC endocarditis guideline added a class I recommendation for surgery in early prosthetic valve endocarditis (under 6 months).
Percutaneous mechanical aspiration is the subject of an advisory for right-sided infective endocarditis, including patient selection and procedural planning.

Antibiotic prophylaxis before invasive dental procedures was associated with lower infective endocarditis incidence in high-risk individuals, with no association shown for low or unknown risk, supporting current AHA and ESC recommendations.
S. aureus is now the most common cause of infective endocarditis, with in-hospital mortality of 14% in the cited review.
Transitioning from intravenous to oral therapy for S. aureus bacteraemia or endocarditis is likely effective in a carefully selected subgroup but needs randomised trials.
In low-risk patients, TAVR gives long-term outcomes similar to SAVR, with more permanent pacemaker implantation.
ESC 2023 guidelines restrict antibiotic prophylaxis strictly to high-risk cardiac conditions undergoing dental procedures involving gingival or periapical manipulation.

uncertainties: Oral step-down evidence is limited.

standard_knowledge.claim: High-risk cardiac categories: prosthetic valves (transcatheter or surgical), prosthetic rings/cords, previous IE, and unrepaired cyanotic congenital heart disease.
The standard prophylaxis regimen is amoxicillin 2 g orally 30 to 60 minutes before the procedure; for penicillin allergy, azithromycin or clarithromycin 500 mg or doxycycline 100 mg is used.
Prophylaxis is NOT recommended for gastrointestinal, urological, respiratory, or routine skin procedures in the absence of established local infection.

page.standard_overview: Antibiotic prophylaxis for infective endocarditis (IE) is restricted to patients at the highest risk of adverse outcomes undergoing high-risk dental procedures involving manipulation of the gingival tissue, periapical region of teeth, or perforation of oral mucosa. High-risk conditions include prosthetic heart valves or prosthetic valve-repair material, previous infective endocarditis, and selected congenital heart disease such as unrepaired cyanotic lesions or repairs with residual hemodynamic abnormalities. The standard prophylactic regimen is a single oral dose of amoxicillin 2g 30-60 minutes pre-procedure.

page.mentor_intro: Antibody-drug conjugate toxicity depends on linker cleavability and payload release. Trastuzumab deruxtecan can cause interstitial lung disease, sacituzumab govitecan causes neutropenia and diarrhoea, and HER2-low reporting needs structured pathology.

teaching_points.claim: A US Delphi consensus guides prevention and management of stomatitis with datopotamab deruxtecan.
International consensus recommends structured HER2 reporting that distinguishes IHC 0 (null), 0+ (ultralow) and HER2-low.
ADCs with cleavable linkers cause premature payload release, raising systemic free payload and associated toxicities.
A meta-analysis of ADC toxicity found more all-grade treatment-related adverse events, with no increase in high-grade events.
Trastuzumab deruxtecan adverse events mostly affect blood, lymphatic and gastrointestinal systems, with interstitial lung disease a notable and potentially serious event.
Sacituzumab govitecan toxicity includes neutropenia, nausea, diarrhoea and anaemia, supporting prophylactic protocols.
Caution is advised when irradiating intracranial sites concurrently with trastuzumab emtansine, and international guidance on combining T-DM1 with radiotherapy is needed.
Enfortumab vedotin (targeting Nectin-4) combined with pembrolizumab established a new first-line standard of care in advanced urothelial carcinoma (EV-302 trial).

uncertainties: Optimal toxicity prophylaxis for each ADC.
mcq_angles: Interstitial lung disease with trastuzumab deruxtecan.

standard_knowledge.claim: Trastuzumab deruxtecan (T-DXd) demonstrated significant progression-free and overall survival improvements over standard therapy in HER2-low metastatic breast cancer (DESTINY-Breast04).

Interstitial lung disease is a recognised class toxicity of trastuzumab deruxtecan and other HER2-directed topoisomerase I conjugates, needing monitoring and prompt steroids; sacituzumab govitecan mainly causes neutropenia and diarrhoea.
The 'bystander killing effect' occurs when membrane-permeable cleaved cytotoxic payloads diffuse into adjacent antigen-negative tumor cells, overcoming intratumoral target heterogeneity.

page.standard_overview: Antibody-drug conjugates are designed to deliver potent cytotoxic payloads preferentially to tumor cells expressing a target surface antigen, using a monoclonal antibody, a cleavable or non-cleavable linker and a payload such as a topoisomerase I inhibitor, auristatin or calicheamicin. Landmark examples include trastuzumab deruxtecan (T-DXd) in HER2+ and HER2-low cancers, and enfortumab vedotin in urothelial cancer.

page.mentor_intro: Anti-CD20 therapy (rituximab) is supported by EULAR for lupus nephritis, in RA-ILD it is a safe option, and B-cell targeting is being reviewed across immune-mediated kidney disease. Cytokine release and infection risk require monitoring.

teaching_points.claim: EULAR 2025 recommendations for SLE with kidney involvement give consensus management adjusted for severity, long-term efficacy, safety, cost and drug availability.
An updated meta-analysis for RA-ILD supports the safety of methotrexate and particularly supports abatacept, rituximab and nintedanib as promising options.
A KDIGO controversies conference on targeting B cells in immune-mediated kidney diseases notes risks of cytokine release syndrome and the need for biomarkers and optimal treatment duration.
NMOSD consensus recommendations cover diagnosis, treatment and pregnancy planning after 12 months of stability.
Chinese guidance for off-label drug use in Sjogren's disease gives 21 recommendations for glandular, systemic and organ-specific manifestations.
Rituximab for myasthenia gravis has been tested in two trials with differing populations and dosing, leading to mixed conclusions.
The 2021 ACR guideline covers rituximab among options for patients with inadequate response to prior therapy, and seropositivity (RF or anti-CCP) predicts a better response.
In the MENTOR trial, rituximab was non-inferior to cyclosporine for remission of primary membranous nephropathy at 12 months and superior at 24 months.

uncertainties: Quality of evidence outside lupus nephritis and ANCA vasculitis.

page.standard_overview: Rituximab is a chimeric monoclonal antibody targeting CD20 on pre-B and mature B lymphocytes, mediating complement-dependent cytotoxicity and antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity. In rheumatology and nephrology, rituximab is used for rheumatoid arthritis refractory to anti-TNF therapy, ANCA-associated vasculitis and primary membranous nephropathy; in systemic lupus erythematosus it is off-label and generally reserved for selected refractory disease rather than being universal standard care.

topic: anticoagulation for atrial fibrillation in chronic kidney disease

page.mentor_intro: DOACs are as effective as and often safer than warfarin in AF, including CKD (CrCl 15 and above); evidence is weaker in dialysis. DOACs should be standard in low-risk AF needing anticoagulation, with correct dosing, and device-detected AF also benefits modestly.

teaching_points.claim: DOACs may increase efficacy and improve safety versus VKAs in AF with CKD (CrCl 15-90), with at least similar results in kidney failure.
In stage 5 CKD, DOACs showed a significant reduction in stroke and a non-significant trend to less major bleeding than VKAs.
In haemodialysis patients with AF, DOACs versus warfarin comparisons need validation by further prospective studies given thrombotic and bleeding risks.
DOACs should be standard of care in low-risk AF patients needing anticoagulation, with dabigatran showing the best balance of stroke prevention and bleeding reduction in one analysis.
A network meta-analysis found no difference in major bleeding, thromboembolism or mortality between DOACs and VKAs, and no DOAC clearly more favourable than others.
Anticoagulation with edoxaban or apixaban reduces stroke in device-detected AF and increases major bleeding.
Off-label underdosed DOACs, particularly rivaroxaban, were associated with increased ischaemic stroke without reduced bleeding, so on-label dosing should be emphasised.
DOACs may be a feasible option in AF with cirrhosis, pending validation.
Dabigatran is 80% renally eliminated and is contraindicated when CrCl < 30 mL/min in European guidelines.
Apixaban requires dose reduction to 2.5 mg BID if the patient meets at least two of the following criteria: age >= 80 years, body weight <= 60 kg, or serum creatinine >= 1.5 mg/dL (133 umol/L).

A KDIGO Controversies Conference on kidney disease and arrhythmias considered DOACs generally preferable to warfarin for atrial fibrillation in CKD stages 1 to 3, with limited trial evidence in advanced CKD.

uncertainties: Best strategy in dialysis patients.
case_hooks: AF patient with CKD stage 4 on warfarin considering a DOAC.

page.standard_overview: Atrial fibrillation is highly prevalent in patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD), significantly increasing stroke and bleeding risks. Direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs: apixaban, rivaroxaban, edoxaban, dabigatran) provide superior or non-inferior stroke prevention compared to warfarin in mild-to-moderate CKD (CrCl 30-50 mL/min). In severe CKD, apixaban may be considered using renal-function- and patient-specific dosing criteria; in dialysis, evidence remains limited and anticoagulant choice should be individualized.

page.mentor_intro: Warfarin remains the anticoagulant for mechanical valves; routine aspirin use beyond guideline indications adds bleeding. DOAC use in mechanical valves is under review, and low-dose vitamin K for supratherapeutic INR has not been shown to cause thromboembolism.

teaching_points.claim: A significant proportion of patients on warfarin for mechanical valves take guideline-discordant aspirin, and aspirin deprescribing in selected patients may safely reduce bleeding events.
A review compares direct-acting oral anticoagulants versus warfarin in mechanical valve patients, with findings needing exploration in specific subgroups.
Portable coagulometers with internet connectivity offer a new model of warfarin management after mechanical valve replacement, improving follow-up and compliance.
In pregnancy with a mechanical valve on non-warfarin anticoagulation, valve thrombosis may present as acute heart failure, and surgery should be prompt if needed.
In mechanical aortic valve patients with warfarin hypersensitivity due to an F9 variant, factor Xa or thrombin inhibitors deserve further investigation.

A systematic review and meta-analysis of vitamin K in mechanical valve patients with supratherapeutic INR addressed the thromboembolism risk of low-dose vitamin K, and more well-designed studies are needed.
AHA/ACC and ESC guidelines establish vitamin K antagonists (warfarin) as the only approved anticoagulation for mechanical heart valves; DOACs are absolutely contraindicated.
The RE-ALIGN trial testing dabigatran in mechanical heart valves was halted early due to an excess of ischemic strokes, valve thrombosis, and major bleeding.

uncertainties: DOACs in mechanical valves remain unproven.

topic: Anticoagulation in atrial fibrillation: CHA2DS2-VASc scoring and DOAC selection

page.mentor_intro: DOACs are as effective as and often safer than warfarin in AF, including CKD (CrCl 15 and above); evidence is weaker in dialysis. DOACs should be standard in low-risk AF needing anticoagulation, with correct dosing, and device-detected AF also benefits modestly.

teaching_points.claim: European Society of Cardiology 2024: Oral anticoagulation is recommended in all patients with AF and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy or cardiac amyloidosis, regardless of CHA2DS2-VA score, to prevent ischaemic stroke and thromboembolism.
DOACs may increase efficacy and improve safety versus VKAs in AF with CKD (CrCl 15-90), with at least similar results in kidney failure.
In stage 5 CKD, DOACs showed a significant reduction in stroke and a non-significant trend to less major bleeding than VKAs.
In haemodialysis patients with AF, DOACs versus warfarin comparisons need validation by further prospective studies given thrombotic and bleeding risks.
DOACs should be standard of care in low-risk AF patients needing anticoagulation, with dabigatran showing the best balance of stroke prevention and bleeding reduction in one analysis.
A network meta-analysis found no difference in major bleeding, thromboembolism or mortality between DOACs and VKAs, and no DOAC clearly more favourable than others.
Anticoagulation with edoxaban or apixaban reduces stroke in device-detected AF and increases major bleeding.
Off-label underdosed DOACs, particularly rivaroxaban, were associated with increased ischaemic stroke without reduced bleeding, so on-label dosing should be emphasised.
DOACs may be a feasible option in AF with cirrhosis, pending validation.
ESC 2024 guidelines recommend DOACs over warfarin as first-line stroke prevention for non-valvular atrial fibrillation (Class I, Level A).

The CHA2DS2-VASc score assigns points: heart failure (1), hypertension (1), age 75 or over (2), diabetes (1), prior stroke/TIA/thromboembolism (2), vascular disease (1), age 65 to 74 (1), female sex (1); ESC 2024 uses the CHA2DS2-VA score, which omits sex.
Meta-analysis of landmark DOAC trials demonstrates a 19% relative reduction in stroke/systemic embolism and a 51% reduction in hemorrhagic stroke compared to warfarin.

uncertainties: Best strategy in dialysis patients.

page.standard_overview: Stroke prevention in non-valvular atrial fibrillation is guided by the CHA2DS2-VASc risk score. Oral anticoagulation is recommended for men with score >= 2 and women with score >= 3, and should be considered for men with score 1 and women with score 2. page.mentor_intro: For cancer-associated VTE, LMWH or DOACs (apixaban, rivaroxaban) are used, with choice by bleeding risk, drug interactions and preference; anticoagulation continues beyond six months in active cancer. Thromboprophylaxis can be given in selected ambulatory patients.

teaching_points.claim: The BSH guideline recommends continuing anticoagulation beyond 6 months for cancer-associated VTE with active cancer, with drug choice guided by interactions and patient preference.

Guideline updates added DOACs as an option for VTE management in cancer patients.
An implementation model delivered VTE risk assessment and prophylaxis to prevent cancer-associated thrombosis in outpatients.
Multidisciplinary awareness programmes are needed to improve guideline adherence in cancer-associated VTE.

The CARAVAGGIO trial demonstrated that oral apixaban was non-inferior to subcutaneous dalteparin for recurrent VTE in cancer patients without an increase in major bleeding.

standard_knowledge.claim: Warfarin crosses the placental barrier and causes warfarin embryopathy (nasal hypoplasia, stippled epiphyses, CNS defects) when taken between 6 and 12 weeks gestation.
Direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) cross the placenta, have documented embryofetal toxicities in animal models, and are strictly contraindicated in pregnancy.
Peripartum management: therapeutic LMWH must be held at least 24 hours (and prophylactic LMWH held 12 hours) prior to planned induction or neuraxial anesthesia.

page.standard_overview: Pregnancy is a prothrombotic state with a 4- to 5-fold increased risk of venous thromboembolism. Low-molecular-weight heparin is the preferred anticoagulant during pregnancy because it does not cross the placenta; after delivery, either LMWH or warfarin can be used when anticoagulation is required. Warfarin can cause fetal embryopathy, particularly with exposure during the first trimester, and DOACs are not recommended during pregnancy because placental transfer is possible and fetal safety data are inadequate.

Ketamine and esketamine nasal spray provide rapid-onset antidepressant effects in treatment-resistant depression with acute suicidal ideation.

page.standard_overview: Major depressive disorder requires systematic, measurement-based pharmacotherapy, using tools such as the PHQ-9 to guide treatment response and stepwise adjustments. The landmark STAR*D trial demonstrated that approximately 33% of patients achieve remission with initial SSRI monotherapy (Step 1). Subsequent steps—switching classes (to bupropion, venlafaxine) or augmenting with bupropion, buspirone, lithium, or second-generation antipsychotics—were reported to reach cumulative remission of about 67%, a figure that later re-analyses suggested was overstated.

page.mentor_intro: Antiseizure medication choice is shaped by pregnancy risk, drug interactions and adverse effects. Folic acid of at least 0.4 mg daily is advised for people with epilepsy of child-bearing potential on ASMs, carbamazepine should not be co-prescribed with clozapine, and cannabidiol can cause liver injury.

teaching_points.claim: Clinicians should prescribe at least 0.4 mg of folic acid daily before and during pregnancy to people with epilepsy of child-bearing potential treated with an antiseizure medication, to reduce neural tube defects and possibly improve neurodevelopmental outcomes.
Carbamazepine should not be co-prescribed with clozapine because of agranulocytosis risk and induction of clozapine metabolism.
ILAE-linked guidance on neonatal seizures recommends a standardised pathway for managing neonatal seizures in each neonatal unit.
A national Delphi consensus in Egypt adapts epilepsy management to resource-limited settings.
Women with epilepsy have worse perinatal outcomes and should receive pregnancy counselling from an epilepsy specialist who can optimise their antiseizure regimen.
Cannabidiol-associated liver enzyme elevations and drug-induced liver injury are common adverse events, so liver function should be monitored.
After paediatric epilepsy surgery with seizure freedom, ASM cessation allows optimisation of intellectual and developmental trajectories.

In the SANAD II trials, lamotrigine was non-inferior and cost-effective compared with levetiracetam or zonisamide for newly diagnosed focal epilepsy, and valproate was superior to levetiracetam for generalised and unclassified epilepsy.

page.standard_overview: Antiseizure medication (ASM) selection is determined by seizure classification (focal vs generalized vs unclassified), patient demographics (age, childbearing potential), comorbidity profiles, and potential drug-drug interactions. Broad-spectrum ASMs (levetiracetam, lamotrigine, valproate, topiramate) are effective for both focal and generalized seizures. Sodium channel blockers (carbamazepine, phenytoin) treat focal seizures but can aggravate generalized absence or myoclonic seizures.

page.mentor_intro: Anti-GBM disease is rare with high renal risk. KDIGO 2021 covers glomerular disease management, double-positive ANCA/anti-GBM cases are difficult to treat, and kidney transplant should wait for 6 months of anti-GBM antibody negativity.

KDIGO 2021: However, if AA V overlaps with anti-GBM antibody GN, plasma exchange should be used.

Kidney transplantation in anti-GBM disease should be performed 6 months after absence of anti-GBM antibodies.
An international consensus recommends indirect immunofluorescence for ANCA testing beyond systemic vasculitis.
A core curriculum on therapeutic plasma exchange discusses its use from a nephrologist's perspective given limited supporting evidence.
Anti-GBM antibodies show high sensitivity and specificity for diagnosing anti-GBM disease, with cohort studies needed to compare immunoassays.
ANCA and anti-GBM double-positive patients are difficult to treat, supporting simultaneous antibody testing and systematic renal biopsy in rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis.
A meta-analysis of anti-GBM disease provides epidemiology, clinical features, risk factors and outcomes, with caution due to observational design.
About one in four children with crescentic glomerulonephritis progress to kidney failure.
The KDIGO 2021 glomerular disease guideline recommends plasma exchange together with cyclophosphamide and glucocorticoids for anti-GBM disease.

Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia prophylaxis with co-trimoxazole is mandatory during cyclophosphamide immunosuppression.

page.standard_overview: Anti-glomerular basement membrane disease is a rare, severe autoimmune small-vessel vasculitis mediated by antibodies against the NC1 domain of the alpha-3 chain of type IV collagen; Goodpasture syndrome describes the pulmonary-renal presentation. Anti-GBM disease can cause rapidly progressive crescentic glomerulonephritis and, in patients with pulmonary involvement, alveolar hemorrhage. Standard treatment is prompt plasma exchange combined with high-dose glucocorticoids and cyclophosphamide, with the cyclophosphamide route and regimen individualized to the patient.

page.mentor_intro: IL-6 receptor blockade is effective in difficult-to-treat RA (tocilizumab 8 mg/4 weeks may be first choice), giant cell arteritis and refractory uveitis, and in hospitalised moderate-to-severe COVID-19. Large-vessel vasculitis guidelines are updated, and upadacitinib is emerging in GCA.

teaching_points.claim: A systematic review informing EULAR PMR/GCA recommendations found multiple trials supporting IL-6, IL-17 and JAK inhibition and B-cell depletion in GCA and PMR, though robust Takayasu trials are lacking.
French recommendations standardise use of immunosuppressants and biologics in giant cell arteritis.
Turkish recommendations note upadacitinib seems promising in GCA but needs more real-life safety data in the elderly with high cardiovascular risk.
A systematic review supports the 2026 JCS guideline on large-vessel vasculitis, with comparable adverse event rates between treatment groups.
Several pharmacological interventions are efficacious and generally safe for managing fatigue in inflammatory rheumatic diseases.
Tocilizumab and rituximab have better efficacy and safety in difficult-to-treat RA, with tocilizumab 8 mg every 4 weeks possibly first choice for remission.
Tocilizumab is a therapeutic option for refractory non-infectious uveitis after failure of conventional immunosuppressants and anti-TNF agents.
Tocilizumab and sarilumab are effective in moderate-to-severe COVID-19 without burden of serious adverse events.
The GiACTA trial demonstrated that tocilizumab combined with a 26-week prednisone taper achieved 56% sustained remission at 52 weeks in giant cell arteritis compared to 14% with placebo.
In hospitalized patients with severe COVID-19 hypoxia and systemic inflammation, tocilizumab significantly reduces 28-day mortality and progression to mechanical ventilation (RECOVERY trial).

page.standard_overview: Antimicrobial stewardship programs (ASPs) optimize clinical outcomes while minimizing unintended consequences of antimicrobial use, including toxicity, selection of pathogenic organisms (such as Clostridioides difficile), and the emergence of antimicrobial resistance. Core strategies include pre-authorization, prospective audit with feedback, evidence-based guidelines, and diagnostic stewardship.

teaching_points.claim: A consensus-validated guideline recommends metformin for preventing antipsychotic-induced weight gain, including co-commencement.
The BAP guideline covers management of weight gain, metabolic disturbance and cardiovascular risk associated with psychotropic drugs.
UK recommendations support optimised use of metformin when managing antipsychotic-induced weight gain.
Metformin is effective for treating antipsychotic-induced weight gain in schizophrenia or schizoaffective disorder, but not for fasting glucose in one analysis.
Second-generation antipsychotics differ in propensity to produce weight gain and in the shapes of their dose-response curves.
GLP-1 agonists such as semaglutide and liraglutide are promising for antipsychotic-induced weight gain, with acceptable adverse effects and no worsening of psychopathology.
Antipsychotic-related weight gain is polygenic and associated with variants in genes coding for pharmacodynamic targets.
A meta-analysis described metabolic risk changes with second-generation antipsychotics from start of treatment to end of follow-up.
ADA/APA consensus guidance advises weight/BMI at baseline and at 4, 8 and 12 weeks then quarterly, and fasting glucose, lipids and blood pressure at baseline, 12 weeks and then annually.

page.mentor_intro: Mid-term outcomes of TAVR and SAVR in low-risk severe aortic stenosis are similar, though pacemaker implantation is more common with TAVR. Cerebral embolic protection is not supported routinely, and urgent TAVI lowers mortality compared with balloon valvuloplasty.

teaching_points.claim: An Italian interdisciplinary consensus addresses anaesthesia for transfemoral TAVI, with individualised decision-making.
Mid-term mortality and disabling stroke rates in severe aortic stenosis were similar with transcatheter and surgical replacement in low-risk patients.
Current evidence does not support routine use of cerebral embolic protection during TAVR given lack of significant benefit in key outcomes.
Urgent TAVI reduced in-hospital and 30-day mortality compared with balloon aortic valvuloplasty, though larger studies are needed.
Sutureless AVR had lower 30-day and one-year mortality and fewer valvular leaks than TAVR in a meta-analysis, with similar in-hospital and two-year mortality.
Unplanned conversion to cardiac surgery during TAVI is not increased in urgent versus elective cases, though AKI and longer stay suggest patient factors contribute to adverse outcomes.
SGLT2 inhibitor benefit after TAVI rests on limited observational evidence and needs randomised trials.
ESC/EACTS and ACC/AHA guidelines recommend single antiplatelet therapy (aspirin) as the standard default antithrombotic strategy in patients without OAC indications.

page.mentor_intro: Retrieved evidence centres on outcomes rather than the diagnostic pathway: type A dissection carries organ-specific malperfusion risk that predicts in-hospital death, and for type B the question is whether and when to add TEVAR to medical therapy. Guideline-level recommendations were not in the retrieved set.

teaching_points.claim: ACC/AHA 2022 aortic disease: In patients with AAS, initial management should include intravenous beta blockers, except in patients with contraindications.
ACC/AHA 2022 aortic disease: In patients with AAS, initial management should include intravenous vasodilators if the BP is not well controlled after initiation of intravenous beta-blocker therapy.

In acute type A aortic dissection, in-hospital survival varies with the type of malperfusion; mesenteric, coronary and cerebral malperfusion carried the highest in-hospital mortality, so organ-specific malperfusion should inform perioperative risk and surgical planning.
Women with type A dissection more often had pericardial effusion or tamponade, while in-hospital surgical mortality did not differ by sex (RR 1.02), suggesting a personalised approach.

A meta-analysis found TEVAR was associated with lower mortality than best medical therapy in type B dissection, especially in patients aged 65 or older, at the cost of longer hospital and ICU stays, with randomised trials still needed.

For uncomplicated type B dissection, the role of TEVAR remains debated: it improves aortic remodelling but there is no definitive survival evidence, and trials and guidelines that include high-risk features are needed.
Meta-analyses of TEVAR timing found the subacute phase (14-90 days from onset) associated with better long-term outcomes, including lower aortic-related death and reintervention.
Retrograde type A dissection after TEVAR is rare but carries high mortality (about 42%), especially in the first month and with proximal bare-stent grafts.
The GERAADA score showed better calibration than EuroSCORE II for 30-day mortality after surgery for acute type A dissection, though discrimination of both was moderate.
AI tools can feasibly detect aortic dissection on CT but do not yet demonstrate clinical applicability, and most studies were low quality.
The ACC/AHA and ESC aortic disease guidelines recommend emergency surgical repair for acute Stanford type A aortic dissection.

uncertainties: Whether pre-emptive TEVAR improves survival in uncomplicated type B dissection.
mcq_angles: Malperfusion type and operative mortality in type A dissection.
Timing of TEVAR in type B dissection.

standard_knowledge.claim: Initial medical management requires anti-impulse therapy: IV beta-blockers (esmolol, labetalol) to reduce heart rate < 60 bpm and shear stress (dP/dt), followed by vasodilators to achieve SBP 100-120 mmHg.

page.standard_overview: Acute aortic dissection is a life-threatening cardiovascular emergency resulting from an intimal tear that creates a false lumen in the aortic media. Stanford Type A involves the ascending aorta (mandates emergent open surgical repair). Stanford type B dissection is confined to the descending aorta and is initially treated with intravenous anti-impulse therapy when uncomplicated; complicated disease requires urgent intervention, and pre-emptive TEVAR may also benefit selected uncomplicated patients, often in the subacute phase.

page.standard_overview: Severe aortic stenosis (AS) is defined on transthoracic echocardiography by an aortic valve area (AVA) <= 1.0 cm2 (or indexed AVA <= 0.6 cm2/m2), mean transvalvular gradient >= 40 mmHg, or peak jet velocity >= 4.0 m/s. Symptomatic severe aortic stenosis has a poor prognosis without valve intervention, with historical survival varying by presentation and often falling to approximately 2-3 years in patients with heart failure or syncope. Low-flow, low-gradient AS requires integrated assessment of severity and flow: dobutamine stress echocardiography is useful mainly with reduced LV ejection fraction, while non-contrast CT aortic-valve calcium scoring can help in selected patients.

standard_knowledge.claim: Large real-world observational comparative effectiveness studies consistently associate apixaban with lower rates of major bleeding and gastrointestinal hemorrhage compared to rivaroxaban.
Rivaroxaban 15 mg and 20 mg tablets must strictly be taken with food to achieve predictable oral bioavailability (bioavailability falls to 66% in the fasting state).
Apixaban requires twice-daily dosing to maintain steady-state anticoagulation, reducing peak-to-trough plasma fluctuations compared to once-daily rivaroxaban.
Both agents are substrate of CYP3A4 and P-glycoprotein, requiring dose adjustment or avoidance with strong dual inhibitors (ketoconazole, ritonavir) or inducers (rifampin, carbamazepine).

page.standard_overview: Apixaban and rivaroxaban are direct factor Xa inhibitors widely prescribed for stroke prevention in non-valvular atrial fibrillation and treatment of venous thromboembolism. Apixaban is administered twice daily (12-hour half-life) and has the lowest renal elimination (~27%) among DOACs. Rivaroxaban dosing depends on the indication; 15 mg and 20 mg doses should be taken with food to ensure absorption, and approximately 35% is renally cleared. Large observational comparative studies show lower gastrointestinal bleeding and mortality with apixaban.

page.standard_overview: Acute appendicitis is a common surgical abdominal emergency; luminal obstruction by a fecalith or lymphoid hyperplasia can initiate distension, bacterial invasion, ischemia and eventual perforation, although the pathogenesis is not obstructive in every case. Diagnosis integrates clinical assessment, decision rules such as Alvarado or AIR, and imaging when needed; ultrasound is often preferred initially in children and pregnancy, while contrast-enhanced CT is commonly used in adults with uncertain diagnosis. Laparoscopic appendectomy remains the definitive standard of care, though selected uncomplicated cases can be managed with antibiotics.

page.standard_overview: Acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) is an acute diffuse inflammatory lung injury characterized by increased pulmonary vascular permeability, alveolar flooding, and severe refractory hypoxemia. The Berlin definition requires onset within 1 week of a known clinical insult, bilateral radiographic opacities not fully explained by effusions, atelectasis or nodules, respiratory failure not fully explained by cardiac failure or fluid overload, and PaO2/FiO2 <=300 mmHg with PEEP >=5 cmH2O. Core ventilatory management uses low tidal volumes, plateau-pressure limitation and minimization of driving pressure; prolonged prone positioning is added early for appropriately selected patients with moderate-to-severe ARDS.

page.standard_overview: Arterial leg ulcers are painful, ischemic, non-healing lower extremity wounds resulting from peripheral artery disease (PAD) and microvascular insufficiency. They are typically deep, punched-out, painful (worse with elevation, relieved by hanging leg over bed), located on distally perfused sites (toes, lateral malleolus, heels), with pale/cyanotic skin and absent pulses. Evaluation includes ABI and arterial duplex ultrasound, with toe pressures or other testing when vessels are non-compressible; patients with chronic limb-threatening ischemia require vascular assessment for revascularization when clinically indicated.

page.standard_overview: Asbestosis is a chronic interstitial pneumonitis and progressive pulmonary fibrosis caused by the inhalation of microscopic asbestos fibers. It typically manifests 20-30 years following substantial occupational exposure (shipyards, construction, insulation). Clinical features include exertional dyspnea, dry bibasilar inspiratory crackles, finger clubbing, and restrictive spirometry with reduced DLCO. HRCT in asbestosis shows subpleural reticulation, curvilinear lines and parenchymal bands; pleural plaques support prior asbestos exposure but may be non-calcified and are not themselves proof of pulmonary fibrosis.

page.standard_overview: Aspiration pneumonia occurs when colonized oropharyngeal or gastric secretions are inhaled into the lower respiratory tract, triggering acute bacterial infection. Dedicated anaerobic coverage is reserved for lung abscess, empyema, or severe periodontal disease.

page.mentor_intro: NSAID-exacerbated respiratory disease is managed with aspirin desensitisation, which can improve quality of life, and with biologics for associated nasal polyps; dupilumab is the most effective biologic for restoring smell. Urinary LTE4 is an investigational biomarker.

teaching_points.claim: The EAACI position paper defines N-ERD diagnosis and management and notes sub-endotypes may guide biological therapy.
Biologics targeting type 2 inflammation offer treatment options for uncontrolled nasal polyps as an alternative to surgery or after persistent symptoms despite surgery.
The chronic rhinosinusitis practice parameter addresses aspirin treatment after desensitisation and the risks of desensitisation.
The adult sinusitis guideline update recommends amoxicillin with or without clavulanate as first-line for acute bacterial rhinosinusitis.

standard_knowledge.claim: AERD is triggered by pharmacologic inhibition of cyclooxygenase-1 (COX-1), diverting arachidonic acid metabolism to the 5-lipoxygenase pathway and causing massive leukotriene release.
Selective COX-2 inhibitors (celecoxib, etoricoxib) do not trigger bronchospasm and are safe alternatives for analgesia in verified AERD.
Dupilumab (anti-IL-4Ralpha) and omalizumab (anti-IgE) achieve significant sinus polyp regression, asthma symptom control, and reduction in leukotriene production in AERD.
Aspirin desensitization followed by high-dose aspirin maintenance therapy (325-650 mg twice daily) provides disease-modifying reduction in nasal polyp recurrence.

page.standard_overview: Aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease (AERD / Samter triad) is a non-IgE-mediated pseudoallergic syndrome characterized by adult-onset asthma, recurrent chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps (CRSwNP), and severe acute upper and lower respiratory reactions following the ingestion of aspirin or other COX-1-inhibiting NSAIDs. Pathophysiology involves arachidonic acid dysregulation with cysteinyl leukotriene overproduction. AERD management includes asthma and nasal-polyposis treatment, avoidance of triggering COX-1 inhibitors and often leukotriene modifiers; biologics or aspirin desensitization followed by aspirin therapy are options for selected patients.

page.mentor_intro: Modern asthma care favours inhaled corticosteroid-containing regimens, with as-needed ICS-formoterol or maintenance-and-reliever therapy rather than SABA alone. Severe asthma needs phenotyping and consideration of biologics, macrolides or triple inhaler therapy.

teaching_points.claim: The 2025 VA/DoD guideline strongly recommends inhaled corticosteroids and suggests ICS combined with a rapid-onset long-acting beta-agonist as both reliever and controller, with step-up by increasing ICS or adding a long-acting anticholinergic.
The ERS/ATS severe asthma guideline suggests a trial of chronic macrolide therapy for persistent symptoms at GINA step 5 and anti-IL-4/13 for severe eosinophilic or corticosteroid-dependent asthma.

The ACCP 2026 guideline gives seven recommendations on choosing a biologic, based on quality of life, lung function, exacerbation frequency, oral steroid use, endotype, biomarkers and comorbidities, while noting no comparative effectiveness trials.
A Spanish study found most guideline quality indicators of asthma care are not followed in practice.

In poorly controlled asthma at GINA step 3 or 4, budesonide-formoterol maintenance and reliever therapy lengthened time to first severe exacerbation compared with stepping up or continuing maintenance ICS-LABA with SABA reliever.
Triple versus dual inhaler therapy in moderate to severe asthma was associated with fewer severe exacerbations and modest control gains, without differences in quality of life or mortality.
Licensed asthma biologics reduce exacerbations and hospitalisations, improve lung function, control and quality of life, and limit systemic corticosteroid use, with greater effect in T2 inflammation.
Clinical remission is achievable for a minority on biologics, with lower rates in those with worse FEV1, longer disease, maintenance oral corticosteroids, depression or obesity.
GINA guidelines recommend as-needed low-dose ICS-formoterol as the preferred reliever across all asthma severities, eliminating short-acting beta-2 agonist (SABA) monotherapy.

uncertainties: Head-to-head comparative efficacy of biologics.

Head-to-head comparisons show small effect size differences with wide confidence interval overlap, and direct pragmatic trials assessing remission are needed.

Real-world anti-IL5 biologics improve outcomes with effect sizes similar to RCTs, though data are largely retrospective.

teaching_points.claim: The Italian paediatric acute-asthma guideline advises against epinephrine, allows IV magnesium sulfate in severe attacks or FEV1 below 60% unresponsive to inhaled therapy, allows heliox in life-threatening attacks, and does not recommend leukotriene receptor antagonists.

A meta-analysis found moderate evidence that high-dose inhaled corticosteroids added to systemic corticosteroids reduce hospital admission (OR 0.73) in ED treatment of moderate-to-severe exacerbations.
In children, intravenous magnesium sulfate improved pulmonary function and reduced hospitalisation and further treatment, whereas nebulised magnesium had no significant effect.
Adherence of 80% or more lowered the odds of severe exacerbation (OR 0.53), and discontinuing therapy raised it.
Blood eosinophils of 200 cells/microlitre or more are associated with exacerbation (a modifiable factor in asthma management).
Inhaler technique education reduced exacerbation rates in older adults with asthma or COPD (pooled risk ratio 0.71).
Oral timolol and infusion propranolol were associated with higher asthma attack risk and should be avoided in patients at risk of asthma.
GORD and asthma exacerbation are only weakly associated.
GINA and BTS/SIGN guidelines mandate early systemic corticosteroids (oral prednisolone 40-50 mg daily) within 1 hour of ED presentation to accelerate resolution and prevent relapse.

A 'normal' or rising PaCO2 (>= 40-45 mmHg) in a severely tachypneic patient signifies impending respiratory muscle fatigue and catastrophic arrest.

page.standard_overview: Acute severe asthma exacerbation is a life-threatening medical emergency. Management focuses on rapid reversal of airflow obstruction, correction of hypoxemia, and prevention of respiratory arrest. Treatment includes repeated inhaled SABA, adding ipratropium bromide for moderate-to-severe attacks, early systemic corticosteroids, controlled oxygen targeting SpO2 93-95% in adults, and intravenous magnesium sulfate for severe attacks not responding to initial therapy.

page.mentor_intro: Modern asthma care favours inhaled corticosteroid-containing regimens, with as-needed ICS-formoterol or maintenance-and-reliever therapy rather than SABA alone. Severe asthma needs phenotyping and consideration of biologics, macrolides or triple inhaler therapy.

teaching_points.claim: The 2025 VA/DoD guideline strongly recommends inhaled corticosteroids and suggests ICS combined with a rapid-onset long-acting beta-agonist as both reliever and controller, with step-up by increasing ICS or adding a long-acting anticholinergic.
The ERS/ATS severe asthma guideline suggests a trial of chronic macrolide therapy for persistent symptoms at GINA step 5 and anti-IL-4/13 for severe eosinophilic or corticosteroid-dependent asthma.

The ACCP 2026 guideline gives seven recommendations on choosing a biologic, based on quality of life, lung function, exacerbation frequency, oral steroid use, endotype, biomarkers and comorbidities, while noting no comparative effectiveness trials.
A Spanish study found most guideline quality indicators of asthma care are not followed in practice.

In poorly controlled asthma at GINA step 3 or 4, budesonide-formoterol maintenance and reliever therapy lengthened time to first severe exacerbation compared with stepping up or continuing maintenance ICS-LABA with SABA reliever.
Triple versus dual inhaler therapy in moderate to severe asthma was associated with fewer severe exacerbations and modest control gains, without differences in quality of life or mortality.
Licensed asthma biologics reduce exacerbations and hospitalisations, improve lung function, control and quality of life, and limit systemic corticosteroid use, with greater effect in T2 inflammation.
Clinical remission is achievable for a minority on biologics, with lower rates in those with worse FEV1, longer disease, maintenance oral corticosteroids, depression or obesity.
GINA guidelines recommend as-needed low-dose ICS-formoterol as the preferred reliever across all asthma severities, eliminating short-acting beta-2 agonist (SABA) monotherapy.

uncertainties: Head-to-head comparative efficacy of biologics.

standard_knowledge.claim: ACOG and GINA guidelines emphasize that it is far safer for pregnant women to take asthma medications than to experience asthma exacerbations or hypoxia.
Inhaled budesonide is the preferred maintenance inhaled corticosteroid in pregnancy due to the largest volume of human safety data.
Acute asthma exacerbations in pregnancy require aggressive treatment: controlled oxygen targeting maternal SpO2 >= 95% to maintain adequate fetal oxygenation.
Systemic corticosteroids (oral prednisolone) should never be withheld in acute severe asthma exacerbations, as maternal hypoxia poses immediate fetal risk.

page.standard_overview: Asthma affects roughly 4 to 8% of pregnant women. Asthma may improve, remain stable or worsen during pregnancy; the traditional 'rule of thirds' is only an approximate heuristic and cannot predict an individual patient's course. Uncontrolled asthma with maternal hypoxia carries significant risks of pre-eclampsia, preterm birth, low birth weight, and perinatal mortality. Inhaled corticosteroids and SABA relievers should be continued when needed during pregnancy; budesonide has extensive safety data, but other effective inhaled corticosteroids are also acceptable.

page.mentor_intro: ACR Appropriateness Criteria (2017, updated 2026) guide imaging for renovascular hypertension. Endovascular treatment gives some blood pressure improvement over medical therapy in an updated meta-analysis, and RAS is common at coronary angiography, with CKD, PAD, older age and severe CAD the strongest predictors.

teaching_points.claim: ACR Appropriateness Criteria for renovascular hypertension guide imaging and treatment selection, updated in 2026.

An updated meta-analysis compared endovascular treatment with medical therapy in hypertensive patients with renal artery stenosis and found improvement with balloon angioplasty with or without stenting, calling for studies in more severe stenosis.
RAS is common in patients undergoing coronary angiography, with CKD, PAD, older age and severe CAD the strongest predictors.
In transplant renal artery stenosis, PTA with stenting appears more effective than PTA alone in stabilising renal function and reducing restenosis.
Catheter-based renal denervation safely reduces ambulatory and office blood pressure versus sham.

AHA/ACC and ESC guidelines restrict renal artery stenting to high-risk clinical presentations: recurrent unexplained flash pulmonary edema (Pickering syndrome) or refractory hypertension resistant to >= 4 medications.
The CORAL trial demonstrated that renal-artery stenting added to medical therapy did not reduce cardiovascular or renal events in atherosclerotic renal-artery stenosis.
The ASTRAL trial showed no evidence of clinically meaningful benefit of renal-artery revascularization on renal function or survival compared to medical therapy.

uncertainties: Benefit of revascularisation in severe stenosis.

page.standard_overview: Atherosclerotic renal artery stenosis (ARAS) is common in elderly patients with generalized vascular disease. Landmark randomized trials, including ASTRAL and CORAL, showed no meaningful routine renal-function or major renal/cardiovascular-event benefit from adding renal artery stenting to optimal medical therapy; CORAL did show a modest systolic blood-pressure difference favoring stenting (-2.3 mmHg). Optimal medical therapy is first-line for most patients with ARAS; revascularization is reserved for selected presentations such as flash pulmonary edema, truly refractory hypertension, or progressive renal dysfunction in appropriate high-grade bilateral or solitary-kidney disease.

page.mentor_intro: Paediatric atopic dermatitis guidelines advise emollients, topical therapy, phototherapy and systemic agents and strongly recommend against systemic corticosteroids. Real-world JAK inhibitor outcomes match trials, and dupilumab should prompt reassessment when cutaneous lymphoma is suspected.

teaching_points.claim: The 2026 paediatric atopic dermatitis guideline conditionally recommends against topical antimicrobials and PUVA phototherapy and strongly recommends against systemic corticosteroids.
Dupilumab may unmask or exacerbate cutaneous T-cell lymphoma, particularly mycosis fungoides and Sezary syndrome, so consensus recommendations guide patient selection and reassessment.
The European living guideline update on atopic eczema includes JAK inhibitors (abrocitinib, baricitinib, upadacitinib) and considerations for paediatric, pregnant and breastfeeding patients.
The ACG evidence-to-recommendation framework for mild and moderate atopic dermatitis weighs benefits, certainty, patient preferences and feasibility.
Real-world effectiveness and safety of JAK inhibitors in atopic dermatitis are comparable to clinical trials.
Increased pollutants and temperature extremes are associated with a higher population burden of atopic dermatitis.
Dupilumab in pregnancy showed no significant increase in miscarriage or congenital malformations, though evidence is limited.
AAD guidelines recommend proactive twice-weekly application of topical calcineurin inhibitors or low-potency steroids to previously affected sites to prevent recurrent flares.

uncertainties: Long-term safety of JAK inhibitors.
