Eczema herpeticum (disseminated cutaneous herpes simplex virus infection) is a dermatological emergency requiring immediate oral or intravenous acyclovir.

page.standard_overview: Atopic dermatitis (eczema) is a chronic, relapsing, pruritic inflammatory skin disease characterized by epidermal barrier dysfunction (often associated with filaggrin mutations) and immune dysregulation with prominent Th2 cytokine activation (IL-4, IL-13). Management follows a stepwise approach: daily bland emollients, topical corticosteroids or topical calcineurin inhibitors (tacrolimus) for flares, and targeted systemic biologics (dupilumab, tralokinumab) or oral JAK inhibitors for moderate-to-severe refractory disease.

page.mentor_intro: Catheter ablation reduces mortality, stroke and heart failure hospitalisation compared with medical therapy in AF, including in AF with heart failure and in HFpEF. A 4-week blanking period may be optimal, and uninterrupted NOACs cut major bleeding periprocedurally.

teaching_points.claim: European Society of Cardiology 2024: When cardioversion is planned, both 3 weeks of OAC and TOE should be considered because thrombi are common in patients with congenital heart disease and atrial arrhythmias.
A review compares guidelines and consensus documents on AF catheter ablation.
In AF with heart failure, catheter ablation reduces mortality and heart failure hospitalisation compared with medical therapy (RR 0.60 for hospitalisation).
Catheter ablation of AF significantly reduces death, stroke and hospitalisation compared with medical therapy alone.
In HFpEF with AF, catheter ablation showed cardiovascular morbidity and mortality benefits compared with standard medical therapy, and lower AF recurrence.
A 4-week blanking period may be the optimal cutoff after AF ablation, supporting revision of the current 3-month period.
Uninterrupted periprocedural NOACs are associated with low stroke or TIA and significantly less major bleeding than uninterrupted VKAs during AF ablation.
Most oesophageal injuries after AF ablation resolved conservatively, while a small percentage of type 2b lesions progressed to perforation or fistula.
ESC 2024 guidelines recommend DOACs over warfarin as first-line stroke prevention for non-valvular atrial fibrillation (Class I, Level A).

The CHA2DS2-VASc score assigns points: heart failure (1), hypertension (1), age 75 or over (2), diabetes (1), prior stroke/TIA/thromboembolism (2), vascular disease (1), age 65 to 74 (1), female sex (1); ESC 2024 uses the CHA2DS2-VA score, which omits sex.
Meta-analysis of landmark DOAC trials demonstrates a 19% relative reduction in stroke/systemic embolism and a 51% reduction in hemorrhagic stroke compared to warfarin.

uncertainties: Early rhythm control beyond ablation is not in the retrieved excerpts.

standard_knowledge.claim: Female sex is a risk modifier rather than an independent risk factor; a woman with no other risk factors does not need anticoagulation.

page.standard_overview: Stroke prevention in non-valvular atrial fibrillation is guided by the CHA2DS2-VASc risk score. Oral anticoagulation is recommended for men with score >= 2 and women with score >= 3, and should be considered for men with score 1 and women with score 2. For eligible patients with non-valvular atrial fibrillation, DOACs such as apixaban, rivaroxaban, dabigatran and edoxaban are generally preferred over warfarin because of their favorable efficacy and safety profile, including a substantial reduction in intracranial hemorrhage.

page.mentor_intro: DOACs are as effective as and often safer than warfarin in AF, including CKD (CrCl 15 and above); evidence is weaker in dialysis. DOACs should be standard in low-risk AF needing anticoagulation, with correct dosing, and device-detected AF also benefits modestly.

teaching_points.claim: DOACs may increase efficacy and improve safety versus VKAs in AF with CKD (CrCl 15-90), with at least similar results in kidney failure.
In stage 5 CKD, DOACs showed a significant reduction in stroke and a non-significant trend to less major bleeding than VKAs.
In haemodialysis patients with AF, DOACs versus warfarin comparisons need validation by further prospective studies given thrombotic and bleeding risks.
DOACs should be standard of care in low-risk AF patients needing anticoagulation, with dabigatran showing the best balance of stroke prevention and bleeding reduction in one analysis.
A network meta-analysis found no difference in major bleeding, thromboembolism or mortality between DOACs and VKAs, and no DOAC clearly more favourable than others.
Anticoagulation with edoxaban or apixaban reduces stroke in device-detected AF and increases major bleeding.
Off-label underdosed DOACs, particularly rivaroxaban, were associated with increased ischaemic stroke without reduced bleeding, so on-label dosing should be emphasised.
DOACs may be a feasible option in AF with cirrhosis, pending validation.
ESC 2024 guidelines recommend DOACs over warfarin as first-line stroke prevention for non-valvular atrial fibrillation (Class I, Level A).

The CHA2DS2-VASc score assigns points: heart failure (1), hypertension (1), age 75 or over (2), diabetes (1), prior stroke/TIA/thromboembolism (2), vascular disease (1), age 65 to 74 (1), female sex (1); ESC 2024 uses the CHA2DS2-VA score, which omits sex.
Meta-analysis of landmark DOAC trials demonstrates a 19% relative reduction in stroke/systemic embolism and a 51% reduction in hemorrhagic stroke compared to warfarin.

uncertainties: Best strategy in dialysis patients.

page.standard_overview: Atrial fibrillation is highly prevalent in patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD), significantly increasing stroke and bleeding risks. Direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs: apixaban, rivaroxaban, edoxaban, dabigatran) provide superior or non-inferior stroke prevention compared to warfarin in mild-to-moderate CKD (CrCl 30-50 mL/min). In severe CKD, apixaban may be considered using renal-function- and patient-specific dosing criteria; in dialysis, evidence remains limited and anticoagulant choice should be individualized.

topic: Atrial fibrillation catheter ablation and early rhythm control

page.mentor_intro: Catheter ablation reduces mortality, stroke and heart failure hospitalisation compared with medical therapy in AF, including in AF with heart failure and in HFpEF. A 4-week blanking period may be optimal, and uninterrupted NOACs cut major bleeding periprocedurally.

teaching_points.claim: European Society of Cardiology 2024: Catheter ablation is recommended as a first-line option within a shared decision-making rhythm control strategy in patients with paroxysmal AF, to reduce symptoms, recurrence, and progression of AF.

In AF with heart failure, catheter ablation reduces mortality and heart failure hospitalisation compared with medical therapy (RR 0.60 for hospitalisation).
Catheter ablation of AF significantly reduces death, stroke and hospitalisation compared with medical therapy alone.
In HFpEF with AF, catheter ablation showed cardiovascular morbidity and mortality benefits compared with standard medical therapy, and lower AF recurrence.
A 4-week blanking period may be the optimal cutoff after AF ablation, supporting revision of the current 3-month period.
Uninterrupted periprocedural NOACs are associated with low stroke or TIA and significantly less major bleeding than uninterrupted VKAs during AF ablation.
Most oesophageal injuries after AF ablation resolved conservatively, while a small percentage of type 2b lesions progressed to perforation or fistula.

page.standard_overview: Atypical pneumonia pathogens include cell-wall-deficient Mycoplasma pneumoniae and intracellular pathogens such as Chlamydia pneumoniae, Legionella pneumophila and Coxiella burnetii, the cause of Q fever. Beta-lactams are not effective treatments for these atypical pathogens: Mycoplasma lacks their peptidoglycan target, while the intracellular pathogens require antibiotics with appropriate intracellular activity. Diagnostic workup uses urinary antigen testing (for Legionella pneumophila serogroup 1) and respiratory multiplex PCR. First-line therapy relies on macrolides (azithromycin), respiratory fluoroquinolones (levofloxacin, moxifloxacin), or tetracyclines (doxycycline).

standard_knowledge.claim: Anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide (anti-CCP) antibodies have high diagnostic specificity (> 96%) for rheumatoid arthritis and predict progressive radiographic erosive joint damage.
Anti-dsDNA antibody titers correlate with disease activity and active lupus nephritis; falling complement (C3, C4) alongside rising anti-dsDNA signals an impending clinical flare.
Anti-Ro/SSA antibodies in pregnant women cross the placenta and carry a 2% risk of causing neonatal lupus erythematosus and irreversible congenital complete heart block in the fetus.

page.standard_overview: Autoantibody panels are essential diagnostic instruments in systemic autoimmune rheumatic diseases (SARD), but must be interpreted strictly within the pre-test clinical context to avoid false-positive misdiagnoses. Antinuclear antibody testing by indirect immunofluorescence on HEp-2 cells is a reference screening assay; the positive titer threshold is assay- and laboratory-dependent, commonly 1:80 or 1:160, rather than universally 1:160. Disease-associated autoantibodies help refine the diagnosis: anti-dsDNA and anti-Sm support SLE; anti-Ro/SSA and anti-La/SSB support Sjögren disease or SLE and relate to congenital heart block risk; anti-Scl-70, anti-centromere and anti-Jo-1 support diffuse systemic sclerosis, limited systemic sclerosis and myositis, respectively; anti-CCP and RF support rheumatoid arthritis; and ANCA supports ANCA-associated vasculitis.

page.standard_overview: Autoimmune encephalitis is a rapidly progressive inflammatory brain disease associated with autoantibodies against neuronal cell-surface or synaptic antigens, such as NMDA receptor, LGI1 and Caspr2, or intracellular onconeuronal antigens, such as Hu and Ma2. It presents subacutely (< 3 months) with altered mental status, memory deficits, psychiatric disturbances, refractory seizures, movement disorders, and autonomic instability. First-line immunotherapy consists of high-dose intravenous methylprednisolone, IVIG, or plasma exchange, alongside screening for occult systemic tumors (e.g. ovarian teratoma in anti-NMDAR).

page.mentor_intro: Autoimmune gastritis is an atrophic gastritis linked to pernicious anaemia, B12 deficiency and other autoimmune diseases, and it carries gastric cancer risk. AGA and ACG guidance covers endoscopic features, surveillance of gastric premalignant conditions, and NICE guidance covers B12 deficiency.

teaching_points.claim: The AGA update on atrophic gastritis describes endoscopic features such as pale mucosa, visible vasculature, loss of gastric folds and, with intestinal metaplasia, light blue crests and white opaque fields.

NICE guidance on vitamin B12 deficiency in people over 16 includes diagnosis and management related to autoimmune gastritis.
A range of autoimmune diseases is associated with gastric cancer, possibly reflecting unreported links with autoimmune gastritis.
Antibody-mediated autoimmune disease is prevalent in type 1 diabetes, especially hypothyroidism and coeliac disease.
Polyautoimmunity is prevalent in autoimmune thyroid disease, and clustering of diseases may define phenotypes.
Patients with chronic spontaneous urticaria have increased risk of autoimmune diseases and should be screened for signs and symptoms.
Endoscopic surveillance (MAPS II guidelines) is recommended every 3-5 years due to increased risks of Type 1 gastric neuroendocrine tumors (from hypergastrinemia) and gastric adenocarcinoma.

standard_knowledge.claim: Destruction of gastric parietal cells leads to achlorhydria, high fasting serum gastrin, and lack of intrinsic factor causing vitamin B12 deficiency (pernicious anemia).
Anti-parietal cell antibodies (APCA) are sensitive (80-90%) but less specific; anti-intrinsic factor antibodies (AIFA) have high diagnostic specificity (> 98%) for pernicious anemia.

Vitamin B12 deficiency produces megaloblastic anemia and subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord (posterior and lateral column demyelination); folic acid alone masks anemia while allowing neurological damage to progress.

page.standard_overview: Autoimmune gastritis (AIG) is a chronic, immune-mediated, organ-specific gastritis directed against gastric parietal cells and their secretory products (H+/K+-ATPase and intrinsic factor). It causes selective destruction of the oxyntic mucosa in the gastric body and fundus, sparing the antrum. Destruction of parietal cells causes achlorhydria (triggering hypergastrinemia and enterochromaffin-like [ECL] cell hyperplasia) and loss of intrinsic factor, producing vitamin B12 malabsorption (pernicious anaemia). Pernicious anemia requires lifelong parenteral or high-dose oral vitamin B12 replacement; iron deficiency should also be treated, and endoscopic surveillance for gastric neuroendocrine tumors and adenocarcinoma should be individualized according to risk and findings.

page.standard_overview: Autoimmune haemolytic anaemia (AIHA) is an immune-mediated disorder characterized by antibody-mediated destruction of red blood cells. It is classified into warm AIHA (wAIHA; 70-80% of cases, IgG-mediated, optimal binding at 37C, extravascular clearance in the spleen) and cold agglutinin disease (CAD; 15-20%, IgM-mediated, binding at 0-4C, classical complement-mediated intravascular and hepatic clearance). Diagnosis is based on laboratory evidence of hemolysis, such as elevated LDH and indirect bilirubin, reticulocytosis and reduced haptoglobin, together with a usually positive direct antiglobulin test; DAT-negative AIHA can occur. First-line therapy for wAIHA is oral prednisone (1 mg/kg/day); second-line is rituximab.

page.standard_overview: Autoimmune hepatitis (AIH) is a chronic, progressive necroinflammatory liver disease characterized by circulating autoantibodies, hypergammaglobulinemia (elevated IgG), and interface hepatitis on liver biopsy. Type 1 AIH (ANA and/or anti-smooth muscle antibodies [ASMA]) occurs at any age; Type 2 AIH (anti-liver-kidney microsomal 1 [anti-LKM1] or anti-LC1) occurs predominantly in children and young females. Standard first-line remission induction uses a systemic corticosteroid such as prednisone or prednisolone, alone or with azathioprine; azathioprine is also commonly used as a steroid-sparing maintenance agent, with timing individualized to the patient.

page.mentor_intro: IgG4-related disease guidelines (UEG/SGF, Japanese consensus) direct autoimmune pancreatitis diagnosis and steroid treatment; if disease activity does not change within three months the diagnosis should be reconsidered. IgG4-RD carries higher cancer risk, especially pancreatic and lymphoma.

teaching_points.claim: European IgG4-related digestive disease recommendations advise that if there is no change in disease activity within 3 months of treatment the diagnosis should be reconsidered, and immunosuppressive drugs added if relapse occurs on treatment.

IgG4-related sclerosing cholangitis guidelines give 14 diagnosis and 4 treatment clinical questions using modified Delphi methodology.
Paediatric recommendations from INSPPIRE standardise diagnosis and management of autoimmune pancreatitis in childhood.
Guidelines on primary sclerosing cholangitis include recommendations to distinguish it from IgG4-related sclerosing cholangitis.
Patients with IgG4-related disease have higher overall cancer risk than the general population, especially pancreatic cancer and lymphoma.
Chronic pancreatitis increases pancreatic cancer risk, rising with disease duration.

The International Consensus Diagnostic Criteria classify autoimmune pancreatitis into type 1 (the pancreatic manifestation of IgG4-related disease) and type 2 (pancreas-specific, associated with inflammatory bowel disease).

standard_knowledge.claim: Type 1 AIP is characterized by elevated serum IgG4 (> 1-2x upper limit of normal), storiform fibrosis, obliterative phlebitis, and abundant IgG4-positive plasma cells (> 10 per HPF).
Oral corticosteroids (prednisone 0.6-0.8 mg/kg daily, typically 30-40 mg daily for 2-4 weeks, then tapered) achieve rapid clinical and radiological remission in > 90% of AIP patients.
Rituximab (anti-CD20) is highly effective for inducing and maintaining remission in steroid-dependent or relapsing Type 1 IgG4-related AIP.

page.standard_overview: Autoimmune pancreatitis (AIP) is a unique form of chronic fibroinflammatory pancreatitis. Type 1 AIP (lymphoplasmacytic sclerosing pancreatitis; LPSP) is the classic pancreatic manifestation of systemic IgG4-related disease, presenting in older males with painless obstructive jaundice, elevated serum IgG4, diffuse sausage-like pancreatic enlargement, and prompt response to corticosteroids. Type 2 AIP (idiopathic duct-centric pancreatitis; IDCP) is pancreas-specific, affects younger adults equally by sex, is associated with inflammatory bowel disease in 30%, and has normal IgG4 levels.

standard_knowledge.claim: APS-1 is diagnosed clinically by the presence of at least 2 of the 3 cardinal features: chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis, hypoparathyroidism, and Addison disease.
APS-1 is caused by loss-of-function mutations in the AIRE gene on chromosome 21q22.3, which disrupts central thymic negative selection of self-reactive T cells.
APS-2 is strongly associated with HLA-DR3 and HLA-DR4 haplotypes; primary adrenal insufficiency is the mandatory component, accompanied by autoimmune thyroiditis or type 1 diabetes.
In patients presenting with concurrent adrenal insufficiency and hypothyroidism, glucocorticoid replacement must always precede levothyroxine to prevent precipitating acute fatal adrenal crisis.

page.standard_overview: Autoimmune polyglandular syndromes (APS) are clusters of multiple endocrine gland deficiencies combined with non-endocrine autoimmune diseases. APS-1 (APECED) is a rare monogenic autosomal recessive disease caused by mutations in the autoimmune regulator (AIRE) gene, presenting in childhood with the classic triad of chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis, hypoparathyroidism, and primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison disease). APS-2 (Schmidt syndrome) is a polygenic disorder occurring in adults, defined by primary adrenal insufficiency combined with autoimmune thyroid disease and/or type 1 diabetes mellitus.

standard_knowledge.claim: Familial Mediterranean Fever (FMF) attacks are short (12-72 hours) with serositis, fever, and erysipelas-like erythema; daily lifelong colchicine prevents attacks and secondary AA amyloidosis.
TRAPS is characterized by prolonged fever episodes lasting 1 to 3 weeks, accompanied by migrating painful erythematous plaques with underlying myalgia and periorbital edema.
CAPS represents a clinical spectrum (FCAS, Muckle-Wells syndrome, NOMID/CINCA) driven by NLRP3 gain-of-function resulting in constitutive inflammasome assembly and excess IL-1beta release.

page.standard_overview: Systemic autoinflammatory diseases are disorders of innate immunity characterized by recurrent or persistent systemic inflammation, usually without high-titer autoantibodies or antigen-specific T cells; many are monogenic. Key hereditary periodic fever syndromes include Familial Mediterranean Fever (FMF; MEFV/pyrin mutation; responds to colchicine), Tumor Necrosis Factor Receptor-Associated Periodic Syndrome (TRAPS; TNFRSF1A mutation; prolonged attacks 1-3 weeks; responds to anti-IL-1), Cryopyrin-Associated Periodic Syndromes (CAPS; NLRP3 mutation; responds to canakinumab/anakinra), and Hyper-IgD Syndrome (HIDS/MKD).

topic: Autonomic dysfunction in cardiovascular disease: POTS, OH, vagal syncope

page.mentor_intro: Orthostatic hypotension is common in Parkinson disease (33.1%) and frailty and drives falls, yet intensive blood pressure treatment still reduces cardiovascular events regardless of orthostatic hypotension. Neurogenic OH shows exaggerated cerebral blood flow falls, and supine hypertension is highly prevalent in alpha-synucleinopathies.

teaching_points.claim: In hypertension trials, intensive therapy reduced cardiovascular disease or all-cause mortality regardless of orthostatic hypotension, without evidence of different effects in those with standing hypotension.
The prevalence of orthostatic hypotension in Parkinson's disease is 33.1%, more in older patients with longer duration and more severe motor symptoms.
Supine hypertension is highly prevalent across alpha-synucleinopathies, varying by disease type and presence of OH.

page.standard_overview: Cardiovascular autonomic dysfunction encompasses disorders of autonomic blood pressure and heart rate regulation, primarily Postural Orthostatic Tachycardia Syndrome (POTS), Neurogenic Orthostatic Hypotension (nOH), and Vasovagal (neurocardiogenic) Syncope. POTS requires chronic symptoms of orthostatic intolerance together with a sustained heart-rate increase of at least 30 bpm, or at least 40 bpm in individuals aged 12-19 years, within 10 minutes of standing or head-up tilt, without orthostatic hypotension. Orthostatic hypotension is defined as a sustained drop in SBP >= 20 mmHg or DBP >= 10 mmHg within 3 minutes of standing. Management emphasizes non-pharmacological volume expansion, compression garments, exercise conditioning, and targeted pharmacotherapy (midodrine, fludrocortisone, droxidopa, pyridostigmine, ivabradine).

topic: Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease tolvaptan

page.mentor_intro: KDIGO 2025 provides the current ADPKD guideline, and tolvaptan selection follows an updated consensus algorithm for rapid progression. mTOR inhibitors and somatostatin analogues are not recommended, statins have consensus support, and nephrectomy is a shared decision after multidisciplinary consultation.

A consensus statement says deciding on nephrectomy and alternatives such as kidney embolisation should be shared decision-making after multidisciplinary consultation.

page.standard_overview: Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD) is the most common monogenic kidney disease, primarily caused by PKD1 (~78%) and PKD2 (~15%) mutations. Tolvaptan, an oral selective vasopressin V2 receptor antagonist, slows kidney cyst growth and decelerates the rate of eGFR decline in rapidly progressing ADPKD (TEMPO 3:4 and REPRISE trials). Candidates are stratified by Mayo Imaging Classification (Classes 1C, 1D, 1E) or rapid eGFR decline (>= 3.0 mL/min/1.73 m2/year). Due to idiosyncratic hepatotoxicity, mandatory monthly liver function monitoring is required for the first 18 months and quarterly thereafter.

page.standard_overview: Avascular necrosis (AVN, osteonecrosis) of bone results from compromised microvascular blood supply leading to osteocyte death, subchondral microfractures, and eventual structural joint collapse, predominantly affecting the femoral head. Major etiologies include high-dose systemic corticosteroid therapy, chronic excess alcohol use, sickle cell disease, trauma (femoral neck fracture), and systemic lupus erythematosus. Early pre-collapse diagnosis is achieved using MRI (pathognomonic 'double-line sign' on T2-weighted sequences). Pre-collapse osteonecrosis is often managed with joint-preserving treatment such as core decompression with or without bone marrow aspirate concentrate; advanced collapse or secondary arthritis often requires total joint arthroplasty, while selected early-collapse disease may still be considered for joint preservation.

page.standard_overview: Acute community-acquired bacterial meningitis is a life-threatening neurologic emergency requiring immediate empiric parenteral bactericidal antibiotics, with adjuvant dexamethasone when indicated. Most common pathogens are Streptococcus pneumoniae, Neisseria meningitidis, and in adults >= 50 or immunocompromised hosts, Listeria monocytogenes. Standard empiric therapy in adults < 50 is IV ceftriaxone (2 g q12h) plus IV vancomycin (15-20 mg/kg q8-12h); adults >= 50 or immunocompromised require the addition of IV ampicillin (2 g q4h) to cover Listeria. Adjuvant dexamethasone 10 mg IV should ideally be given before or with the first antibiotic dose; in high-income settings it reduces mortality in pneumococcal meningitis and reduces hearing loss in bacterial meningitis.

page.standard_overview: Metabolic and bariatric surgery (MBS) is the most effective and durable intervention for severe obesity and related cardiometabolic comorbidities. The ASMBS/IFSO 2022 guidelines recommend metabolic and bariatric surgery for individuals with BMI of at least 35 kg/m2 regardless of comorbidities and state that it should be considered for those with BMI 30-34.9 kg/m2 and metabolic disease. The STAMPEDE trial showed that Roux-en-Y gastric bypass or sleeve gastrectomy plus intensive medical therapy produced greater 5-year improvements in glycemic control and reductions in weight and medication use than intensive medical therapy alone, with diabetes remission in some surgical patients. RYGB has higher rates of internal hernia, marginal ulcers, and micronutrient malabsorption (iron, calcium, vitamin B12, copper), whereas sleeve gastrectomy has higher risks of de novo or worsening gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD).

page.standard_overview: Barrett's esophagus (BE) is the replacement of normal stratified squamous esophageal epithelium by specialized intestinal metaplasia with goblet cells, predisposing to esophageal adenocarcinoma. Diagnosis requires endoscopically visible columnar epithelium >= 1 cm proximal to the gastroesophageal junction (Prague C & M criteria) and histological confirmation of intestinal metaplasia. ACG guidelines recommend endoscopic surveillance every 3-5 years for non-dysplastic BE. For confirmed low-grade dysplasia, endoscopic eradication therapy with resection of visible nodular lesions followed by radiofrequency ablation is preferred, although surveillance remains an alternative; high-grade dysplasia and intramucosal carcinoma should be treated with endoscopic eradication after appropriate staging and expert assessment.

Vismodegib and sonidegib inhibit smoothened in the Hedgehog pathway, with objective response rates of roughly 40 to 60% in locally advanced basal cell carcinoma and lower (about 30%) in metastatic disease (ERIVANCE, BOLT).

page.standard_overview: Basal cell carcinoma (BCC) is the most common human malignancy, driven by ultraviolet radiation-induced oncogenic mutations activating the Hedgehog (PTCH1/SMO) signaling pathway. Clinical subtypes include nodular (pearly papule with telangiectasias and rolled borders), superficial (erythematous scaly plaque), and infiltrative/morpheaform (firm scar-like plaque). Treatment is risk-stratified: low-risk lesions may be treated with standard surgical excision or, in selected sites and subtypes, electrodessication and curettage; Mohs micrographic surgery is preferred for many high-risk or recurrent lesions, including critical facial sites and aggressive histology. Locally advanced or metastatic BCC that is not amenable to surgery or radiotherapy may be treated with an oral Hedgehog inhibitor such as vismodegib or sonidegib; cemiplimab is used after Hedgehog-inhibitor progression, intolerance or contraindication.

standard_knowledge.claim: BCP crystals (hydroxyapatite) are submicroscopic and non-birefringent under compensated polarized light, distinguishing them from birefringent monosodium urate and CPPD crystals.
Alizarin Red S staining demonstrates characteristic bright red-orange crystal clumps under light microscopy, facilitating rapid identification of BCP deposition.
Milwaukee shoulder syndrome is characterized by rapid destructive arthropathy of the glenohumeral joint, massive rotator cuff disruption, and large non-inflammatory serosanguinous joint effusions.
Surgical management of advanced Milwaukee shoulder requires reverse total shoulder arthroplasty (rTSA) to restore shoulder kinematics in the absence of an intact rotator cuff.

page.standard_overview: Basic calcium phosphate (BCP) crystal deposition encompasses carbonate-substituted hydroxyapatite, octacalcium phosphate, and tricalcium phosphate. BCP crystals deposit in periarticular structures (calcific tendinitis of the rotator cuff) or cause destructive arthropathy, most notably Milwaukee shoulder syndrome (rapidly destructive cuff-tear arthropathy). Milwaukee shoulder predominantly affects elderly women, presenting with large, cool, non-inflammatory hemorrhagic joint effusions, extensive rotator cuff tearing, and severe glenohumeral osteolysis. Synovial fluid is non-inflammatory (< 2,000 WBC/uL) with negative polarizing microscopy (BCP crystals are submicroscopic and non-birefringent, requiring Alizarin Red S staining or electron microscopy). Management consists of joint aspiration, intra-articular corticosteroids, NSAIDs, and reverse total shoulder arthroplasty.

page.mentor_intro: Guidelines for BPSD vary between statements, and non-pharmacological and person-centred approaches are favoured for emotional symptoms and sleep, with atypical antipsychotics reserved for severe symptoms because of a trade-off between benefit and harm. Reminiscence therapy and home-based activity help.

teaching_points.claim: A systematic review of BPSD guidelines found variability in recommendation statements and insufficient consideration of applicability, which may hamper implementation.
In a guideline review, non-pharmacological treatments may suit emotional symptoms and sleep disorders, with atypical antipsychotics a better choice for severe symptoms.
A network meta-analysis supports a trade-off between effectiveness and safety of atypical antipsychotics in dementia-related symptoms.
Person-centred care interventions improve BPSD and cognitive function in persons with dementia.
Dyadic psychological interventions should involve both the person with dementia and the caregiver, targeting anxiety, quality of life and carer burden.

page.standard_overview: Behavioural and psychological symptoms of dementia (BPSD) - including agitation, aggression, psychosis, depression, apathy, and wandering - occur in > 80-90% of dementia patients over the course of illness. Initial management emphasizes non-pharmacological care: identify and treat underlying triggers such as pain, infection, constipation, delirium or sensory deficits, and use individualized behavioral strategies such as the DICE approach (Describe, Investigate, Create, Evaluate). Pharmacotherapy with atypical antipsychotics (risperidone, olanzapine) should be restricted to patients with severe, distressing, or dangerous aggression/psychosis where non-pharmacological interventions fail, due to an increased risk of stroke and mortality (black-box warning). Brexpiprazole is the first FDA-approved medication specifically for agitation associated with Alzheimer's dementia.

page.standard_overview: Behçet's disease is a systemic variable-vessel vasculitis characterized by recurrent painful oral aphthous ulcers, genital ulcers, inflammatory ocular disease (relapsing panuveitis, retinal vasculitis), and cutaneous lesions (erythema nodosum, pseudofolliculitis). The pathergy test (development of a pustule 24-48 hours after sterile needle prick) is highly specific. Venous thromboembolism (deep vein thrombosis, Budd-Chiari, dural venous sinus thrombosis) and pulmonary artery aneurysms are classic severe vascular complications. EULAR guidelines recommend colchicine for mucocutaneous manifestations, topical corticosteroids for aphthous ulcers, azathioprine or TNF inhibitors (adalimumab, infliximab) for sight-threatening uveitis and vascular disease, and high-dose glucocorticoids + cyclophosphamide for pulmonary artery aneurysms. Before anticoagulation, pulmonary artery aneurysm should be considered and assessed with CT or MR angiography when clinically suspected; immunosuppression is the mainstay of vascular treatment, and anticoagulation should be individualized cautiously after assessing bleeding risk.

page.standard_overview: Targeted biologics have transformed the management of systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) with active disease refractory to standard-of-care antimalarials (hydroxychloroquine) and corticosteroids. Belimumab is a human monoclonal antibody that neutralizes soluble B-lymphocyte stimulator (BLyS/BAFF), inhibiting autoreactive B-cell survival. In TULIP-2, anifrolumab significantly improved BICLA response and skin manifestations (TULIP-1 missed its SRI-4 primary endpoint) in moderate-to-severe SLE.

page.standard_overview: Bell's palsy is an acute, unilateral peripheral facial nerve (CN VII) paresis of idiopathic etiology, frequently linked to reactivation of herpes simplex virus type 1 (HSV-1) within the geniculate ganglion. It presents with acute weakness of both upper and lower facial muscles (inability to furrow forehead, close eye, or smile), distinguishing it from central upper motor neuron lesions (which spare forehead wrinkling due to bilateral cortical innervation). AAO-HNS strongly recommends oral corticosteroids within 72 hours of symptom onset for patients aged 16 years or older without contraindications; a common regimen is prednisone 50-60 mg daily, using a fixed course or a short course followed by a taper. Antiviral monotherapy is not recommended; adding an antiviral to corticosteroids may have little or no effect on incomplete recovery, including in severe paralysis, but may reduce long-term sequelae and remains a treatment option. Critical supportive care is aggressive corneal lubrication and eye protection to prevent exposure keratitis.

page.standard_overview: Benign Paroxysmal Positional Vertigo (BPPV) is the most common peripheral vestibular disorder, caused by free-floating otoconia (calcium carbonate crystals) detached from the utricle that enter the semicircular canals (canalithiasis, > 90% posterior canal). It presents with brief recurrent episodes of spinning vertigo (< 60 seconds) triggered by head position changes (rolling over in bed, looking upward). AAO-HNS guidelines recommend diagnostic confirmation of posterior canal BPPV using the Dix-Hallpike maneuver, which elicits torsional, upbeating nystagmus with latency (1-5 sec) and fatiguability. Posterior-canal BPPV is treated with the Epley canalith-repositioning maneuver, which is highly effective; routine vestibular-suppressant medication is not recommended, although limited short-term symptom relief may occasionally be considered.

page.standard_overview: Benign pleural diseases associated with environmental or occupational asbestos exposure include pleural plaques, benign asbestos pleural effusion (BAPE), diffuse pleural thickening (DPT), and rounded atelectasis (Blesovsky syndrome). Pleural plaques are the most common manifestation (occurring 20-30 years post-exposure), characterized by well-circumscribed, bilateral fibrocalcific plaques on the parietal pleura (posterolateral chest wall and diaphragm) that are asymptomatic and do not undergo malignant degeneration into mesothelioma. In contrast, diffuse pleural thickening involves visceral-parietal pleural symphysis, classically over more than 25% of the hemithorax, and can cause restrictive ventilatory impairment and dyspnea. Benign asbestos pleural effusion is an exudative, sometimes hemorrhagic effusion that often occurs earlier after exposure than plaques and may resolve spontaneously, although recurrence or subsequent diffuse pleural thickening can occur.

page.standard_overview: Benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) is an age-dependent, non-malignant adenomatous proliferation of the prostatic transitional zone leading to lower urinary tract symptoms (LUTS: storage symptoms [urgency, frequency, nocturia] and voiding symptoms [hesitancy, weak stream, intermittency, straining]). Initial evaluation includes symptom assessment, often with the IPSS, and urinalysis; post-void residual measurement is useful in selected patients, and serum PSA is appropriate when the result would change management. First-line medical therapy for moderate-to-severe symptoms includes alpha-1 blockers (tamsulosin, alfuzosin, silodosin) for rapid symptom relief, and 5-alpha reductase inhibitors (5-ARIs: finasteride, dutasteride) for enlarged prostates (> 30 mL) to reduce prostate volume, prevent acute urinary retention, and reduce the need for surgery. Phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors (tadalafil 5 mg daily) are indicated for concurrent LUTS and erectile dysfunction.

topic: benzodiazepine deprescribing in anxiety and insomnia

page.mentor_intro: Deprescribing benzodiazepines and Z-drugs is feasible with structured support and may be done by pharmacists, though evidence quality is low. Withdrawal rates vary by intervention type, psychotherapy and tapering support help, and inpatient withdrawal needs an individualised taper.

teaching_points.claim: A narrative review proposes a systematic, individualised taper for inpatient benzodiazepine withdrawal, especially in complex patients with co-occurring disorders and protracted symptoms.
Deprescribing benzodiazepines and Z-drugs is feasible depending on the process and support employed, with very low to low quality evidence of effectiveness (intervention versus routine care RR 3.26).
Withdrawal of benzodiazepines and hypnotics is feasible in older people, though withdrawal rates vary by intervention type and sustainability is unclear.
Pharmacists may contribute to deprescribing benzodiazepines in older outpatients.
A review of interventions to improve tapering success in older adults notes psychotherapy costs as an issue and calls for research on pharmaceutical adjuvants.

After catatonia has been fully treated and maintenance lorazepam established, lorazepam should be discontinued in line with benzodiazepine discontinuation guidelines to minimise catatonia re-emergence.

AGS Beers Criteria and Deprescribing Guidelines strongly recommend tapering and discontinuing benzodiazepines and Z-drugs in older adults due to elevated risks of falls, fractures, delirium, and cognitive decline.

Structured, gradual dose-reduction (for example 10 to 25% every 2 to 4 weeks) combined with patient education (EMPOWER trial) led to benzodiazepine discontinuation in about a quarter of chronic users versus 5% with usual care.

AGS Beers Criteria strongly recommend avoiding benzodiazepines in older adults for insomnia or anxiety. Deprescribing requires patient engagement, structured shared decision-making, and a gradual dose reduction schedule (typically decreasing 10-25% of the baseline dose every 2-4 weeks over months to over a year) to prevent withdrawal syndromes (rebound insomnia, autonomic instability, delirium, seizures). Switching to a longer-acting agent (diazepam) may facilitate smooth tapering in difficult cases. Cognitive Behavioral Therapy for Insomnia (CBT-I) is the recommended first-line substitute therapy for chronic insomnia.

standard_knowledge.claim: The Beryllium Lymphocyte Proliferation Test (BeLPT) is the gold standard diagnostic test, measuring in vitro proliferation of memory T-cells exposed to beryllium salts in blood or BAL fluid.
The HLA-DPB1 Glu69 allele is strongly associated with beryllium sensitisation and progression to chronic beryllium disease.
ATS criteria for definite CBD require: 1) documented occupational exposure, 2) positive blood or BAL BeLPT, and 3) lung biopsy demonstrating non-caseating granulomas.
First-line therapy for symptomatic or progressive CBD is oral corticosteroids (prednisone 0.5 mg/kg daily tapered over months), with methotrexate or azathioprine as steroid-sparing alternatives.

page.standard_overview: Chronic Beryllium Disease (CBD, berylliosis) is an occupational granulomatous lung disease caused by a cell-mediated hypersensitivity reaction to inhaled beryllium dust or fumes, primarily in aerospace, telecommunications, electronics, nuclear defense, and dental alloy manufacturing. It is strongly linked to genetic susceptibility conferred by the HLA-DPB1 allele containing a glutamic acid at position 69 (Glu69). Pathologically, CBD is characterized by non-caseating granulomas and may cause interstitial fibrosis; it can closely mimic sarcoidosis clinically and radiologically. Diagnosis requires demonstration of beryllium-specific sensitization via the Beryllium Lymphocyte Proliferation Test (BeLPT) in blood or bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) fluid, coupled with biopsy evidence of non-caseating granulomas. Management includes cessation of beryllium exposure, with systemic corticosteroids reserved for clinically significant or progressive disease and other immunosuppression considered when needed.

topic: best initial test for suspected pulmonary embolism in a stable patient

page.mentor_intro: In a haemodynamically stable patient the first step is a pre-test probability assessment, then D-dimer in non-high probability, then imaging. Age-adjusted D-dimer and the YEARS algorithm reduce imaging while staying safe.

teaching_points.claim: D-dimer interpretation depends on assay performance characteristics, and international guidelines differ in how they allow age-adjusted and pretest-adjusted thresholds.
In pregnancy, introducing the pregnancy-adapted YEARS guideline increased investigation for PE, and over 5 years there were no known missed cases among women assessed with D-dimer alone.
Original and simplified Wells rules combined with age-adjusted D-dimer have similar performance for ruling out PE, and the simplified Wells rule is preferred for ease of use.
Age-adjusted D-dimer cutoffs combined with low clinical probability rule out PE with fewer false positives than conventional D-dimer, across 47,720 patients with non-high clinical probability.
The YEARS algorithm had pooled sensitivity of 96% and specificity of 50%, with a risk ratio of 0.78 for advanced imaging use, suggesting it is effective and safe.

In cancer patients, D-dimer with clinical decision rules had failure rates similar to standard imaging, with the highest yield (26%) from revised Geneva with age-adjusted D-dimer and the YEARS algorithm.
In COVID-19, D-dimer of at least 1000 micrograms/L may help select patients for CT pulmonary angiography.
Double low-dose CT pulmonary angiography is feasible, with reduced radiation and contrast dose without compromising diagnostic image quality.
The ADJUST-PE trial proved that using an age-adjusted D-dimer cutoff (age x 10 ug/L in patients aged > 50 years) increases diagnostic specificity without missing PE events.

page.standard_overview: The diagnostic evaluation of suspected acute pulmonary embolism (PE) in a hemodynamically stable patient relies on sequential pre-test clinical probability assessment, age-adjusted D-dimer testing, and definitive imaging to minimize unnecessary radiation. Validated prediction rules (Wells score or revised Geneva score) stratify patients into low, intermediate, or high probability. In low-risk patients, the Pulmonary Embolism Rule-out Criteria (PERC rule: age < 50, HR < 100, SpO2 >= 95%, no prior DVT/PE, no recent surgery/trauma, no hemoptysis, no estrogen use, no unilateral leg swelling) safely excludes PE without laboratory testing (PROPER trial). For patients with non-high or PE-unlikely clinical probability, including low-risk patients who are PERC-positive, a negative high-sensitivity D-dimer can rule out PE; the age-adjusted cutoff is age x 10 ug/L in patients older than 50 years (ADJUST-PE). When imaging is required, Computed Tomography Pulmonary Angiography (CTPA) is the diagnostic gold standard; Ventilation/Perfusion (V/Q) planar/SPECT scintigraphy is preferred in severe renal impairment or severe contrast allergy.

topic: Beta-blockers in heart failure: carvedilol, bisoprolol, metoprolol succinate titration

page.mentor_intro: In heart failure beta-blocker use is established, but in HFpEF observational data show mortality association without effect on rehospitalisation. Evidence for long-term beta-blockers after uncomplicated MI is weak, and heart rate remains high in many HFrEF patients despite titration.

teaching_points.claim: Higher heart rate was frequent in HFrEF even after aggressive titration and was associated with worse outcomes.
A consensus statement from India recommends the place of bisoprolol in heart failure management.

Beta-blocker therapy in HFpEF was associated with lower mortality in observational studies but did not affect rehospitalisation for heart failure or the composite with mortality, and large randomised trials are needed.
Prolonged beta-blocker treatment does not change peak VO2 but improves functional status in heart failure patients.
Oral beta-blockers for a year or more after MI do not reduce mortality in patients without heart failure in the reperfusion era.
In patients without heart failure or LV systolic dysfunction after ACS in the PCI era, beta-blocker therapy at discharge may still be associated with lower all-cause death.
The impact of beta-blocker maintenance on decompensated heart failure remains uncertain and needs more randomised trials.
Short-acting metoprolol tartrate was inferior to carvedilol in reducing all-cause mortality in the COMET trial and should not be used for HFrEF.

Titration must be gradual, doubling doses every 2-4 weeks in euvolemic patients toward target doses: carvedilol 25 mg BID (50 mg BID if > 85 kg), bisoprolol 10 mg daily, or metoprolol succinate 200 mg daily.

During acute decompensated heart failure, continuation of beta-blocker therapy (at current or slightly halved dose) is associated with lower post-discharge mortality compared to withdrawal, unless cardiogenic shock is present.

page.standard_overview: Evidence-based beta-blockers constitute one of the four foundational pillars of guideline-directed medical therapy (GDMT) in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF; LVEF <= 40%). Landmark randomized trials proved that only three specific beta-blockers reduce all-cause mortality and hospitalizations: bisoprolol (CIBIS-II), carvedilol (COPERNICUS, US Carvedilol), and sustained-release metoprolol succinate (MERIT-HF). Atenolol and immediate-release metoprolol tartrate have not shown equivalent mortality reduction in HFrEF, and nebivolol showed benefit only on a composite outcome in older patients (SENIORS). Initiation should begin at low doses in clinically stable, euvolemic patients and be titrated slowly (doubling dose every 2-4 weeks) toward target clinical trial doses (carvedilol 25-50 mg BID, bisoprolol 10 mg daily, metoprolol succinate 200 mg daily). Beta-blockers should NOT be abruptly discontinued during mild-to-moderate decompensation unless cardiogenic shock or profound bradycardia is present.

page.standard_overview: Approximately 10% of the population reports a penicillin allergy, yet > 90-95% are not truly allergic when formally evaluated with skin testing or direct oral challenge. Inappropriate penicillin allergy labels lead to the use of broader-spectrum, less effective, and more toxic alternative antibiotics (fluoroquinolones, vancomycin, carbapenems), driving increased risks of Clostridioides difficile infection, surgical site infections, antimicrobial resistance, prolonged hospitalizations, and higher healthcare costs. Validated risk stratification algorithms (such as the PEN-FAST score: Penicillin allergy < 5 years = 2 pts, Anaphylaxis/Angioedema or Severe cutaneous adverse reaction = 2 pts, Treatment required for allergy = 1 pt) accurately identify low-risk patients (PEN-FAST score < 3) who can safely undergo direct oral challenge without preceding skin testing (PALACE trial).

page.standard_overview: Biliary strictures represent narrowing of the extrahepatic or intrahepatic bile ducts resulting from benign (iatrogenic post-cholecystectomy, chronic pancreatitis, primary sclerosing cholangitis [PSC], IgG4-related sclerosing cholangitis, anastomotic post-liver transplant) or malignant (cholangiocarcinoma, pancreatic adenocarcinoma, gallbladder cancer) etiologies. Diagnostic evaluation begins with magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography (MRCP) to non-invasively map stricture anatomy. Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) allows direct therapeutic stenting and tissue acquisition via brush cytology and fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH), although routine cytology has low sensitivity (30-40%). Digital single-operator cholangioscopy enables direct visualization and targeted intraductal biopsy and can improve the diagnostic assessment of indeterminate strictures, with sensitivity varying by cohort and by visual versus histologic assessment. Benign strictures are managed with progressive balloon dilation and serial insertion of multiple plastic stents or fully covered self-expandable metal stents (FCSEMS).

page.standard_overview: Biliary tract cancers (BTCs) encompass intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma (iCCA), extrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma (perihilar [Klatskin] and distal), and gallbladder carcinoma. Surgical resection with negative margins (R0) and regional lymphadenectomy offers the only potentially curative option. The landmark phase 3 BILCAP trial established adjuvant oral capecitabine (1,250 mg/m2 BID, days 1-14 q3w for 8 cycles) as the global standard of care post-resection, with a median overall survival of about 50 to 53 months versus 36 months for observation (significant in the per-protocol but not the intention-to-treat analysis). In unresectable, locally advanced, or metastatic disease, the phase 3 TOPAZ-1 trial established first-line systemic chemoimmunotherapy with durvalumab (anti-PD-L1) plus gemcitabine and cisplatin as standard of care, significantly improving overall survival (median OS 12.8 vs 11.5 months; 2-year OS 24% vs 10%). Comprehensive molecular profiling is recommended for advanced biliary tract cancer, particularly intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma, to identify actionable alterations including FGFR2 fusions, IDH1 mutations, HER2 amplification, BRAF V600E and NTRK fusions that can guide matched targeted therapy.

topic: Biofilm-associated infections: chronic wounds, prosthetics, catheters, rifampicin strategies

page.mentor_intro: Biofilms are highly prevalent in chronic wounds and form on implants and tubing; the 2025 International Consensus on musculoskeletal infection sets research priorities. Standardised biofilm detection and anti-biofilm therapies remain unmet needs.

Biofilms have a high prevalence in chronic wounds, despite methodological heterogeneity of studies.

page.standard_overview: Biofilm-associated infections involving prosthetic joints, vascular grafts, chronic wounds, and indwelling central catheters are characterized by bacterial communities encased in an extracellular polymeric substance (EPS) matrix. Bacteria within biofilms enter a low-metabolic 'persister' phenotype conferring extreme tolerance to standard cell wall-active antibiotics. In staphylococcal prosthetic joint infections (PJI), the landmark Zimmerli trials established that debridement, antibiotics, and implant retention (DAIR) requires combination bactericidal biofilm-active therapy—specifically oral rifampicin paired with a companion agent (fluoroquinolone, cotrimoxazole, or fusidic acid)—to eradicate adherent surface biofilms. Rifampicin monotherapy is strictly contraindicated due to rapid emergence of single-step rpoB point mutation resistance.

page.standard_overview: Severe eosinophilic asthma (SEA) represents a distinct, adult-onset Type 2-high inflammatory endotype driven by interleukin-5 (IL-5), the master cytokine governing eosinophil differentiation, activation, and survival. page.standard_overview: Antidepressant monotherapy is generally not recommended for bipolar I depression because evidence for efficacy is limited and some antidepressants can precipitate mania or mixed symptoms, with risk varying by drug and patient. Lithium and lamotrigine are recommended first-line maintenance treatments for bipolar I disorder and are also first-line options for acute bipolar I depression.

standard_knowledge.claim: Lithium has a unique anti-suicidal effect independent of its mood-stabilising action, reducing suicide and suicide attempts substantially (by roughly 60% in meta-analyses) compared with other agents or placebo.

Lamotrigine demonstrates preferential efficacy in preventing depressive relapses rather than manic relapses; slow upward dose titration (25 mg daily for 2 weeks, doubling every 2 weeks) is mandatory to prevent life-threatening Stevens-Johnson syndrome.

Therapeutic drug monitoring is essential for lithium maintenance, targeting serum trough concentrations of 0.6 to 0.8 mmol/L (up to 1.0 mmol/L during acute stabilization), with regular 6-month surveillance of renal function (eGFR) and thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH).

page.standard_overview: Maintenance pharmacotherapy aims to prevent manic and depressive relapse and attenuate subthreshold mood instability; lithium additionally has evidence suggesting reduced suicide risk, although randomized meta-analysis estimates for suicide attempts and completed suicide were not statistically significant. Lithium remains a first-line maintenance mood stabilizer with long-term evidence for relapse prevention and possible suicide-risk reduction, but the cited randomized meta-analysis did not show statistically significant reductions in suicide attempts or completed suicide. In the landmark BALANCE trial, both combined lithium plus valproate and lithium monotherapy were more effective than valproate monotherapy in preventing relapse. Lamotrigine is a first-line maintenance option, particularly for depressive recurrence, whereas antipsychotics are not uniformly mainly antimanic: quetiapine is also a first-line option for bipolar I depression.

standard_knowledge.claim: Divalproex sodium (sodium valproate) is highly effective for acute mania, mixed features, and rapid-cycling presentations; rapid loading with oral divalproex (20-30 mg/kg/day) achieves therapeutic serum concentrations (> 50-100 ug/mL) and symptom relief within 48-72 hours.

Valproate should be avoided in women of childbearing potential because of its teratogenicity (neural tube defects, cardiac malformations) and risk of neurodevelopmental disorders in up to 30 to 40% of exposed children.

page.standard_overview: Acute bipolar mania represents a psychiatric emergency characterized by grandiosity, decreased need for sleep, pressured speech, racing thoughts, severe impulsivity, and psychotic features. Rapid control of agitation, psychosis, and mood elevation is necessary to prevent bodily harm, social disruption, and exhaustion. In Cipriani et al.'s Lancet multiple-treatments meta-analysis, antipsychotics—including haloperidol (a typical antipsychotic), risperidone, olanzapine, quetiapine, and aripiprazole—were overall significantly more effective than mood stabilizers for acute mania. For acute mania, CANMAT/ISBD recommends lithium, divalproex, or several antipsychotics, alone or in combination, as first-line treatment options.

topic: Bisphosphonates in osteoporosis: alendronate, zoledronate, drug holidays, atypical fractures

page.mentor_intro: The living ACP guideline suggests individualised bisphosphonate use in women over 65 with osteopenia. Antiresorptives do not raise dental implant failure, teriparatide and denosumab increase BMD more than bisphosphonates, and romosozumab cardiovascular concerns appear smaller than feared.

teaching_points.claim: American College of Physicians 2023: Treatments to Reduce Fractures in Adults Diagnosed With Osteoporosis Recommendation 1a: ACP recommends that clinicians use bisphosphonates for initial pharmacologic treatment to reduce the risk of fractures in postmenopausal females diagnosed with primary osteoporosis (strong recommendation; high-certainty evidence).

The living ACP guideline suggests an individualised decision about starting a bisphosphonate in females over 65 with osteopenia to reduce fractures (conditional recommendation, low-certainty evidence).
Implants may be placed safely with concomitant bisphosphonate or denosumab use in osteoporosis, without evidence of higher implant failure.
Adjuvant bisphosphonates in early breast cancer did not consistently reduce recurrence in any subset, per the ASCO-OH guideline.
The Endocrine Society guideline gives a framework for managing hypercalcaemia of malignancy.
Updated myeloma bone disease guidance suggests biomarkers for guiding antiresorptive therapy and strategies to enhance osteoblastic activity.
Teriparatide and denosumab were more efficacious than bisphosphonates in increasing BMD at the femoral neck, total hip and lumbar spine.
Romosozumab cardiovascular concerns seem less significant than previously suggested, though real-world data are required.

In the Fracture Intervention Trial in women with existing vertebral fractures, alendronate reduced new morphometric vertebral fractures (8.0% vs 15.0%; relative risk 0.53) and hip fractures (relative hazard 0.49).

The HORIZON-PFT trial (NEJM) demonstrated that once-yearly intravenous zoledronic acid (5 mg) reduced vertebral fractures by 70% and hip fractures by 41% over 3 years, with proven compliance advantages.

The FLEX trial (Black et al., JAMA) demonstrated that after 5 years of alendronate, women who discontinued therapy maintained stable bone mineral density and experienced no increase in non-vertebral fractures over the subsequent 5 years, supporting the safety of a drug holiday.

uncertainties: Treatment duration and drug holidays are not covered by the retrieved excerpts.

standard_knowledge.claim: The ASBMR Task Force defines atypical femur fractures (AFF) as non-comminuted, transverse or short oblique fractures along the subtrochanteric or diaphyseal femoral shaft associated with cortical thickening (beaking); patients on long-term bisphosphonates presenting with thigh or groin pain must immediately undergo bilateral femoral radiography.

page.standard_overview: Bisphosphonates (oral alendronate or risedronate and intravenous zoledronic acid) are first-line antiresorptive options for postmenopausal osteoporosis; patients at very high fracture risk may instead start romosozumab or teriparatide followed by a bisphosphonate. By binding bone hydroxyapatite and inhibiting farnesyl pyrophosphate synthase (FPPS) in osteoclasts, nitrogen-containing bisphosphonates reduce vertebral fractures by roughly half to 70% and hip fractures by about 40–50% in the FIT and HORIZON-PFT trials. Because bisphosphonates persist in bone, treatment should be reassessed after about 5 years of oral or 3 years of intravenous therapy to determine whether a drug holiday is appropriate; long-term use is associated with a small increase in medication-related osteonecrosis of the jaw, and FLEX found that many women can discontinue alendronate after 5 years without higher overall fracture risk, except for clinical vertebral fractures.

page.mentor_intro: The second international BK polyomavirus consensus guides kidney transplant management; leflunomide, cidofovir, quinolones and IVIG are not supported. standard_knowledge.claim: Sustained plasma BK viral load > 10,000 copies/mL (or > 4 log10 copies/mL) for > 3 weeks is the clinically validated threshold defining 'presumptive BK polyomavirus nephropathy' triggering prompt intervention.

The primary, evidence-based first-line therapy for BK viremia and nephropathy is the systematic reduction of maintenance immunosuppression (typically reducing mycophenolate dose by 50% or stopping it, followed by lowering tacrolimus trough targets to 4-6 ng/mL).

Renal allograft biopsy confirms definitive BKPyVN, characterized by intranuclear viral inclusion bodies, positive SV40 large T-antigen immunohistochemistry, and variable tubulitis and interstitial fibrosis under the Banff 2018 classification.

page.standard_overview: BK polyomavirus nephropathy (BKPyVN) is an important cause of renal allograft dysfunction and premature allograft loss. BKPyVN results from reactivation of latent polyomavirus in the urinary tract under immunosuppression; tacrolimus regimens and acute rejection are established risk factors for BKPyV viremia and nephropathy. KDIGO 2009 suggests screening all kidney transplant recipients for BK virus with quantitative plasma NAT monthly for the first 3-6 months, then every 3 months to the end of the first post-transplant year, and whenever creatinine rises unexpectedly or after treatment for acute rejection (grade 2C/2D). Plasma BKPyV-DNAemia persisting above 1,000 copies/mL or exceeding 10,000 copies/mL should trigger predefined stepwise immunosuppression reduction to limit allograft damage; biopsy-proven nephropathy is managed similarly.

overview_support.note: KDIGO 2009 13.1.1: "We suggest screening all KTRs for BKV with quantitative plasma NAT (2C) at least monthly for the first 3-6 months... then every 3 months until the end of the first post-transplant year". It is a suggestion, not a universal standard.

standard_knowledge.claim: The Banff 2018 classification stratifies BKPyVN into Class 1 (minimal viral load and <= 10% fibrosis), Class 2 (intermediate), and Class 3 (extensive fibrosis > 50%), with Class 3 carrying an allograft loss rate exceeding 50% at 24 months.

Intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG 1-2 g/kg) contains high titers of neutralizing anti-BK virus antibodies and is frequently employed as an adjuvant rescue therapy, particularly in patients experiencing concurrent acute allograft rejection and BK viremia.
Retransplantation after allograft loss from BKPyVN is safe and achieves excellent graft survival, provided that BK viremia has completely cleared to undetectable levels in plasma prior to relisting.

page.standard_overview: When reduction of baseline immunosuppression fails to clear viremia or when allograft rejection co-exists, clinicians have historically explored adjuvant therapies (leflunomide, ciprofloxacin, intravenous immunoglobulin [IVIG], or low-dose cidofovir). Current evidence does not support routine adjuvant leflunomide, cidofovir, quinolones, or IVIG; appropriate randomized trials are lacking, and stepwise immunosuppression reduction remains the primary intervention.

page.mentor_intro: Non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer risk stratification includes T1 substaging and NLR, with active surveillance proposed for low-grade disease and immune checkpoint inhibitors under study for BCG-unresponsive disease. AFU, EAU and ASTRO guidance cover perioperative chemo-immunotherapy and radiotherapy.

teaching_points.claim: An international Delphi gives the first expert-driven framework for active surveillance in low-grade NMIBC, including exit criteria.
Real-world data challenge management guidance for very high-risk NMIBC, so treatment decisions should be individualised.
French AFU recommendations update NMIBC induction and maintenance regimens and cystectomy indications, and the 2025 update includes perioperative chemotherapy with immunotherapy.
The ASTRO guideline gives evidence-based recommendations on radiation therapy for bladder cancer for local control or palliation.
T1 substaging systems prognosticate recurrence and progression in NMIBC, with Rete Oncologica Lombarda substaging showing promise.
Neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio is associated with recurrence and progression in NMIBC after BCG.
Immune checkpoint inhibitors show therapeutic response in BCG-unresponsive NMIBC, though variability and adverse events call for randomised trials.

European Association of Urology (EAU) guidelines stratify NMIBC using EORTC risk tables into low, intermediate, and high risk; high-risk NMIBC (T1, high-grade, CIS) mandates adjuvant intravesical BCG maintenance for 1-3 years.

In the landmark SWOG 8710 randomized trial (Grossman et al., NEJM), neoadjuvant methotrexate, vinblastine, doxorubicin, and cisplatin (MVAC) followed by radical cystectomy significantly improved median overall survival (77 vs 46 months) and increased pathologic complete response (38% vs 15%) compared with cystectomy alone.

In locally advanced or metastatic urothelial carcinoma, the phase 3 EV-302 trial established enfortumab vedotin plus pembrolizumab as the superior frontline regimen, nearly doubling median overall survival compared to traditional platinum chemotherapy.

uncertainties: Optimal management of BCG-unresponsive disease.

page.standard_overview: Blood cultures are the definitive diagnostic gold standard for bloodstream infections and infective endocarditis, yet diagnostic sensitivity and clinical utility depend critically on rigorous venipuncture technique. Multiple blood culture sets should be collected by separate venipunctures before antimicrobial administration whenever this does not dangerously delay treatment; increasing consecutive sets improves pathogen recovery. page.standard_overview: The traditional dogma mandating prolonged 6-week courses of intravenous antibiotic therapy for complex bone and joint infections (osteomyelitis, native joint septic arthritis, and prosthetic joint infections) was fundamentally overturned by the landmark OVIVA trial. page.standard_overview: Borderline Personality Disorder (BPD) is characterized by pervasive emotional dysregulation, unstable interpersonal relationships, identity disturbance, severe impulsivity, and chronic non-suicidal self-injury (NSSI) and recurrent suicidal behaviors. Randomized evidence shows that DBT can reduce suicide attempts and hospitalization for suicidal ideation compared with expert community therapy; Cochrane found low-quality evidence that DBT reduces self-harm versus treatment as usual. DBT integrates four modular skill training domains: mindfulness, distress tolerance, emotion regulation, and interpersonal effectiveness.

standard_knowledge.claim: Botulism classically presents with symmetric, descending flaccid paralysis without sensory loss, beginning with bulbar cranial nerve palsies (diplopia, fixed dilated pupils, dysarthria, dysphagia) and progressing downward to upper extremities, trunk, and respiratory muscles.

Equine-derived heptavalent botulinum antitoxin (HBAT, covering toxin types A through G) should be administered immediately upon clinical suspicion without waiting for confirmatory laboratory results (mouse bioassay or PCR), as antitoxin only neutralizes free, unbound circulating toxin.

In infant botulism (< 1 year old), Human Botulism Immune Globulin Intravenous (BabyBIG) is the treatment of choice, significantly reducing hospital stay and ICU length of stay; equine antitoxin is avoided in infants due to anaphylaxis and serum sickness risks.

In wound botulism, extensive surgical debridement of the anaerobic focus and high-dose intravenous penicillin G are required after antitoxin infusion; aminoglycosides and neuromuscular blocking agents are strictly contraindicated as they exacerbate presynaptic neuromuscular blockade.

page.standard_overview: Botulism is a rare, neuroparalytic emergency caused by botulinum neurotoxins (types A-G) produced by Clostridium botulinum, which irreversibly cleave SNARE proteins at presynaptic cholinergic neuromuscular junctions, blocking acetylcholine exocytosis. Major naturally occurring forms are foodborne botulism from ingested preformed toxin, wound botulism from bacterial wound colonization, and infant or adult intestinal botulism from intestinal colonization; iatrogenic and inhalational botulism are also recognized. Patients present with the classic triad: afebrile, alert, and symmetric descending flaccid paralysis starting with cranial nerves ('the 4 Ds': Diplopia, Dysarthria, Dysphagia, Dysphonia) progressing to diaphragmatic arrest. Prompt botulinum antitoxin and meticulous intensive-care respiratory support are essential; heptavalent antitoxin is used for symptomatic noninfant botulism where indicated, whereas infant intestinal botulism is treated with human-derived botulism immune globulin intravenous (BIG-IV).

Rectal cancer requires specialized pelvic MRI staging to evaluate distance to the mesorectal fascia (CRM); threatened margins (< 1 mm) mandate neoadjuvant total neoadjuvant therapy (TNT: chemoradiation and consolidation chemotherapy) prior to total mesorectal excision (TME).

page.standard_overview: Most colorectal cancers develop through the adenoma–carcinoma sequence, with serrated pathways also contributing; screening enables detection of precancerous lesions and early cancer. Average-risk adults should begin colorectal cancer screening at age 45; ACS recommends annual high-sensitivity FIT among preferred stool-based options, with timely colonoscopy after any positive noncolonoscopy test. Staging requires complete colonoscopy with biopsy, cross-sectional imaging (contrast CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis), and high-resolution pelvic MRI for rectal cancers to assess circumferential resection margin (CRM). For resectable colon cancer, oncologic en bloc surgical resection with regional lymphadenectomy provides definitive local therapy and accurate prognostic staging.

page.standard_overview: Bowel obstruction is broadly classified into mechanical obstruction (physical luminal blockage from adhesions, hernias, or neoplasms) and functional obstruction (paralytic ileus or acute colonic pseudo-obstruction [Ogilvie syndrome]). Mechanical small-bowel obstruction typically causes abdominal pain, nausea and vomiting, abdominal distention, and constipation or obstipation; CT is highly sensitive and specific for detection and characterization, while bowel sounds may be hypoactive as well as increased. Acute colonic pseudo-obstruction (Ogilvie syndrome) causes massive colonic distension without mechanical blockage, often after surgery or severe illness; the Ponec trial enrolled patients with cecal diameter of at least 10 cm who had not responded to conservative treatment. In the Ponec randomized trial of acute colonic pseudo-obstruction unresponsive to conservative therapy, intravenous neostigmine 2 mg produced prompt colonic decompression in 10 of 11 patients (91%) versus 0 of 10 receiving placebo.

page.standard_overview: Breast cancer management is governed by biological subtyping based on estrogen receptor (ER), progesterone receptor (PR), human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2), and proliferation index (Ki-67). Clinicopathological surrogate groups include luminal A-like (hormone receptor-positive, HER2-negative, low Ki-67), luminal B-like (hormone receptor-positive with higher Ki-67 and/or HER2-positive), HER2-positive disease (hormone-receptor status variable), and triple-negative disease (ER-, PR-, HER2-); these surrogates are not identical to intrinsic gene-expression subtypes. Early-stage management incorporates breast-conserving surgery (lumpectomy) with sentinel lymph node biopsy (SLNB) and adjuvant whole-breast radiotherapy, or mastectomy. Adjuvant systemic therapy is guided by multi-gene expression assays (Oncotype DX) and targeted therapies.

Chemotherapy is strictly contraindicated during the first trimester due to high teratogenic risks (malformation rates 10-20%) and must be stopped by week 35-37 of gestation (or 3 weeks prior to planned delivery) to avoid delivery during maternal and fetal neutropenic nadirs.

HER2-targeted agents (trastuzumab, pertuzumab) cause oligohydramnios and fetal renal failure and tamoxifen is associated with congenital malformations, so both are deferred until after delivery; radiotherapy is also deferred because of fetal radiation exposure.

page.standard_overview: Pregnancy-associated breast cancer (PABC)—defined as breast cancer diagnosed during gestation or within one year postpartum—presents unique clinical challenges balancing maternal oncologic cure against fetal safety. In an international cohort adjusted for clinical and treatment factors, breast cancer diagnosed during pregnancy had similar overall survival to nonpregnant patients, and disease-free survival did not differ significantly, supporting treatment while continuing pregnancy.

page.standard_overview: Bronchial provocation (challenge) testing is indicated to confirm or exclude airway hyperresponsiveness (AHR) in patients with symptoms suggestive of asthma who have normal baseline spirometry without documented reversible airflow obstruction. A positive methacholine challenge is defined by a 20% fall in FEV1; the current ERS technical standard recommends reporting the provocative delivered dose (PD20) rather than concentration (PC20) to improve comparability across devices and protocols.

page.standard_overview: Bronchiectasis is a chronic, heterogeneous pulmonary syndrome characterized by permanent abnormal dilation of the bronchi, impaired mucociliary clearance, chronic wet or productive cough, and recurrent infectious exacerbations. page.standard_overview: Frequent infectious exacerbations in bronchiectasis accelerate lung function decline, worsen quality of life, and increase hospital admissions. Long-term azithromycin reduces exacerbations in non-CF bronchiectasis: EMBRACE used 500 mg three times weekly for 6 months (exacerbation rate ratio 0.38), and BAT used 250 mg daily for 12 months (median 0 versus 2 exacerbations); ERS strongly recommends long-term macrolides for patients at high exacerbation risk. standard_knowledge.claim: Routine diagnostic testing (chest radiography, complete blood count, and viral PCR panels) is not recommended in uncomplicated bronchiolitis, as imaging does not alter management and increases inappropriate antibiotic prescribing.

Pharmacological therapies—including inhaled bronchodilators (salbutamol), nebulized adrenaline, systemic corticosteroids, and antibiotics—do not alter disease resolution, hospital admission, or oxygen duration, and should not be administered routinely.

page.standard_overview: Acute viral bronchiolitis is the leading cause of hospitalization in infants under 12 months of age, most commonly caused by Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV), followed by rhinovirus, metapneumovirus, and parainfluenza. Pathophysiology involves viral replication in respiratory epithelial cells causing epithelial necrosis, intense submucosal edema, mucus hypersecretion, and airway plugging. American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) and NICE guidelines emphasize that bronchiolitis is a clinical diagnosis and recommend against routine chest radiographs, viral testing, or blood investigations. Management is strictly supportive: fluid maintenance, minimal handling, and judicious oxygen supplementation.

standard_knowledge.claim: Age and clinical history distinguish the two conditions: acute bronchiolitis presents in infants < 12-24 months with coryza, bilateral crackles, and tachypnea, whereas viral wheeze occurs in preschool children (1-5 years) with discrete polyphonic wheezing without crackles.

While salbutamol is universally ineffective in viral bronchiolitis, a monitored trial of inhaled salbutamol via spacer (2-4 puffs) is recommended in preschool children presenting with acute viral wheezing to assess clinical reversibility.

Systemic corticosteroids (oral prednisolone) provide no clinical benefit in preschool children with episodic viral wheeze in the absence of a personal or family atopic asthma diathesis, and are ineffective in infant bronchiolitis.

Underlying risk factors for severe or atypical course include prematurity (< 32-35 weeks' gestation), low birth weight, congenital heart disease, bronchopulmonary dysplasia, and neuromuscular weakness.

page.standard_overview: Acute viral bronchiolitis in infants and recurrent episodic viral wheeze in preschool children differ in pathophysiology and bronchodilator responsiveness, although their clinical features can overlap. Bronchiolitis causes inflammation, mucus production and plugging of small airways; inhaled therapies are generally ineffective, so routine salbutamol is not recommended. In episodic viral wheeze or wheezing bronchitis, reversible bronchoconstriction contributes more prominently, and salbutamol administered with a holding chamber may relieve symptoms.

Young age (< 6 weeks) and prematurity (< 35 weeks) are strong independent risk factors for life-threatening central apnea complicating RSV infection, requiring continuous cardiorespiratory monitoring.

Fluid management is a cardinal supportive pillar: enteral hydration via nasogastric or orogastric tube is as effective as intravenous fluids, causes fewer electrolyte shifts, and is preferred unless the infant is in impending respiratory failure.

page.standard_overview: Risk stratification in acute viral bronchiolitis focuses on identifying infants at high risk for rapid clinical deterioration, central apnea, and severe hypoxemic respiratory failure. High-risk features include chronological age < 6-8 weeks, history of prematurity, hemodynamically significant congenital heart disease, chronic lung disease of prematurity, and inadequate fluid intake (< 50% of normal). In infants requiring supplemental oxygen outside intensive care, high-flow nasal cannula therapy reduced escalation of care for treatment failure compared with standard oxygen, and subsequent evidence suggests reduced treatment escalation with possible modest reductions in hospital stay and oxygen duration.

standard_knowledge.claim: Absence of interlobar collateral ventilation—verified using the Chartis balloon catheter system or high-resolution fissure analysis (> 90-95% fissure completeness)—is the mandatory prerequisite for achieving lobar atelectasis and clinical success with endobronchial valves.

Pneumothorax is the primary and most common serious procedure-related complication, occurring in 20-25% of patients within 72 hours of valve placement due to rapid parenchymal shift and compensatory expansion of the untreated ipsilateral lobe.
Patients must be hospitalized under close observation for at least 3 to 4 days post-procedure with immediate chest tube thoracostomy capabilities available to manage post-atelectatic pneumothorax.

page.standard_overview: Bronchoscopic Lung Volume Reduction (BLVR) utilizing one-way endobronchial valves (EBVs; Zephyr or Spiration valves) has emerged as an effective, minimally invasive therapeutic alternative to surgical lung volume reduction (LVRS) for severe heterogeneous pulmonary emphysema. EBVs allow air and secretions to exit the targeted hyperinflated lobe during expiration while preventing air re-entry during inspiration, inducing total lobar atelectasis and decompressing the diaphragm. Randomized trials of endobronchial valves show modest improvements in FEV1 and clinical responder rates in appropriately selected patients, although benefits in six-minute walk distance were not consistent across trials.

page.mentor_intro: Triple antibiotic therapy is more effective than dual therapy for human brucellosis without added side effects. Diagnosis relies on serology and other tests needing standardisation, and neurobrucellosis has dedicated consensus guidance.

teaching_points.claim: A Chinese expert consensus on neurobrucellosis covers assessment, diagnosis, differential diagnosis, therapeutic strategies and prognosis.
Triple antibiotic therapy has better efficacy than dual therapy for human brucellosis without increasing side effects.
A diagnostic systematic review highlights a need for standardisation, improved reporting and advancing test development for human brucellosis.
Pooled brucellosis prevalence was estimated at 15.53%, with more studies needed in developing and low-income countries.
Livestock vaccination with S19 and RB51 prevents abortion and infection at suitable doses.
Domestic animal contact is associated with higher seroprevalence in wildlife, supporting buffalo as a reservoir species.
