World Health Organization (WHO) and international consensus guidelines recommend oral doxycycline (100 mg BID for 6 weeks) combined with either intramuscular streptomycin (1 g daily for the first 2-3 weeks) or oral rifampicin (600-900 mg daily for 6 weeks) for uncomplicated brucellosis.

In a randomized double-blind study of human brucellosis, doxycycline plus rifampin and doxycycline plus streptomycin had similar efficacy: therapeutic failure or relapse at 12 months was 14.4% versus 5.9% (difference not significant), and 4.9% versus 4.3% when patients with spondylitis were excluded.

page.standard_overview: Brucellosis is a worldwide zoonotic infection caused by Brucella species (predominantly B. melitensis, B. abortus, B. suis) transmitted through direct contact with infected livestock (farmers, slaughterhouse workers, veterinarians) or ingestion of unpasteurized dairy products. It presents insidiously with undulant fever, profuse nocturnal sweats, arthralgias, hepatosplenomegaly, and osteoarticular complications (sacroiliitis, spondylodiscitis). Diagnosis relies on compatible clinical features with culture and/or serologic testing; Rose Bengal testing, IgG/IgM ELISA and PCR can be highly accurate, but no single serum-agglutination threshold should be treated as universally confirmatory without reference to the assay and clinical setting. Management mandates prolonged multi-drug regimens with high intracellular penetration (doxycycline for 6 weeks combined with aminoglycosides or rifampicin) to eliminate intracellular bacterial reservoirs and prevent relapse.

Due to extraordinary tumor proliferation rates (doubling time < 24-48 hours), emergency pre-treatment rasburicase (recombinant urate oxidase) and vigorous intravenous hydration are mandatory to prevent catastrophic acute uric acid nephropathy and lethal tumor lysis syndrome.
Intrathecal CNS prophylaxis (intrathecal methotrexate and cytarabine) is an essential component of all curative Burkitt regimens due to the high risk (> 20-30%) of leptomeningeal relapse.

page.standard_overview: Burkitt lymphoma is an exceptionally aggressive mature B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma characterized by deregulation of the MYC oncogene through the t(8;14)(q24;q32) translocation with the immunoglobulin heavy chain (IGH) locus, driving the highest proliferation index (Ki-67 nearly 100%) of any human malignancy. It manifests in three distinct epidemiological settings: endemic (jaw tumors in African children, EBV-driven), sporadic (abdominal ileocecal mass, ascites), and immunodeficiency-associated (HIV). Treatment requires prompt risk-adapted chemoimmunotherapy with CNS-directed treatment and careful tumor-lysis prophylaxis; effective regimens include lower-intensity EPOCH-R in appropriate patients as well as more intensive protocols.

page.mentor_intro: Complement-targeted agents such as iptacopan and pegcetacoplan are now indicated in C3 glomerulopathy to reduce proteinuria or clear C3 deposits, and proteinuria is an acceptable marker of treatment effect. Classification relies on immunofluorescence and electron microscopy.

teaching_points.claim: Iptacopan is indicated in adults with C3 glomerulopathy to reduce proteinuria, with unknown benefit in rapidly progressive disease or severe chronic kidney injury.
Pegcetacoplan response includes clear removal of C3 build-up on follow-up kidney biopsy, with reassessment at least yearly and budget impact considerations.
The Mayo/Renal Pathology Society report gives a pathogenesis-based classification of glomerulonephritis and standardised reporting.
A review updates understanding of C3G as a complement-mediated disease.
Complement-targeted therapies may specifically address unmet needs in primary and secondary glomerular diseases.
A systematic review of C3G and primary IC-MPGN emphasises the need for new targeted treatments, and proteinuria is an acceptable marker for assessing treatment efficacy on long-term kidney outcomes.
A narrative review of complement-targeted therapies for C3G and atypical HUS notes outcomes should be priorities and percentages are not pooled estimates.

Diagnosis under KDIGO guidelines requires predominant glomerular C3 staining on immunofluorescence (C3 intensity at least two orders of magnitude greater than any other immunoglobulin: IgG, IgM, IgA, or C1q).
In the phase 3 APPEAR-C3G trial, the oral factor B inhibitor iptacopan reduced 24-hour urine protein-to-creatinine ratio by 35.1% relative to placebo at 6 months in C3 glomerulopathy.

page.standard_overview: C3 Glomerulopathy (C3G) is a rare, severe kidney disease characterized by abnormal, uncontrolled activation of the alternative complement pathway, resulting in glomerular C3 fragment deposition with minimal or absent immunoglobulins. C3G is classified histopathologically into Dense Deposit Disease (DDD; dense osmiophilic ribbon-like intramembranous deposits on electron microscopy) and C3 Glomerulonephritis (C3GN; subendothelial, mesangial, and subepithelial deposits). Autoantibodies (C3 nephritic factors [C3NeF], stabilizing the C3 convertase) or genetic mutations in complement regulatory proteins (CFH, CFI, CFHR) drive the disease. Emerging targeted complement inhibitors (such as the oral factor B inhibitor iptacopan) are changing treatment, with iptacopan reducing proteinuria in a randomized trial.

topic: CABG versus PCI multivessel coronary disease

page.mentor_intro: Meta-analyses suggest CABG gives sustained lower cumulative all-cause mortality than PCI in multivessel disease without left main involvement, particularly in diabetes and complex anatomy, with lower MI and repeat revascularisation but upfront stroke risk. Left main outcomes are comparable.

teaching_points.claim: An individual patient data meta-analysis showed sustained lower cumulative all-cause mortality with CABG than PCI for multivessel disease without left main involvement.
Mortality benefit of CABG over PCI was seen in diabetes and higher coronary complexity, with no benefit for CABG in left main disease.
CABG is associated with a significant benefit regarding future myocardial infarction versus PCI in multivessel or left main CAD.
In chronic total occlusion eligible for both strategies, CABG is associated with superior survival, fewer MI and fewer repeat revascularisations.
With left ventricular dysfunction, CABG has long-term benefits for mortality and revascularisation but higher upfront stroke rate.
In ACS with unprotected left main disease, CABG reduced repeat revascularisation with a trend to more stroke.
Alternative approaches to CABG such as hybrid revascularisation merit exploration for combined benefits.

2021 ACC/AHA/SCAI revascularization guidelines recommend a multidisciplinary Heart Team approach utilizing the SYNTAX score: PCI is reasonable for low complexity (SYNTAX <= 22), whereas CABG is strongly preferred for intermediate-to-high complexity (SYNTAX >= 23) and diabetes.
In the 10-year follow-up of the SYNTAX trial, all-cause mortality did not differ significantly overall, but in three-vessel disease CABG had lower mortality than PCI (about 21% versus 28%).
In the FREEDOM trial of diabetic patients with multivessel disease, CABG reduced 5-year all-cause mortality (10.9% versus 16.3% with PCI) and myocardial infarction, with a higher early stroke rate.

page.standard_overview: The choice between Coronary Artery Bypass Grafting (CABG) and Percutaneous Coronary Intervention (PCI) in multivessel coronary artery disease is governed by coronary anatomical complexity (SYNTAX score), the presence of diabetes mellitus, and left ventricular systolic function. At 10-year follow-up of SYNTAX, there was no significant overall mortality difference between CABG and PCI, but CABG conferred a significant survival advantage in patients with three-vessel disease; the trial did not show a significant linear treatment-effect trend across SYNTAX-score tertiles. In patients with diabetes and multivessel coronary disease, FREEDOM found that CABG significantly reduced death and myocardial infarction compared with PCI using drug-eluting stents, but increased stroke.

topic: CADASIL: genetic features, MRI findings, clinical course

page.mentor_intro: CADASIL is caused by NOTCH3 mutations (common arginine variants), with MRI changes and white matter alterations linked to cognition. In CADASIL migraine, beta-blockers may be relatively contraindicated, and cholinesterase inhibitors help vascular cognitive impairment generally.

teaching_points.claim: The most common NOTCH3 mutations causing CADASIL include p.R75P, p.R141C, p.R182C and p.R544C, with possible founder effects.
Cysteine-sparing NOTCH3 missense mutations can present with clinical CADASIL and typical MRI findings, with less anterior temporal lobe involvement.
In CADASIL migraine, antimigraine prophylaxis with beta-blockers may be contraindicated relative to other therapies, and controlled studies are needed.
White matter alterations relate to domain-specific cognitive impairment in cerebral small vessel disease.
The parahippocampal gyrus may be a reliably affected brain region in CADASIL.
Impaired neurovascular coupling is associated with cerebral small vessel disease including CAA and CADASIL.
Donepezil 5 mg improves cognition slightly in vascular cognitive impairment according to network meta-analysis.
CADASIL is caused by autosomal dominant mutations in the NOTCH3 gene, specifically missense mutations creating or abolishing a cysteine residue in the extracellular EGF-like repeat domain.
Management of CADASIL is supportive with strict vascular risk control; thrombolysis is used cautiously because of the risk of haemorrhage from microbleeds.

page.standard_overview: Cerebral Autosomal Dominant Arteriopathy with Subcortical Infarcts and Leukoencephalopathy (CADASIL) is the most common hereditary small vessel disease causing premature ischemic stroke and vascular dementia. CADASIL is usually caused by stereotyped NOTCH3 missense variants on chromosome 19 that alter cysteine-residue numbers in extracellular EGF-like repeats; NOTCH3 protein aggregation and granular osmiophilic material in vessel walls are characteristic pathological findings. Cardinal neuroimaging features on T2/FLAIR MRI include early, highly characteristic symmetric hyperintensities in the anterior temporal lobes and external capsules, alongside widespread leukoaraiosis and subcortical lacunar infarcts.

standard_knowledge.claim: CHADD predominantly affects the shoulder rotator cuff (supraspinatus tendon > 80% of cases), with acute, excruciating shoulder pain and erythema occurring during the spontaneous resorptive phase when crystals trigger a massive leukocytic inflammatory response.

Radiographs demonstrate dense, homogeneous, cloud-like amorphous calcifications without cortical bone trabeculation within the tendon; during the resorptive phase, calcifications become fluffy, ill-defined, and may migrate into the subacromial-subdeltoid bursa.

Ultrasound-guided percutaneous needle barbotage (lavage and aspiration) combined with subacromial corticosteroid injection is the most effective non-surgical intervention, achieving rapid pain relief and calcium clearance in > 70-80% of symptomatic refractory cases.

Extracorporeal shock wave therapy (ESWT) is an effective non-invasive alternative that fragments hydroxyapatite deposits and stimulates revascularization in chronic, non-resolving formative calcifications.

page.standard_overview: Calcium Hydroxyapatite Deposition Disease (CHADD)—most commonly presenting clinically as calcific tendinitis—is characterized by the pathological deposition of basic calcium phosphate (BCP / hydroxyapatite) crystals within periarticular tendons, capsules, and bursae, predominantly affecting the supraspinatus tendon of the rotator cuff. It manifests through three evolutionary phases: pre-calcific (metaplastic fibrocartilage transformation), formative/resting (dense chalk-like crystal deposition), and resorptive phase (vascular invasion, macrophage phagocytosis, intense acute throbbing pain mimicking septic arthritis or acute gout). Management utilizes NSAIDs, ultrasound-guided percutaneous needle barbotage (lavage), and subacromial corticosteroid injection.

standard_knowledge.claim: Chondrocalcinosis appears on plain radiographs as punctate or linear radiodense striations within hyaline cartilage and fibrocartilage, most characteristically in the menisci of the knee, triangular fibrocartilage of the wrist, and pubic symphysis.

Crowned dens syndrome results from CPP crystal deposition in the retro-odontoid cruciform and transverse ligaments of C1-C2, presenting with severe occipital/cervical pain, neck rigidity, and fever; non-contrast CT of the cervical spine is the diagnostic gold standard.

First-line therapy for acute CPP crystal arthritis comprises joint aspiration and intra-articular corticosteroid injection, oral colchicine (0.5 mg BID), or short-course NSAIDs; systemic corticosteroids are preferred in elderly patients with polyarticular flares or renal impairment.

page.standard_overview: Calcium Pyrophosphate Deposition (CPPD) encompasses a spectrum of clinical phenotypes driven by the deposition of calcium pyrophosphate dihydrate crystals in articular and fibrocartilage (chondrocalcinosis). Clinical manifestations include acute CPP crystal arthritis ('pseudogout': abrupt severe monoarthritis, classically affecting the knee or wrist), chronic CPP inflammatory arthritis resembling RA, osteoarthritis with CPPD, and 'crowned dens syndrome' (crystal deposition around the odontoid process causing severe acute neck pain, rigid stiffness, and high inflammatory markers in older adults, mimicking polymyalgia rheumatica or meningitis). Diagnosis is confirmed by synovial fluid analysis demonstrating rhomboid-shaped crystals with weak positive birefringence.

standard_knowledge.claim: Hereditary hemochromatosis is strongly associated with CPPD; classic findings include involvement of the 2nd and 3rd metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joints with square-shaped bone ends and prominent hook-like (beak) osteophytes on plain radiography.

Hypomagnesemia promotes CPP crystallization because magnesium is an essential cofactor for alkaline phosphatase and inorganic pyrophosphatases that normally hydrolyze and solubilize inorganic pyrophosphate (PPi).
Prophylactic low-dose oral colchicine (0.5 mg once or twice daily) significantly reduces the frequency of recurrent acute crystal arthritis flares in patients with frequent pseudogout attacks.

page.standard_overview: Most CPPD is sporadic and strongly age-associated; onset at a younger age or extensive polyarticular disease should prompt evaluation for secondary metabolic or inherited causes. The four cardinal secondary etiologies are hemochromatosis (iron overload), primary hyperparathyroidism (hypercalcemia), hypomagnesemia (Gitelman syndrome), and hypophosphatasia. Hemochromatosis-associated arthropathy characteristically involves the second and third metacarpophalangeal joints and may produce hook-like osteophytes; this arthropathy can coexist with CPPD but is not unique to crystal deposition.

page.mentor_intro: SGLT2 inhibitors reduce kidney outcomes across the range of GFR and albuminuria, including stage 4 CKD and in non-diabetic CKD, and reduce cardiovascular events and mortality. Adding an MRA lowers albuminuria and blood pressure further, and GLP-1 agonist benefits are independent of SGLT2 inhibitor use.

SGLT2 inhibitors improve kidney outcomes across the full spectrum of GFR and albuminuria, including stage 4 CKD or minimal albuminuria, among patients with type 2 diabetes, CKD or heart failure.
SGLT2 inhibitors significantly reduced the primary renal outcome in CKD patients, with differences by patient features and underlying disease.
SGLT2 inhibitors help delay progression of non-diabetic kidney disease.
Empagliflozin kidney benefits were evident regardless of diabetes status, heart failure status, cause of kidney disease or the size of the initial eGFR dip.

page.standard_overview: The landmark CREDENCE randomized trial demonstrated that the sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 (SGLT2) inhibitor canagliflozin provides profound renoprotection in patients with type 2 diabetes and high-risk diabetic kidney disease (eGFR 30-90 mL/min/1.73m2 and urinary albumin-to-creatinine ratio > 300 to 5,000 mg/g). page.standard_overview: The landmark CANTOS trial (Canakinumab Anti-inflammatory Thrombosis Outcomes Study) definitively validated the 'inflammatory hypothesis of atherothrombosis' in humans. In 10,061 patients with prior myocardial infarction and persistent high-sensitivity C-reactive protein (hsCRP >= 2 mg/L) despite optimal statin therapy, selective inhibition of interleukin-1beta with canakinumab (150 mg SC every 3 months) significantly reduced major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE: CV death, non-fatal MI, non-fatal stroke) by 15% (hazard ratio 0.85, p=0.02) without lowering LDL cholesterol. Canakinumab increased fatal infection, and its benefit-risk profile has limited routine use in coronary disease; separately, low-dose colchicine has shown modest cardiovascular event reductions, although trial results have been inconsistent.

page.standard_overview: Cancer-associated thrombosis is a major cause of morbidity and is associated with recurrent VTE, major bleeding and early mortality in patients with cancer. Historic standard of care was low-molecular-weight heparin (LMWH; dalteparin in the CLOT and CATCH trials). However, contemporary practice has been transformed by large-scale randomized clinical trials (Hokusai-VTE Cancer, SELECT-D, and CARAVAGGIO) demonstrating that direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs: apixaban, edoxaban, rivaroxaban) are non-inferior to LMWH in preventing recurrent VTE. In CARAVAGGIO, apixaban was noninferior to dalteparin for recurrent VTE without increasing major bleeding; DOACs are now recommended treatment options, with LMWH often favored when gastrointestinal or genitourinary bleeding risk, impaired absorption, or drug interactions are concerns.

standard_knowledge.claim: Cachexia evolves through three clinical stages: pre-cachexia (early metabolic changes with weight loss <= 5%), established cachexia, and refractory cachexia (profound wasting in advanced cancer with life expectancy < 3 months where active oncologic therapy is impossible).

page.standard_overview: Cancer cachexia is a multifactorial metabolic syndrome characterized by progressive, involuntary loss of skeletal muscle mass (sarcopenia) with or without loss of adipose tissue, which cannot be fully reversed by conventional nutritional support. Under international consensus criteria (Fearon et al., Lancet Oncology), cachexia is formally diagnosed by weight loss > 5% over 6 months, or weight loss > 2% in individuals with a BMI < 20 kg/m2 or sarcopenia. Cancer cachexia is associated with systemic inflammation and cytokine networks involving IL-6 and TNF-alpha, together with abnormal metabolism and negative protein-energy balance, and leads to functional impairment and poorer clinical outcomes.

standard_knowledge.claim: Hereditary Breast and Ovarian Cancer (HBOC) syndrome is driven by autosomal dominant germline mutations in BRCA1 (lifetime breast cancer risk 65-75%, ovarian risk 40-50%) and BRCA2 (breast risk 60-70%, ovarian risk 15-20%), with risk-reducing bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy (RRSO) reducing all-cause mortality by > 60-70%.

Lynch syndrome (hereditary non-polyposis colorectal cancer) is caused by germline mutations in DNA mismatch repair (MMR) genes (MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, PMS2); universal screening of all colorectal and endometrial cancers with IHC or MSI PCR is recommended by NCCN guidelines.

In Lynch syndrome, high-quality colonoscopy performed every 1-2 years starting at age 20-25 significantly reduces colorectal cancer incidence and mortality by detecting and removing rapidly progressing adenomas.

Familial Adenomatous Polyposis (FAP) is caused by germline APC gene mutations, resulting in hundreds to thousands of colorectal adenomatous polyps with a near 100% lifetime risk of colorectal cancer by age 40 without prophylactic proctocolectomy.

page.standard_overview: Approximately 5-10% of all cancers are driven by highly penetrant, inherited germline mutations conferring dramatically elevated lifetime risks of malignancy. Identifying hereditary cancer syndromes—such as Hereditary Breast and Ovarian Cancer syndrome (HBOC; BRCA1, BRCA2), Lynch syndrome (HNPCC; MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, PMS2), Li-Fraumeni syndrome (TP53), and Familial Adenomatous Polyposis (FAP; APC gene)—enables life-saving personalized surveillance protocols, risk-reducing prophylactic surgeries, and targeted therapeutics (such as PARP inhibitors in BRCA carriers and immune checkpoint inhibitors in Lynch-associated mismatch repair deficiency).

standard_knowledge.claim: Dilated fundoscopic examination by an ophthalmologist is mandatory for all non-neutropenic patients with candidemia (optimally within the first week of diagnosis) to evaluate for ocular candidiasis (chorioretinitis or endophthalmitis).

Echocardiography (transthoracic or transesophageal) is recommended in all patients with candidemia to exclude Candida infective endocarditis, particularly in those with prosthetic heart valves, persistent fungemia, or new cardiac murmurs.

Early removal of all indwelling central venous catheters (CVCs) is strongly recommended when the catheter is the suspected source or when candidemia persists, significantly accelerating clearance of fungemia and improving survival.

page.standard_overview: Candidemia (Candida bloodstream infection) carries a high in-hospital mortality rate (30-40%) and must never be disregarded as a benign skin contaminant or colonization. For most patients with candidemia, guidelines recommend prompt initial therapy with an echinocandin such as caspofungin, micafungin or anidulafungin, with subsequent treatment tailored to species, susceptibility and clinical response. A dilated ophthalmologic examination is recommended to assess for ocular involvement in appropriate patients with candidemia; echocardiography is indicated when endocarditis is suspected, such as with persistent candidemia, a compatible murmur, prosthetic material or embolic findings, rather than routinely for every patient. Early removal of an infected or presumed-source central venous catheter should be considered and is generally recommended when feasible, with timing individualized to the likely source, vascular access and the patient's condition.

page.standard_overview: Invasive candidiasis—encompassing candidemia and deep-seated intra-abdominal candidiasis—is a frequent cause of severe sepsis in intensive care units, occurring particularly in surgical patients with anastomotic leaks, repeated abdominal operations, total parenteral nutrition (TPN), and prolonged broad-spectrum antibacterial exposure. The Candida score combines severe sepsis, total parenteral nutrition, surgery and multifocal Candida colonization to estimate risk in non-neutropenic critically ill colonized patients, but it should not by itself be used to justify routine empiric antifungal therapy. Serum 1,3-beta-D-glucan can aid assessment of invasive candidiasis, but a negative result cannot universally rule it out or independently justify stopping empiric antifungals; predictive values depend on prevalence, assay and clinical context.

standard_knowledge.claim: In patients receiving empirical antifungal therapy, structured reassessment at 48-72 hours with negative blood cultures and negative beta-D-glucan should trigger immediate antifungal discontinuation to avoid resistance emergence (such as FKS-mutant Candida glabrata).

page.standard_overview: The management of suspected invasive fungal infections in critically ill, non-neutropenic ICU patients requires balancing the danger of delayed treatment in true invasive candidiasis against the hazards and costs of widespread indiscriminate antifungal overuse. The landmark EMPIRICUS multicenter randomized clinical trial (Timsit et al., JAMA) rigorously tested the strategy of empirical micafungin versus placebo in 260 mechanically ventilated ICU patients with ICU-acquired sepsis, Candida colonization, and multi-organ failure. EMPIRICUS found no significant improvement in 28-day invasive-fungal-infection-free survival with empirical micafungin, although new invasive fungal infections were reduced; the results do not support routine empirical micafungin for this broad high-risk ICU population.

standard_knowledge.claim: Capacity is legally presumed in all adults unless proven otherwise; an unusual, eccentric, or medically unwise decision does not in itself constitute evidence of lack of capacity.

The functional test of capacity requires the patient to: (1) understand information relevant to the decision; (2) retain that information long enough; (3) weigh the information (benefits, risks, alternatives); and (4) communicate their decision.

To find that a patient lacks capacity, the functional inability must be directly caused by an impairment of, or disturbance in the functioning of, the mind or brain (e.g., delirium, dementia, severe head trauma, intoxication).

When a patient lacks capacity, decisions must be made in their 'best interests' taking into account their past wishes, beliefs, values, and consulting family or named lasting powers of attorney (LPA), choosing the least restrictive option.

page.standard_overview: Mental capacity assessment is a fundamental clinical skill required whenever an adult patient's ability to make a specific healthcare decision is called into question. Under statutory frameworks (such as the UK Mental Capacity Act 2005) and international ethical standards, capacity is decision-specific and time-specific: a patient may lack capacity to make complex financial or major surgical decisions while retaining full capacity to consent to simple nursing interventions. Five core statutory principles govern practice: (1) presumption of capacity; (2) taking all practicable steps to support decision-making; (3) right to make an unwise decision; (4) best interests principle; and (5) least restrictive option.

page.standard_overview: Small bowel capsule endoscopy (SBCE) is a non-invasive diagnostic modality providing high-resolution visualization of the entire small intestinal mucosa beyond the reach of standard esophagogastroduodenoscopy (OGD) and ileocolonoscopy. Major clinical indications defined by European Society of Gastrointestinal Endoscopy (ESGE) guidelines include obscure gastrointestinal bleeding (OGIB; unexplained iron deficiency anemia or overt melena with normal upper/lower endoscopy), suspected or refractory Crohn disease, small bowel polyposis syndromes, and refractory celiac disease. Capsule retention is the principal complication, particularly in patients with known or suspected strictures; cross-sectional imaging and/or a patency capsule should be used according to risk, and ESGE recommends a patency capsule before SBCE in established Crohn disease.

page.standard_overview: Carbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales—including Klebsiella pneumoniae, Escherichia coli and Enterobacter species—are urgent antimicrobial-resistance threats associated with substantial mortality in bloodstream and other invasive infections. Resistance mechanisms are categorized into carbapenemase producers (CPE: serine beta-lactamases like KPC, oxacillinases like OXA-48, and metallo-beta-lactamases like NDM, VIM, IMP) and non-carbapenemase producers (porin loss with ESBL/AmpC). IDSA guidance favors newer agents selected by carbapenemase type and susceptibility—such as ceftazidime-avibactam, meropenem-vaborbactam, imipenem-cilastatin-relebactam and, in selected settings, cefiderocol—over polymyxin-based regimens.

page.mentor_intro: Diagnosing ATTR cardiac amyloidosis by bone scintigraphy requires excluding light chain disease with a monoclonal protein screen. Management relies on expert opinion in the absence of trials: SGLT2 inhibitors may be associated with better prognosis, heart failure drugs behave differently, and transplant has Mayo consensus.

teaching_points.claim: AHAACC 2024: In patients for whom a diagnosis of transthyretin cardiac amyloidosis is m ade, genetic testing with TTR gene sequencing is recommended to differen tiate hereditary variant from wild-type transthyretin cardiac amyloidosis.
The ACC/AHA quality measures update stresses a monoclonal protein screen to exclude light chain amyloidosis when interpreting bone scintigraphy for transthyretin cardiac amyloidosis.
A consensus on non-amyloid-specific treatment of ATTR cardiac amyloidosis relies on expert opinion and retrospective studies given the lack of randomised trials.
Guideline-directed heart failure drugs based on LVEF should be reconsidered in the context of ATTR cardiomyopathy.
A Mayo Clinic consensus gives recommendations for pretransplant evaluation and post-transplant management in cardiac amyloidosis.
An Italian consensus gives diagnostic-therapeutic pathways for suspected or established cardiac amyloidosis.
SGLT2 inhibitors may be associated with more favourable prognosis in ATTR cardiomyopathy, with observational evidence needing validation in RCTs.
CT-derived myocardial extracellular volume has high diagnostic accuracy and is useful for detecting amyloidosis in preoperative TAVR CT.

In the landmark prospective ATTR-ACT phase 3 trial (Maurer et al., NEJM), tafamidis (a selective kinetic stabilizer of the transthyretin tetramer) significantly reduced all-cause mortality (29.5% vs 42.9%, HR 0.70) and cardiovascular hospitalizations by 32% in patients with ATTR cardiac amyloidosis.

The non-biopsy diagnostic criteria established by Gillmore et al. (Circulation) confirm ATTR cardiac amyloidosis with 100% specificity when bone scintigraphy (99mTc-DPD, PYP, or HMDP) demonstrates Perugini Grade 2 or 3 cardiac uptake AND monoclonal protein testing (serum free light chains, serum/urine immunofixation) is completely negative.

page.standard_overview: Cardiac amyloidosis is a progressive, underdiagnosed infiltrative cardiomyopathy caused by extracellular amyloid-fibril deposition; typical findings can include concentric ventricular thickening, restrictive physiology, low QRS voltage despite increased wall thickness, and heart failure across the ejection-fraction spectrum. The two major forms are AL (light chain) amyloidosis (plasma cell clone producing monoclonal immunoglobulin light chains; medical emergency) and Transthyretin (ATTR) amyloidosis (wild-type in older males or hereditary/mutant [TTRv]). In a landmark multicenter study (Gillmore et al., Circulation), a validated non-biopsy diagnostic algorithm utilizing 99mTc-DPD/PYP bone scintigraphy (Perugini Grade 2-3 myocardial uptake) coupled with the rigorous exclusion of monoclonal light chains reliably diagnoses ATTR without endomyocardial biopsy.

page.mentor_intro: The 2025 ERC and AHA resuscitation guidelines are the current references for adult ALS, post-resuscitation care and special circumstances. Post-arrest care covers temperature control, seizures, prognostication and organ donation.

teaching_points.claim: The ERC 2025 adult ALS guidelines emphasise early and effective ALS interventions to improve survival from in- or out-of-hospital cardiac arrest.
The ERC 2025 special circumstances guidelines describe modifications to basic and advanced life support for prevention and treatment of cardiac arrest in specific situations.
ERC/ESICM 2025 post-resuscitation care covers haemodynamic monitoring, seizure control, temperature control, intensive care management, prognostication, rehabilitation and organ donation.

The ILCOR 2025 consensus on science for advanced life support provides treatment recommendations and lists priority knowledge gaps.
ERC 2025 adult basic life support embeds technology use into the relevant sections.

International resuscitation guidelines (ERC and AHA) recommend targeted temperature management targeting strict normothermia (avoiding fever > 37.7°C) for at least 72 hours post-ROSC in all comatose patients, alongside delayed multimodal neuroprognostication >= 72 hours.

In the PARAMEDIC-2 trial, epinephrine increased 30-day survival (3.2% vs 2.4%) but did not significantly increase survival with a favourable neurological outcome (2.2% vs 1.9%), and more survivors in the epinephrine group had severe neurological impairment (31.0% vs 17.8%).

In the international TTM2 randomized trial of 1,900 comatose post-cardiac arrest adults (Dankiewicz et al., NEJM), targeted hypothermia at 33°C did not reduce all-cause mortality (50% vs 48%) or functional disability at 6 months compared with targeted normothermia (early treatment of fever with target <= 37.5°C).

uncertainties: Evidence gaps are listed in the ILCOR consensus.

standard_knowledge.claim: In maternal cardiac arrest at >= 20 weeks' gestation, immediate manual left uterine displacement is required to relieve aortocaval compression; if ROSC is not achieved within 4 minutes, emergency resuscitative hysterotomy (perimortem caesarean section) must be performed at the site of arrest by minute 5.

Resuscitative hysterotomy in maternal cardiac arrest is primarily a maternal resuscitation intervention: evacuating the uterus restores 60-80% of maternal venous return and cardiac output, significantly increasing maternal survival.

In deep accidental hypothermia (core temperature below 30 C), continue CPR but withhold adrenaline and limit defibrillation to three shocks until rewarmed above 30 C, ideally with extracorporeal rewarming.

When pulmonary embolism is the suspected cause of cardiac arrest, emergency administration of a systemic thrombolytic agent (e.g., tenecteplase or alteplase 50 mg) is recommended, and CPR should be continued for at least 60 to 90 minutes to allow drug circulation and clot lysis.

page.standard_overview: Cardiac arrest occurring under special clinical circumstances requires rapid modification of standard ALS algorithms to reverse unique precipitating pathophysiology. In maternal cardiac arrest with a uterus at or above the umbilicus, aortocaval compression can impede resuscitation; perform immediate manual left uterine displacement and prepare resuscitative delivery early, aiming to perform it by about five minutes of arrest if ROSC has not occurred. In accidental hypothermic cardiac arrest below 30°C, defibrillation may be limited to three attempts and adrenaline is generally withheld until rewarmed above 30°C; urgent extracorporeal rewarming should be considered in appropriate refractory cases. In pulmonary embolism-induced arrest, immediate intravenous thrombolysis (alteplase 50 mg IV bolus) and continuing CPR for 60-90 minutes is indicated.

page.standard_overview: Acute cardiac arrhythmias are classified clinically into tachyarrhythmias (heart rate > 100 bpm) and bradyarrhythmias (heart rate < 60 bpm), requiring immediate assessment for adverse life-threatening features: shock, syncope, myocardial ischemia, or acute heart failure. Unstable tachyarrhythmia with a pulse generally requires immediate synchronized electrical cardioversion, except rhythms that cannot be synchronized reliably—particularly polymorphic ventricular tachycardia or ventricular fibrillation—which require unsynchronized high-energy defibrillation. For stable regular narrow-complex SVT, vagal maneuvers—preferably the modified Valsalva technique—followed by rapid intravenous adenosine when needed are standard treatments and often terminate AV-node-dependent SVT. For symptomatic bradycardia, intravenous atropine (0.5 mg, up to 3 mg total) followed by transcutaneous pacing or isoprenaline/adrenaline infusions provides essential chronotropic support.

standard_knowledge.claim: Applying a clinical doughnut magnet directly over an ICD immediately suspends tachyarrhythmia detection and shock delivery without affecting underlying pacemaker functionality, providing safe emergency suppression of inappropriate shock storms.

Applying a magnet over a pacemaker initiates asynchronous fixed-rate pacing (DOO or VOO mode at the magnet rate, typically 85-100 bpm), protecting pacemaker-dependent patients from electromagnetic interference (EMI) during electrocautery or MRI.

Failure to capture (pacemaker spike not followed by a P wave or QRS complex) is caused by lead dislodgement, myocardial exit block, severe hyperkalemia, antiarrhythmic toxicity, or lead fracture, requiring emergency threshold interrogation and pacing output increase.

T-wave oversensing and conductor lead fractures (characterized by abrupt non-physiological high-frequency signals and lead impedance spikes > 2,000 ohms) are the primary hardware causes of inappropriate shocks, requiring lead revision or replacement.

page.standard_overview: Cardiac implantable electronic device (CIED) malfunctions encompass pacemaker failures (failure to pace, failure to sense [undersensing/oversensing], failure to capture) and implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD) complications (inappropriate shocks and electrical storm). Inappropriate ICD shocks occur in up to 10-15% of patients, predominantly triggered by supraventricular tachycardias (atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response), T-wave oversensing, or lead fractures (conductor coil failure or insulation defect). A clinical magnet placed over an ICD generally suspends tachyarrhythmia detection and further therapy while it remains in place, without changing bradycardia pacing in most devices; continuous monitoring and urgent device interrogation are required because responses vary by device and programming.

page.standard_overview: Infection of cardiac implantable electronic devices (CIEDs: pacemakers, ICDs, CRT devices) represents a life-threatening complication occurring in 1-2% of implants, carrying an in-hospital mortality rate of 8-15%. Infection presents as localized pocket infection (erythema, swelling, erosion, purulent drainage) or systemic bacteremia/endocarditis with transvenous lead vegetations. The landmark international WRAP-IT randomized trial (Tarakji et al., NEJM) proved that an absorbable antibacterial-eluting envelope (rifampin and minocycline) reduced major CIED infections by 40%. Established CIED pocket or systemic infection generally requires systemic antibiotics plus complete removal of the infected generator and transvenous leads, with rare exceptions such as superficial incisional infection that does not involve the device.

page.mentor_intro: Cardiac myxoma has low surgical mortality (4.7 per 1000 person-years) and low recurrence, and timely excision is warranted. Embolism risk factors include an irregular tumour surface and narrow base, and cerebral aneurysm is a rare complication.

standard_knowledge.claim: Cardiac myxomas predominantly arise in the left atrium (75-80%), followed by the right atrium (15-20%), and characteristically attach by a fibrovascular stalk to the limbus of the fossa ovalis on the interatrial septum.

Systemic constitutional symptoms (fever, malaise, weight loss, arthralgias, Raynaud phenomenon) occur in 50% of patients, mediated by tumor secretion of interleukin-6 (IL-6), and rapidly resolve following surgical resection.

Systemic embolization occurs in 30-40% of left atrial myxomas, with cerebral embolization (embolic stroke or TIA) being the most devastating presenting manifestation, particularly in tumors with a friable, villous gelatinous surface.

Emergency surgical resection with full-thickness resection of the septal attachment cuff is the definitive curative standard of care; familial myxomas (Carney complex, PRKAR1A mutation) carry an elevated recurrence rate (15-20% vs 1-2% for sporadic).

page.standard_overview: Cardiac myxoma is the most common primary benign cardiac neoplasm in adults, with > 75-80% originating in the left atrium, typically arising from the fossa ovalis border of the interatrial septum. Myxomas present through a classic clinical triad: (1) intracardiac mechanical obstruction (mitral stenosis mimic, dyspnea, syncope, positional pulmonary edema, 'tumor plop' sound in early diastole); (2) embolic phenomena (cerebral transient ischemic attacks, stroke, retinal occlusion, visceral infarcts); and (3) constitutional systemic symptoms (fever, weight loss, arthralgias, elevated ESR/CRP) driven by autonomous tumor production of interleukin-6 (IL-6). Prompt surgical excision is the treatment of choice, usually gives excellent outcomes and substantially reduces further tumor-embolization risk, but follow-up is required because residual/recurrent tumor and delayed complications can occur.

page.mentor_intro: Cardiac rehabilitation referral and patient education are core quality measures after coronary events. page.standard_overview: Cardiac Resynchronization Therapy (CRT via biventricular pacing) restores synchronous mechanical contraction between the interventricular septum and left ventricular lateral wall in patients with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) and ventricular dyssynchrony. According to 2021 ESC guidelines, patient selection depends on four primary criteria: (1) symptomatic heart failure (NYHA Class II-IV ambulatory) despite >= 3 months of optimal medical therapy; (2) left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) <= 35%; (3) sinus rhythm; and (4) QRS morphology and duration. The greatest clinical benefit (Class I indication) occurs in patients with true Left Bundle Branch Block (LBBB) morphology and QRS duration >= 150 ms.

page.standard_overview: The landmark COMPANION trial (Comparison of Medical Therapy, Pacing, and Defibrillation in Heart Failure; Bristow et al., NEJM) was a pivotal multicenter randomized controlled trial evaluating 1,520 patients with advanced heart failure (NYHA Class III or IV), LVEF <= 35%, and QRS duration >= 120 ms. COMPANION compared optimal pharmacologic medical therapy alone against CRT with a pacemaker (CRT-P) or CRT with a defibrillator (CRT-D). CRT-D significantly reduced all-cause mortality by 36% versus optimal pharmacologic therapy in COMPANION (hazard ratio 0.64, p=0.003), supporting its use in appropriately selected patients with advanced dyssynchronous heart failure.

standard_knowledge.claim: Classic clinical examination reveals Beck's triad (hypotension, raised jugular venous pressure with absent y-descent, and muffled heart sounds) and pulsus paradoxus (inspiratory systolic blood pressure drop > 10-12 mmHg).

Key echocardiographic diagnostic hallmarks of cardiac tamponade include: (1) early diastolic collapse of the right ventricular free wall; (2) late diastolic collapse of the right atrium; (3) a plethora of the inferior vena cava (IVC dilated > 2.1 cm with < 50% inspiratory collapse); and (4) exaggerated respiratory variation in transvalvular Doppler flows (> 25% across the mitral valve).

Emergency ultrasound-guided pericardiocentesis (subxiphoid or apical approach) with placement of an indwelling pigtail catheter is the treatment of choice for unstable tamponade, producing immediate hemodynamic restoration.

Surgical pericardial window or open thoracotomy drainage is indicated for purulent pericarditis, hemopericardium secondary to aortic dissection (type A) or cardiac trauma, loculated posterior effusions, or recurrent malignant effusions.

page.standard_overview: Cardiac tamponade is an acute, life-threatening hemodynamic emergency caused by accumulation of pericardial fluid under elevated pressure, compressing the cardiac chambers, impairing diastolic filling, and leading to low-output circulatory collapse. Classic presentation comprises Beck's triad (hypotension, jugular venous distension, and muffled/distant heart sounds) and pulsus paradoxus (an abnormally large decrease in systolic blood pressure > 10 mmHg during inspiration). Transthoracic echocardiography is the diagnostic imaging modality of choice; supportive findings include early diastolic right-ventricular collapse, right-atrial systolic collapse and a dilated inferior vena cava with reduced inspiratory collapse. Emergency ultrasound-guided pericardiocentesis is life-saving.

page.standard_overview: Cardiogenic shock is a state of critical end-organ hypoperfusion caused by primary cardiac pump failure, characterized by persistent hypotension (systolic BP < 90 mmHg for > 30 minutes or requiring vasopressors), elevated cardiac filling pressures (pulmonary capillary wedge pressure > 15 mmHg), and severely depressed cardiac index (< 2.2 L/min/m2) with evidence of tissue hypoperfusion (elevated blood lactate, cool extremities, oliguria, altered mental status). Acute myocardial infarction with left ventricular failure accounts for > 60-70% of cases. In the landmark DanGer Shock trial (Moller et al., NEJM), microaxial flow pump mechanical circulatory support (Impella CP) significantly reduced 180-day mortality in STEMI-related cardiogenic shock compared to standard care.

standard_knowledge.claim: Stage C ('Classic' cardiogenic shock) is clinically defined by relative hypoperfusion (cool extremities, oliguria < 30 mL/h, serum lactate >= 2 mmol/L) requiring inotropic or mechanical support to restore organ perfusion.

Stage D ('Deteriorating') indicates failure to respond to initial inotropes or device therapy within 1-2 hours, signaling the need for immediate escalation of mechanical circulatory support (Impella, VA-ECMO) or pulmonary artery catheterization.

page.standard_overview: The SCAI shock staging system provides a widely used five-stage framework: A (at risk), B (beginning hemodynamic instability without hypoperfusion), C (classic shock with hypoperfusion requiring intervention), D (deteriorating despite initial therapy), and E (extremis with refractory collapse or cardiac arrest). Multicenter registries show a graded association between higher SCAI shock stage and inpatient mortality, although absolute mortality varies by cohort, setting and treatment.

page.standard_overview: The routine use of the Intra-Aortic Balloon Pump (IABP) in acute myocardial infarction complicated by cardiogenic shock was fundamentally demoted by the landmark IABP-SHOCK II randomized trial. In 600 patients with infarct-related cardiogenic shock undergoing early revascularization, adding counterpulsation with an IABP did not reduce 30-day all-cause mortality (39.7% vs 41.3%, p=0.69). At six-year follow-up, IABP-SHOCK II found no significant differences in mortality, recurrent myocardial infarction, other cardiovascular outcomes or survivors' quality of life between IABP and control groups. page.standard_overview: Multivessel coronary artery disease occurs in 70-80% of patients presenting with acute myocardial infarction complicated by cardiogenic shock. The practice of immediate, complete multivessel PCI during the index catheterization was shown to be inferior in the landmark CULPRIT-SHOCK randomized trial (706 patients). In CULPRIT-SHOCK (Thiele et al., NEJM), immediate PCI of only the culprit lesion significantly reduced 30-day all-cause mortality or severe renal failure requiring dialysis by 17% compared with immediate multivessel PCI (45.9% vs 55.4%, p=0.01). Immediate non-culprit PCI may prolong and complicate the index procedure and increase contrast exposure, but CULPRIT-SHOCK did not establish contrast toxicity or worsened myocardial stunning as the mechanisms of its worse outcomes.

The 2022 ESC guidelines recommend risk-stratified baseline and surveillance assessment with echocardiography and biomarkers in appropriate patients; a relative global-longitudinal-strain reduction greater than 15% from baseline is a marker of subclinical cancer-therapy-related cardiac dysfunction.

standard_knowledge.claim: Peak oxygen consumption (peak VO2) is the most robust prognostic marker in heart failure: peak VO2 <= 12-14 mL/kg/min (or <= 50% of predicted) is an established Class I criterion for listing for orthotopic heart transplantation or mechanical circulatory support.

The VE/VCO2 slope reflects ventilatory efficiency: elevated values (> 34-36) demonstrate increased pulmonary dead space, early metabolic lactic acidemia, and excessive chemoreceptor reflex drive, independently predicting mortality in HFrEF.

The anaerobic threshold (AT)—identified via the V-slope method where VCO2 begins to rise faster than VO2—occurs at 50-60% of peak VO2; an AT < 11 mL/kg/min predicts high perioperative cardiopulmonary complications after major abdominal surgery.

CPET accurately differentiates cardiac limitation (reduced peak VO2, normal breathing reserve > 30%, normal pulse oximetry) from pulmonary ventilatory limitation (exhausted breathing reserve < 15-20%, exertional desaturation, abnormal oxygen pulse).

page.standard_overview: Cardiopulmonary Exercise Testing (CPET) is the gold-standard, non-invasive assessment of integrated cardiovascular, respiratory, and metabolic physiological reserves during progressive incremental physical exertion. By measuring breath-by-breath gas exchange (oxygen uptake [VO2], carbon dioxide output [VCO2], and minute ventilation [VE]), CPET objectively evaluates unexplained dyspnea, stratifies surgical risk prior to major cavitary operations, and determines prognosis and transplant listing in heart failure. Cardinal physiological metrics include peak oxygen consumption (peak VO2), the anaerobic threshold (AT), and the ventilatory equivalent for carbon dioxide (VE/VCO2 slope).

page.standard_overview: In-hospital cardiac arrest (IHCA) occurring within an intensive care unit (ICU) presents distinct clinical features compared to out-of-hospital arrest, as patients are monitored, frequently intubated, and suffer from advanced multi-organ failure. Advanced post-resuscitation care focuses on the prevention of secondary hypoxic-ischemic brain injury and myocardial stunning. Grounded in the landmark TTM2 trial (Dankiewicz et al., NEJM) and ERC/ESICM guidelines, post-cardiac arrest management requires: (1) strict normothermia (target core temperature <= 37.5°C, actively avoiding fever) for at least 72 hours; (2) hemodynamic optimization targeting mean arterial pressure >= 65-75 mmHg; (3) lung-protective normocapnia (PaCO2 35-45 mmHg); and (4) delayed, multimodal neuroprognostication.

Elevated central venous pressure (CVP) and high renal venous congestion, rather than low cardiac index or reduced systemic blood pressure, correlate most strongly with worsening renal function during acute decompensated heart failure.

A transient rise in serum creatinine during effective decongestive therapy does not indicate true tubular injury if hemoconcentration and symptomatic relief occur; discontinuing disease-modifying therapies in this setting worsens post-discharge mortality.

page.standard_overview: Cardiorenal syndrome (CRS) reflects bidirectional organ dysfunction where acute or chronic decompensation of either heart or kidney accelerates failure in the other. Renal venous congestion and elevated central venous pressure are major hemodynamic contributors to worsening renal function in acute heart failure, alongside reduced effective perfusion, neurohormonal activation and other mechanisms. Management prioritizes effective decongestion, usually with protocolized intravenous loop-diuretic escalation and adjunctive sequential nephron blockade when needed; urine sodium can guide response, and RAAS or SGLT2 inhibitors should be reviewed individually rather than stopped automatically for every transient creatinine rise.

In the CARRESS-HF trial of patients with acute heart failure and worsening renal function, stepped pharmacologic therapy was superior to ultrafiltration for preserving renal function, with ultrafiltration causing significantly higher rates of adverse events (72% vs 57%) and no difference in net weight loss.

Earlier data from the UNLOAD trial showed that early ultrafiltration reduced 90-day heart failure readmissions compared to usual-care diuretics, but the study lacked standardized high-dose diuretic protocols and did not focus on patients with preexisting cardiorenal worsening.

The AVOID-HF trial demonstrated a trend toward prolonged time to first heart failure event with ultrafiltration versus adjustable diuretic therapy, but was terminated early and observed significantly more serious adverse events including line sepsis and bleeding in the ultrafiltration arm.

The ADVOR trial demonstrated that sequential nephron blockade using IV acetazolamide added to IV loop diuretics significantly increases successful decongestion incidence (42.2% vs 30.5%) without excess renal impairment, solidifying pharmacologic escalation before considering extracorporeal therapies.

page.standard_overview: Extracorporeal ultrafiltration was conceptualized as an effective mechanical alternative to overcome loop diuretic resistance and achieve rapid isotonic decongestion in cardiorenal syndrome. CARRESS-HF found stepped pharmacologic therapy superior to ultrafiltration for preserving renal function at 96 hours, with similar weight loss and more serious adverse events in the ultrafiltration group. Ultrafiltration is generally reserved for selected patients with persistent congestion despite optimized pharmacologic therapy or with conventional extracorporeal-therapy indications, rather than used routinely for cardiorenal syndrome.

standard_knowledge.claim: Transmural extent of late gadolinium enhancement inversely predicts functional recovery after revascularization: segments with under 25% transmural scar exhibit high likelihood of contractility recovery, whereas segments with over 50% transmural enhancement rarely recover.

page.standard_overview: Cardiovascular magnetic resonance (CMR) is the gold standard imaging modality for myocardial tissue characterization, structural quantification, and viability assessment. Late gadolinium enhancement helps distinguish ischemic from non-ischemic disease: subendocardial or transmural enhancement in a coronary territory indicates infarction, whereas mid-wall or subepicardial patterns suggest non-ischemic injury; amyloidosis more typically produces diffuse subendocardial or transmural enhancement with characteristic nulling abnormalities. Updated Lake Louise criteria combine T1- and T2-based markers, often including parametric mapping, to support diagnosis of acute myocardial inflammation; separately, LGE extent and distribution can contribute to arrhythmic-risk assessment in several cardiomyopathies.

In the EMPA-REG OUTCOME trial, empagliflozin significantly reduced 3-point MACE (HR 0.86), cardiovascular death (HR 0.62), and heart failure hospitalization (HR 0.65) in patients with type 2 diabetes and established cardiovascular disease.

The LEADER trial demonstrated that liraglutide significantly reduced 3-point MACE (HR 0.87) and cardiovascular mortality (HR 0.78) in patients with type 2 diabetes at high cardiovascular risk, driven by reductions in atherosclerotic events.

The SUSTAIN-6 trial showed that once-weekly semaglutide significantly reduced major adverse cardiovascular events (HR 0.74), primarily driven by a 39% reduction in non-fatal stroke, alongside significant glycemic and weight reductions.

In the DECLARE-TIMI 58 trial, dapagliflozin reduced the composite of cardiovascular death or hospitalization for heart failure (HR 0.83) across a broad primary and secondary prevention population, with consistent renal composite benefit.

page.standard_overview: Systematic cardiovascular risk modification integrates multivariable risk quantification with individualized, stepwise interventions targeting atherogenic lipoproteins, systemic hypertension, smoking, and lifestyle behaviors. Contemporary clinical guidelines recommend calibrated algorithms (SCORE2/SCORE2-OP) to estimate 10-year fatal and non-fatal cardiovascular events in asymptomatic individuals, categorizing patients into low-to-moderate, high, and very high risk tiers. Prevention uses risk-based intensive LDL lowering with statin, ezetimibe and PCSK9-inhibitor escalation when indicated, together with individualized blood-pressure targets; lower systolic targets can benefit selected high-risk patients but require monitoring for adverse events.

standard_knowledge.claim: Clinical presentation of carotid dissection classically features ipsilateral neck or facial pain, headache, and a partial Horner's syndrome (ptosis and miosis without anhidrosis) prior to retinal or cerebral ischemic symptoms.

Partial Horner's syndrome occurs because sympathetic fibers for facial sudomotor function travel with the external carotid artery, sparing sweating when the internal carotid artery is selectively dissected.

page.standard_overview: Spontaneous or traumatic cervical artery dissection (carotid or vertebral) is a leading cause of ischemic stroke in young and middle-aged adults. Pathophysiologically, an intimal tear produces an intramural hematoma, leading to arterial stenosis, pseudoaneurysm, or downstream thromboembolism. The therapeutic debate between antiplatelets and full anticoagulation was rigorously evaluated in landmark randomized trials (CADISS and TREAT-CAD). CADISS found no significant difference between antiplatelet and anticoagulant strategies, while TREAT-CAD did not demonstrate aspirin noninferiority to vitamin K antagonists; either approach may be reasonable after individual assessment of ischemic and bleeding risks, and evidence for DOACs remains insufficient.

page.standard_overview: Carpal tunnel syndrome (CTS) is the most prevalent compressive entrapment neuropathy of the upper extremity, resulting from median nerve compression within the fibro-osseous carpal canal. Characterized by nocturnal paresthesia and numbness in the median nerve distribution, diagnosis combines clinical provocation maneuvers with electrodiagnostic studies (EMG/NCS) and neuromuscular ultrasound. Stepwise conservative therapy with neutral nocturnal wrist splinting and local corticosteroid injections provides effective short-term to medium-term symptomatic relief, while open or endoscopic surgical transection of the transverse carpal ligament provides definitive decompression for persistent, severe, or denervating disease.

standard_knowledge.claim: Durkan's carpal compression test exhibits higher diagnostic sensitivity (up to 87%) and specificity compared to traditional Phalen's maneuver or Tinel's percussion sign in systematic reviews of physical examination maneuvers.

page.standard_overview: Diagnosis of carpal tunnel syndrome begins with compatible symptoms and examination findings; electrodiagnostic studies or neuromuscular ultrasound can confirm the diagnosis when additional objective testing is needed. Provocative signs, including Phalen's maneuver, Tinel's percussion sign, and Durkan's carpal compression test, exhibit varying diagnostic sensitivities and specificities. Neurophysiologic grading (Bland scale) objectively measures sensory and motor conduction delays, identifying demyelinating slowing versus axonal denervation. Neutral-position splinting is a common initial conservative treatment, while randomized evidence shows greater clinical improvement with surgical release than with splinting; however, surgical complications are more frequent and superiority is less certain for mild symptoms.

page.standard_overview: Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell therapy has revolutionized the therapeutic landscape of relapsed and refractory B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (B-ALL). By engineering autologous T cells to express synthetic CAR constructs targeting surface CD19 coupled to intracellular signaling and costimulatory domains (4-1BB or CD28), CAR T cells mediate robust, MHC-independent leukemia clearance. The landmark ELIANA and ZUMA-3 trials reported overall remission rates of 81% in children and young adults and 71% in adults, respectively, in heavily pretreated relapsed or refractory B-ALL. Clinical success depends on vigilant recognition and preemptive mitigation of life-threatening toxicities, including Cytokine Release Syndrome (CRS) and neurotoxicity.

page.standard_overview: Axicabtagene ciloleucel (axi-cel) is an autologous anti-CD19 CAR T-cell product utilizing a CD28 costimulatory domain that induces rapid and potent effector activation. In the landmark ZUMA-1 trial, axi-cel established durable remissions in chemotherapy-refractory large B-cell lymphoma (LBCL). The randomized phase 3 ZUMA-7 trial changed management of primary refractory or early-relapsing large B-cell lymphoma by showing superior event-free survival and response with second-line axi-cel compared with salvage platinum-based immunochemotherapy followed by autologous stem-cell transplantation in responders. Axi-cel is a recommended second-line option for eligible patients with large B-cell lymphoma that is primary refractory or relapses within 12 months of first-line chemoimmunotherapy.

page.standard_overview: The therapeutic paradigm of relapsed/refractory large B-cell lymphoma (LBCL) features multiple CD19-directed CAR-T products distinguished by their costimulatory architecture and cell manufacturing formulations. page.standard_overview: The clinical delivery of CD19 CAR T-cell therapy in large B-cell lymphoma requires standardized recognition and management of its hallmark systemic toxicities: Cytokine Release Syndrome (CRS) and Immune effector Cell-Associated Neurotoxicity Syndrome (ICANS). Standardized consensus grading by the American Society for Transplantation and Cellular Therapy (ASTCT) stratifies severity based on fever, hypotension, hypoxia, and neurologic encephalopathy scoring (ICE score). Current toxicity-management protocols use early tocilizumab and/or corticosteroids according to severity and product-specific protocols; an exploratory axi-cel cohort using prophylactic dexamethasone and earlier intervention reported no grade 3 or higher CRS and high response rates, but universal prevention of organ failure or absence of any effect on efficacy has not been proven.

PARP inhibitor benefit in mCRPC is greatest with BRCA alterations, strong with PALB2 or CDK12, and absent with ATM or CHEK2.

page.standard_overview: Castration-resistant prostate cancer (CRPC) is defined by biochemical or radiographic disease progression despite castrate serum testosterone levels (<50 ng/dL or <1.7 nmol/L). The therapeutic management of metastatic CRPC (mCRPC) has transformed with the integration of potent androgen receptor signaling inhibitors (abiraterone, enzalutamide), taxane chemotherapies (docetaxel, cabazitaxel), PARP inhibitors for homologous recombination repair (HRR) gene alterations (olaparib), and radioligand therapy with lutetium-177-PSMA-617. Treatment selection depends on prior androgen deprivation exposure, molecular biomarker profiling (BRCA1/2, ATM), PSMA PET expression, and disease tempo.

standard_knowledge.claim: The Bush-Francis Catatonia Rating Scale (BFCRS) standardizes the clinical assessment of catatonia; presence of 2 or more of the first 14 screening items reliably confirms the catatonic syndrome with high inter-rater reliability.

The lorazepam challenge test (1 to 2 mg IV or IM) produces rapid, dramatic symptomatic improvement within 15-30 minutes in up to 60-80% of catatonic patients, serving as both a diagnostic confirmation and first-line therapeutic initiation.

Electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) is the definitive treatment for severe, benzodiazepine-refractory catatonia and malignant catatonia characterized by autonomic instability, hyperthermia, and hemodynamic collapse.

Antipsychotics should be immediately withheld or avoided during acute catatonia because dopamine D2 blockade markedly increases the risk of precipitating or aggravating malignant catatonia and neuroleptic malignant syndrome.

page.standard_overview: Catatonia is a severe, life-threatening neuropsychiatric syndrome characterized by motor, behavioral, and autonomic dysregulation arising secondary to mood disorders, psychotic illness, or systemic medical and neurological conditions. Core clinical features include mutism, stupor, catalepsy, waxy flexibility, negativism, and echophenomena. The standardized Bush-Francis Catatonia Rating Scale (BFCRS) guides diagnostic screening and monitoring. Management includes prompt assessment and treatment of underlying causes, review and cessation of a suspected precipitating antipsychotic when appropriate, first-line lorazepam with monitored dose titration, and early electroconvulsive therapy for malignant catatonia or an inadequate response to benzodiazepines.

page.mentor_intro: For cancer-associated VTE, LMWH or DOACs (apixaban, rivaroxaban) are used, with choice by bleeding risk, drug interactions and preference; anticoagulation continues beyond six months in active cancer. Thromboprophylaxis can be given in selected ambulatory patients.

teaching_points.claim: CHEST 2021 Antithrombotic therapy VTE second update: In patients with acute VTE in the setting of cancer (cancer-associated thrombosis) we recommend an oral Xa inhibitor (apixaban, edoxaban, rivaroxaban) over low molecular weight heparin (LMWH) for the initiation and treatment phases of therapy (strong recommendation, moderate-certainty evidence).

Lancet Oncol 2022: Prophylaxis of catheter-related thrombosis International Advisory Panel ranking: 8·52 out of 9·00 1 Use of anticoagulation for routine prophylaxis of catheterrelated thrombosis is not recommended (grade 1A).
The BSH guideline recommends continuing anticoagulation beyond 6 months for cancer-associated VTE with active cancer, with drug choice guided by interactions and patient preference.

The 2022 international guideline suggests LMWH or DOACs (rivaroxaban or apixaban) for ambulatory patients with locally advanced or metastatic pancreatic cancer on anticancer therapy and low bleeding risk.
The Canadian treatment algorithm tailors anticoagulation to cancer type, bleeding risk and drug interactions, and adapts therapy as cancer status changes.
Guideline updates added DOACs as an option for VTE management in cancer patients.
An implementation model delivered VTE risk assessment and prophylaxis to prevent cancer-associated thrombosis in outpatients.
Multidisciplinary awareness programmes are needed to improve guideline adherence in cancer-associated VTE.

A meta-analysis found DOACs versus LMWH for cancer thrombosis associated with significantly increased major bleeding and a trend to more clinically relevant non-major bleeding, with small absolute differences (2-3%).

The CHEST guideline recommends therapeutic anticoagulation for catheter-associated upper extremity deep vein thrombosis (UEDVT) without routine catheter removal if the catheter is functional, correctly positioned, and clinically required.

The CHEST 2021 update recommends direct oral anticoagulants (apixaban, rivaroxaban) or low-molecular-weight heparin (LMWH) for at least 3 months for upper extremity DVT, continuing anticoagulation for the duration the catheter remains in situ.

ASCO clinical practice guidelines advise against routine primary pharmacologic thromboprophylaxis solely for the presence of an indwelling central venous catheter in cancer outpatients due to bleeding risks without significant overall survival benefit.

standard_knowledge.claim: Indications for immediate catheter removal in catheter-associated thrombosis include non-functioning catheter, catheter sepsis/bacteremia, progressive thrombosis despite therapeutic anticoagulation, or loss of clinical need for vascular access.

page.standard_overview: Catheter-associated venous thrombosis (CAT) is a frequent and serious complication of central venous access devices (CVADs), peripherally inserted central catheters (PICCs), and hemodialysis catheters, particularly in oncologic and critically ill cohorts. Catheter-associated thrombosis reflects venous-wall injury during insertion, disturbed blood flow and stasis around an intravascular foreign body, together with patient- and disease-related hypercoagulability. Clinical guidelines from CHEST and ASCO emphasize that a functional, uninfected catheter should NOT be routinely removed simply due to thrombosis; instead, therapeutic anticoagulation should be initiated with the catheter retained in situ if central access remains clinically essential. Anticoagulation is maintained for at least 3 months and continued as long as the catheter remains in place.

page.standard_overview: Cauda equina syndrome (CES) is a true neurosurgical emergency resulting from compression of the lumbosacral nerve roots below the conus medullaris, most frequently secondary to massive central lumbar disc herniation. Clinical presentation spans a critical spectrum from incomplete CES (CES-I, preserved bladder control but altered perineal sensation or urinary flow) to established CES with retention (CES-R, painless urinary retention and overflow incontinence). Post-void residual measurement can contribute to assessment of bladder dysfunction in suspected cauda equina syndrome, but no single volume threshold reliably excludes or confirms bladder denervation and it must not delay urgent MRI. Suspected cauda equina syndrome requires urgent MRI, usually of the lumbosacral spine unless wider imaging is clinically indicated, and prompt surgical decompression as early as feasible to reduce the risk of permanent bladder, bowel, motor and sexual dysfunction.

page.standard_overview: Celiac disease is a systemic, immune-mediated enteropathy triggered by dietary gluten ingestion in genetically susceptible individuals expressing HLA-DQ2 or HLA-DQ8. The cornerstone of initial diagnostic testing is serology with IgA anti-tissue transglutaminase (tTG-IgA) paired with total serum IgA measurement to rule out selective IgA deficiency. In adult patients, confirmation conventionally requires multiple duodenal mucosal biopsies demonstrating villous atrophy and intraepithelial lymphocytosis (Marsh classification) while on a gluten-containing diet. page.standard_overview: Cellulitis is an acute, spreading bacterial infection of the deep dermis and subcutaneous tissues, most commonly affecting the lower extremities. Erysipelas involves superficial cutaneous lymphatics and upper dermis with sharply demarcated borders and early high fever, whereas standard cellulitis involves deeper dermis and subcutaneous fat with diffuse, poorly demarcated margins.

page.standard_overview: Misdiagnosis of lower extremity cellulitis is exceptionally common in clinical practice, with roughly 30% of patients admitted with a diagnosis of cellulitis found to have another condition and driving significant antibiotic overuse and avoidable hospitalizations. Distinguishing true bacterial dermohypodermitis from non-infectious pseudo-cellulitis mimics is paramount. Erysipelas is a superficial dermal infection characterized by a sharply demarcated, raised, fiery-red border with acute onset and high fevers, driven mainly by group A Streptococcus. Common mimics have differing patterns: stasis dermatitis and lipodermatosclerosis are often bilateral with chronic epidermal or venous changes, contact dermatitis follows an exposure-related distribution, and deep-vein thrombosis is usually unilateral without primary epidermal change; fever and leukocytosis may be absent in any of them.

page.standard_overview: Central line-associated bloodstream infection (CLABSI) remains a primary cause of preventable nosocomial bacteremia, associated with prolonged hospital stay, increased healthcare costs, and attributable mortality. For surveillance, CLABSI is a qualifying bloodstream infection occurring while a central line has been in place for more than two consecutive calendar days on the event date, with no infection at another site to which the bloodstream infection is attributable. Microbiological confirmation distinguishes catheter-related bloodstream infection (CRBSI) using paired blood cultures demonstrating a differential time to positivity (DTTP >=2 hours earlier from the catheter) or quantitative culture ratios (>=3:1 catheter to peripheral). Therapeutic decision-making hinges on whether catheter retention is viable or whether immediate extraction is mandatory (e.g., Staphylococcus aureus, Candida species, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, severe sepsis, or tunnel tract infection).

page.standard_overview: The implementation of standardized insertion and maintenance bundles has transformed central line-associated bloodstream infection (CLABSI) from an accepted complication of critical care into a largely preventable adverse event. Landmark quality improvement trials established the power of multi-faceted safety bundles combining chlorhexidine skin antisepsis, full-barrier drapes, subclavian preference, and daily line audits. When catheter-related bloodstream infection is suspected, obtain appropriate paired peripheral and catheter-drawn blood cultures before antimicrobial therapy whenever this can be done without materially delaying urgent treatment. Treatment mandates pathogen-directed antimicrobial selection, determining the need for line extraction, and duration of therapy ranging from 5-7 days for uncomplicated coagulase-negative staphylococci to 4-6 weeks for complicated S. aureus endovascular seeding.

The randomized 3SITES trial revealed distinct clinical tradeoffs between internal jugular, subclavian, and femoral catheterization: the subclavian route yields the lowest rates of bloodstream infection and symptomatic thrombosis, but carries an elevated risk of pneumothorax. In a multicenter cluster-randomized ICU trial, daily bathing with 2% chlorhexidine-impregnated cloths reduced hospital-acquired bloodstream infections by 28% and acquisition of multidrug-resistant organisms by 23% compared with nonantimicrobial cloths.

page.mentor_intro: The 2023 ESO guideline is the first comprehensive European GRADE guideline on PACNS. Angiography and biopsy-defined disease differ, diagnostic tests often disagree, and adult PACNS has frequent relapses and high mortality.

page.standard_overview: Primary angiitis of the central nervous system (PACNS) is an uncommon, severe, immune-mediated inflammatory disorder confined to the cerebral and leptomeningeal arteries, veins, and capillaries without evidence of systemic vasculitis. Patients typically present with insidious headache, cognitive decline, encephalopathy, and multifocal recurrent ischemic strokes. Brain MRI is abnormal in approximately 93% of reported PACNS cases, but findings are nonspecific and can include multifocal infarcts, white-matter or mass-like lesions and, in some patients, parenchymal or leptomeningeal enhancement. Digital subtraction angiography may show multifocal stenosis and dilatation ('beading'), while leptomeningeal and cortical biopsy can provide histopathologic confirmation; neither test is universally definitive because discordance and false-negative results occur. Distinguishing PACNS from reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome is essential because their treatments differ; suspected PACNS should be managed by an expert multidisciplinary team, often using glucocorticoid-based immunosuppression with cyclophosphamide for selected severe or progressive cases, although treatment evidence is very limited.

topic: Central Sleep Apnea and Cheyne-Stokes respiration

page.mentor_intro: The 2025 AASM guideline covers treatment of central sleep apnoea by aetiology (primary, heart failure, medication, treatment-emergent, medical condition), with mostly conditional, very-low-certainty recommendations. PAP does not prevent cardiovascular events or death in sleep apnoea, and adaptive servo-ventilation is restricted to defined populations.

teaching_points.claim: The 2025 AASM guideline gives treatment recommendations for central sleep apnoea by aetiology: primary, heart failure, medication or substance, treatment-emergent, and medical condition; certainty is very low in places.
Updated adaptive servo-ventilation recommendations apply only to the target populations, with LVEF above 45% or mild CHF-related central sleep apnoea syndrome addressed explicitly.
A meta-analysis found PAP therapy for sleep apnoea does not support treatment aimed at preventing cardiovascular events or death, though PAP has other benefits.
Acetazolamide improved both obstructive and central sleep apnoea in a meta-analysis, though long-term data are needed.
Sleep-related breathing disorders are common in dementia, particularly Alzheimer's and Parkinson's dementia.

In the CANPAP trial of heart failure patients with central sleep apnea, CPAP successfully reduced the central apnea-hypopnea index and improved left ventricular ejection fraction, but failed to improve overall transplant-free survival.

The landmark SERVE-HF trial showed that adaptive servo-ventilation (ASV) in patients with HFrEF (LVEF <=45%) and predominant central sleep apnea significantly increased all-cause mortality (HR 1.28) and cardiovascular mortality (HR 1.34), leading to an absolute contraindication.

Transvenous phrenic nerve stimulation demonstrated significant reduction in central apnea-hypopnea index and improved sleep quality and quality of life in a pivotal randomized trial, offering an implantable neurostimulation alternative for moderate-to-severe CSA.

uncertainties: Evidence certainty for most treatments is low.

page.standard_overview: Central sleep apnea (CSA) and its classic periodic breathing manifestation, Cheyne-Stokes respiration (CSR), represent a ventilatory control disorder characterized by recurrent crescendo-decrescendo fluctuations in tidal volume punctuated by central apneas without respiratory effort. In heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, Cheyne-Stokes respiration is sustained by prolonged circulation time, pulmonary congestion-related hyperventilation and increased chemosensitivity, allowing PaCO2 to fall below the apneic threshold; central sleep apnea also occurs with stroke and several other conditions. CANPAP showed that CPAP attenuated central sleep apnea but did not improve survival, whereas SERVE-HF found increased all-cause and cardiovascular mortality with adaptive servo-ventilation in HFrEF with LVEF 45% or less and predominant moderate-to-severe CSA, leading to contraindication of that therapy in this population.

page.standard_overview: Cerebral amyloid angiopathy (CAA) is a leading cause of non-traumatic lobar intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH) and cognitive decline in older adults. It is characterized histopathologically by progressive amyloid-beta peptide deposition in the walls of cortical and leptomeningeal small arteries, arterioles, and capillaries. Clinical manifestations include spontaneous and recurrent lobar intracerebral hemorrhage, transient focal neurological episodes ('amyloid spells') and cognitive impairment or dementia. The Boston criteria v2.0 build on v1.5, which incorporated cortical superficial siderosis (cSS), a potent MRI marker of high recurrent hemorrhage risk, alongside strictly lobar cerebral microbleeds on blood-sensitive MRI sequences (T2*-GRE and SWI), and add non-haemorrhagic white-matter markers. Anticoagulation in CAA requires individualized weighing of recurrent intracranial hemorrhage risk against the thromboembolic indication, considering prior hemorrhage, cortical superficial siderosis, microbleed burden and available stroke-prevention alternatives.
