In the randomized CHANCE trial, clopidogrel plus aspirin initiated within 24 hours of acute minor ischemic stroke (NIHSS <=3) or high-risk TIA (ABCD2 >=4) significantly reduced 90-day recurrent stroke from 11.7% to 8.2% (HR 0.68) without increasing hemorrhage.

In the POINT trial, clopidogrel plus aspirin reduced major ischaemic events compared with aspirin alone (5.0% vs 6.5%; hazard ratio 0.75) in acute ischaemic stroke and high-risk TIA, with a higher risk of major hemorrhage.

The TARDIS trial demonstrated that triple antiplatelet therapy (aspirin + clopidogrel + dipyridamole) did not reduce stroke recurrence compared to guideline-directed dual or single therapy, but significantly increased major bleeding, establishing a ceiling on antiplatelet escalation.

page.standard_overview: The risk of recurrent stroke is highest during the first 48 to 72 hours following an acute minor ischemic stroke or high-risk transient ischemic attack (TIA). The landmark CHANCE trial in China and the international POINT trial established that short-course dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT) with clopidogrel plus aspirin is significantly superior to aspirin monotherapy in preventing early recurrent ischemic stroke. For eligible non-cardioembolic minor ischemic stroke or high-risk TIA not treated with thrombolysis, DAPT should be started within 24 hours; a 21-day clopidogrel-plus-aspirin course is commonly used, with duration individualized to the trial regimen and bleeding risk before de-escalation to monotherapy. Longer DAPT increases major bleeding, and its net benefit is greatest in the early high-risk period; extending clopidogrel-plus-aspirin DAPT beyond 90 days is not recommended after minor stroke or high-risk TIA.

page.standard_overview: Clostridioides difficile infection (CDI) is the leading cause of healthcare-associated infectious diarrhea and pseudomembranous colitis. Pathogenesis is triggered by broad-spectrum antibiotic disruption of the colonic microbiota, facilitating C. difficile spore germination and the production of large clostridial exotoxins (Toxin A and Toxin B) that cause mucosal inflammation and epithelial necrosis. Testing should be limited to unformed stool from patients with clinically compatible diarrhea; one accepted multistep algorithm uses GDH screening and toxin A/B enzyme immunoassay with NAAT for discordant results, although other validated algorithms may be used and clinical context is needed to distinguish infection from colonization. IDSA guidance prefers oral fidaxomicin 200 mg twice daily for 10 days over vancomycin, while ACG accepts fidaxomicin or vancomycin; metronidazole is no longer preferred and is generally reserved for selected non-severe cases when the preferred agents are unavailable.

page.standard_overview: Clinical stratification of Clostridioides difficile infection directs intensity of antimicrobial therapy and urgent surgical involvement. Non-severe disease (WBC <=15,000/uL and serum creatinine <1.5 mg/dL) and severe disease (WBC >=15,000/uL or serum Cr >1.5 mg/dL) respond to oral fidaxomicin (200 mg bid) or oral vancomycin (125 mg qid). Fulminant CDI with hypotension, shock, ileus, or megacolon requires urgent high-dose enteral vancomycin, typically 500 mg four times daily, plus intravenous metronidazole; add rectal vancomycin if ileus is present and obtain early surgical consultation, with colectomy or diverting loop ileostomy considered in selected cases. For recurrent CDI, options include extended-pulsed fidaxomicin, a vancomycin taper, bezlotoxumab (anti-toxin B; availability has been withdrawn in some regions), and faecal microbiota products, which help restore colonisation resistance and reduce relapse.

page.standard_overview: Clozapine-induced myocarditis is an acute, life-threatening hypersensitivity or toxic inflammatory myocardial injury occurring in approximately 1% to 3% of patients initiating clozapine. Most clozapine-associated myocarditis occurs early, particularly during the first 2-4 weeks, but onset can be later and continued clinical vigilance is required. Clinical symptoms are frequently non-specific and easily mistaken for benign drug fever or respiratory infection: persistent resting tachycardia (>100-110 bpm out of proportion to fever), fever, chest discomfort, shortness of breath, and postural hypotension. Standardized monitoring using baseline and weekly troponin and C-reactive protein during the first 4 weeks can aid early detection of clozapine-associated myocarditis, although the optimal protocol and its effect on mortality have not been established. Prompt recognition, immediate clozapine discontinuation, and urgent cardiology assessment are essential to reduce the risk of fatal deterioration; any later rechallenge requires individualized specialist assessment after recovery.

page.standard_overview: Cluster headache is the most severe and distinctive trigeminal autonomic cephalalgia (TAC), colloquially known as 'suicide headache' due to its excruciating, devastating pain intensity. Cluster headache causes strictly unilateral severe orbito-temporal pain lasting 15-180 minutes, often with circadian and circannual periodicity and nocturnal attacks that can awaken patients from sleep. Episodes are accompanied by prominent ipsilateral parasympathetic activation and sympathetic paralysis: conjunctival injection, lacrimation, nasal congestion, rhinorrhea, eyelid edema, miosis, and ptosis (partial Horner syndrome). A key characteristic clinical feature distinguishing cluster headache from migraine is intense motor agitation and restlessness (patients pace the room, rock back and forth, or hit their head), whereas migraineurs seek stillness in a dark, quiet room.

page.standard_overview: The pharmacological management of cluster headache comprises three distinct, coordinated strategies: acute attack abortive therapy, short-term transitional bridging prophylaxis, and long-term maintenance prophylaxis. Oral analgesics and oral triptans are generally too slow because of delayed absorption relative to the rapid (peak within minutes) attack tempo. High-flow normobaric 100% oxygen (12 to 15 L/min delivered via a tight-fitting non-rebreather mask for 15 minutes) was validated in a landmark randomized trial by Cohen et al., providing pain freedom or adequate relief at 15 minutes in about 78% of attacks (versus about 20% with air). Subcutaneous sumatriptan (6 mg) provides rapid rescue. For transitional prophylaxis, a greater occipital nerve (GON) suboccipital steroid injection rapidly suppresses bouts. Verapamil (titrated from 240 mg to 960 mg daily with mandatory serial ECGs to monitor for PR prolongation and AV block) is the gold-standard maintenance preventive agent.

page.standard_overview: Cytomegalovirus (CMV) causes severe opportunistic end-organ disease in immunocompromised hosts, including solid organ transplant (SOT) recipients, allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplant (HSCT) patients, and individuals with advanced HIV infection (CD4 count <50 cells/uL). Clinical manifestations depend on the host: CMV retinitis with necrotizing hemorrhagic retinal lesions is characteristic of advanced HIV, whereas gastrointestinal disease and potentially life-threatening pneumonitis are important presentations in transplant recipients. International consensus guidelines endorse intravenous ganciclovir (5 mg/kg every 12 hours) or oral valganciclovir (900 mg twice daily) as first-line induction therapy; the landmark VICTOR trial established the non-inferiority of oral valganciclovir for non-life-threatening disease. For refractory or ganciclovir-resistant CMV (harboring UL97 kinase or UL54 DNA polymerase mutations), foscarnet, cidofovir, or maribavir provide targeted salvage.

page.standard_overview: Coagulation disorders encompass inherited deficiencies of clotting factor proteins (Hemophilia A [Factor VIII], Hemophilia B [Factor IX], and von Willebrand disease [vWD]) and complex acquired consumptive coagulopathies, notably Disseminated Intravascular Coagulation (DIC). Laboratory evaluation relies on systematic interpretation of the prothrombin time (PT/INR), activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT), thrombin time, and mixing studies. An isolated prolonged aPTT that corrects on immediate 1:1 mixing with normal plasma suggests an intrinsic-pathway factor deficiency and should prompt specific factor assays; failure to correct suggests an inhibitor or lupus anticoagulant, with anticoagulant interference also considered. The management of severe Hemophilia A underwent a revolution with the introduction of emicizumab—a recombinant humanized bispecific monoclonal antibody that bridges activated Factor IX and Factor X, mimicking FVIII cofactor activity—proven in the landmark HAVEN trials to drastically slash bleeding rates with subcutaneous dosing, regardless of FVIII inhibitor presence.

standard_knowledge.claim: Epidemiological surveillance by NIOSH demonstrates a dramatic, modern resurgence of severe coal worker's pneumoconiosis and progressive massive fibrosis in underground coal miners, driven by mechanized mining cutting into silica-containing rock.

Progressive massive fibrosis (PMF) is characterized on chest imaging by large, confluent fibrotic masses >1 cm in diameter, predominantly in the upper lung zones, associated with architectural distortion, bullae, and restrictive-obstructive impairment.

Caplan syndrome represents the distinct clinical constellation of coal worker's pneumoconiosis in patients with rheumatoid arthritis, presenting radiographically with multiple, well-defined peripheral round nodules measuring 0.5 to 5 cm in diameter.

There are no curative pharmacological treatments to reverse coal dust fibrosis; medical management mandates complete removal from dust exposure, smoking cessation, pulmonary rehabilitation, supplemental oxygen, and lung transplantation evaluation.

page.standard_overview: Coal Worker's Pneumoconiosis (CWP)—commonly known as 'black lung disease'—is an occupational fibrotic lung disorder caused by the chronic inhalation and pulmonary accumulation of respirable coal mine dust. Inhaled dust particles (<5 um) are engulfed by alveolar macrophages, inciting chronic inflammatory signaling, reactive oxygen species generation, and fibroblastic proliferation. Pathologically, CWP spans from simple CWP (characterized by 1 to 5 mm pigmented coal macules and nodules with focal surrounding centrilobular emphysema in upper lung zones) to complicated CWP, known as Progressive Massive Fibrosis (PMF). PMF is defined by large confluent fibrotic masses (>10 mm in diameter) that cause progressive, irreversible lung destruction, cavitation, severe hypoxemia, and cor pulmonale. A critical clinical variant is Caplan syndrome: the co-occurrence of CWP with rheumatoid arthritis, manifesting as rapidly developing, multiple rounded peripheral necrobiotic pulmonary nodules.

page.standard_overview: Coeliac disease is a chronic, systemic immune-mediated enteropathy triggered by dietary gluten ingestion in genetically predisposed individuals expressing HLA-DQ2 or HLA-DQ8. The small bowel mucosal pathology is defined by the Marsh-Oberhuber classification: intraepithelial lymphocytosis (Marsh 1), crypt hyperplasia (Marsh 2), and progressive villous blunting (Marsh 3a-3c). Beyond classic gastrointestinal malabsorption, coeliac disease frequently manifests with extraintestinal presentations, including iron deficiency anemia, early-onset osteopenia, elevated transaminases, recurrent aphthous stomatitis, and dermatitis herpetiformis (pathognomonic granular IgA deposition within dermal papillae). Treatment mandates strict, lifelong gluten exclusion. In patients with persistent symptoms despite strict GFD, refractory coeliac disease must be evaluated and subclassified into Type 1 (polyclonal T-cells) or Type 2 (aberrant clonal intraepithelial lymphocytes), the latter carrying high risks of enteropathy-associated T-cell lymphoma (EATL).

page.standard_overview: The clinical approach to the collapsed patient requires immediately distinguishing true syncope—defined as transient loss of consciousness (TLoC) caused by self-limited global cerebral hypoperfusion characterized by rapid onset, short duration, and spontaneous complete recovery—from non-syncopal collapse (generalized epileptic seizures, hypoglycemia, psychogenic pseudosyncope, accidental falls, and catastrophic vascular events like subarachnoid hemorrhage). page.standard_overview: Advanced Life Support (ALS) guidelines established by the European Resuscitation Council (ERC) and American Heart Association (AHA) provide standardized, evidence-based algorithms for cardiac arrest resuscitation. The central branch point divides arrest rhythms into Shockable (Ventricular Fibrillation [VF] and Pulseless Ventricular Tachycardia [pVT]) and Non-Shockable (Pulseless Electrical Activity [PEA] and Asystole). Shockable management prioritizes immediate defibrillation, continuous high-quality chest compressions (100-120 bpm, 5-6 cm depth), intravenous amiodarone or lidocaine after the 3rd shock, and adrenaline every 3 to 5 minutes starting after the 3rd shock. Non-shockable management mandates early adrenaline and immediate identification and treatment of reversible causes structured by the '4 Hs and 4 Ts'. After ROSC in patients who remain unresponsive, active temperature control and fever prevention are components of post-arrest care; TTM2 found no mortality benefit from targeted hypothermia at 33°C compared with targeted normothermia with early fever treatment.

Because recurrence rates exceed 50% to 60% following successful endoscopic decompression alone, definitive semi-elective sigmoid resection during the index hospitalization is strongly recommended for operable patients.

For cecal volvulus, endoscopic reduction is contraindicated due to low success rates (<30%) and high perforation risks; emergency surgical resection (right hemicolectomy or ileocecectomy) is the mandatory treatment of choice.

page.standard_overview: Colonic volvulus is torsion of a redundant mobile segment of large bowel around its mesenteric axis and is a leading cause of large-bowel obstruction, accounting for roughly 5% of cases in many series. Sigmoid volvulus (comprising roughly 60 to 75% of cases) characteristically affects elderly, debilitated, institutionalized patients with chronic constipation and neuropsychiatric disease. Abdominal radiography and CT demonstrate a dilated, inverted U-shaped loop resembling a 'coffee bean' with its apex pointing toward the right upper quadrant. Management dictates urgent rigid or flexible endoscopic detorsion/decompression with placement of a flatus tube in the absence of peritonitis, followed by elective sigmoid resection during the same hospitalization due to extreme recurrence rates (>50%). Cecal volvulus generally requires urgent surgery because endoscopic decompression is usually ineffective; resection is standard for nonviable or severely dilated bowel, while cecopexy may be considered in selected patients with viable bowel.

page.standard_overview: Colorectal cancer (CRC) is the third most common cancer globally, arising through distinct genomic and epigenetic pathways. The classical adenoma-carcinoma sequence (Fearon-Vogelstein model) accounts for 70-80% of sporadic cases, driven by chromosomal instability (CIN) initiated by APC tumor suppressor loss, followed by KRAS activation and TP53 inactivation. Approximately 15% arise via defective DNA mismatch repair (dMMR) leading to high microsatellite instability (MSI-H), seen in hereditary Lynch syndrome (germline MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, PMS2 mutations) and sporadic hypermethylated tumors (CIMP / BRAF V600E). Clinical presentation differs by anatomy: right-sided tumors manifest with insidious occult bleeding, fatigue, and iron deficiency anemia, whereas left-sided tumors cause altered bowel habits, pencil-thin stools, and obstruction. Accurate clinical-radiological staging (contrast CT and high-resolution pelvic MRI for rectal cancer) directs multidisciplinary curative resection.

page.standard_overview: After curative R0 resection, adjuvant chemotherapy targets micrometastatic disease and reduces recurrence and improves survival in stage III colon cancer and in appropriately selected high-risk stage II disease. In stage III node-positive colon cancer, oxaliplatin-based doublet chemotherapy with FOLFOX or CAPOX is standard; MOSAIC established the benefit of adding oxaliplatin to fluorouracil-leucovorin, while other trials established CAPOX. A practice-changing breakthrough emerged from the international IDEA collaboration: in low-risk stage III disease (T1-3, N1), 3 months of adjuvant CAPOX achieved non-inferior disease-free survival compared to 6 months while drastically slashing rates of debilitating, permanent oxaliplatin-induced peripheral sensory neurotoxicity. In high-risk stage III disease (T4 or N2), 6 months remains standard. In stage II disease, adjuvant chemotherapy is restricted to high-risk features (T4, obstruction, perforation, <12 lymph nodes harvested, lymphovascular/perineural invasion); critically, tumors exhibiting deficient mismatch repair (dMMR/MSI-H) derive no benefit from single-agent 5-FU adjuvant therapy.

page.standard_overview: Population-level screening for colorectal cancer (CRC) effectively reduces disease incidence and disease-specific mortality by detecting asymptomatic early-stage invasive carcinomas and enabling the endoscopic removal of pre-cancerous adenomatous and serrated polyps. Current USPSTF guidelines recommend initiating routine screening in all average-risk adults beginning at age 45 (lowered from age 50 due to rising incidence of early-onset CRC). Non-invasive screening is anchored by the quantitative Fecal Immunochemical Test (FIT), which selectively detects human globin with high sensitivity and eliminates dietary restrictions. In COLONPREV, biennial FIT was non-inferior to one-off colonoscopy for 10-year colorectal cancer mortality, while NordICC (invitation to colonoscopy versus no screening) showed a smaller than expected benefit largely because of limited uptake, emphasizing that adherence and participation dictate population-level effectiveness.

page.standard_overview: Systemic therapy for metastatic colorectal cancer (mCRC) is dictated by comprehensive molecular biomarker testing (RAS [KRAS/NRAS], BRAF V600E, HER2, and mismatch repair / microsatellite stability status) alongside primary tumor sidedness. In KEYNOTE-177, first-line pembrolizumab doubled median progression-free survival to 16.5 versus 8.2 months with chemotherapy in dMMR/MSI-H metastatic CRC, establishing it as a standard first-line immunotherapy option. For pMMR/MSS disease, chemotherapy is combined with a biologic according to molecular profile and sidedness: anti-EGFR antibodies are generally preferred for RAS wild-type, left-sided tumors, particularly without BRAF V600E mutation, while bevacizumab is commonly preferred for right-sided or RAS-mutated disease. For previously treated BRAF V600E-mutant metastatic CRC, encorafenib plus cetuximab is an approved targeted regimen supported by BEACON CRC; treatment in other lines depends on current approvals and regimen-specific evidence.

page.standard_overview: Common variable immunodeficiency (CVID) is the most common clinically significant primary immunodeficiency in adults, characterized by impaired B-cell differentiation and defective antibody production. Diagnostic criteria mandate marked reduction in serum IgG (at least two standard deviations below age-adjusted mean, typically <5.0 g/L) combined with marked reduction in serum IgA and/or IgM, accompanied by absent or severely impaired specific antibody responses to vaccination (e.g., protein tetanus/diphtheria and polysaccharide pneumococcal vaccines), after excluding secondary hypogammaglobulinemia. Clinical manifestations include recurrent sinopulmonary infections (Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae) leading to bronchiectasis, alongside non-infectious immune dysregulation (enteropathy, granulomatous-lymphocytic interstitial lung disease [GLILD], autoimmune cytopenias, and lymphoma). Immunoglobulin replacement with IVIG or SCIg is foundational, usually long-term therapy; the dose and trough IgG target should be individualized to infections and clinical response rather than applying a universal >7-8 g/L threshold.

page.standard_overview: Community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) is a common and potentially life-threatening lower respiratory tract infection acquired outside of hospital or healthcare environments. While Streptococcus pneumoniae remains the predominant bacterial etiology, contemporary molecular epidemiological studies (such as the CDC EPIC study) demonstrate that respiratory viruses (rhinovirus, influenza, RSV, SARS-CoV-2) are detected in a substantial proportion of hospitalized patients, often as co-pathogens. Atypical pathogens (Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Chlamydophila pneumoniae, and Legionella pneumophila) account for 15-20% of cases. Clinical presentation classically combines acute cough, purulent sputum, dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, and fever with focal auscultatory crackles. Diagnosis requires radiographic demonstration of a new pulmonary infiltrate or consolidation on chest radiography or CT. Validated risk stratification directs appropriate outpatient versus inpatient management.

page.standard_overview: Hospitalized community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) encompasses a high-risk spectrum ranging from general medical ward admissions to life-threatening acute respiratory failure and septic shock. Inpatient management requires immediate severity triage to determine if direct intensive care unit (ICU) admission is indicated. The ATS/IDSA guidelines define severe CAP by validated major criteria (invasive mechanical ventilation or septic shock requiring vasopressors) or the presence of at least three minor criteria (respiratory rate >=30, PaO2/FiO2 ratio <=250, multilobar infiltrates, acute confusion, uremia BUN >=20 mg/dL, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, hypothermia, or hypotension requiring aggressive fluid resuscitation). In severe CAP, obtain indicated blood and sputum cultures and urinary antigen tests without materially delaying parenteral antibiotics, which should be started promptly, especially immediately in septic shock. Procalcitonin may be used as an adjunct to support stopping antibiotics, although the 2019 ATS/IDSA guideline advises against using it to decide whether to start them.

page.standard_overview: Empiric antimicrobial selection for community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) is guided by patient setting (outpatient vs inpatient non-ICU vs ICU), underlying comorbidities, and local pathogen resistance patterns. For healthy outpatients without chronic disease, updated ATS/IDSA guidelines strongly endorse high-dose oral amoxicillin (1 g three times daily) or doxycycline (100 mg twice daily); macrolide monotherapy is restricted strictly to regions where pneumococcal macrolide resistance is documented to be <25%. In outpatients with chronic cardiopulmonary, renal, or metabolic comorbidities, combination therapy (amoxicillin-clavulanate plus a macrolide/doxycycline) or respiratory fluoroquinolone monotherapy (levofloxacin, moxifloxacin) is recommended. In hospitalized non-ICU patients with clinically suspected CAP, CAP-START found a beta-lactam monotherapy strategy noninferior to beta-lactam-macrolide or fluoroquinolone strategies for 90-day mortality. Treat uncomplicated CAP for at least 5 days and until clinical stability is achieved, extending therapy when indicated by persistent instability, complications, or the pathogen.

page.standard_overview: Objective risk assessment in community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) guides site-of-care decisions, reducing avoidable hospital admissions and associated nosocomial complications. The two primary validated scoring systems are CURB-65 and the Pneumonia Severity Index (PSI). CURB-65 assigns 1 point each for confusion, urea >7 mmol/L, respiratory rate >=30/min, systolic BP <90 or diastolic BP <=60 mmHg, and age >=65; scores 0-1 often suit outpatient care, score 2 may warrant supervised or short inpatient care, and scores 3-5 indicate higher mortality risk requiring urgent hospital assessment and consideration of ICU care. PSI incorporates 20 variables and demonstrates higher sensitivity for safely triaging low-risk patients (Classes I-III) to outpatient care. When atypical-pathogen coverage is indicated, use a macrolide, tetracycline, or respiratory fluoroquinolone because beta-lactams do not reliably treat Mycoplasma, Chlamydophila, or intracellular Legionella; healthy outpatients do not always require atypical coverage.

page.standard_overview: Comprehensive management of community-acquired pneumonia spans rapid diagnostic confirmation, risk-adapted antimicrobial therapy, timely oral step-down, and planned recovery surveillance. Diagnosis combines clinical signs with radiographic verification. Routine microbiologic testing is not required for every hospitalized CAP patient; blood and sputum cultures and pneumococcal or Legionella urinary antigen testing are prioritized in severe CAP and when resistant-pathogen risks or specific epidemiologic indications exist. Parenteral therapy is transitioned to oral step-down as early as day 2 to 3 once the patient is hemodynamically stable, afebrile, and able to absorb oral medications, significantly shortening hospital length of stay without compromising cure rates. Some guidelines (BTS) advise a follow-up chest radiograph at about 6 weeks for patients over 50, smokers, or those with persisting symptoms to document resolution and exclude underlying bronchogenic carcinoma, whereas ATS/IDSA does not recommend routine follow-up imaging.

page.standard_overview: Severe community-acquired pneumonia (sCAP) requiring intensive care admission is associated with mortality rates exceeding 20% to 30%, driven by septic shock, multiorgan dysfunction, and acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS). standard_knowledge.claim: The Pneumonia Severity Index (PSI/PORT score) stratifies CAP into five risk classes based on 20 demographic, comorbid, physical, and laboratory variables; Classes I and II (<70 points) exhibit 30-day mortality below 1% and are strongly recommended for outpatient care, whereas Class IV (91-130 points) and Class V (>130 points) confer mortality rates of 9% and 27%, requiring inpatient hospitalization.

CURB-65 assigns 1 point each for Confusion, Urea >7 mmol/L (BUN >19 mg/dL), Respiratory rate >=30/min, Blood pressure (systolic <90 mmHg or diastolic <=60 mmHg), and Age >=65; a score of 0-1 indicates low risk (<3% mortality, outpatient management), a score of 2 indicates moderate risk (9% mortality, short-stay inpatient or supervised outpatient), and a score >=3 indicates severe pneumonia (15-40% mortality, urgent inpatient admission).

SMART-COP (Systolic BP, Multilobar, Albumin, Respiratory rate, Tachycardia, Confusion, Oxygen low, arterial pH) specifically identifies patients at risk for intensive respiratory or vasopressor support (IRVS); a score >=3 detects 92% of patients requiring IRVS, outperforming PSI and CURB-65 for mechanical ventilation triage.

page.standard_overview: Risk stratification in community-acquired pneumonia dictates site-of-care decisions, diagnostic depth, and empirical antibiotic selection. Clinical judgment alone can misestimate CAP severity, particularly in older patients with atypical presentations; validated tools should supplement rather than replace clinical assessment. Standardized risk tools—chiefly the CURB-65 score and the Pneumonia Severity Index (PSI/PORT score)—provide objective 30-day mortality estimates. While CURB-65 prioritizes rapid bedside triage, PSI provides superior discriminative accuracy for identifying low-risk candidates safe for ambulatory management. In severe presentations, neither tool accurately predicts acute deterioration requiring mechanical ventilation or septic shock resuscitation, necessitating specialized scoring via SMART-COP or the ATS/IDSA severe CAP criteria.

standard_knowledge.claim: Hospital-acquired pneumonia is defined as pneumonia developing >=48 hours post-admission that was not incubating upon hospitalization, whereas ventilator-associated pneumonia develops >=48 hours post-endotracheal intubation; the former HCAP category is abandoned to prevent unnecessary broad-spectrum toxicity.

In HAP/VAP, empiric coverage for methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) using vancomycin or linezolid is indicated only if the patient has received IV antibiotics within the prior 90 days, is in an ICU where MRSA prevalence among S. aureus isolates exceeds 20%, or is at high risk of mortality (requiring ventilatory support or septic shock).

Two antipseudomonal agents from different classes (e.g., piperacillin-tazobactam or cefepime plus an aminoglycoside or ciprofloxacin) are recommended empirically for HAP/VAP only in patients with prior IV antibiotics within 90 days, septic shock, high risk of death, or when local Gram-negative monotherapy resistance rates exceed 10%.

A 7-day course of antimicrobial therapy is non-inferior to longer courses (10-14 days) for HAP and VAP in patients who achieve clinical stability, significantly reducing antibiotic selection pressure and Clostridioides difficile superinfection without increasing recurrence rates.

page.standard_overview: Differentiating community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) from hospital-acquired pneumonia (HAP) and ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP) is fundamental to preventing both antimicrobial under-treatment and inappropriate broad-spectrum overuse. Current ATS/IDSA guidelines have retired the legacy 'healthcare-associated pneumonia' (HCAP) category because it led to excessive carbapenem and vancomycin consumption without mortality benefit. True HAP is defined as pneumonia developing 48 hours or more after hospital admission, not incubating at admission, whereas VAP develops 48 hours or more following endotracheal intubation. Empirical regimens must reflect validated individual risk factors for multidrug-resistant (MDR) pathogens—specifically prior intravenous antibiotic exposure within 90 days and local unit antibiograms—rather than institutional residence alone.

standard_knowledge.claim: The cardinal diagnostic finding of early acute compartment syndrome is pain out of proportion to injury and exquisite pain upon passive stretching of the muscles traversing the affected fascial compartment; paresthesia reflects early sensory nerve ischemia, while loss of distal pulses is a late sign signifying irreversible muscle infarction.

A delta pressure (diastolic blood pressure minus measured intracompartmental pressure) <=30 mmHg represents inadequate tissue perfusion and is a validated, objective threshold for emergent fasciotomy, outperforming absolute compartment pressure (>30 mmHg) in preventing inappropriate surgery in hypertensive patients or missed ischemia in hypotensive patients.

In the lower leg, emergent decompression mandates complete release of all four distinct fascial compartments (anterior, lateral, superficial posterior, and deep posterior), typically achieved via a dual-incision (anterolateral and posteromedial) technique.

Immediate initial management prior to surgical intervention involves cutting all circumferential casts, splints, and dressings down to bare skin (which can reduce intracompartmental pressure by up to 50-85%) and positioning the limb at heart level, strictly avoiding elevation which reduces arterial perfusion pressure.

page.standard_overview: Acute compartment syndrome (ACS) is a time-critical surgical emergency where elevated tissue pressure within an unyielding osteofascial envelope compromises capillary perfusion, culminating in ischemic necrosis of muscles and nerves. The earliest, most sensitive clinical finding is severe pain disproportionate to the underlying injury, exacerbated by passive stretch of the muscle groups within the involved compartment. Pulselessness, pallor, paralysis, and poikilothermia are late signs that may indicate advanced ischemia; they must never be awaited before diagnosing and treating compartment syndrome. Diagnosis is primarily clinical, but intracompartmental pressure monitoring using needle manometry is indispensable in obtunded, intubated, or equivocal patients. Definitive management demands immediate release of all constrictive casts or dressings and emergent decompressive fasciotomy.

standard_knowledge.claim: Deficiencies in terminal complement pathway components (C5, C6, C7, C8, and C9) or alternative pathway properdin result in a 1,000- to 10,000-fold increased risk of recurrent invasive Neisseria meningitidis and disseminated Neisseria gonorrhoeae infections due to the inability to assemble the lytic membrane attack complex (C5b-9).

Early classical pathway deficiencies (C1q, C1r/s, C4, and C2) impair apoptotic cell and immune complex clearance, predisposing predominantly to severe encapsulated bacterial infections (Streptococcus pneumoniae, H. influenzae) and severe autoimmune disorders, with >90% of C1q-deficient individuals developing systemic lupus erythematosus.

Screening for complement deficiencies requires total hemolytic complement (CH50) to evaluate classical and terminal pathways, and alternative pathway hemolytic activity (AH50); an undetectable CH50 with normal AH50 indicates an early classical component defect (C1, C4, C2), while undetectable levels in both assays indicate a shared terminal pathway defect (C5 through C9).

Therapeutic complement inhibition with monoclonal anti-C5 antibodies (eculizumab, ravulizumab) mimics terminal complement deficiency, requiring immunization against meningococcal serogroups A, C, W, Y and B at least 2 weeks prior to therapy, coupled with long-term oral penicillin or macrolide chemoprophylaxis.

page.standard_overview: The complement cascade is a fundamental arm of innate immunity comprising classical, alternative, and lectin activation pathways converging on terminal membrane attack complex (MAC, C5b-9) assembly and opsonization via C3b. Congenital or pharmacologically induced deficiencies in complement components generate distinct, predictable patterns of infectious vulnerability and autoimmune pathology. Early classical pathway deficiencies (C1q, C1r/s, C4, C2) impair immune complex clearance and opsonization of encapsulated bacteria (Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae) while strongly predisposing to systemic lupus erythematosus. In contrast, terminal pathway deficiencies (C5, C6, C7, C8, C9) and alternative pathway defects (properdin) selectively disable serum bactericidal lysis, resulting in an extreme susceptibility to recurrent, invasive Neisserial infections, particularly Neisseria meningitidis.

standard_knowledge.claim: CRPS Type 1 develops in the absence of a definable major peripheral nerve lesion (representing >90% of clinical cases, typically following distal radius fractures or sprains), whereas CRPS Type 2 is characterized by electrophysiologically or anatomically confirmed structural damage to a major nerve trunk.

page.standard_overview: Complex Regional Pain Syndrome (CRPS) is a debilitating neuropathic pain condition that characteristically develops in an extremity following trauma, fracture, or surgery, presenting with continuing pain that is disproportionate in degree and duration to the inciting event. Diagnosis uses the clinical Budapest Criteria: continuing disproportionate pain, at least one symptom in at least three of four categories, at least one sign in at least two categories, and exclusion of a better alternative diagnosis. CRPS is bifurcated into Type 1 (formerly reflex sympathetic dystrophy), in which no overt major peripheral nerve lesion is demonstrable, and Type 2 (formerly causalgia), where a discrete major nerve injury is confirmed. Management emphasizes early recognition and individualized, graded multidisciplinary rehabilitation with desensitization and functional mobilization; drugs and interventional procedures are adjuncts for selected patients, with variable supporting evidence.

page.standard_overview: Complicated intra-abdominal infections (cIAI) are defined by extension of inflammation and microbial contamination beyond a hollow viscus into the peritoneal space, manifesting as localized abscess formation or diffuse peritonitis. STOP-IT showed that after adequate source control, a fixed antibiotic course of approximately 4 days produced similar rates of surgical-site infection, recurrent intra-abdominal infection, and death to a longer course averaging 8 days.

standard_knowledge.claim: Community-acquired mild-to-moderate cIAI is reliably treated with single-agent cefoxitin, ertapenem, or moxifloxacin, or combination therapy with cefazolin, cefotaxime, or ceftriaxone plus metronidazole; routine coverage for Enterococcus faecalis or Pseudomonas aeruginosa is unnecessary in this setting.

Empirical coverage against Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Enterococcus species is strictly indicated in healthcare-associated, postoperative, or tertiary peritonitis, utilizing piperacillin-tazobactam, cefepime plus metronidazole, or meropenem.

Empirical antifungal therapy directed against Candida albicans and non-albicans Candida (using an echinocandin such as caspofungin or micafungin) is indicated for cIAI only in high-risk patients: recurrent gastrointestinal perforations, anastomotic leaks, severe necrotizing pancreatitis, or sustained septic shock in prolonged ICU admissions.

Transition to oral antimicrobial therapy (e.g., ciprofloxacin plus metronidazole, amoxicillin-clavulanate, or oral trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole plus metronidazole) is safe as soon as the patient tolerates oral intake, is hemodynamically stable, and demonstrates resolving inflammatory markers, completing a total antibiotic course of 4 to 5 days.

page.standard_overview: Microbiological risk stratification in complicated intra-abdominal infections (cIAI) determines the necessity of covering multidrug-resistant (MDR) pathogens, enterococci, and fungi. Community-acquired cIAI is usually polymicrobial with enteric Gram-negative bacilli, streptococci, and anaerobes; beta-lactam/beta-lactamase inhibitors or a cephalosporin plus metronidazole are empiric options, selected by severity and local susceptibility. In contrast, healthcare-associated or postoperative cIAI is heavily enriched for Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Enterobacterales expressing extended-spectrum beta-lactamases (ESBL), Enterococcus faecium, and Candida species. Achieving early microbiological eradication while preserving antimicrobial stewardship requires risk-tailored regimens and prompt oral step-down once gastrointestinal motility returns.

standard_knowledge.claim: A complicated urinary tract infection is defined by the presence of factors that compromise the host defenses or urinary tract drainage—including male sex, nephrolithiasis, urethral stricture, neurogenic bladder, indwelling catheter, renal failure, or immunosuppression—mandating pre-treatment urine culture and susceptibility testing.

In patients presenting with complicated UTI and signs of obstructive uropathy (e.g., infected hydronephrosis from obstructing ureteral calculi), emergent urological decompression via ureteral stenting or percutaneous nephrostomy is life-saving and takes precedence over antibiotic adjustments.

Novel carbapenem-sparing beta-lactamase inhibitor combinations, such as ceftazidime-avibactam and cefepime-enmetazobactam, achieve superior or non-inferior clinical cure and microbiological eradication rates compared to carbapenems (doripenem) or piperacillin-tazobactam in cUTI caused by ESBL-producing Enterobacterales.

A 7-day treatment course with fluoroquinolones (ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin) or trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (when susceptible) is non-inferior to 14 days in hemodynamically stable patients with complicated UTI who demonstrate prompt clinical resolution and source relief.

page.standard_overview: Complicated urinary tract infections (cUTI) occur in patients with anatomical, functional, or metabolic host abnormalities that increase the risk of therapeutic failure, recurrent infection, and secondary bacteremia. These factors include urinary tract obstruction, indwelling catheters, male sex, pregnancy, neurogenic bladder, urinary tract instrumentation, and renal transplantation. The microbiological spectrum of cUTI is diverse and heavily enriched with antimicrobial resistance, prominently extended-spectrum beta-lactamase (ESBL)-producing Enterobacterales, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, and enterococci. Treatment requires immediate identification and relief of underlying urinary tract obstruction alongside urine-penetrating empirical antimicrobials tailored to local resistance data, transitioning rapidly to pathogen-directed oral agents.

standard_knowledge.claim: Classic 21-hydroxylase deficiency presents in neonates with life-threatening salt-wasting adrenal crisis (hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, hypovolemia, hypoglycemia) typically between days 7 and 21 of life, accompanied by virilization of external genitalia (Prader stages I-V) in 46,XX infants, driven by marked elevation of 17-hydroxyprogesterone (17-OHP).

Hydrocortisone (10-15 mg/m2/day divided three times daily) is the preferred glucocorticoid in growing children to minimize growth impairment, whereas longer-acting agents (prednisone, dexamethasone) are often utilized in adults to achieve adequate nocturnal ACTH suppression and suppress morning androgen peaks.

All patients with classic salt-wasting CAH require mineralocorticoid replacement with fludrocortisone (0.05-0.2 mg daily) and sodium chloride supplementation in infancy, titrated to maintain normal blood pressure and plasma renin activity (PRA) in the upper-normal reference range.

Crinecerfont, a novel oral non-peptide corticotropin-releasing factor type 1 (CRF1) receptor antagonist, significantly reduces elevated androstenedione and 17-OHP levels in adults and adolescents with classic CAH while allowing substantial reductions in daily glucocorticoid doses toward physiological replacement levels.

page.standard_overview: Congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH) encompasses a group of autosomal recessive enzymopathies characterized by impaired cortisol biosynthesis, of which >95% are caused by 21-hydroxylase deficiency (CYP21A2 mutations). Cortisol deficiency abolishes negative feedback inhibition on the pituitary gland, driving excessive ACTH secretion and massive adrenal cortical hyperplasia with shunting of precursor steroids into androgen pathways. Classic CAH can present with neonatal salt-wasting crises and 46,XX genital virilization, while non-classic CAH usually presents later with androgen excess such as hirsutism, menstrual irregularity, acne, or infertility. The therapeutic challenge involves balancing adequate glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid replacement to suppress adrenal androgen hypersecretion without inducing iatrogenic Cushingoid morbidity, growth arrest, or metabolic syndrome.

page.standard_overview: Connective tissue disease-associated interstitial lung disease (CTD-ILD) represents a major cause of morbidity and a leading cause of disease-related mortality in systemic sclerosis (SSc) and an important one in rheumatoid arthritis (RA). While high-resolution computed tomography (HRCT) typically demonstrates a non-specific interstitial pneumonia (NSIP) pattern in SSc, inflammatory myopathies, and mixed connective tissue disease, a usual interstitial pneumonia (UIP) pattern predominates in RA-ILD. Treatment assessment integrates the CTD, symptoms, pulmonary-function trend, and HRCT pattern: ground-glass opacity may reflect inflammatory disease, whereas traction bronchiectasis indicates fibrosis, but imaging alone does not determine reversibility. In systemic sclerosis-associated ILD, trials support mycophenolate and cyclophosphamide as immunosuppressive options, while nintedanib and tocilizumab can slow FVC decline in appropriate patients; evidence and indications differ across other CTD-ILDs.

standard_knowledge.claim: Anti-MDA5 antibody-positive dermatomyositis is strongly associated with rapidly progressive interstitial lung disease (RPILD) that can progress to fatal hypoxemic respiratory failure within weeks; serum ferritin serves as a critical biomarker of disease activity and mortality risk.

Standard corticosteroid monotherapy is notoriously ineffective in anti-MDA5 RPILD; early, simultaneous triple therapy combining high-dose pulsed methylprednisolone, a calcineurin inhibitor (tacrolimus or cyclosporine), and intravenous cyclophosphamide or a JAK inhibitor (tofacitinib) significantly improves 6-month survival.

Anti-synthetase syndrome, characterized by autoantibodies against aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases (anti-Jo-1, anti-PL-7, anti-PL-12), presents with ILD, non-erosive arthritis, Raynaud phenomenon, 'mechanic's hands', and myositis, responding favorably to glucocorticoids combined with azathioprine, mycophenolate, or rituximab.

page.standard_overview: CTD-related ILD includes indolent fibrotic disorders and occasional rheumatologic emergencies, making recognition of rapidly progressive disease essential. Most catastrophic among these is rapidly progressive interstitial lung disease (RPILD) occurring in clinically amyopathic dermatomyositis (CADM) associated with anti-melanoma differentiation-associated gene 5 (anti-MDA5) autoantibodies. Anti-MDA5 RPILD can cause characteristic ulcerative or palmar skin lesions, marked hyperferritinemia, and hypoxemic respiratory failure over weeks, with high early mortality in severe historical cohorts and poor outcomes with glucocorticoid monotherapy. Early expert-led combination immunosuppression is advocated, commonly high-dose glucocorticoids with a calcineurin inhibitor and/or cyclophosphamide; JAK inhibitors may be considered in selected cases, but evidence is largely observational and no single four-drug regimen is universal.

page.mentor_intro: The 2026 AHA/ACC/ADA/ASN guideline frames cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic syndrome across cardiology, endocrinology and nephrology. A living guideline covers cardiovascular, kidney and weight effects of type 2 diabetes drugs, and KDIGO 2026 covers CKD anaemia. Frailty and renal dose adjustment are recurring management problems.

teaching_points.claim: The 2026 AHA/ACC/ADA/ASN guideline addresses prevention, detection, evaluation and management of cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic syndrome for cardiologists, endocrinologists, nephrologists and primary care.
A living guideline on type 2 diabetes therapeutics covers cardiovascular, kidney-related and weight loss effects, and notes cost and availability limit implementation.
The KDIGO 2026 guideline gives recommendations for management of anaemia in chronic kidney disease.
A consensus report on frailty in CKD links serial frailty measurement to decisions on assisted home dialysis and transplant eligibility.
Renal dose adjustment guideline adherence is inconsistent, and non-adherence to dosing recommendations was associated with adverse consequences and higher healthcare use.
An Indian consensus aims to standardise online haemodiafiltration practice in kidney replacement therapy.

The KDIGO 2024 Clinical Practice Guideline recommends structured shared decision-making regarding kidney replacement therapy versus comprehensive conservative management, utilizing validated 2- and 4-year kidney failure risk equations and frailty assessments to guide discussions.

standard_knowledge.claim: In patients aged 75 years and older with advanced CKD and high comorbidity scores (particularly cardiovascular disease and ischemic cardiomyopathy), initiating maintenance dialysis provides no significant overall survival benefit compared to comprehensive conservative management, while markedly increasing hospitalizations and invasive procedures.

Comprehensive conservative kidney management involves active non-dialytic disease-modifying therapy: optimizing blood pressure, restricting dietary sodium and phosphorus, correcting metabolic acidosis with sodium bicarbonate, and managing volume overload with high-dose loop diuretics combined with thiazide-like agents (metolazone).

Symptom control in conservative kidney care uses targeted drugs: gabapentin or pregabalin at renally reduced doses (or difelikefalin in haemodialysis) for uraemic pruritus, ESAs for symptomatic anaemia (haemoglobin about 10 to 11.5 g/dL), and non-renally cleared opioids such as fentanyl, buprenorphine or methadone for pain.

page.standard_overview: Comprehensive conservative kidney management (CKM) is a planned, patient-centered, holistic treatment pathway for advanced chronic kidney disease (CKD G5, eGFR <15 mL/min/1.73m²) without kidney replacement therapy (hemodialysis, peritoneal dialysis, or kidney transplantation). For some very frail older adults with multimorbidity or major functional impairment, observational evidence suggests that dialysis may offer limited survival advantage and can add substantial treatment burden and hospital time; outcomes vary, so decisions require individualized shared assessment. Conservative management does not signify therapeutic abandonment; rather, it entails active medical management to delay CKD progression, meticulous symptom palliation (controlling fluid retention, pruritus, fatigue, and pain), advance care planning, and seamless transition to end-of-life palliative care.

topic: Conservative oxygen therapy in mechanically ventilated patients

page.mentor_intro: Pooled analyses find conservative oxygen therapy does not consistently reduce mortality in ICU, ventilated, acute medical or post-cardiac-arrest patients. An earlier IOTA meta-analysis found liberal oxygen increases mortality, and benefit may be limited to fewer ventilator-free days or organ failure; targets above SpO2 94-96% may be unfavourable.

teaching_points.claim: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2012: We recommend use of sedation with a sedation goal in critically ill mechanically ventilated patients with sepsis (grade 1D).
Implementing a conservative oxygenation guideline changed attitudes and practice and improved adherence to targets.
The IOTA meta-analysis of acutely ill adults found liberal oxygen increases mortality, with supplemental oxygen possibly unfavourable above SpO2 94-96%.
Conservative oxygen therapy did not reduce all-cause mortality in ICU patients, affecting only mechanical-ventilation-free days.
A meta-analysis found conservative oxygen did not reduce mortality but decreased ventilation time, new organ failure and renal replacement therapy risk in critical care.
For ventilated ICU patients, conservative oxygen was not significantly superior to liberal oxygen on clinical outcomes.
In acutely ill medical patients, conservative oxygen therapy was not associated with decreased mortality.
After cardiac arrest, conservative oxygen did not decrease mortality, improve neurologic recovery or shorten ICU stay in a meta-analysis of RCTs.
An individual-level analysis after cardiac arrest found lower mortality with conservative oxygen with low to very low certainty.

In mechanically ventilated ICU patients, the ICU-ROX trial demonstrated that a conservative oxygen regimen (targeting SpO2 91-96% and titrating FiO2 down to 0.21 if SpO2 >=91%) resulted in comparable ventilator-free days and 90-day mortality to liberal oxygen therapy, confirming the feasibility and safety of avoiding hyperoxia.

The HOT-ICU trial in 2,928 ICU patients with acute hypoxemic respiratory failure showed that targeting a lower oxygenation threshold (PaO2 60 mmHg / 8 kPa) yielded identical 90-day mortality (42.9% vs 42.4%) and percentage of days alive without life support compared to a higher target (PaO2 90 mmHg / 12 kPa).

uncertainties: Effect in specific populations.

standard_knowledge.claim: Liberal oxygen therapy in acutely ill medical and surgical adults is associated with increased in-hospital and 30-day mortality (IOTA systematic review and meta-analysis of 25 RCTs involving 16,037 patients, Relative Risk 1.21 for in-hospital mortality), leading to strong international recommendations to avoid SpO2 >96%.

Physiological harms of hyperoxia include absorption atelectasis (due to denitrogenation of poorly ventilated alveoli), coronary and cerebral vasoconstriction, increased systemic vascular resistance with decreased cardiac output, and direct pulmonary epithelial and capillary endothelial injury mediated by reactive oxygen species.

page.standard_overview: Oxygen is one of the most frequently administered therapeutics in the intensive care unit, yet hyperoxia exerts substantial toxic biological effects. Excess oxygen exposure and hyperoxemia can promote oxidative injury, vasoconstriction, absorption atelectasis, and pulmonary inflammation; SpO2 99%-100% alone does not define the arterial oxygen tension or tissue hyperoxia. IOTA, ICU-ROX, and HOT-ICU do not support routine liberal oxygen administration; conservative targets avoiding both hypoxemia and hyperoxemia are reasonable, but major ICU trials have not shown uniform mortality or organ-support superiority for one target range in all ventilated adults.

standard_knowledge.claim: Dyssynergic defecation is defined by paradoxical contraction or failure of >20% relaxation of the anal sphincter and puborectalis muscle during defecation, accompanied by inadequate intra-abdominal propulsive forces and an abnormal balloon expulsion test (>1 minute to evacuate a 50-mL water-filled balloon).

Pelvic floor biofeedback therapy is the first-line, evidence-based treatment for dyssynergic defecation, achieving sustained clinical improvement and restoration of normal anorectal coordination in 70-80% of patients, markedly outperforming laxatives, sham biofeedback, or muscle relaxants.

In patients with slow transit constipation who fail dietary fiber and osmotic laxatives (polyethylene glycol), prescription intestinal secretagogues (guanylate cyclase-C agonists like linaclotide, or chloride channel activators like lubiprostone) increase intraluminal fluid secretion and accelerate transit.

Prucalopride, a high-affinity, selective 5-HT4 receptor agonist, stimulates colonic giant migrating contractions and significantly improves spontaneous complete bowel movements and patient satisfaction in severe chronic constipation refractory to standard over-the-counter laxatives.

page.standard_overview: Chronic constipation is a heterogeneous disorder affecting up to 15% of the general population, categorized into normal transit constipation, slow transit constipation (colonic inertia), and defecatory disorders (pelvic floor dyssynergia). Dyssynergic defecation—characterized by the paradoxical contraction or failure of involuntary relaxation of the puborectalis muscle and external anal sphincter during attempted evacuation—accounts for over one-third of refractory chronic constipation cases. Patients typically complain of excessive straining, feelings of incomplete evacuation, and the need for digital disimpaction. Recognizing pelvic-floor dyssynergia is important because laxatives or secretagogues alone often provide inadequate relief, and treatment should include pelvic-floor biofeedback rather than simply escalating medication. Definitive diagnosis requires high-resolution anorectal manometry and balloon expulsion testing, and the treatment of choice is pelvic floor biofeedback therapy.

topic: Constrictive pericarditis: haemodynamic features, pericardiectomy indications

page.mentor_intro: BNP and NT-proBNP are lower in constrictive pericarditis than restrictive cardiomyopathy, and Mayo Clinic echocardiographic criteria have good accuracy for differentiating them. Tuberculosis is an important cause, especially with HIV in Africa, and pericardiectomy outcomes are worse in non-idiopathic aetiologies.

teaching_points.claim: BNP and NT-proBNP were significantly lower in constrictive pericarditis than restrictive cardiomyopathy, with BNP showing good pooled diagnostic accuracy.
All echocardiographic parameters from the Mayo Clinic criteria have good diagnostic accuracy for differentiating constrictive pericarditis from restrictive cardiomyopathy.
HIV infection complicates a significant portion of constrictive pericarditis in Africa, and early mortality has improved globally but remains high.

In pericardiectomy for constrictive pericarditis, post-radiation and other non-idiopathic aetiologies carry higher mortality than idiopathic, with heterogeneity and a possible need for randomised trials.
Pericardiectomy for constrictive tuberculous pericarditis has operative mortality with significant heterogeneity and methodological concerns.
Tuberculous cardiac involvement is frequent and can lead to heart failure, constrictive pericarditis or death, so early detection of complications is key.
Cochrane evidence on tuberculous pericarditis interventions shows low-certainty findings, with colchicine and steroid effects uncertain.
Intrapericardial fibrinolysis to prevent complications of effusion has very low certainty of efficacy and safety.

Characteristic echocardiographic features of constrictive pericarditis (Mayo criteria) include respirophasic ventricular septal shift, preserved or increased medial mitral annular e' velocity (about 9 cm/s or more), annulus reversus (medial e' greater than lateral e'), and expiratory diastolic flow reversal in the hepatic veins.

standard_knowledge.claim: Cardiac catheterization demonstrates dissociation of intrathoracic and intracardiac pressures, manifesting as simultaneous left and right ventricular pressure discordance during respiration (during inspiration, LV peak systolic pressure falls while RV peak systolic pressure rises), along with early rapid diastolic filling and sudden plateau ('dip-and-plateau' or square root sign).

Pericardial thickness on cardiac CT or MRI may be normal (<2 mm) in up to 18-20% of patients with surgically proven constrictive pericarditis; therefore, normal pericardial thickness does not rule out constriction when classic hemodynamics are present.

Complete radical pericardiectomy (phrenic-to-phrenic resection) is the definitive treatment for chronic, permanent constrictive pericarditis, with early surgical intervention prior to end-stage hepatic dysfunction (cardiac cirrhosis), severe NYHA class IV symptoms, or myocardial atrophy yielding superior long-term survival.

page.standard_overview: Constrictive pericarditis is a chronic condition characterized by fibrotic, thickened, and often calcified pericardial layers that impede normal diastolic cardiac filling. The hallmark pathophysiology is the rigid shell that shields cardiac chambers from normal respiratory intrathoracic pressure swings, leading to dissociation between intrathoracic and intracardiac pressures, exaggerated ventricular interdependence, and equalization of end-diastolic pressures across all four chambers. Clinically, patients present with signs of right-sided heart failure (elevated jugular venous pressure with prominent y descent, hepatomegaly, ascites, peripheral edema) and the classic Kussmaul sign (lack of inspiratory JVP decline or paradoxical rise). Differentiating constrictive pericarditis from restrictive cardiomyopathy is essential, as constrictive disease is potentially curable with surgical pericardiectomy.

standard_knowledge.claim: Allergic contact dermatitis is a Type IV cell-mediated delayed hypersensitivity reaction requiring an initial sensitization phase and subsequent elicitation upon re-exposure, manifesting 48-72 hours later with intense pruritus, erythema, and vesiculation, frequently spreading beyond the contact boundary.

Irritant contact dermatitis accounts for approximately 80% of occupational contact dermatitis cases, resulting from direct cytotoxic damage to keratinocytes and stratum corneum lipid disruption without prior immunological sensitization, manifesting as burning or stinging sharply demarcated to contact areas.

Diagnostic patch testing is the gold standard for diagnosing ACD; standardized allergen panels are applied to uninvolved skin of the upper back for 48 hours, with mandatory subsequent readings at 48 hours and 72-96 hours (and occasionally day 7) to detect delayed reactions and distinguish allergic crescendo patterns from decrescendo irritant responses.

First-line pharmacological management of acute severe ACD consists of mid-to-high potency topical corticosteroids (e.g., clobetasol 0.05% or mometasone 0.1%) applied once to twice daily for 2 to 4 weeks; facial and intertriginous involvement requires topical calcineurin inhibitors (tacrolimus, pimecrolimus) to avoid steroid-induced skin atrophy.

page.standard_overview: Contact dermatitis encompasses two fundamentally distinct pathophysiological processes that require accurate clinical differentiation: irritant contact dermatitis (ICD) and allergic contact dermatitis (ACD). ICD is non-immunologic barrier injury caused by sufficient or repeated exposure to irritants such as wet work, solvents, and detergents; it is usually concentrated at the contact site, with acute burning or stinging and more chronic eczematous changes after repeated exposure. In contrast, ACD is a Type IV cell-mediated delayed hypersensitivity reaction orchestrated by allergen-specific memory T cells following prior sensitization, frequently spreading beyond the contact site and presenting with intense pruritus and vesiculation 48 to 72 hours post-exposure. Diagnostic patch testing remains the definitive standard to identify causative contact allergens, whereas treatment demands barrier restoration, identification and avoidance of culprits, and topical anti-inflammatory therapy.

topic: Continuous EEG monitoring in the ICU: non-convulsive status epilepticus

page.mentor_intro: Continuous EEG is advised for patients with altered mental status after convulsive status epilepticus, while diagnostic criteria for nonconvulsive status epilepticus in comatose patients remain unsettled. cEEG also aids neonatal seizure assessment, and neurophysiology contributes to prognostication after hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy.

teaching_points.claim: Guidelines and consensus statements recommend continuous EEG monitoring for patients with altered mental status after convulsive status epilepticus.
The modified Salzburg and updated ACNS criteria for nonconvulsive status epilepticus in comatose patients have unresolved diagnostic accuracy.
Very low cortical SSEP amplitudes (approximately 0.5 µV or less) strongly predict poor outcome after hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy, though not yet in guidelines.
A practical approach to ICU encephalopathy notes dexmedetomidine is effective for delirium in ventilated patients, while haloperidol has minimal effect.
Continuous EEG should be used to diagnose neonatal seizures and assess severity, remission and drug efficacy.
Diagnosis and management of adult status epilepticus in resource-limited settings is non-uniform, highlighting the need for appropriate guidelines.
In COVID-19, EEG commonly shows encephalopathy correlating with severity, with frontal findings proposed as a biomarker.

Non-convulsive status epilepticus (NCSE) in comatose patients without known epileptic encephalopathy is defined by the Salzburg Criteria as continuous epileptiform discharges >2.5 Hz for >=10 seconds, or epileptiform discharges <=2.5 Hz with either dynamic spatiotemporal evolution or clinical/electrophysiological response to a rapid-acting intravenous antiseizure medication.

standard_knowledge.claim: In critically ill patients with altered mental status following cardiac arrest, intracerebral hemorrhage, or severe traumatic brain injury, non-convulsive seizures occur in 15% to 40% of cases, with over 80% lacking any outward motor manifestations, making continuous EEG indispensable for detection.

A cumulative electrographic seizure burden exceeding 20% of any recorded hour (>=12 minutes per hour) is independently associated with secondary metabolic brain crisis, hippocampal atrophy, and worsened long-term neurological disability in comatose patients with acute brain injury.

Initial emergent pharmacotherapy for established status epilepticus consists of intravenous benzodiazepines (lorazepam 0.1 mg/kg or midazolam 10 mg IM), followed immediately by second-line non-sedating IV antiseizure medications (levetiracetam 60 mg/kg, fosphenytoin 20 mg PE/kg, or valproate sodium 40 mg/kg), escalating to continuous anesthetic infusions (propofol or midazolam) titrated to electrographic burst suppression if seizures persist beyond 30 minutes.

page.standard_overview: Continuous electroencephalography (cEEG) monitoring in the intensive care unit is essential for detecting subclinical seizures and non-convulsive status epilepticus (NCSE) in comatose, encephalopathic, or critically brain-injured patients. Up to 20-30% of comatose patients following traumatic brain injury, subarachnoid hemorrhage, intracranial hemorrhage, or resuscitation from cardiac arrest harbor electrographic seizures that lack overt motor signs. According to the 2015 Salzburg Criteria and the 2021 ACNS Standardized Critical Care EEG Terminology, electrographic status epilepticus is defined by continuous epileptiform activity lasting >=10 minutes or occupying >=20% of any 60-minute recording. Uncontrolled electrographic seizure activity precipitates secondary excitotoxic neuronal injury, severe brain edema, and elevated intracranial pressure, demanding urgent stepwise therapeutic suppression.

topic: Continuous glucose monitoring CGM: time-in-range targets, hybrid closed loop

page.mentor_intro: CGM adds benefit across settings: in hospitalised non-critically ill adults it improves control and reduces hypoglycaemia over point-of-care testing, in pregnancy it lowers HbA1c and possibly large-for-gestational-age risk, and in non-insulin-treated type 2 diabetes it supports lifestyle change. An Italian guideline supports wider T2D use.

teaching_points.claim: An Italian guideline supports a shift to wider use of CGM in type 2 diabetes, with CGM becoming mandatory for people on insulin therapy and reimbursement needing adaptation.
An international guideline defines study design, comparator measurements and minimum accuracy requirements for CGM system assessment.
In non-critically ill hospitalised adults with diabetes, adding CGM to point-of-care testing for insulin dosing gave superior glycaemic control and less hypoglycaemia.
CGM in pregnancy reduces HbA1c and possibly large-for-gestational-age risk, with greatest benefit in type 1 diabetes, then gestational diabetes.
CGM in non-insulin-treated type 2 diabetes improves outcomes and patient experience, reduces resource use, and has acceptable cost-effectiveness.
CGM guides lifestyle choices and nutrition in type 2 diabetes with benefits for glycaemia and body weight.
Real-world evidence shows commercially available automated insulin delivery systems differ in glycaemic outcomes including time in range, with age influencing outcomes.

International consensus targets for continuous glucose monitoring in non-pregnant adults with type 1 and type 2 diabetes recommend: Time in Range (TIR, 70-180 mg/dL) >70% (equating to >16 hours 48 minutes/day), Time Below Range (TBR <70 mg/dL) <4% (<1 hour/day), severe hypoglycemia (<54 mg/dL) <1% (<15 minutes/day), and Coefficient of Variation (CV) <=36% to indicate stable glycemic control.

Hybrid closed-loop (automated insulin delivery) systems, combining real-time CGM with automated insulin pump dosing algorithms (e.g., Control-IQ), significantly increase Time in Range by 11 percentage points (2.6 hours/day) and markedly reduce nocturnal hypoglycemia compared to sensor-augmented pump therapy alone (Control-IQ trial).

uncertainties: Real-world evidence biases for AID systems.

page.standard_overview: CGM has become a cornerstone of management for many people with insulin-treated diabetes by displaying glucose trends and variability, but capillary glucose testing remains necessary for selected patients and situations, including discordant symptoms and some device-specific calibration or confirmation needs. Interpretation is standardized through the Ambulatory Glucose Profile (AGP) report, anchored by internationally validated consensus metrics: Time in Range (TIR, 70-180 mg/dL), Time Below Range (TBR, <70 mg/dL and <54 mg/dL), Time Above Range (TAR, >180 mg/dL and >250 mg/dL), and the Glucose Management Indicator (GMI). Incorporating real-time CGM data into advanced automated insulin delivery (AID) or hybrid closed-loop (HCL) systems has achieved unprecedented improvements in TIR while reducing hypoglycemia, establishing AID as the primary standard of care for type 1 diabetes.

page.mentor_intro: CGM adds benefit across settings: in hospitalised non-critically ill adults it improves control and reduces hypoglycaemia over point-of-care testing, in pregnancy it lowers HbA1c and possibly large-for-gestational-age risk, and in non-insulin-treated type 2 diabetes it supports lifestyle change. An Italian guideline supports wider T2D use.

teaching_points.claim: An Italian guideline supports a shift to wider use of CGM in type 2 diabetes, with CGM becoming mandatory for people on insulin therapy and reimbursement needing adaptation.
An international guideline defines study design, comparator measurements and minimum accuracy requirements for CGM system assessment.
In non-critically ill hospitalised adults with diabetes, adding CGM to point-of-care testing for insulin dosing gave superior glycaemic control and less hypoglycaemia.
CGM in pregnancy reduces HbA1c and possibly large-for-gestational-age risk, with greatest benefit in type 1 diabetes, then gestational diabetes.
CGM in non-insulin-treated type 2 diabetes improves outcomes and patient experience, reduces resource use, and has acceptable cost-effectiveness.
CGM guides lifestyle choices and nutrition in type 2 diabetes with benefits for glycaemia and body weight.
Real-world evidence shows commercially available automated insulin delivery systems differ in glycaemic outcomes including time in range, with age influencing outcomes.

For pregnant women with type 1 diabetes, consensus CGM targets are more stringent: Time in Range (63-140 mg/dL [3.5-7.8 mmol/L]) >70%, Time Below Range (<63 mg/dL) <4%, severe hypoglycemia (<54 mg/dL) <1%, and Time Above Range (>140 mg/dL) <25%.

In adults with type 2 diabetes treated with basal insulin without prandial insulin, the randomized MOBILE trial demonstrated that real-time CGM use significantly decreased mean HbA1c from 9.1% to 8.0% compared to blood glucose fingerstick monitoring (adjusted difference -0.4%), while increasing Time in Range by 3.8 hours/day without increasing hypoglycemia.

In pregnancy with type 1 diabetes, the CONCEPTT trial showed real-time CGM raised time in range (68% versus 61%) and was associated with fewer large-for-gestational-age infants and fewer neonatal ICU admissions longer than 24 hours (odds ratios about 0.5).

In adults with type 1 diabetes using multiple daily insulin injections (MDI), the DIAMOND randomized trial demonstrated that real-time CGM produced a sustained 0.6% reduction in HbA1c and reduced hypoglycemia compared to capillary blood glucose testing, independent of baseline numeracy or education.

page.standard_overview: CGM use has expanded beyond type 1 diabetes to type 2 diabetes treated with basal insulin, selected people using non-insulin regimens, and pregnancy with pre-existing diabetes, with evidence strength and indications differing by population. By replacing episodic fingerstick capillary glucose checks with continuous trend arrows and customizable threshold alarms, real-time CGM (rtCGM) and intermittently scanned CGM (isCGM) empower patients to make immediate behavioral adjustments and facilitate proactive clinical medication titration. In basal insulin-treated type 2 diabetes, MOBILE demonstrated that CGM improved HbA1c and increased time in range compared with fingerstick monitoring. In pregnant women with pre-existing diabetes, CGM implementation was associated in CONCEPTT (type 1 diabetes) with more time in range and fewer large-for-gestational-age babies and neonatal intensive care admissions.

standard_knowledge.claim: CPAP therapy confers definitive, robust clinical benefits in improving daytime sleepiness (measured by the Epworth Sleepiness Scale), vitality, depression scores, health-related quality of life, and reducing motor vehicle crash risks in adult patients with symptomatic OSA.

Subgroup analyses from randomized trials and observational cohorts indicate that clinically meaningful reductions in blood pressure (particularly nocturnal systolic and diastolic blood pressure) and potential cardiovascular risk reduction require strict CPAP adherence of at least 4 hours per night.

page.standard_overview: OSA is characterized by recurrent upper-airway collapse during sleep, causing intermittent hypoxemia, recurrent arousals, and sympathetic activation; sustained nocturnal hypercapnia may occur in severe disease or with comorbid hypoventilation. These pathophysiological insults generate profound oxidative stress, systemic endothelial dysfunction, elevated nighttime blood pressure, and left atrial remodeling. Continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) is the gold-standard therapeutic intervention to splint the upper airway, eliminating nocturnal desaturations and daytime hypersomnolence. SAVE showed that CPAP improves sleepiness and health-related quality of life but did not significantly prevent major cardiovascular events in patients with moderate-to-severe OSA and established cardiovascular disease; average adherence was limited.

page.standard_overview: Continuous Renal Replacement Therapy (CRRT) is generally preferred for hemodynamically unstable critically ill patients (trials have not shown a survival advantage over intermittent dialysis) with acute kidney injury (AKI) and multiorgan failure in the intensive care unit. The physiological advantage of CRRT lies in slow, continuous solute and volume removal over 24 hours, preventing the rapid hemodynamic shifts, intradialytic hypotension, and intracranial pressure spikes characteristic of intermittent hemodialysis. Determining the optimal timing of initiation has been clarified by landmark multinational trials (STARRT-AKI and AKIKI), which established that routine early or accelerated initiation of renal replacement therapy provides no mortality benefit compared to a conservative strategy that waits for absolute emergent indications, while exposing patients to unnecessary vascular catheterization and dialysis-associated complications.

standard_knowledge.claim: Convection in CVVH removes solutes via solvent drag driven by a transmembrane hydrostatic pressure gradient across a high-flux membrane, achieving superior clearance of middle and larger molecules (500-30,000 Da) compared to purely diffusive modalities.

Diffusion in CVVHD clears small solutes (<500 Da, including urea, creatinine, and potassium) down a concentration gradient generated by countercurrent flow of dialysate solution running opposite to blood flow, without requiring convective fluid ultrafiltration or replacement solutions.

page.standard_overview: Prescribing Continuous Renal Replacement Therapy (CRRT) requires precise understanding of solute clearance physics across its three primary modalities: Continuous Veno-Venous Hemofiltration (CVVH), Continuous Veno-Venous Hemodialysis (CVVHD), and Continuous Veno-Venous Hemodiafiltration (CVVHDF). CVVH relies entirely on convection (solvent drag across a semipermeable membrane driven by transmembrane hydrostatic pressure), providing superior clearance of middle-to-larger molecular weight solutes (500 to 30,000 Da, including cytokines, myoglobin, and beta-2 microglobulin). CVVHD relies on diffusion driven by concentration gradients across the membrane via countercurrent dialysate flow, excelling at small-solute clearance (<500 Da, such as urea and potassium). CVVHDF merges both mechanisms. Landmark trials (ATN and RENAL) established that a delivered effluent dose of about 20 to 25 mL/kg/hour is adequate (prescribing 25 to 30 mL/kg/hour allows for downtime), with higher doses giving no added benefit.

page.mentor_intro: Contrast-associated AKI risk is raised by hypertension, and the potential need for dialysis should be explained, especially after intra-arterial contrast. Biomarkers such as NGAL, cystatin-C and KIM-1 may predict it; RenalGuard-guided hydration may be safer than conventional hydration.

teaching_points.claim: The risk of dialysis should be communicated to patients undergoing procedures requiring contrast, especially intra-arterial exposure.
Hypertension is an independent risk factor for contrast-associated AKI and can be used for risk stratification.
RenalGuard is more secure than conventional hydration for preventing contrast-associated AKI, though its role in TAVR is questionable.
NGAL had the highest diagnostic performance for contrast-induced nephropathy, followed by cystatin-C and urinary KIM-1.
Pre-angiography CRP and some haematological indices are associated with contrast-induced nephropathy, and NLR shows potential as a cost-effective predictor.
SGLT2 inhibitors may help prevent contrast-induced nephropathy in diabetic patients undergoing coronary angiography or PCI, but clinical trials are needed.

Consensus statements from the American College of Radiology (ACR) and National Kidney Foundation (NKF) state that the true risk of contrast-induced AKI is clinically negligible when eGFR is >=30 mL/min/1.73m²; prophylactic volume expansion with isotonic saline is indicated only in high-risk patients with eGFR <30 mL/min/1.73m² not on chronic maintenance dialysis.

The randomized PRESERVE trial (4,993 patients) conclusively demonstrated that neither intravenous sodium bicarbonate (compared to intravenous 0.9% normal saline) nor oral N-acetylcysteine (compared to placebo) reduced the 90-day incidence of death, need for dialysis, or persistent decline in kidney function following angiography.

The prospective randomized AMACING trial showed that withholding prophylactic intravenous hydration prior to elective contrast-enhanced CT in patients with eGFR 30-59 mL/min/1.73m² was non-inferior to intravenous normal saline hydration, demonstrating no difference in post-contrast AKI incidence (2.6% vs 2.7%) while eliminating hydration-related costs and heart failure exacerbations.

page.standard_overview: Contrast-associated AKI is acute kidney injury occurring within roughly 48-72 hours after intravascular iodinated contrast, defined by standard creatinine or urine-output criteria and denoting temporal association rather than proven causality. In contrast, true contrast-induced nephropathy (CIN) refers specifically to kidney injury causally attributable to contrast toxicity. The risk of causal kidney injury after modern intravenous contrast is low in patients with stable eGFR >=30 mL/min/1.73m², but it is not zero and risk assessment must account for AKI, severe CKD, comorbidity, and intra-arterial administration. The landmark PRESERVE trial dismantled decades of clinical dogma by proving that oral N-acetylcysteine and intravenous sodium bicarbonate provide no benefit over intravenous isotonic saline. Furthermore, the European AMACING trial demonstrated that prophylactic intravenous hydration can be safely withheld in elective outpatients with eGFR 30-59 mL/min/1.73m².
